Separate evidence-rule validation into two stages: (a) historical benign cohort (100–200 per site, false-positive rate 7–13%), (b) adversarial synthetic cohort (20–30 scenarios per site, false-negative rate <10%); deliver Calibration Confidence Memo with both validations locked by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23) or trigger Phase One delay. 3. Embed confidence-interval methodology and mechanical verdict-scoring rule in the bilateral instrument by Month 1 (2026-11-08), not as planning documents; numeric thresholds lock at Month 5.5 (2027-03-23); specify that an interval straddling a criterion threshold means Modify (no co-chair discretion). 4. Pre-authorize adjudication surge staffing (USD 2–3M for 8–12 specialists, dual-country) by Month 4 (2027-02-08) and confirm evidence-rule miscalibration scenarios (false positives 15–20%) are modeled with costs allocated before Phase One. 5. Define reciprocal-access parity using quantitative metrics (inspector-hour balance ≥90%, exercise distribution parity, data-access turnaround ≤3 days, challenge-outcome agreement ≥80%) by Month 4 (2027-02-08) and lock in the bilateral instrument, not TBD.

Unoptimized waterfall. Parallel work not modelled here.

Part 2: Supporting analysis

Persuasive elevator pitch.

US–China Bilateral Frontier-Computing Verification Consortium: Phase One Operational Test

Project Overview

Imagine two great powers verifying the other's frontier-computing hardware without exposing secrets or breaking trust. The Consortium is the first bilateral US–China mechanism to prove this is possible: a 90-day operational test verifying declared equipment changes at matched datacenters, using tamper-evident ledgers, reciprocal inspections and provisional validated thresholds. With USD 5 billion in committed appropriations, full mirrored teams and independent exercises, it answers whether credible detection is achievable between adversaries. Success brings strategic stability; failure informs what not to do next. This is not arms control as usual—it is verification engineering at the edge of feasibility.

The project scope is strictly bounded: declared-equipment change verification at participating declared sites only. The program is a sovereign public-sector national-security initiative with no commercial elements.

Target Audience

The primary audience comprises US and Chinese national co-chairs, bilateral oversight bodies, and legislative appropriations committees evaluating strategic investment. Secondary audiences include participating inspectorates, operators and vendors assessing participation costs and benefits; third-country neutral facility hosts and independent auditors; and arms-control experts and academic verification researchers seeking precedent and lessons.

The pitch must convince sovereigns that the mission is worth USD 5 billion, operationally feasible and honest about limits.

Risks and Mitigation Strategies

Entry gates slip, compressing the test and widening statistical uncertainty. Mitigation: binding roadmap with 2-week escalation and 4-week re-scope backstop. Any gate slipping over 2 weeks triggers an emergency co-chair summit within 5 days; if the entry gate is not certified by Month 9 (2027-07-08), a formal Stop/re-scope decision is invoked.

Asymmetric access undermines parity. Mitigation: pre-clock reciprocal-access audit and hard stop on shielding. If access is found to be asymmetric or material unverifiable equipment exceeds thresholds (over 10% at a site or overall), the project halts.

Thin exercise data makes the verdict ambiguous. Mitigation: pre-register thresholds, lock before the clock, and default to Modify when intervals straddle a decision boundary.

Ledger divergence blocks evidence. Mitigation: rehearsed key recovery and hourly digest exchange with alerts. Local recording occurs at event time (at most 5 minutes); counterpart signed-digest exchange occurs at least every 1 hour; alerts trigger when an exchange is overdue by 30 minutes; mismatch is escalated within 4 hours with a reconciliation target of 72 hours.

Funding is withheld by either country. Mitigation: synchronized tranches with 14-day escalation and 30-day stop trigger. Tranche delay over 14 days escalates to co-chair review; delay over 30 days or unequal deposits unresolved activates the stop trigger.

Inspectors are exposed to counterintelligence threats. Mitigation: compartmentalization, filtered evidence, and CI Oversight Board oversight. Inspectors are compartmentalized by role and site with debriefs and monitored cooling-off before reassignment; no personal phones on site. A CI Oversight Board of 3 officers per side investigates breaches within 48 hours, recommends within 72 hours, and decides within 7 days.

Staffing attrition in 24/7 shifts. Mitigation: staggered rotations and leave buffers built into the staffing model.

Metrics for Success

Detection capability is measured as:

  • At least 70% of planned-event class (unreported arrival, substitution)
  • At least 50% of unplanned class (vendor refusal, reluctant operator)
  • Class thresholds for the remaining three event types to be determined at pre-registration

Data quality and parity are measured as:

  • False positives at most 10%
  • Unverifiable equipment at most 5%
  • Reciprocal-access parity at least 85%
  • No discrepancy older than 21 days at conclusion
  • Fewer than 5 open material discrepancies

Ledger integrity is measured as:

  • Zero unauthorized signings
  • Hourly digest exchange with mismatch escalation within 4 hours
  • Reconciliation within 72 hours

Exercise Authority performance is measured as:

  • 54 total exercises in 90 days (6 per month per country-pair across 3 pairs)
  • Scenario coverage across all seven event types
  • Independent scoring by mixed-nationality teams

Inspectorate deployment is measured as:

  • 80% certification by Month 5 (2027-03-08)
  • Full deployment by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23)
  • Zero production disruption
  • Zero confirmed IP or cyber breaches

Audit completeness is measured as:

  • 100% envelope mapping sampled
  • At most 2% exceptions

Adjudication workload is measured as:

  • Planned capacity of 15 cases per month
  • Escalation if exceeded

Go verdict threshold: At least 4 of 5 scored criteria met (detection, false positives, unverifiable equipment, reciprocal-access parity, discrepancy age), fewer than 5 open material discrepancies, no hard stop trigger, and intervals not straddling a threshold.

Stakeholder Benefits

Co-chairs gain a credible test of bilateral verification feasibility, a framework for detecting undeclared equipment changes, and documented operational lessons that shape future policy.

Inspectorates gain full-time employment, training in frontier-computing inspection, and a pathway to permanent roles.

Operators secure home-government compensation, controlled access limits, and demonstrated fairness through reciprocal inspection.

Vendors participating in fallback exercises gain credibility as trustworthy; those declining gain documented exclusion.

Auditors and neutral hosts gain paid engagements and reputation as guarantors of integrity.

Legislative bodies gain transparency on spending, envelope mapping and stopping conditions, plus proof that verification of sensitive domains is achievable.

Ethical Considerations

This project is built on double-key governance: neither country unilaterally controls the outcome. Compartmentalized inspectors protect sensitive technology without hiding evidence—filtered packages are certified by independent auditors, and raw evidence is available in a joint reading room after formal challenge.

Entry gates and hard stop triggers are pre-registered to block political gaming of ambiguous results. The verdict defaults to Modify when statistical intervals are ambiguous, not to Go based on hope. Provisional thresholds are validated against historical data before deployment.

Operator and vendor compensation is transparent and administered by home governments. Language of record is dual-authoritative with a controlled glossary to prevent translation weaponization. All spending is mapped to envelopes and independently audited.

Failure is accepted and informative: a Stop verdict or key suspension does not require confession, only transparent deadlock procedures.

Collaboration Opportunities

  • Independent Exercise Authority: Mixed-nationality core team of 8 staff plus red teams from both countries design and score all 54 blind challenges.
  • Neutral facility host: Joint neutral secure facility (Geneva or Singapore; site choice to be decided by Month 1 = 2026-11-08), at least 1,000 sq m, operational by Month 3 (2027-01-08).
  • Independent filter auditor: Third-country auditor certifies that evidence packages omit nothing event-relevant before counterpart disclosure.
  • Envelope and compliance auditors: Conduct envelope reconciliation and compliance testing (100% sampling of high-risk categories).
  • Accredited independent examiners: From both countries, execute vendor-refusal fallback ladders.
  • Technical specialists: From both sides, form rotating evidence-weighting committees, validated against blind outcomes.
  • Arms-control institutes and academic verification researchers: Observe declassified process and outcomes to build precedent.
  • Bilateral legal implementation team: Ensures instrument consistency and enforceability.

Long-term Vision

Phase One is a 90-day proof-of-concept of declared-equipment change verification at matched sites. If the Go verdict is reached, Phase Two (not yet funded) could extend to additional sites, longer duration or broader equipment scope. If Modify, the verdict specifies rework: stronger evidence rules, more exercises, tighter synchronization bounds, or revised thresholds. If Stop, the outcome documents what broke: access asymmetry, shielding, ledger failure or statistical insufficiency—knowledge that shapes whether verification of frontier computing is feasible at scale.

Beyond this bilateral frame, success establishes a replicable model for three-country, regional or treaty-based verification of sensitive technology. Lessons on double-key governance, compartmentalization, tamper-evident ledgers and reciprocal challenge exercises are relevant to future arms-control regimes.

The project does not aim to solve verification permanently; it aims to prove that the problem is tractable, establish the operational and political costs, and inform the next iteration.

Call to Action

Both governments must sign the bilateral instrument by Month 1 (2026-11-08) and enact domestic appropriations by Month 2 (2026-12-08), triggering the first tranche (USD 625 million per country). The 90-day clock starts at Month 6 (2027-04-08), after the entry gate is certified.

Co-chairs must sign off on matched-pair selections by Month 3 (2027-01-08) and certify the entry gate by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23). If either milestone slips more than 2 weeks, a 5-day emergency co-chair summit is convened. If the entry gate is not certified by Month 9 (2027-07-08), the scope-reduction backstop is invoked.

Operators must submit Statements of Cooperation and access schedules before matched-pair approval at Month 3 (2027-01-08); the parity definition and aggregation method are locked with them before Month 3 (2027-01-08), and Month 5.5 (2027-03-23) is kept only for dry-run confirmation. Whether the commitments are binding is to be stated in the bilateral instrument.

Independent auditors and neutral-facility hosts should signal availability by Month 1 (2026-11-08).

The 90-day clock starts only when all gates are certified (target Month 5.5 = 2027-03-23); the verdict is delivered by Month 9.5 (2027-07-23).

Goal Statement: Run a 90-day Phase One operational test (Months 6-9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08) of The Consortium, a US–China mechanism verifying declared frontier-computing equipment changes at 3 matched pairs of declared datacenters, within a USD 5.0 billion cap (USD 2.5 billion each), and reach a Go/Modify/Stop decision by Month 9.5 (2027-07-23).

SMART Criteria

  • Specific: Verify arrivals, installations, removals, transfers, maintenance changes and decommissioning of declared equipment at matched participating sites, then issue a Go, Modify or Stop decision. Excludes total-capacity estimates, workload or model-weight checks, hidden-facility detection and foreign-hosted infrastructure.
  • Measurable: Five scored criteria: detection (at least 70% planned class, at least 50% unplanned class; proposed thresholds), false positives at most 10%, unverifiable equipment at most 5%, parity at least 85% (definition TBD), no discrepancy older than 21 days. Go needs 4 of 5 plus no hard Stop trigger. All thresholds provisional, validated on pilot data.
  • Achievable: Both leaders back the mission and can compel participation. Funding is fixed at USD 2.5 billion per country, about 180 full-time staff per country (estimate) and 54 exercises are planned. Limits: no trust, thin statistics (pooled about ±12% at 95%, per type about ±32%; estimate) and strict entry gates.
  • Relevant: Tests whether declared-equipment change verification is credible between distrustful powers, protecting national security and political control. Public value is mission justification and fiscal accountability; commercial elements are Not applicable.
  • Time-bound: Entry gates Months 0-5 (2026-10-08 to 2027-03-08).5 (start Month 0 = 2026-10-08), 90-day clock Months 6-9 (2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08), verdict scored within 5 days, final decision by Month 9.5 (2027-07-23). Any gate slipping over 2 weeks triggers a summit; no certification by Month 9 (2027-07-08) forces a Stop/re-scope decision.

Dependencies

  • Bilateral instrument signed by both governments
  • Both contributions appropriated and domestic access authority enacted
  • Participating sites selected as matched pairs with parity confirmed
  • Inspectors approved and operator and vendor participation secured
  • Provisional covered-equipment schedule adopted

Resources Required

  • Replicated tamper-evident ledger, attestation, evidence and secure communications systems
  • Mirrored full-time national inspection and specialist units
  • Joint neutral secure facility for ledger hosting, key custody and reading rooms
  • Independent Exercise Authority, red teams and accredited examiner teams
  • Independent auditors and bilateral legal implementation team

Related Goals

  • Bilateral authority and reciprocity gate
  • Site eligibility and matched selection
  • Live challenge exercises
  • Discrepancy adjudication and suspension
  • Possible Modify-directed rework or later phase (funding OPEN)

Tags

  • Arms control verification
  • US-China
  • Frontier computing
  • Tamper-evident ledger
  • Public-sector

Risk Assessment and Mitigation Strategies

Key Risks

  • Entry gates slip, compressing the test and widening statistical uncertainty
  • Asymmetric access or operator shielding undermines parity
  • Thin exercise data makes the verdict ambiguous or contested
  • Ledger divergence or key-custody failure blocks evidence
  • Tranche delay or withheld funding by either country

Diverse Risks

  • Counterintelligence breach or IP exposure by inspectors
  • Vendor refusal leaves equipment unverifiable (full fallback ladder cannot finish before entry)
  • Evidence rule miscalibration overloads adjudication (about 15 cases per month planned)
  • Exercises disrupt production
  • Staffing shortfall or attrition in 24/7 mirrored shifts

Mitigation Plans

  • Entry task force with binding roadmap; parallel tracks; summit within 5 days of a gate slipping over 2 weeks; compression reserve USD 50-100M (estimate); re-scope rather than extend
  • Pre-clock parity audit; exclude asymmetric pairs; fall back to 2 pairs; hard Stop on shielding
  • Pre-register thresholds, lock before the clock, report intervals openly; default to Modify when intervals straddle thresholds
  • Validate evidence rule on 100-200 historical events per site; rehearse key recovery; hourly digest exchange with alerts
  • Synchronized tranches with 14-day escalation and 30-day Stop trigger; contingency draw triggers at 30%, 50% and 75%
  • Compartmentalized inspectors, filtered evidence, 3-officer CI board; run exercises only in staging, spare, maintenance or expansion areas

Stakeholder Analysis

Primary Stakeholders

  • US national co-chair and office
  • Chinese national co-chair and office
  • Mirrored inspection and technical units
  • Independent Exercise Authority
  • Ledger, cybersecurity and counterintelligence units

Secondary Stakeholders

  • Participating datacenter operators
  • Critical equipment vendors and maintenance providers
  • Independent auditors and third-country filter auditor
  • Legislative oversight bodies of both countries
  • Customs and logistics agencies

Engagement Strategies

  • Co-chairs: weekly dashboard, double-key decisions, emergency summit on gate slips
  • Inspection and specialist units: regular briefings, rapid answers to information requests, rotation and debrief schedules
  • Operators and vendors: written commitments, access baselines, home-government compensation, fallback options
  • Auditors and filter auditor: monthly unclassified findings and milestone reports
  • Legislatures and agencies: periodic declassified summaries and notice of significant scope or timeline changes

Regulatory and Compliance Requirements

Permits and Licenses

  • Bilateral instrument and domestic access authority in each country
  • Appropriation acts for each USD 2.5 billion contribution
  • Inspector security clearances and site access approvals
  • Export-control and data-handling authorizations for evidence and equipment inspection
  • Host-country permits for the neutral facility (Geneva or Singapore; OPEN)

Compliance Standards

  • Double-key authorization with no casting vote
  • Public financial management and envelope mapping (100% sampled)
  • Classified-information and cybersecurity standards
  • Operator confidentiality and evidence-preservation requirements
  • Scope limits: monitored changes at participating declared sites only

Regulatory Bodies

  • Both governments' appropriations and audit authorities
  • National security and counterintelligence agencies
  • Export control and customs authorities
  • Neutral host-country authorities
  • Independent third-country auditors

Compliance Actions

  • Sign instrument and enact access authority before the clock
  • Lock deadlock, impaired-confidence and suspension thresholds in the instrument
  • Schedule monthly envelope reconciliation and independent audits
  • Apply for neutral facility permits and clearances for all personnel
  • Certify entry gate by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23) and publish verdict within 5 days

Primary Decisions

The vital few decisions that have the most impact.

The Critical levers (Layered Evidence Weighting, Inspector Information Firewall, Blind Challenge Exercise Control, Verdict Threshold Calibration, Deadlock and Suspension) address the core tensions: verification strength versus protection of sensitive technology, detection credibility versus production disruption, and stalling versus brittle suspension under equal co-chairs. High levers govern cost, parity and exposure trade-offs. No major strategic dimension appears missing, though operator and host-government compliance incentives are only indirectly covered.

Decision 1: Layered Evidence Weighting Model

Lever ID: c2bc2403-915c-45b2-a589-b97885c08f92

The Core Decision: Specifies the rule by which attestation, physical inspection, customs and shipment records, identifiers, maintenance logs, infrastructure changes and witnessed movement combine into an equipment-identity confidence rating. It must honor the principle that no single source is decisive. Success metrics: calibration of confidence against blind-exercise ground truth, false-positive and false-negative rates, and adjudication caseload generated per month.

Why It Matters: This lever decides how attestation, physical inspection, customs and shipment records, identifiers, maintenance logs, infrastructure changes and witnessed movement combine into an equipment-identity confidence rating. A transparent rule makes findings defensible to both governments. A rigid rule can be gamed by an operator who knows which evidence types carry the most weight, and a loose one produces disputes that overload adjudication.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Apply a published rule requiring corroboration from a minimum number of independent evidence categories, with no category sufficient alone, and keep the category list in the confidential versioned schedule.
  2. Use a confidential, rotating combination rule set by accountable specialists from both sides, so operators cannot learn which evidence combinations suffice, with weights validated against blind-exercise outcomes.
  3. Score identity confidence by contradiction rather than accumulation, so any unresolved conflict between two evidence layers lowers the rating regardless of how much other evidence supports identity.

Trade-Off / Risk: Contradiction-based scoring resists gaming and fits the rule that no single source is decisive, but it may flag benign record errors as discrepancies and push adjudication workload above what the inspectorate can absorb.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Supplies the scoring basis for Verdict Threshold Calibration Method and works with Covered-Equipment Schedule Revision Rhythm, because the confidential schedule defines which evidence categories exist and can be reweighted as equipment changes.

Conflict: Conflicts with Deadlock and Suspension Mechanics and Inspector Information Firewall Doctrine: stricter or contradiction-based scoring raises discrepancy counts and aging pressure, while filtered evidence limits the layers inspectors may combine.

Justification: Critical, Central hub: converts all evidence layers into identity confidence, feeds verdict scoring, vendor fallback credit and schedule alignment. Controls the false-positive/negative versus adjudication-load trade-off and the 'no single source decisive' principle, and conflicts with firewall and deadlock levers.

Decision 2: Deadlock and Suspension Mechanics

Lever ID: 65da5760-ec8d-4347-90c0-b34edded6de6

The Core Decision: Defines how the equal co-chairs' deadlocks over budgets, protocol changes, site findings and sanctions are handled, and when impaired-confidence or automatic suspension applies without a casting vote. It protects the mission from both stalling and brittle shutdowns. Success metrics: time to resolve deadlocks, unresolved discrepancy age, suspension frequency and duration, and share of verification kept running.

Why It Matters: This lever determines what happens when the co-chairs cannot agree on a budget, protocol change, site finding or sanction. Without a casting vote, the design of deadlock, impaired-confidence and automatic-suspension rules decides whether a dispute pauses the mission safely or lets one side stall. Rules that suspend too readily make the program fragile, and rules that suspend too rarely allow unresolved findings to build up.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Pause only the disputed function through automatic partial suspension after a fixed period, leaving unrelated verification running and recording each pause in the ledger as an event.
  2. Refer deadlocked findings to a standing panel of technical specialists nominated equally by both sides, whose advisory conclusion is non-binding but is published to both co-chairs and logged.
  3. Link suspension to the age of unresolved discrepancies, so a finding left open past a set limit moves the site into impaired-confidence status without a decision by either co-chair.

Trade-Off / Risk: Age-triggered impaired-confidence status removes the need for a joint decision, yet the age limit is itself a figure both governments must agree on, so the stalling problem is shifted to its calibration.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Reinforces Appropriations Tranche and Audit Cadence, since funding disputes can use the same pause rules, and Verdict Threshold Calibration Method, by tying aged discrepancies to explicit Modify or Stop triggers.

Conflict: Conflicts with Layered Evidence Weighting Model and Ledger Synchronization Bounds: higher discrepancy volume or ledger divergence accelerates suspension triggers, while the agreed age limit moves the stalling risk into calibration.

Justification: Critical, Controls the foundational governance tension of equal co-chairs with no casting vote: stalling versus brittle shutdown. Connects to evidence volume, ledger divergence, funding, schedule amendments and verdict triggers, making it a hub for mission continuity.

Decision 3: Blind Challenge Exercise Control

Lever ID: 1474c892-bbc3-4e7a-85cc-9fe1974499b2

The Core Decision: Sets who designs, schedules, executes and scores the live challenge exercises that produce the only direct detection evidence in Phase One. Key success metrics are scenario coverage across all seven event types, scorer independence accepted by both governments, zero interruption of active computation, and enough trials per event type to state detection rates with explicit, labeled uncertainty.

Why It Matters: This lever decides who designs, schedules and scores the live exercises covering unreported arrival, substituted equipment, inaccurate records, delayed access, disputed identity, vendor refusal and a reluctant operator. Control over the design affects whether detection results are credible to both governments. Independent control costs more and complicates operator coordination, and exercises must run in staging, spare-inventory, maintenance or expansion areas without interrupting active computational work.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Fund an independent test authority with mixed-nationality staff to design and run all exercises, with each government's inspectorate blind to the scenarios until execution.
  2. Have each country's red team design challenges for the other country's inspectorate, so each side tests the verification it has the most reason to doubt, with an independent referee scoring results.
  3. Interleave unannounced challenges with routine operations throughout the test rather than scheduling discrete exercise windows, so inspectors cannot adjust their behavior for known test periods.

Trade-Off / Risk: Unannounced challenges give more realistic detection data, but they raise the risk of production disruption and operator resistance, and a few events per type may be too few to support any statistical claim about false negatives.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Supplies the detection data that Verdict Threshold Calibration Method needs to score Go, Modify or Stop. It also stress-tests the Vendor Refusal Fallback Ladder and Mirrored Shift Coverage Architecture under realistic, unannounced conditions.

Conflict: Unannounced or interleaved challenges strain Mirrored Shift Coverage Architecture and risk production disruption. Exercise secrecy also competes with Matched Site Selection Doctrine, because operators must still grant staging-area access and coordinate cover.

Justification: Critical, Exercises produce the only direct detection evidence in Phase One, so credibility of the Go/Modify/Stop decision depends on who designs and scores them. Hub linking site selection, shift coverage, vendor ladder and verdict calibration, with production-disruption trade-offs.

Decision 4: Verdict Threshold Calibration Method

Lever ID: 719358dc-940c-4de4-93a1-e852e5d255cc

The Core Decision: Converts exercise outcomes (detection by event type, false positives and negatives, unverifiable equipment, parity) into Go, Modify or Stop. It determines whether the final decision reads as technical or negotiated. Success means thresholds fixed before results are known, each marked provisional or TBD with a stated validation path, and statistical limits from few events per type stated openly.

Why It Matters: This sets how detection rates, false positives and unverifiable equipment are converted into Go, Modify or Stop. Fixed numeric cutoffs give clarity but would rest on figures that cannot be validated before the first exercises. Judgment-based thresholds adapt to evidence but invite dispute and political reading of ambiguous results. The choice determines whether the final decision is seen as technical or negotiated.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Set provisional thresholds before the first exercise, mark each as provisional or TBD, and lock them only after a mirrored panel validates them against pilot data.
  2. Define thresholds as bands rather than points, so results inside a band trigger Modify by default and only results clearly outside it support Go or Stop.
  3. Have an independent testing body, not the co-chairs, score exercise results against a pre-registered rubric, with the co-chairs allowed only to confirm or contest the scoring through double-key procedure.

Trade-Off / Risk: Pre-registered thresholds resist post-hoc bargaining, but with only a short operational test and few events per type, the statistical basis is thin, so confidence in any numeric cutoff must be labeled provisional.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Builds directly on data from Blind Challenge Exercise Control and on the evidence confidence outputs of Layered Evidence Weighting Model, giving the final decision a traceable, pre-registered basis that both governments can audit.

Conflict: Strict pre-registered cutoffs constrain Appropriations Tranche and Audit Cadence, since funding releases may depend on interim results. They also conflict with Covered-Equipment Schedule Revision Rhythm when mid-test schedule changes make results non-comparable.

Justification: Critical, Converts exercise data into Go, Modify or Stop and decides whether the outcome is technical or negotiated. Consumes outputs of exercises and evidence weighting and ties to suspension triggers and funding; thin statistics make its design decisive for credibility.

Decision 5: Inspector Information Firewall Doctrine

Lever ID: 31c8cfb6-de4f-4767-b4d9-8d881591e887

The Core Decision: Governs what inspectors can observe, carry, record and disclose, and how knowledge is contained after rotation, protecting workloads, topology, source code and unrelated infrastructure. It sets the trust balance between operator confidence and inspector ability to resolve identity questions. Metrics: IP or cybersecurity incidents, unverifiable-equipment count, filter-dispute rate, and the audit trail of raw-observation access.

Why It Matters: Controls what inspectors may see, carry, record and say, and how their knowledge is contained after rotation. Tighter firewalls protect workloads, topology and source code but can leave inspectors unable to resolve ambiguous identity evidence, raising the unverifiable-equipment count and pushing more cases to adjudication.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Run inspectors through a sealed observation-and-report model in which they hold only the filtered evidence interface, with raw observations retained in site custody for later audited review.
  2. Pair each inspector with an operator-side security officer who pre-screens each view and recording, trading some speed for operator confidence that no unrelated infrastructure was exposed.
  3. Compartmentalize inspector knowledge by role and site, with post-assignment debriefs and monitored cooling-off periods before any reassignment to other duties.

Trade-Off / Risk: A sealed interface best protects sensitive technology, but it makes inspectors depend on the filtering rules, so disputes shift from what was seen to who wrote the filter and whether it hides discrepancies.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Pairs with Counterpart Evidence Disclosure Tiers, which sets what filtered evidence reaches the other side, and with Root-of-Trust Key Custody Architecture, which can secure raw observations held in site custody.

Conflict: Tighter firewalls work against Vendor Refusal Fallback Ladder and Layered Evidence Weighting Model, because filtered views leave less evidence for identity confidence. That raises unverifiable counts and adjudication load.

Justification: Critical, Controls the core tension between protecting sensitive technology and giving inspectors enough evidence to verify. Determines unverifiable counts, adjudication load and incident risk, and conflicts with evidence weighting, vendor fallback and shift coverage, making it a foundational hub.

Secondary Decisions

These decisions are less significant, but still worth considering.

Decision 6: Matched Site Selection Doctrine

Lever ID: d352cbea-8bbf-460f-a173-29715cf307e8

The Core Decision: Defines how the small set of declared datacenters is nominated, paired and confirmed before the Phase One clock starts. Scope covers pairing logic, veto or reconciliation rights, and documented rationale for each pairing. Success metrics: reciprocal-access parity score, share of exercise-eligible staging, spare-inventory, maintenance and expansion areas per pair, and time to complete site selection as an entry condition.

Why It Matters: This lever sets how the small set of declared datacenters is chosen and paired. It determines whether reciprocal-access parity can be demonstrated and whether the exercises are representative or flattering. Sites that are easy to inspect make the test pass but say little about harder cases. Sites that are too sensitive may stall the entry conditions before the 90-day clock starts.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Pair sites by functional equivalence of staging, spare-inventory and maintenance areas, with each side proposing candidates and the other holding a veto over any site it judges unrepresentative.
  2. Pair sites through a sealed, simultaneous exchange of nominations, then reconcile mismatches in a structured negotiation that weights parity of inspector access over similarity of facility scale.
  3. Pair each declared site with a deliberately contrasting counterpart, such as a hyperscale operator against a government-run facility, so the test exposes asymmetries in operator reluctance and legal authority.

Trade-Off / Risk: Functional equivalence makes parity measurable, but no two datacenters across both systems are truly equivalent, so every pairing embeds a judgment that either side can later cite as grounds for discounting an unfavorable result.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Feeds Mirrored Shift Coverage Architecture, since site count and layout drive staffing, and strengthens Blind Challenge Exercise Control by supplying representative, comparable areas where unreported-arrival and substitution tests can be run.

Conflict: Pressures Vendor Refusal Fallback Ladder and Counterpart Evidence Disclosure Tiers: sites chosen for comparable access may host vendors or equipment that resist disclosure, and sensitive sites may stall entry conditions.

Justification: High, Determines whether reciprocal-access parity is demonstrable and whether exercises are representative. Feeds staffing and exercise design and pressures vendor and disclosure levers. It is an entry condition, so it can stall the clock, but it is largely a one-time gate decision.

Decision 7: Ledger Synchronization Bounds

Lever ID: f86475f4-cfae-44c1-b1a9-4be1ec3739f4

The Core Decision: Sets the timing and mechanism by which locally recorded events become visible in the counterpart's ledger copy, and how divergence is detected and reconciled. It governs the trade-off between tamper-detection window and cross-border exposure. Success metrics: event-recording latency, synchronization latency, divergence incidents, reconciliation time, and number of unresolved ledger divergences.

Why It Matters: This lever sets how quickly local events become visible to the counterpart and how divergence between the two national copies is detected and resolved. Tighter bounds shrink the window for undetected tampering but increase network exposure and operational burden at sites. Looser bounds reduce the attack surface but allow divergence to build before anyone can see it.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Record every event locally at once and exchange signed digests with the counterpart copy on a fixed short interval, escalating automatically when any digest fails to match.
  2. Synchronize only at defined custody handover points, such as completion of intake or exit dispositions, and rely on witnessed local recording in between, which reduces continuous cross-border data flow.
  3. Introduce a neutral third-party notary for digest escrow only, holding no event content, so a divergence dispute can be resolved by checking against an independently held commitment.

Trade-Off / Risk: A third-party notary adds a tie-breaker for divergence, but it introduces a party neither government fully controls, and the premise of double-key governance with no casting vote makes its acceptance politically uncertain.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Depends on and reinforces Root-of-Trust Key Custody Architecture, since signed digests need trustworthy keys, and supports Departure Disposition Closure Rules by timestamping custody handovers so exits stay verifiable within the boundary.

Conflict: Trades off against Inspector Information Firewall Doctrine and Mirrored Shift Coverage Architecture: tighter synchronization widens network exposure and adds shift workload, while looser bounds weaken the evidence base for discrepancy adjudication.

Justification: High, Governs the tamper-detection window versus cross-border exposure trade-off for the core ledger. Depends on key custody and supports exit closure, but it is a technical parameter choice with fewer system-wide strategic consequences than the evidence or governance levers.

Decision 8: Vendor Refusal Fallback Ladder

Lever ID: 732264f2-7f1a-4800-8ac0-6fcc15081e37

The Core Decision: Determines how the Consortium responds when a critical vendor declines reporting, escort or evidence-preservation duties, and how each fallback method is credited toward verification. It governs whether equipment is classed as unverifiable and whether a site fails Phase One. Success metrics: vendor-refusal outcomes by rung, unverifiable-equipment count, and evidence sufficiency per fallback.

Why It Matters: This lever sets the order and conditions under which vendor-supervised testing, filtered evidence, accredited independent examiners, clean-room procedures or validated attestations are used when a critical vendor refuses. A fixed ladder gives predictability, but a vendor can aim for the weakest rung. Whether equipment ends up classed as unverifiable, and whether a site fails Phase One, depends on how each rung is credited.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Follow a fixed escalation order from vendor-supervised testing to accredited independent examination, and classify equipment as unverifiable once the last rung has been tried without sufficient evidence.
  2. Let the receiving national team choose the fallback for each refusal, subject to the counterpart's right to demand a stronger method, so neither side is bound to a method it distrusts.
  3. Make vendor participation a condition of listing equipment on the covered schedule, so refusal is settled at entry by excluding the item or the site rather than discovered later during operations.

Trade-Off / Risk: Settling refusal at the entry gate avoids mid-test surprises, but it lets vendors shape which equipment is verifiable at all, and the resulting schedule may omit exactly the items the Consortium most needs to see.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Works with Layered Evidence Weighting Model, which determines how much evidentiary credit each fallback rung earns, and with Blind Challenge Exercise Control, which tests vendor-refusal scenarios against the ladder.

Conflict: Constrains Covered-Equipment Schedule Revision Rhythm and Matched Site Selection Doctrine: entry-gate exclusion lets vendors shape the schedule and site set, while a fixed ladder invites aiming at the weakest rung.

Justification: High, Decides when equipment becomes unverifiable and whether a site fails Phase One, a direct Stop trigger. Linked to evidence weighting, exercises, schedule and site selection, but it addresses one specific scenario rather than the whole system.

Decision 9: Covered-Equipment Schedule Revision Rhythm

Lever ID: 95d82a58-50fa-4a12-b4d8-63c145be0524

The Core Decision: Governs how the confidential, versioned technical schedule of covered equipment is amended so it stays technology-neutral and does not lapse into a product list. It sets amendment timing, approval path, effective-time rules and version traceability. Success is measured by coverage gaps found, amendment cycle time, scope disputes opened, and exercise results that remain comparable across schedule versions.

Why It Matters: This determines how the confidential, versioned technical schedule is amended as hardware generations, form factors and performance characteristics change. A tight rhythm keeps coverage relevant and prevents the schedule from lapsing into a product list. It also gives each side frequent openings to argue scope and to learn what the other treats as frontier-relevant. A loose rhythm reduces negotiation friction but risks gaps that undercut credibility of detection.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Freeze the provisional schedule for the entire Phase One test and defer all amendments to the final decision, trading coverage freshness for stability and fewer scope disputes.
  2. Allow amendments at fixed review points set by the accountable specialists, with each version double-key approved and applied only to events recorded after its effective time.
  3. Maintain a standing mirrored technical panel that proposes amendments continuously, with each change held in escrow and activated only after the counterpart panel independently reproduces the classification logic.

Trade-Off / Risk: Frequent revisions keep the schedule from being outflanked by new hardware, but each amendment is a double-key negotiation that can stall under deadlock, and mid-test changes complicate comparing exercise results across versions.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Keeps the Layered Evidence Weighting Model aligned with current hardware, so identity and attestation evidence classify correctly. A stable version history also supports Verdict Threshold Calibration Method by making exercise results comparable.

Conflict: Each amendment needs double-key approval, so frequent revisions load Deadlock and Suspension Mechanics. They also reveal frontier-relevance judgments, pulling against Counterpart Evidence Disclosure Tiers, which aim to limit what the counterpart learns.

Justification: Medium, Keeps the confidential schedule technology-neutral and preserves comparability of results, but within a 90-day test a freeze or fixed review points is a manageable option. Moderate coupling to deadlock and disclosure levers; mainly an optimization.

Decision 10: Counterpart Evidence Disclosure Tiers

Lever ID: e993aa9d-6f74-47e1-9ec6-e3db52e53680

The Core Decision: Defines how much of each event record and its underlying evidence the counterpart national team can see, from identifiers only to supervised full-detail reading. It sets the balance between challengeability and protection of workloads, topology, security architecture and unrelated infrastructure. Metrics include disputes caused by opaque records, IP or cybersecurity incidents, filtering-certification latency and the share of findings the counterpart can check.

Why It Matters: This defines what the counterpart national team sees of each event record: identifiers only, filtered images and attestations, or full detail inside a controlled room. Wider disclosure raises the ability to challenge a finding but exposes network layout, security architecture and unrelated infrastructure. Narrower disclosure protects intellectual property but pushes more disputes into adjudication because the counterpart cannot check the basis for a record.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Give the counterpart only hashed event summaries and equipment identifiers by default, releasing underlying evidence solely when a discrepancy is formally opened by double-key authorization.
  2. Provide the counterpart with filtered evidence packages prepared by the host side's inspectors, with an independent examiner certifying that filtering removed nothing event-relevant.
  3. Hold raw evidence in a joint secure reading room where counterpart specialists can query it under supervision but cannot copy or retain it, trading convenience for tighter exposure control.

Trade-Off / Risk: Tiered disclosure protects sensitive detail, but filtering is itself a point where a host can omit inconvenient evidence, so the filtering step needs independent certification that adds latency and cost.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Strengthens Inspector Information Firewall Doctrine by applying the same boundaries to counterpart access, and gives Layered Evidence Weighting Model credible inputs because each side can check the basis of a record.

Conflict: Narrow tiers push disputes into Deadlock and Suspension Mechanics, since the counterpart cannot verify records. Wider tiers add exposure risk and certification delay, which can lengthen the synchronization times set by Ledger Synchronization Bounds.

Justification: High, Sets the challengeability versus IP-protection balance between national teams. Narrow tiers push disputes into deadlock, wide tiers add exposure and latency. Strongly coupled with firewall, evidence weighting and ledger timing, though overlapping the firewall lever.

Decision 11: Root-of-Trust Key Custody Architecture

Lever ID: 7cb65114-fa5d-4343-9281-05785a8b8877

The Core Decision: Specifies who generates, holds, rotates, recovers and revokes the signing keys that make ledger entries and validated attestations trustworthy to both countries. Scope covers ceremonies, hardware modules, compromise response and recovery. Success metrics include zero unauthorized signings, key-rotation timeliness, recovery time after a lost or contested key, and cross-certification disputes that cause ledger divergence.

Why It Matters: Determines who generates, holds and rotates the signing keys behind the tamper-evident ledger and validated attestations. Split custody strengthens the double-key principle but adds ceremony overhead and recovery complexity, and a lost or contested key can stall evidence validity at a site until the deadlock procedures resolve it.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Generate keys in joint ceremonies at a neutral secure facility, with each country holding a non-reconstructable share and both shares required for any ledger signing or attestation validation.
  2. Give each country fully independent signing hierarchies for its own national ledger copy, cross-certified through audited exchange, so neither side's evidence depends on the other's key material.
  3. Issue short-lived signing keys from hardware modules sealed inside inspection zones and destroyed on a fixed cycle, so compromise exposure is bounded even if custody procedures are later challenged.

Trade-Off / Risk: Shared key shares match the double-key design, but they create a single ceremony chokepoint; independent hierarchies avoid that and instead push the risk into cross-certification disputes that could surface as ledger divergence.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Underpins Ledger Synchronization Bounds by making each replicated copy verifiable, and reinforces the double-key principle in Deadlock and Suspension Mechanics through shared custody and clear key-contest procedures.

Conflict: Joint-share ceremonies create chokepoints that can stall Ledger Synchronization Bounds and Mirrored Shift Coverage Architecture during round-the-clock recording. Independent hierarchies avoid this but risk disputes that Deadlock and Suspension Mechanics must resolve.

Justification: Medium, Underpins ledger trustworthiness and the double-key principle, but is largely an enabling security mechanism. Its main impact flows through ledger synchronization and deadlock procedures, so it is important to implement well yet less of a strategic choice.

Decision 12: Departure Disposition Closure Rules

Lever ID: 4a4a2789-ec70-4325-b658-b90fa7c74631

The Core Decision: Sets the ledger rules that turn every departure into one of the five Exit Protocol dispositions: witnessed destruction, verified permanent disablement, transfer to another participating site, documented release beyond the monitored system, or unresolved disposition. Key metrics are the share of departures closed within window, unresolved discrepancy age, and the rate of closures later contested. Closure windows (proposed, TBD) need validation in exercises.

Why It Matters: Governs how each removal is classified and closed in the ledger, and when an open disposition becomes a finding. Strict closure deadlines keep the ledger honest about the monitored boundary, but they can force premature classification of unresolved items and trigger suspensions from ordinary logistics delays.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Require every departure to reach one of the defined dispositions within a fixed period, and automatically escalate any item still open to a formal discrepancy at expiry.
  2. Allow tiered closure windows by disposition type, giving transfers between participating sites a shorter period and destruction or disablement witnessing a longer, scheduled period.
  3. Treat release beyond the monitored system as a terminal ledger state that records the handover point only, and bar any later inspector entries about that equipment's whereabouts.

Trade-Off / Risk: Terminal release entries respect the rule against implying knowledge beyond the boundary, but they also let a party move equipment out cleanly; the closure deadline then does little to address what the release hides.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Works with Layered Evidence Weighting Model, which supplies the evidence standard for each disposition, and Deadlock and Suspension Mechanics, which gives expired open items a defined route to formal discrepancy and suspension.

Conflict: Strict deadlines pressure Mirrored Shift Coverage Architecture, since witnessing destruction or transfers on schedule needs inspectors available. They also tighten Verdict Threshold Calibration Method, because ordinary logistics delays can inflate unresolved counts.

Justification: Medium, Operationalizes the Exit Protocol and closure deadlines for ledger honesty, with links to evidence standards, shift scheduling and unresolved counts. Mostly a procedural rule set whose effects are contained to departures rather than the core trade-offs.

Decision 13: Mirrored Shift Coverage Architecture

Lever ID: 547dc5ad-0929-4c4c-bbef-e871d96babf5

The Core Decision: Determines how mirrored national teams are rostered at each participating site, including shift patterns, minimum paired presence, leave cover and surge capacity. It converts site count and coverage choices into full-time headcount, so it drives the inspector envelope and exposure to operator friction. Metrics: detection rate for unreported arrivals, coverage gaps per shift, roster fill rate, and personnel cost per site (TBD).

Why It Matters: Defines whether inspectors are continuously present or deployed around expected events, which drives headcount, leave coverage and surge needs. Continuous presence improves detection of unreported arrivals but multiplies personnel cost within the inspector envelope and increases operator friction and counterintelligence exposure.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Station mirrored teams at each site around the clock in rotating shifts, with fixed minimum paired presence in staging and spare-inventory areas at all times.
  2. Maintain continuous coverage of staging and loading points only, and cover maintenance and expansion areas through scheduled and short-notice event-triggered deployments.
  3. Use a hybrid roster with a continuous core crew and a pooled national surge unit that deploys to whichever site shows rising event volume or unresolved discrepancies.

Trade-Off / Risk: Continuous presence maximizes detection of unreported arrivals but strains the USD 750 million personnel envelope; event-triggered coverage saves headcount but leaves gaps that a determined party can schedule around.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Amplifies Blind Challenge Exercise Control, because continuous presence in staging and spare areas gives exercises a fair test of detection. It also supports Departure Disposition Closure Rules by making witnessed removals schedulable.

Conflict: Heavy headcount competes with Appropriations Tranche and Audit Cadence for the fixed USD 750 million personnel envelope. Continuous presence also strains Inspector Information Firewall Doctrine, since more inspector hours mean more exposure to protect.

Justification: High, Drives headcount, the USD 750 million personnel envelope, detection of unreported arrivals and operator friction. Strongly connected to exercises, exit scheduling, firewall exposure and funding, governing a major cost versus detection trade-off.

Decision 14: Language of Record and Interpretive Authority

Lever ID: c0308540-c69b-4ade-9d36-c505d5a58ea1

The Core Decision: Defines which language text governs protocols, ledger entries and findings, and how translation disputes are resolved before they harden into contested findings. It sizes the translation unit and sets leakage risk when sensitive evidence is translated. Metrics: translation turnaround, count of divergence rulings, findings returned for terminology disputes, and adjudication cycle time (targets TBD).

Why It Matters: Establishes which language version of protocols, evidence entries and findings is authoritative and how translation disputes are resolved. This choice shapes how fast discrepancies are adjudicated and whether a mistranslated term can itself become a contested finding. It also affects translation unit size and the risk of information leakage during translation.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Designate both language versions as equally authoritative, with a joint terminology board issuing a controlled glossary and ruling on divergences before they enter the ledger.
  2. Record evidence entries in a structured, language-neutral schema with coded fields, limiting free text and using translation only for narrative annotations and findings.
  3. Require independent bilingual reviewers from each country to back-translate every finding before double-key sign-off, rejecting any finding whose back-translations materially differ.

Trade-Off / Risk: Dual authoritative texts avoid a language hierarchy but invite divergent readings; coded schemas reduce ambiguity yet may squeeze out context that inspectors need to describe an unusual discrepancy.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Strengthens Ledger Synchronization Bounds, because shared coded fields and a controlled glossary make the two national copies easier to reconcile. It also supports Counterpart Evidence Disclosure Tiers by standardizing what each tier means in both languages.

Conflict: Back-translation and glossary rulings slow Deadlock and Suspension Mechanics, which depend on timely findings. Coded schemas can also limit the context that Layered Evidence Weighting Model needs to describe unusual discrepancies.

Justification: Low, Affects translation turnaround and terminology disputes but is mostly a supporting, tactical standard. Its synergies with ledger and disclosure levers are real yet secondary, and its slowing effect on adjudication can be managed through glossary design.

Decision 15: Appropriations Tranche and Audit Cadence

Lever ID: 783534e4-1c16-4932-9535-bd26bb241c0a

The Core Decision: Specifies how the two USD 2.5 billion contributions are drawn down and audited against the seven-envelope map, with every expense mapped to an envelope. It makes funding timeliness and audit exceptions measurable and supports the Stop condition for withheld funding. Metrics: deposit parity, days of tranche delay, envelope reconciliation exceptions, and contingency draw rate. Domestic operator compensation is charged to each government's own contribution.

Why It Matters: Sets how the two equal contributions are drawn down and audited against the envelope map. Frequent tranches and audits expose funding shortfalls and mis-mapped expenses early, which supports the stop condition on withheld funding, but they create recurrent leverage points where either government can slow disbursement.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Release both contributions in synchronized tranches tied to entry-condition milestones, with the next tranche conditional on matching deposits and clean envelope reconciliation.
  2. Hold each country's full contribution in escrow-style national accounts under joint visibility and let drawdown occur on invoice, with independent auditors testing envelope mapping continuously.
  3. Fund inspectorate and ledger envelopes first and defer site preparation and testing draws until site eligibility is confirmed, limiting committed spend if a gate fails.

Trade-Off / Risk: Synchronized tranches make withholding visible and symmetric, but each release is a veto point; escrow-style accounts lessen that leverage while relying on audit quality to catch misuse, which the plan cannot yet demonstrate.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Supports Deadlock and Suspension Mechanics by giving funding delay a defined trigger and visibility. Also supports Mirrored Shift Coverage Architecture by letting surge and contingency spending be planned against audited envelopes.

Conflict: Tranche gates create veto points that can delay Matched Site Selection Doctrine and site preparation. Frequent audit cycles also add administrative load on Mirrored Shift Coverage Architecture and inspectorate staffing.

Justification: Medium, Makes funding timeliness and audit exceptions measurable and supports the withheld-funding Stop condition. Creates veto points affecting site selection and staffing, but is mainly financial-governance optimization rather than a driver of detection credibility.

Choosing our strategic path.

The Strategic Context

Understanding the core ambitions and constraints that guide our decision.

Ambition and Scale: Very high ambition at national-security scale: a first-of-kind bilateral US–China verification mechanism with a USD 5 billion budget (user constraint), split 50/50, full-time mirrored inspectorates and replicated national ledgers. Operational scope is deliberately narrow: a 90-day Phase One test at a small matched set of declared sites, limited to declared-equipment change verification.

Risk and Novelty: High novelty and high political and technical risk. There is no direct precedent for hardware-change verification of frontier computing equipment between adversaries. Trust is assumed absent. Main risks are IP exposure, operator or government shielding, gaming of evidence rules, thin statistics from few events per exercise type, and disputes over thresholds. Phase One is an experimental proof-of-concept whose clock starts only after strict entry conditions are met.

Complexity and Constraints: Very complex. Constraints: equal co-chairs with double-key authorization and no casting vote; defined deadlock, impaired-confidence and automatic-suspension procedures; no single decisive evidence source; no workload, model-weight or hidden-facility verification; exercises must not interrupt active computation; thresholds must be marked provisional or TBD with a validation path. Staffing is large, mirrored and full-time, with separation of duties. Budget envelopes are fixed, and every expense must map to one.

Domain and Tone: Sovereign public-sector arms-control-style verification. The tone is formal, impersonal and governance-heavy. Commercial elements (revenue, investors, customers) are not applicable and are replaced by mission justification, appropriations governance and fiscal accountability.

Holistic Profile: A rigorous but bounded, reciprocity-driven experimental verification pilot between mutually distrustful great powers. It needs credible detection and visible parity to both sides, preserves operations and sensitive technology, resists gaming and stalling without brittle shutdowns, and states its statistical limits honestly. Its ideal strategy balances rigor with workability, with reciprocal test design, partial suspension and provisional validated thresholds.

The Path Forward

This scenario aligns best with the project's characteristics and goals.

The Pragmatic Foundation: Reciprocal Proof with Controlled Risk

Strategic Logic: This pathway balances rigor and workability. Confidential rotating evidence rules validated against blind outcomes resist gaming without the false-positive load of pure contradiction scoring. Each side's red team tests the verification it most doubts, under an independent referee, which builds reciprocal confidence. Partial suspension keeps unrelated verification running, and thresholds are provisional until validated, which fits the thin data from a short test.

Fit Score: 9/10

Why This Path Was Chosen: Rotating confidential evidence rules resist gaming, each side's red team tests what it doubts most (directly supporting reciprocal-access parity), and partial suspension keeps unrelated verification running. Provisional, validated thresholds match the thin-data reality and the plan's provisional/TBD requirement. Compartmentalized inspectors fit the information-barrier workstream.

Key Strategic Decisions:

  • Layered Evidence Weighting Model: Use a confidential, rotating combination rule set by accountable specialists from both sides, so operators cannot learn which evidence combinations suffice, with weights validated against blind-exercise outcomes.
  • Deadlock and Suspension Mechanics: Pause only the disputed function through automatic partial suspension after a fixed period, leaving unrelated verification running and recording each pause in the ledger as an event.
  • Blind Challenge Exercise Control: Have each country's red team design challenges for the other country's inspectorate, so each side tests the verification it has the most reason to doubt, with an independent referee scoring results.
  • Verdict Threshold Calibration Method: Set provisional thresholds before the first exercise, mark each as provisional or TBD, and lock them only after a mirrored panel validates them against pilot data.
  • Inspector Information Firewall Doctrine: Compartmentalize inspector knowledge by role and site, with post-assignment debriefs and monitored cooling-off periods before any reassignment to other duties.

The Decisive Factors:

  • Fit with the plan's profile: The plan is an ambitious but bounded first-of-kind test between distrustful parties. It needs credible detection, visible reciprocity and operational safety at once, and the Pragmatic Foundation balances all three.
  • Reciprocity: Cross-designed red-team challenges under an independent referee directly test parity. Each side probes the verification it doubts most.
  • Anti-gaming without overload: Confidential rotating evidence rules, validated against blind outcomes, resist gaming and avoid the false-positive load of contradiction scoring.
  • Resilient governance: Partial suspension of only the disputed function fits double-key rules with no casting vote and keeps verification running.
  • Honest statistics: Provisional thresholds, locked after validation, match the thin 90-day data.
  • Why not the Pioneer's Gambit: Its unannounced challenges and automatic suspension risk production disruption and brittle shutdowns.
  • Why not the Conservative Anchor: Its operator-side screening invites shielding, and its advisory-only panel and Modify-default bands weaken detection credibility and deadlock resolution.

Alternative Paths

The Pioneer's Gambit: Maximum Detection Pressure

Strategic Logic: This pathway treats Phase One as a hard stress test of the verification concept. It uses contradiction-based identity scoring, unannounced interleaved challenges, automatic age-triggered impaired-confidence status, and independent scoring. It accepts higher adjudication load, more operator friction and some disruption risk in exchange for the most realistic detection data. It also removes any chance for a government or operator to stall or bargain over outcomes.

Fit Score: 5/10

Assessment of this Path: Maximizes detection realism and removes stalling, but contradiction scoring, unannounced interleaved challenges and a sealed interface raise false positives, adjudication overload and production-disruption risk. Age-triggered automatic impaired-confidence can also cause brittle suspension in a 90-day test with thin data, and it conflicts with the no-interruption constraint.

Key Strategic Decisions:

  • Layered Evidence Weighting Model: Score identity confidence by contradiction rather than accumulation, so any unresolved conflict between two evidence layers lowers the rating regardless of how much other evidence supports identity.
  • Deadlock and Suspension Mechanics: Link suspension to the age of unresolved discrepancies, so a finding left open past a set limit moves the site into impaired-confidence status without a decision by either co-chair.
  • Blind Challenge Exercise Control: Interleave unannounced challenges with routine operations throughout the test rather than scheduling discrete exercise windows, so inspectors cannot adjust their behavior for known test periods.
  • Verdict Threshold Calibration Method: Have an independent testing body, not the co-chairs, score exercise results against a pre-registered rubric, with the co-chairs allowed only to confirm or contest the scoring through double-key procedure.
  • Inspector Information Firewall Doctrine: Run inspectors through a sealed observation-and-report model in which they hold only the filtered evidence interface, with raw observations retained in site custody for later audited review.

The Conservative Anchor: Proven Rules, Wide Bands, Operator Comfort

Strategic Logic: This pathway puts stability, operator acceptance and protection of sensitive infrastructure first. It uses a published corroboration rule, an advisory technical panel for deadlocks, an independent test authority running all exercises, outcome bands that default to Modify when results are ambiguous, and operator-side security officers on every view. It gives up some speed, detection sharpness and gaming-resistance to lower the risk of IP exposure, production disruption and early political breakdown. The advisory panel and operator-side officers also carry risks: weaker deadlock resolution and possible operator shielding, which the Stop criteria must catch.

Fit Score: 4/10

Assessment of this Path: Protects operators and IP, but operator-side screeners on every view invite the shielding the plan lists as a Stop trigger. An advisory-only deadlock panel is weak against stalling, a published corroboration rule is easier to game, and bands defaulting to Modify weaken the credible-detection requirement for Go.

Key Strategic Decisions:

  • Layered Evidence Weighting Model: Apply a published rule requiring corroboration from a minimum number of independent evidence categories, with no category sufficient alone, and keep the category list in the confidential versioned schedule.
  • Deadlock and Suspension Mechanics: Refer deadlocked findings to a standing panel of technical specialists nominated equally by both sides, whose advisory conclusion is non-binding but is published to both co-chairs and logged.
  • Blind Challenge Exercise Control: Fund an independent test authority with mixed-nationality staff to design and run all exercises, with each government's inspectorate blind to the scenarios until execution.
  • Verdict Threshold Calibration Method: Define thresholds as bands rather than points, so results inside a band trigger Modify by default and only results clearly outside it support Go or Stop.
  • Inspector Information Firewall Doctrine: Pair each inspector with an operator-side security officer who pre-screens each view and recording, trading some speed for operator confidence that no unrelated infrastructure was exposed.

Purpose

Purpose: business, neither for profit nor non-profit (e.g., a government programme, an agreement between countries, a public-private hybrid). No owner profits from it; judge it by its outcomes for the parties involved and by funding accountability, and use revenue or return on investment only for parts of the plan that earn money.

Purpose Detailed: Sovereign public-sector national-security and arms-control-style verification program: a jointly governed bilateral mechanism (equal co-chairs, double-key authorization) with a replicated tamper-evident ledger, intake and exit protocols, mirrored full-time inspectorates, live challenge exercises, discrepancy adjudication and a final Go/Modify/Stop decision. Scope is limited to monitored changes at participating declared sites. It is not a commercial venture. Revenue, investors, customers and market-demand elements are not applicable and are replaced by mission justification, public value, strategic necessity, appropriations governance and fiscal accountability.

Topic: Bilateral US–China "Consortium" verifying changes (arrival, installation, removal, transfer, maintenance, decommissioning) to declared frontier-relevant computing equipment at a small matched set of declared datacenters, via a 90-day Phase One operational test with a USD 5 billion budget funded 50/50

Domain

Primary domain: Arms Control Verification

Secondary domains: Hardware Supply Chain Security, Counterintelligence and Cybersecurity, Treaty Verification Law

Rationale: Arms Control Verification is the only outcome role and scores highest (5×5), matching the bilateral inspection-based verification mission and Go/Modify/Stop decision. Supply chain security, cryptography, red teaming, law and diplomacy are subordinate methods, constraints or stakeholders.

Plan Type

This plan requires one or more physical locations. It cannot be executed digitally.

Explanation: The plan is classified as physical. The Consortium is a bilateral US–China mechanism that verifies changes to computing equipment at declared datacenters, and its core activities need real-world presence and resources. (1) Inspectors must be deployed to participating datacenters, with full-time mirrored national teams working in shifts. (2) The Intake Protocol checks equipment identity in controlled staging areas before installation, using physical inspection, equipment identifiers and witnessed movement. (3) The Exit Protocol covers witnessed destruction, verified permanent disablement, transfers between sites and documented release, and each of these takes place in person. (4) Evidence is layered from shipment and customs records, maintenance records, infrastructure changes and physical inspection, so it depends on physical logistics and custody chains. (5) The live challenge exercises (unreported arrival, substituted equipment, disputed identity, vendor refusal, reluctant operator) are run in staging, spare-inventory, maintenance and expansion areas of real datacenters. (6) Site preparation, operator compensation, secure facilities, clean rooms and secure communications need construction, setup and physical security. (7) The mandatory entry conditions (signed instrument, site selection, inspector approval, vendor participation) involve in-person government and operator engagement. (8) The USD 5 billion budget funds personnel, facilities and equipment. The replicated tamper-evident ledger is digital, but it only records and synchronizes events that happen physically, and its national copies need secure hosting. Nothing in the plan can be done entirely online without benefit from physical presence, so it is physical.

Physical Locations

This plan implies one or more physical locations.

Requirements for physical locations

  • Declared frontier-relevant computing datacenters with existing operational infrastructure
  • Staging, spare-inventory, maintenance and expansion areas suitable for live challenge exercises without interrupting active computation
  • Reciprocally accessible sites: matched pairs demonstrating functional parity of inspector access
  • Capacity to support full-time mirrored national inspectorates (estimated 150–200+ personnel per country across multiple sites in shifts)
  • Secure facilities meeting physical and electronic security standards for classified ledger hosting, evidence review, key custody and counterintelligence
  • Facilities for continuous monitoring and witness capability during intake, installation, maintenance and exit procedures
  • Space and infrastructure for secure clean-room procedures, vendor-supervised testing and accredited independent examinations
  • Proximity or accessibility to customs, logistics and shipment tracking infrastructure for intake verification
  • Capacity to host secured reading rooms and joint secure governance spaces accessible to both national teams
  • Isolated secure areas for post-rotation inspector debriefs and cooling-off periods to enforce information barriers
  • Network infrastructure capable of supporting tamper-evident ledger synchronization with bounded latency and signed-digest exchange
  • Physical separation enabling independent national ledger copies and secure key custody

Location 1

United States

Tier-1 hyperscale datacenter regions (Northern Virginia, Oregon, Texas, or equivalent critical computing hubs)

Declared hyperscale operator facilities with multiple isolated staging and maintenance areas, existing access-control infrastructure, and capacity for sustained 24/7 inspectorate presence

Rationale: US sites must host frontier-relevant computing equipment and demonstrate existing operational security standards, physical logistics infrastructure for equipment intake/exit, and capacity for continuous mirrored staffing. Northern Virginia and Oregon align with established US computing infrastructure and federal-security precedent. Hyperscale operators have documented equipment-change procedures and maintenance areas suitable for blind-challenge exercises without disrupting active workloads.

Location 2

China

Major regional computing hubs (e.g., Beijing, Shanghai, Shenzhen, or state-approved tier-1 datacenter zones)

Declared state-operated or state-approved frontier computing facilities with government-controlled access, documented equipment schedules, and existing maintenance and spare-equipment areas

Rationale: Chinese sites must be selected through bilateral Matched Site Selection Doctrine and represent frontier-relevant computing capacity. Selection at major regional hubs (Beijing, Shanghai) reflects where state-directed frontier research and computing infrastructure concentrate. The sites must be government-accessible under the domestic-authority provision and include documented procedures for equipment arrival, installation, maintenance and removal. Pairing with US hyperscale sites requires functional equivalence in staging and spare-inventory areas.

Location 3

Neutral or joint secure facility location (proposed: Geneva, Singapore, or equivalent diplomatically neutral jurisdiction)

Secure bilateral governance and evidence-review facility outside both countries' direct territorial control, with established secure-communications and classified-document handling standards

Joint secure facility housing: dual national ledger-hosting infrastructure, bilateral co-chair workspace, secure reading rooms for counterpart evidence review, key-custody ceremonies, inspector debriefing and cooling-off spaces, and independent auditor workspace

Rationale: The Consortium's equal co-chair governance, double-key authorization, no-casting-vote structure and Inspector Information Firewall Doctrine require a neutral space where neither government has unilateral physical control. A Geneva-based facility (aligning with precedent in IAEA, OPCW and START verification) or Singapore (neutral in US–China context, strong secure-infrastructure capability) supports joint operations without territorial sovereignty complications. This facility hosts the replicated ledgers, hosts bilateral dispute adjudication, secures root-of-trust key material and provides secure evidence review rooms that apply Counterpart Evidence Disclosure Tiers without either side controlling the filtering environment.

Location Summary

The Consortium is a bilateral US–China verification mechanism with inherently localized, physical operations. Phase One requires declared datacenters in both countries as the primary operational sites where inspectors deploy full-time, where intake and exit protocols are executed, where staged equipment is physically inspected, and where live challenge exercises are conducted in staging, spare-inventory, maintenance and expansion areas. The plan explicitly constrains these to "a small, matched set of declared datacenters" selected through a bilateral gate before the 90-day clock begins. Additionally, secure facilities are needed to host the replicated national ledgers, conduct evidence review in secure reading rooms, hold key-custody ceremonies, staff full-time mirrored inspectorates, run training and translation units, and maintain counterintelligence capability. The bilateral mechanism itself requires joint secure spaces for co-chair governance, double-key authorization protocols and dispute adjudication.

Currency Strategy

This plan involves money.

Currencies

  • USD: Primary budget currency (user constraint). All bilateral budgeting, appropriations governance, tranche disbursement, envelope tracking, auditing and final reporting are conducted in USD. Each country's USD 2.5 billion contribution is tracked and reconciled in USD.
  • CNY: Chinese domestic expenses. Operator compensation, site preparation, personnel and facility costs within China are incurred and administered in CNY by the Chinese government, then converted to USD equivalents at agreed bilateral exchange-rate milestones for consolidated envelope reconciliation.

Primary currency: USD

Currency strategy: USD is the primary currency for all bilateral governance, auditing and reporting. Domestic expenses within each country are incurred in local currency (USD in the United States, CNY in China) but reconciled to USD equivalents at fixed bilateral exchange-rate milestones (entry conditions, Phase One start, final audit) to ensure budget accountability, prevent currency-fluctuation disputes and support the symmetric 50/50 appropriations structure. This approach aligns with arms-control-style verification precedent, where international settlement occurs in a stable reference currency while domestic administration remains in local currency.

Identify Risks

Risk 1 - Regulatory & Permitting

Entry conditions (signed bilateral instrument, appropriations, domestic access authority, site selection, inspector approval, vendor participation, covered-equipment schedule) are mandatory gates before the 90-day clock starts. Each is subject to political or bureaucratic review, veto or amendment. Misalignment on which sites qualify as 'matched' or 'frontier-relevant' can stall site selection indefinitely. Vendor participation requirements create leverage points where a critical vendor's refusal can block a site from entering Phase One or force unresolvable schedule disputes.
