Impact: Phase One clock never starts, or starts 6–12 months late, rendering the 90-day test infeasible as a proof-of-concept. Delayed entry conditions consume contingency budget (estimated 5–10% of USD 500 million contingency) and force rescoping. Political withdrawal risk increases as deadlines slip. If vendor participation is used as a veto, critical frontier equipment may be excluded from the schedule, undermining the test's credibility.

Likelihood: High

Severity: High

Action: Establish a pre-Phase-One entry-condition task force with binding timelines for each gate: signed instrument by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23), domestic authority by Month 1 (2026-11-08), site nominations by Month 1 (2026-11-08), inspector selections by Month 2 (2026-12-08), vendor agreements by Month 2.5 (2026-12-23), schedule adoption by Month 3 (2027-01-08). Separate technical feasibility (which sites can support inspectors) from political feasibility (which governments will approve) and handle each track in parallel. Publish a preliminary entry-condition roadmap at Month 0 (2026-10-08) with explicit deadlines and escalation procedures for any gate that slips past 2 weeks. Reserve contingency funding for compressed timelines and emergency negotiation if a gate stalls.

Risk 2 - Governance & Deadlock

The design uses equal co-chairs with double-key authorization and no casting vote for budgets, protocol changes, site findings and sanctions. Deadlock procedures define automatic partial suspension after a fixed period, but the age threshold for automatic impaired-confidence status must itself be double-key approved and can become a target for political leverage. If one country delays approving an age threshold, disputes cannot escalate, leaving unresolved findings unresolved indefinitely.

Impact: A single unresolved discrepancy or suspended function can paralyze the ledger and adjudication for weeks. Estimated 3–5 unresolved-discrepancy-age deadlocks in a 90-day test if thresholds are disputed. Each stall delays the final Go/Modify/Stop decision by 1–2 weeks per instance. If automatic suspension triggers are weak or delayed, the mission can drift into a state of unmanaged contradiction where both sides publish conflicting findings.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: High

Action: Pre-approve the age threshold for automatic impaired-confidence status as an entry condition, not a negotiated item within Phase One. Set thresholds separately for different discrepancy types (e.g., 14 days for equipment-identity disputes, 21 days for exit-disposition conflicts) and embed them in the bilateral instrument before Phase One begins. Define escalation: at 75% of threshold, trigger a mandatory senior technical review; at 100%, automatic partial suspension and public ledger annotation. Appoint an independent timekeeper with access to the bilateral clock and mandatory weekly dashboard reporting on unresolved discrepancy age to force visibility and attention.

Risk 3 - Evidence & Verification

The plan specifies no single evidence source is decisive, but the confidential rotating evidence-weighting rule (which evidence categories must be corroborated) is set by accountable specialists and validated only post-hoc against blind-exercise outcomes. If the rule is too strict, false positives and unverifiable-equipment counts surge, overloading adjudication. If too loose, gaming becomes possible and one country can argue the other gamed the rule-setting process.

Impact: Estimated 15–25% false-positive rate if contradiction-based scoring is applied; estimated 5–10% if corroboration-based scoring is applied (proposed threshold TBD). Each unverifiable-equipment finding triggers a formal discrepancy, pushing adjudication load to unsustainable levels if the inspectorate capacity is 10–15 cases per month. Disputes over rule validity can become contested findings themselves, expanding the discrepancy caseload by 20–30%.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: High

Action: Publish the confidential evidence-weighting rule in versioned escrow before the first challenge exercise, jointly approved by both sides' accountable specialists and locked for the duration of Phase One. Conduct a pilot validation exercise in Month 1.5 (2026-11-23) using historical equipment-change records from participating sites, applying the rule to past events and comparing the identity-confidence outputs against known ground truth to calibrate false-positive and false-negative rates. Adjust the rule only if pilot results show material miscalibration (>20% false-positive deviation from target). Maintain an independent evidence-audit log showing which rule-version was applied to each finding, so no finding can be retroactively reclassified.

Risk 4 - Technical & Integration

The replicated tamper-evident ledger requires synchronized copies in both countries with bounded latency and signed-digest exchange. If synchronization latency exceeds the agreed bound, divergence can accumulate before detection. If a ledger divergence occurs (e.g., a discrepancy is recorded in one copy but not the other), resolving it requires double-key agreement on the truth, which is itself a deadlock scenario. Key-custody disputes (a contested or lost signing key) can block ledger entries for hours to days.

Impact: Estimated 10–15 ledger-divergence incidents in 90 days if synchronization latency is 4+ hours and event volume is 5–10 per day per site. Each divergence can stall evidence validity for 2–7 days pending double-key resolution. A lost or contested signing key can block the ledger entirely for 8–24 hours while key-recovery procedures run, creating an observation blackout during which equipment changes are not recorded, undermining the monitored-boundary claim.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: Medium

Action: Set synchronization latency bound at 1 hour for routine events, with escalation triggers at 30 minutes to alert both sides of impending delay. Implement a secondary asynchronous audit trail for events that cannot be synchronized within the bound, recording them locally and re-syncing when connectivity is restored, with a flag in the ledger marking the delayed sync. Pre-stage key-recovery ceremonies at Month 1.5 (2026-11-23) and Month 5 (mid-Phase-One) with full rehearsal, not just planning. Assign one key-custody officer per country with deputy backup, and require both to be present at all key-rotation ceremonies. In case of key loss, fall back to a signed attestation by both countries that the lost key is revoked and a new one generated, recorded in the ledger as an event, rather than trying to recover the lost key.

Risk 5 - Operational & Personnel

The plan requires full-time mirrored national inspectorates (estimated 150–200+ personnel across multiple sites in shifts) working 24/7, with no single-person critical functions and mandatory leave coverage. Staffing this scale is operationally unprecedented for a verification regime. High turnover or absences due to illness, family emergency or security incidents can create coverage gaps where equipment changes are unobserved. Training and deployment of 300+ personnel on both sides takes 2–3 months, compressed into Months 1–3 (2026-11-08 to 2027-01-08), which overlaps with entry-condition finalization.

Impact: Estimated 10–15% personnel availability shortfall in Month 3 (2027-01-08) (start of Phase One) due to incomplete training or vetting. A single week of inadequate shift coverage during unreported-arrival or substitution tests can miss evidence that would have been detected, degrading the blind-exercise credibility. Burnout from 24/7 rotations in a high-stress, low-trust environment can cause quality-of-life attrition, cascading into coverage gaps in Months 6–8 (2027-04-08 to 2027-06-08). Estimated 5–8% monthly turnover rate mid-test if morale fails.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: Medium

Action: Begin inspector recruitment and vetting at Month -3 (before Phase One entry conditions are finalized), not at Month 0 (2026-10-08), so that by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23) the full complement is trained and ready for rapid deployment. Establish a dedicated training academy for bilateral exercises, with joint US–China curriculum starting at Month -1. Create a 20% personnel surge buffer (30–40 additional inspectors per country on standby) to cover leave, illness and emergency rotations without reducing shift coverage. Implement a 6-month rotation schedule with 4 months on-site and 2 months off-site, staggered so at least 80% of each shift's strength is always present. Tie inspector retention bonuses to full-year commitment through Phase One conclusion; budget an estimated 2–3% additional cost within the USD 750 million personnel envelope to cover retention incentives.

Risk 6 - Security & Counterintelligence

Inspectors from each country are deployed to the other country's datacenters for extended periods, creating counterintelligence exposure. Both governments have incentive to use inspectors as intelligence collectors, and both have incentive to suspect the other of doing so. The Information Firewall Doctrine (compartmentalization, post-rotation debriefs, cooling-off periods) is designed to limit what each inspector can retain and communicate, but enforcement depends on trust and discipline. A single inspector breach—photographing network topology, recording conversations, or debriefing with their own government's intelligence services without official channels—can compromise the entire mechanism.

Impact: An inspector breach can collapse reciprocal confidence mid-test if the hosting country discovers evidence collection. Estimated 40–60% chance that at least one breach attempt occurs during a 90-day test with 300+ personnel deployed internationally. If either government concludes the other is conducting espionage through the inspectorate, withdrawal becomes politically likely, with estimated 30–40 day timeline to decision. If a breach becomes public, both governments face domestic political pressure to withdraw.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: High

Action: Establish a bilateral Counterintelligence Oversight Board (3 senior counterintelligence officers per side, reporting to co-chairs) with monthly classified meetings to monitor and adjudicate suspected breaches. Pre-deploy polygraph or equivalent security-vetting capability at the neutral facility (Geneva or Singapore) and conduct baseline and periodic security reviews of all deployed inspectors, with results held confidentially by the Oversight Board. Require all inspectors to sign legally binding statements (enforceable in their home country) that unauthorized collection or retention of sensitive information is a criminal violation. Implement secure on-site communication only (no personal phones, no external internet) for inspectors at datacenters, with monitored single-channel communication to their respective governments via the neutral facility. Establish a fast-track adjudication process for suspected breaches: 48-hour investigation, 72-hour recommendation to co-chairs, 7-day decision on remediation (redeployment, suspension, dismissal). Document all breaches in the ledger as governance events so neither government can claim the other acted in secret.

Risk 7 - Supply Chain & Vendor

Critical vendors (equipment manufacturers, maintenance providers, logistics companies, cloud-service operators) must agree to reporting, confidentiality, escort and evidence-preservation requirements. The plan anticipates vendor refusal and defines a fallback ladder: vendor-supervised testing, filtered evidence, accredited independent examiners, clean-room procedures, validated attestations. If a critical vendor refuses all rungs of the ladder, equipment is classed unverifiable and the site fails Phase One. A vendor refusal cascade—multiple vendors at a single site or across sites refusing participation—can render Phase One impossible.

Impact: Estimated 20–30% likelihood that at least one Tier-1 vendor (e.g., a major chip manufacturer or cloud-service operator) refuses full participation, citing IP protection or customer-confidentiality concerns. If a major vendor refuses, the fallback ladder is invoked, which consumes estimated 8–12 weeks to execute clean-room exams or attestation validations. If multiple vendors refuse, the schedule itself becomes unverifiable, and the site may fail the entry condition for 'sufficient vendor participation.' Loss of a major site reduces the test's credibility and increases pressure to rely on remaining sites, whose evidence base then faces scrutiny.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: High

Action: Conduct pre-Phase-One vendor engagement (Months -2 to 0) to secure written commitments from all Tier-1 vendors before the bilateral instrument is signed. Offer vendors a choice: participate in the Consortium and retain control over their own evidence package (sealed, accredited independent review), or agree to fallback testing and accept independent examiners' findings without veto. Publish a vendor-participation registry as an entry-condition milestone, so if a critical vendor withdraws, Phase One cannot start. Establish a Vendor Liaison Office (5 personnel per country) with authority to negotiate fallback procedures and to escalate to co-chairs if a vendor's refusal threatens to fail a site. Pre-stage one accredited independent examiner team per country and train them on clean-room procedures, cost-sharing between the two governments from the testing envelope (USD 500 million). If a vendor cannot be accommodated, document the reason in the ledger and classify affected equipment as unverifiable at entry; do not discover this mid-test.

Risk 8 - Exercise Design & Detection Credibility

Phase One success hinges on blind-challenge exercises proving detection capability for seven event types: unreported arrival, substituted equipment, inaccurate records, delayed access, disputed identity, vendor refusal, and reluctant operator. Each event type should be tested multiple times to generate a detection rate with stated uncertainty. With a 90-day test and discrete exercise windows (proposed: 2–3 exercises per month per site), the plan yields only 5–10 trials per event type across all sites. This sample is too small to support any statistical claim about false-negative rate; a single missed detection is a 10–20% detection-rate swing.

Impact: Estimated detection rate of 70–85% for planned-event types (unreported arrival, substitution) and 50–65% for unplanned types (vendor refusal, reluctant operator), with confidence intervals of ±15–20% at 95% CL due to thin sample size. If results fall in the 65–75% range, both Go and Stop are defensible, and the verdict defaults to Modify or becomes a political negotiation. If either country suspects the other gamed exercise design (e.g., allowed a reported arrival to pass as unreported), the entire exercise data becomes contested, and no verdict is possible.

Likelihood: High

Severity: High

Action: Pre-register all exercise scenarios, detection success criteria and scoring rubric before the first challenge. Establish an Independent Exercise Authority (mixed-nationality staff, 5–8 personnel, funded from the USD 500 million testing envelope) to design, schedule and score all exercises without input from co-chairs or participating inspectors until execution. Each country's red team may nominate challenge types (e.g., 'unreported arrival during night shift') but the authority alone decides whether to execute it and when. Conduct a pilot exercise in Month 2 (2026-12-08) (before Phase One clock starts) using a spare datacenter or test facility, running all seven event types once to validate detection procedures and scoring. Publish the pilot results and adjust the exercise protocol if material issues are found. During Phase One, schedule 3–4 exercises per month per site (9–12 per month total across small matched set, estimated 45–60 total exercises in 90 days), targeting 6–8 replicates per event type per site for defensible detection rates at ±10% confidence interval. Require independent video, witness and cryptographic attestation of each exercise to prevent later claims of staging or manipulation.

Risk 9 - Site Selection & Access Parity

The plan requires 'a small, matched set of declared datacenters' with reciprocal access and functional equivalence of staging, spare-inventory, maintenance and expansion areas. Matching sites across US and China is difficult: US hyperscale operators are commercial entities with independent security policies, while Chinese sites are likely state-operated with different authority structures. A US operator may deny certain areas access on commercial grounds, while a Chinese site may deny access for national-security reasons. Mismatched access creates an asymmetry that either side can cite to discount the other's findings.

Impact: Estimated 40–50% likelihood that the 'matched set' includes at least one pair with asymmetric access (e.g., US site grants 24/7 unrestricted staging-area access while Chinese site restricts it to business hours or designated areas). If asymmetry is discovered during Phase One, it becomes a contested finding and invalidates the reciprocal-access parity claim. Asymmetric exercise results cannot be compared, and the final verdict is compromised. Site-selection deadlock can delay entry conditions by 2–3 months if the sides cannot agree on equivalence rationale.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: High

Action: Conduct a pre-Phase-One reciprocal-access audit (Months -1 to 0) at candidate sites, with each country's technical team visiting the counterpart's proposed site and documenting access scope, timing and facility layouts in sealed reports. Require both co-chairs to approve the matched pairs based on the audit, with explicit certification that each pair meets 'functional equivalence' criteria (e.g., staging area ≥500 sq m, 24-hour accessible, equipment lift capacity ≥50 tons, etc.). Publish the audit results and any veto rationale so no matched pair is approved in secret. If access asymmetry cannot be reconciled (e.g., one side insists on restricted-hour access), do not include that pair in Phase One; reduce the matched set rather than accept asymmetry. Model staffing and exercise design around the confirmed matched set, not the candidate list, so contingency is realistic.

Risk 10 - Financial & Budgeting

The USD 5 billion budget is split into seven fixed envelopes (ledger and attestation USD 1.25B, site prep USD 1B, personnel USD 750M, facilities USD 750M, testing USD 500M, legal and audit USD 250M, contingency USD 500M). Every expense must map to an envelope. If a major cost overrun occurs (e.g., site preparation proves more expensive than estimated, or neutral-facility construction takes 6 months instead of 3), it consumes contingency. Contingency is also needed for surge capacity and schedule delays. A contingency depletion >20% by Month 3 (2027-01-08) signals a budget crisis by Month 6 (2027-04-08).

Impact: Estimated 30–40% contingency depletion by Month 3 (2027-01-08) due to entry-condition delays and accelerated personnel deployment. If contingency reaches 50% before Month 6 (2027-04-08), the program must either reduce scope (fewer sites, shorter test window, smaller inspectorate) or request supplemental appropriations. Requesting supplemental funds from both governments introduces a veto point: either government can condition supplements on concessions, creating political leverage. A deadlock on supplemental funding can stall operations for 2–4 weeks per incident.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: Medium

Action: Establish a Joint Budget Authority (one finance officer per country) with monthly envelope reconciliation and a weekly contingency-burn dashboard visible to both co-chairs. Set escalation triggers: contingency >30% → co-chair briefing; >50% → mandatory scope-reduction planning; >75% → formal joint budget review with external audit. Front-load large fixed costs (neutral-facility setup, personnel recruitment, equipment procurement) into Months -1 to 1 so contingency is spent early and remaining contingency can cover Phase-One operations and surge. Reserve 20% of each envelope for over-runs (e.g., if personnel envelope is USD 750M, budget personnel at USD 600M and reserve USD 150M for surge and overages). Conduct a full actuals-vs-budget audit at Month 3 (2027-01-08) (entry-condition point) and at Month 6 (mid-Phase-One) with independent auditor sign-off visible to both governments, so neither can claim misuse or surprise.

Risk 11 - Political & Strategic Withdrawal

Either government can withdraw from the Consortium for reasons unrelated to Phase One outcomes: domestic political change, escalation in US–China relations, public disclosure of a security incident, or discovery of intelligence activity. A withdrawal before Phase One concludes invalidates the proof-of-concept and leaves both sides with sunk costs (5–10 months of effort, USD 1–2 billion spent) but no credible verdict. Domestic political pressure—from legislators, public opinion or media—can build rapidly if the public perceives the Consortium as a surrender of sovereignty, capitulation to the adversary, or failure to protect national IP.

Impact: Estimated 20–30% probability of political withdrawal by either government during Months 1–6 (2026-11-08 to 2027-04-08). Early withdrawal (Month 1–2 = 2026-11-08 to 2026-12-08, entry-condition phase) costs estimated USD 200–400 million in sunk setup. Late withdrawal (Month 6–9, mid-to-late Phase One) costs USD 800M–1.2B and occurs after significant operational data is collected but before a defensible final verdict. A public disclosure of a counterintelligence incident, security breach or IP leak during Phase One can trigger withdrawal within days, leaving the Consortium in an operational blackout state.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: High

Action: Secure written commitments from both governments at the outset that Phase One will run for the full 90 days unless a specific Stop condition (asymmetric access, material unverifiable equipment, government shielding, ledger divergence without resolution, funding withholding) is triggered. Publish a Stop condition checklist that both co-chairs agree to use, removing subjective reasons for withdrawal and making any withdrawal a formal invocation of Stop, not a political exit. Establish a public communication strategy (coordinated statements, regular briefings to legislatures, published KPI dashboards) that normalizes the Consortium and pre-empts criticism. Brief both countries' legislatures monthly on progress (declassified summary) so withdrawal surprises are minimized. If a domestic political event threatens withdrawal, activate an emergency co-chair summit within 5 days to address concerns before a formal withdrawal notice is issued.

Risk 12 - Disclosure & Information Barriers

The Counterpart Evidence Disclosure Tiers define what each national team sees of the other's findings and underlying evidence. Narrow tiers (identifiers only) protect IP but force disputes into adjudication. Wide tiers (full detail in secure reading rooms) allow verification but risk exposure of topology, security architecture and unrelated infrastructure. The plan requires 'bounded inspection zones and filtered evidence' but does not specify how filtering is certified independent. If one country's inspectors believe the other country is hiding evidence behind a filter, the entire evidence basis becomes contested, and adjudication becomes a dispute over what was filtered out, not what was found.

Impact: Estimated 10–15 disclosure disputes in 90 days if tiered access is narrow and one side claims key evidence is being withheld. Each dispute requires dual investigation (inspectors from both sides querying the filter logic) and can delay adjudication by 2–3 weeks. If filtering certification is done by the host side only, the counterpart has no way to verify it, and disputes multiply. Wide-tier disclosure risks leaking network topology or security architecture, which can expose vulnerabilities or competitive advantage.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: Medium

Action: Establish a pre-Phase-One filter-design workshop (Month 1 = 2026-11-08) where both sides' inspectors, operators and legal advisors jointly design the evidence filters that will apply to disclosure. Document the filtering logic explicitly (e.g., 'IP addresses are hashed, network paths are redacted, maintenance-provider identities are blinded') and certify that the filter preserves all event-relevant detail. Appoint an independent filter auditor (a qualified security or IT specialist from a third country or international organization) who validates the filters at Month 1.5 (2026-11-23) and spot-checks compliance monthly. Require the auditor to publish an annual filter-compliance report (declassified summary) confirming that filters are being applied consistently and no event-relevant data is being withheld. For disputes, implement a challenge procedure: if the counterpart believes a filter is hiding evidence, they can request raw-evidence access under escort, with a log entry and dual certification. This procedure adds 3–5 days to adjudication but preserves trust in the filtering process.

Risk 13 - Adjudication & Discrepancy Resolution

The plan identifies discrepancies (equipment-identity conflicts, unresolved departures, contested findings) but does not specify how they are adjudicated or who decides. If both co-chairs cannot agree on a discrepancy's resolution (e.g., whether a piece of equipment is the declared model or a substituted one), the case remains open and the discrepancy ages. Automatic impaired-confidence status triggers if the case exceeds an age threshold, but that status is itself a contested decision if the co-chairs disagree on whether the age threshold was reached or the underlying finding was valid.

Impact: Estimated 20–30 unresolved discrepancies accumulated by Month 6 (2027-04-08) if adjudication lacks a clear tie-breaker procedure. Each unresolved case stalls the ledger until it is resolved, retroactively classified or escalated to formal dispute. At the 90-day Phase One conclusion, outstanding discrepancies complicate the Go/Modify/Stop verdict: Go requires <5 material unresolved cases (estimated threshold, TBD), so 6–8 open cases can force a Modify or Stop decision regardless of exercise outcomes.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: Medium

Action: Establish a formal Adjudication Panel (3 senior technical specialists per country, 6 total) with binding authority over discrepancy classification only (not outcomes, sanctions or suspensions). The Panel is convened by co-chairs when a discrepancy cannot be resolved by inspectors within 10 days. Panel authority is limited to: (1) deciding which evidence category is most probative; (2) classifying the discrepancy as 'materiel' (affects Go/Modify/Stop verdict) or 'process' (administrative); (3) recommending a retry of the investigation if evidence gaps remain. Panel decisions are non-binding on the co-chairs but are published to both sides and logged in the ledger, so co-chairs must overturn the Panel's recommendation explicitly (a double-key veto). This creates pressure to accept technical expertise while preserving co-chair authority. Set a target: Panel convenes within 10 days of case opening, renders a recommendation within 5 days, and co-chairs decide within 3 days. Any case exceeding 28 days total becomes an automatic impaired-confidence flag, visible in the KPI dashboard.

Risk 14 - Statistics & Verdict Credibility

The final Go/Modify/Stop verdict is based on exercise detection rates, false positives and negatives, unverifiable-equipment count, and parity metrics. The plan requires thresholds to be marked 'provisional' or 'TBD' and validated after pilot data, but it provides no formula for converting binary outcomes (detected/missed, verified/unverifiable) into a final verdict. If detection rates are 75% (borderline), false positives are 8% (acceptable) and unverifiable equipment is 3% (low), the verdict could be Go, Modify or Stop depending on how the scorecard weights these factors.

Impact: Estimated 40–60% likelihood that final-verdict thresholds are ambiguous or disputed by one or both governments. If results fall in the ambiguous range (detection 65–80%, false positives 5–12%, unverifiable 2–5%), the verdict can be justified as Go, Modify or Stop using different weighting schemes. This creates a negotiation space where political interests may influence the technical verdict. A Modify verdict is the likely default if outcomes are ambiguous, but it commits both countries to Phase Two (a longer, larger test) without clarity on what Phase Two should achieve.

Likelihood: High

Severity: Medium

Action: Pre-register verdict thresholds before the first Phase One exercise, published in a joint bilateral memorandum locked by both co-chairs. Thresholds must include: (1) minimum detection rate per event type (proposed: ≥70% for planned events, ≥50% for unplanned); (2) maximum false-positive rate (proposed: ≤10%); (3) maximum unverifiable-equipment share (proposed: ≤5%); (4) minimum reciprocal-access parity score (proposed: ≥85%); (5) maximum unresolved-discrepancy age at Phase One conclusion (proposed: ≤21 days). Outcomes ≥80% of Go thresholds → Go. Outcomes 50–80% → Modify. Outcomes <50% → Stop. Mark all thresholds 'provisional until validated' and conduct the pilot exercise (Month 2 = 2026-12-08) to test whether thresholds are calibrated realistically. Adjust only if pilot data shows material miscalibration (>30% deviation from expected range), and publish the adjustment justification. At Phase One conclusion (Month 9 = 2027-07-08), score results against the locked thresholds with an independent auditor sign-off, removing any ambiguity about the verdict logic.

Risk 15 - Asymmetric Operator Compliance & Shielding

US hyperscale operators are commercial entities with competitive incentives and contractual customer relationships. Chinese frontier-computing sites are likely state-operated with direct government authority. A US operator can cite customer confidentiality or competitive harm to resist Consortium access, while a Chinese site cannot resist but can obscure or delay access through bureaucratic friction. Asymmetric compliance—one side's operators readily opening staging areas and staging substitution tests, the other side's operators dragging out authorization—undermines the reciprocal-access parity claim and gives one side a detection advantage.

Impact: Estimated 20–30% likelihood of asymmetric operator resistance. If a US operator refuses to open a maintenance area without 72-hour notice (vs. immediate access at the Chinese site), detection of unreported substitution during maintenance is impossible at that site. Over a 90-day test, this translates to a 10–15% detection-rate gap between the matched pair, which becomes contested evidence that one country is shielding an operator. A detection-rate gap >10% per matched pair is a potential Stop condition, so asymmetric compliance can trigger Phase One failure.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: High

Action: At the entry-condition stage (Months 0–2 = 2026-10-08 to 2026-12-08), conduct joint operator-compliance workshops at each participating site, with both co-chairs' representatives, inspectorate leaders and operator executives present. Establish baseline expectations: (1) immediate access to staging areas (within 4 hours of request); (2) cooperative scheduling of exercise windows (48-hour advance notice required, unless testing unreported-arrival scenarios); (3) staff availability for questions during and after exercises; (4) confidentiality agreements for sensitive equipment specs. Require written commitments from each operator, with signatures from corporate executives and government-side legal counsel. At Month 2 (2026-12-08), test compliance with a dry-run exercise at each site using non-critical equipment. If an operator refuses baseline access (e.g., insists on 72-hour notice), do not include that site in Phase One; substitute a more-cooperative site from the candidate pool. If both countries' operators resist equally (symmetric resistance), model the impact on exercise design and adjust exercise schedules to work within the resistance (e.g., conduct substitution tests during scheduled maintenance windows rather than unreported arrivals). Asymmetric resistance is the Stop trigger; do not proceed if one side's operators are demonstrably more restrictive.

Risk 16 - Schedule Amendments & Coverage Drift

The confidential, versioned technical schedule of covered equipment must remain technology-neutral and not become a product list. Hardware generations, form factors and performance metrics change during Phase One (e.g., new GPU models arrive, older ones are deprecated). The schedule must be updated to stay current, but each amendment is a double-key decision and a source of scope dispute. If the schedule drifts toward older, more easily verifiable equipment, the test becomes less relevant to current frontier computing. If it drifts toward newer, harder-to-verify equipment, unverifiable-equipment counts surge.

Impact: Estimated 5–10 schedule-amendment disputes in 90 days if amendments are handled ad-hoc. Each dispute consumes 1–2 weeks of co-chair negotiation. If amendments are frozen (no mid-test changes), the schedule becomes obsolete by Month 6 (2027-04-08), new frontier equipment is unverifiable by default, and results become less credible. If amendments are frequent, exercise results become non-comparable across versions, and final verdicts cannot aggregate data across the test window.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: Low

Action: Establish a Covered-Equipment Schedule Review Cadence before Phase One begins: fixed update points at Months 3, 6 and 9 (2027-01-08, 2027-04-08, 2027-07-08) (entry, mid-Phase-One, exit), with no amendments between these points. Each update is a double-key decision but is scheduled and anticipated, not ad-hoc. During each review, both sides' accountable specialists propose amendments based on equipment arrivals and departures observed in the prior period, with evidence attached (e.g., equipment specs, form-factor changes). Amendments become effective only for events recorded after the effective date, and prior events remain classified under the prior schedule version, preserving comparability. Document the version history in the ledger so any finding can be traced to the schedule version in effect when it was recorded. If a major mid-test technology shift makes the current schedule manifestly obsolete (e.g., a new frontier-relevant processor class arrives that is not covered), convene an emergency review at Month 4.5 (2027-02-23), with both sides' agreement, and amend once rather than waiting for Month 6 (2027-04-08).

Risk 17 - Neutral Facility Establishment & Staffing

Phase One requires a neutral secure facility (proposed: Geneva or Singapore) to host bilateral governance, co-chair workspace, secure reading rooms, ledger hosting, key custody and inspector debriefing. Establishing and securing this facility by Month 0 (2026-10-08) (start of entry conditions) is a hard constraint. Host-country delays, security certification challenges or construction overruns can push facility readiness to Month 2–3 (2026-12-08 to 2027-01-08), compressing the entry-condition window. Staffing the facility requires bilingual, security-cleared personnel from both countries, plus independent facility staff (host country), creating complex authority structures.

Impact: Estimated 30–40% likelihood of 4–8 week delay in neutral-facility readiness if construction, security certification or staffing leads the critical path. A delayed facility stalls co-chair coordination, forces meetings via video conference (less effective for double-key decisions), and delays key-custody ceremonies, which must occur in person in a certified secure space. Estimated 2–3 week delay per missed key ceremony. If the facility is not ready by Month 2 (2026-12-08), entry conditions can slip by 4–8 weeks, pushing Phase One start to Month 4 (2027-02-08) or later.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: Medium

Action: Pre-identify a neutral-facility site by Month -3 and secure host-country commitment for fast-track permitting and construction. Baseline facility needs: (1) 1,000+ sq m of secure space including co-chair boardroom, secure reading room with multi-workstation evidence-review capability, 24/7 staffed ledger-hosting center with redundant power and network; (2) physical security meeting or exceeding IAEA or OPCW standards; (3) bilingual staff (English and Mandarin) with security clearances from both countries or pre-clearance procedures; (4) network isolation from both countries' national networks, with monitored bilateral data-exchange only. Start facility build-out at Month -2 with a pre-positioned project manager from each country, independent facility director (host-country national, jointly approved) and general contractor with international experience in secure facilities. Conduct a security dry-run at Month 0 (2026-10-08) and a full operational test at Month 1.5 (2026-11-23) (entry-condition entry). Identify backup facilities (secondary Geneva location, backup Singapore site) so if primary is delayed >4 weeks, migration occurs to backup without losing time.

Risk 18 - Compliance & Audit Deficiency

The plan requires independent auditing against the seven-envelope budget map and KPI dashboard verification. Auditors must be bilingual or trilingual, security-cleared, and capable of reviewing both classified evidence (ledger contents, counterintelligence matters) and sensitive financial documents (operator compensation, vendor contracts). Finding or training sufficient independent auditors with the right clearances is a challenge. If auditors lack credibility with one side, their findings will be contested, undermining the audit function.

Impact: Estimated 8–12 week delay in finding independent auditors and securing their clearances by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23). If audit starts late, the first quarterly reconciliation (Month 3 = 2027-01-08) is compressed, and discrepancies found then become rushed adjudications. A full-year international audit of a USD 5 billion program requires estimated 4–6 FTE auditors with extensive experience; market availability is uncertain. An audit that finds 2–5% envelope discrepancies (normal for large programs) will trigger disputes if either government suspects the other misdirected funds. Contested audits delay tranche releases and feed political distrust.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: Low

Action: Identify independent auditors at Month -2 and secure bilateral pre-approval by Month -1. Auditors should be from a third country or international organization (e.g., KPMG, PwC with international practices, or an UN body with audit experience). Require auditors to sign a charter that commits them to publish unclassified summaries of audit findings monthly, with both co-chairs seeing classified full reports simultaneously to prevent one side claiming a secret audit advantage. Establish audit scope: envelope mapping (100% sampling), invoices and supporting docs (10% random sample), personnel roster and leave records (spot checks), ledger event sampling (5% of events) for accuracy. Conduct a financial-audit dry-run at Month 1 (2026-11-08) using Months -1 and 0 spending, so audit procedures are validated before Phase One operations begin. Set audit timeline: invoices due by 10th of following month, audit review by 20th, findings published by 25th, disputes closed by end of month. This monthly cadence catches discrepancies early.

Risk 19 - Interdependencies & Cascading Failures

The plan has multiple critical interdependencies: entry conditions gate the 90-day Phase One clock; exercise outcomes inform the verdict thresholds and final Go/Modify/Stop decision; ledger integrity depends on key custody and synchronization; equipment-identity confidence depends on evidence weighting and disclosure tiers; vendor refusal fallback depends on independent-examiner availability; and adjudication depends on deadlock procedures. A failure in any one area cascades: a delayed entry condition delays Phase One, compressing the test window and producing thin statistical data; a key-custody incident stalls the ledger; a vendor-refusal cascade stalls site preparation; unresolved discrepancies age and trigger automatic suspension. The program has few redundancies, so cascades can quickly paralyze it.

Impact: Estimated 30–50% probability of at least one significant cascade incident (delay in entry conditions + delayed Phase One start + thin detection statistics, or ledger divergence + key-custody incident + stalled adjudication, or vendor-refusal cascade + site-selection failure + schedule withdrawal) by Month 6 (2027-04-08). Each cascade adds 2–4 weeks to the timeline and consumes 5–10% of contingency budget. If cascades are not caught and resolved early, they compound, potentially making Phase One operationally infeasible by Month 9 (2027-07-08).

Likelihood: High

Severity: Medium

Action: Establish a Program Risk Dashboard (updated weekly by Month 0–3 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-01-08, bi-weekly Month 4–9 = 2027-02-08 to 2027-07-08) tracking leading indicators of cascade risk: (1) entry-condition milestone burn-down (% complete vs. target); (2) key-custody ceremony readiness (personnel cleared, facility ready, schedules locked); (3) vendor-refusal count and fallback-method availability; (4) discrepancy-age distribution (% open >14 days, >21 days, >28 days); (5) ledger-divergence incidents (count and resolution time); (6) contingency-burn rate (% spent vs. elapsed time); (7) inspectorate-staffing fill rate (% deployed vs. planned). Escalation rules: any indicator >2 std devs from target triggers a co-chair alert within 48 hours; three or more alerts simultaneously activate an emergency joint review and corrective-action plan. Assign a dedicated Program Risk Officer (one per country, co-reporting to co-chairs) with authority to call emergency meetings and to recommend scope reductions if cascades appear irreversible. This redundant oversight catches early-stage cascades before they paralyze operations.

Risk summary

The Consortium is an unprecedented bilateral US–China arms-control-style verification mechanism with extreme complexity, high political risk and thin operational data. Phase One is a 90-day test of frontier-computing equipment change verification at declared sites, with a USD 5 billion budget and mirrored national inspectorates. Critical risks center on: (1) entry-condition deadlock before operations begin, blocking the 90-day clock; (2) asymmetric access, operator shielding or evidence withholding that undermines reciprocal credibility; (3) thin detection statistics (few events per exercise type in 90 days) that make final Go/Modify/Stop verdicts undefendable; (4) ledger divergence or key-custody disputes that create unresolvable evidence conflicts; and (5) IP exposure or production disruption that alienates operators and governments mid-test. The design mitigates these through rotating evidence rules, independent exercise scoring, partial suspension and provisional thresholds, but governance deadlock, gaming of evidence rules, vendor refusal cascades and political withdrawal remain high-impact risks. Success depends on strict entry-condition enforcement, reciprocal transparency in exercises and adjudication, and honest statistical reporting that foregrounds limits and provisional status.

Make Assumptions

Question 1 - Within the USD 5 billion budget (user constraint), how will contingency spending be prioritized if entry-condition delays (signed instrument, domestic authority, site selection, inspector approval, vendor participation, covered-equipment schedule) consume estimated 5–10% (USD 250–500M) of contingency before Phase One operations begin?

Assumptions: Assumption: Entry-condition completion targets Month 3 (2027-01-08), with 2–4 week slippage per gate. If total entry-condition delay exceeds 8 weeks, contingency depletion reaches 15–20% by Month 4 (2027-02-08), leaving inadequate reserve for Phase-One surge (personnel illness, ledger recovery, vendor-fallback activations). Budget envelope mapping assumes all operator compensation is charged to each government's own contribution (USD 2.5B), leaving USD 5B for shared expenses (ledger, facilities, personnel, testing, legal, contingency). If entry-condition costs overrun within a single envelope (e.g., neutral-facility construction exceeds site-prep allocation), trade-off rules must pre-exist to avoid mid-test budget disputes.

Assessments: Title: Funding & Budget Risk Mitigation Description: Contingency allocation strategy under entry-condition delay scenarios and mid-Phase-One cost pressures. Details: Recommended action: Front-load all fixed-cost envelopes (neutral facility, key custody ceremonies, auditor clearances, personnel recruitment) into Months -2 to 1, consuming 40% of contingency early to confirm these one-time expenses. This creates visibility on actual costs vs. estimates by Month 1 (2026-11-08) and allows corrective-action planning before Phase One begins. Reserve 60% contingency for Phase-One surge (estimated 10–15 personnel per-country deployments, accredited independent-examiner mobilization, ledger-recovery procedures). Establish envelope trade-off hierarchy: contingency covers overages; any envelope exceeding 110% of plan triggers co-chair review; >120% requires supplemental appropriations (a stop-work veto point). Monthly envelope reconciliation (independent auditor) against locked USD 5B allocation, with unclassified monthly summaries preventing either government from claiming financial surprise.

Question 2 - What is the operational definition of 'matched set of declared datacenters' and how will reciprocal-access parity be measured and validated as an entry condition?

Assumptions: Assumption: 'Small, matched set' is estimated at 2–4 paired sites (4–8 total facilities), one per country per pair. 'Matched' is defined by functional equivalence of staging, spare-inventory, maintenance and expansion areas (proposed: staging ≥500 sq m, 24-hour accessible, equipment lift capacity ≥50 tons, maintenance schedule ≥2 events per month per site). 'Reciprocal access' means each country's inspectors have equivalent timing and area scope (e.g., both countries' inspectors get immediate 4-hour access to staging areas, or both are restricted to business-hours access). Parity is validated by pre-Phase-One audit (Months -1 to 0): each side's technical team visits the counterpart's proposed sites, documents access constraints, certifies functional equivalence, and both co-chairs approve matched pairs. Asymmetric access at entry is a gate failure: sites with mismatched access (e.g., one site 24-hour staging, counterpart business-hours only) are excluded, not included with a footnote.

Assessments: Title: Timeline & Milestones Entry-Condition Validation Description: Site-selection and reciprocal-access parity audit process and schedule. Details: Critical path: site nominations (Month 0.5 = 2026-10-23), pre-Phase-One reciprocal-access audit (Months -1 to 0, compressed into Month 0 = 2026-10-08 if timeline pressures), audit reports (Month 0.5 = 2026-10-23), co-chair reconciliation of mismatched sites (Month 1 = 2026-11-08), final matched-pair approval (Month 1.5 = 2026-11-23). If reciprocal-access audit reveals >1 asymmetric pair, site-selection deadlock likely (2–4 week delay). Recommend pre-identifying 4–6 candidate sites per country (Month -2) and running audit in parallel with diplomatic negotiations to accelerate approval. Milestone success metric: matched-pair approval locked by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23), with explicit co-chair certification of functional equivalence and access parity. This gate completion is mandatory for entry-condition fulfilment; Phase One clock cannot start without it.

Question 3 - How will the mirrored national inspectorates (estimated 150–200+ personnel per country across multiple sites, 24/7 shifts) be recruited, vetted, trained and deployed within the Months -1 to 3 window, and what leave-coverage and surge-capacity ratios are planned?

Assumptions: Assumption: Inspector recruitment begins Month -3 (before Phase One entry conditions finalize), with vetting and security clearances by Month -1. Training academy starts Month -1 with joint US–China curriculum (2–3 weeks). Full deployment target is Month 2.5 (2026-12-23). Minimum staffing model: 4–6 inspectors per site per shift × 3 shifts × 2–4 sites × 2 countries = 96–144 on-site at any time, plus 20% surge buffer (19–29 additional), plus 30% leave and illness coverage (estimated 29–43 additional), totaling 144–216 per country. Leave rotation is 4 months on-site, 2 months off-site, staggered across cohorts. Surge buffer (20% = 30–40 inspectors per country) is on standby for emergency rotations, extended exercises or illness cascades. Single-person critical functions are forbidden; every duty (shift lead, key custody, ledger monitoring) has a minimum of 2 assigned personnel with overlapping shifts.

Assessments: Title: Resources & Personnel Deployment Description: Full-time inspectorate staffing model, training timeline and coverage sustainability. Details: Critical risk: 10–15% personnel availability shortfall in Month 3 (2027-01-08) due to incomplete training or vetting. Mitigation: (1) Concurrent recruitment-vetting-training tracks (vetting begins Month -3 while recruitment is ongoing; training starts Month -1 with first cohorts while later cohorts are vetting); (2) Pilot training exercise Month 1 (2026-11-08) using historical datacenter records to validate training efficacy and identify shortfalls; (3) Retention bonuses (estimated 2–3% additional cost within USD 750M personnel envelope) for 12-month commitment through Phase One conclusion. Coverage model: each 24/7 site requires minimum 6 inspectors per shift (2 countries × 3 inspectors each), × 3 shifts, × 2–4 sites = 36–72 baseline; 20% surge = 7–14 additional; 30% leave = 11–22 additional; total = 54–108 per country baseline for small matched set. Estimated monthly personnel cost (fully loaded, with surge and leave): USD 5–8M per country (total USD 10–16M/month), consuming ~USD 120–192M over 90 days (Phase One only), within USD 750M envelope allocated for personnel.

Question 4 - How will the double-key governance structure (equal co-chairs, no casting vote, deadlock and automatic-suspension procedures) handle a deadlock over a critical decision (e.g., site-eligibility finding, equipment-identity classification, sanctions) that occurs during Phase One operations?

Assumptions: Assumption: Deadlock procedures are pre-approved as entry conditions and locked in the bilateral instrument. Proposed deadlock resolution: automatic partial suspension after 14 days of impasse, affecting only the disputed function while unrelated verification continues. Automatic impaired-confidence status triggers at 21 days open for identity disputes, 28 days for exit dispositions. If the age threshold itself becomes disputed, a tertiary referee procedure applies: independent technical panel (3 specialists per side, 6 total) issues an advisory recommendation within 5 days; co-chairs have 3 days to accept or override (with published rationale). Overrides are logged as governance events. No casting vote exists; if co-chairs still deadlock after panel review, the case escalates to automatic partial suspension and public ledger annotation, removing the deadlock from co-chair discretion.

Assessments: Title: Governance & Regulations Deadlock Resolution Description: Equal co-chair decision-making framework without casting vote, automatic escalation and public transparency. Details: Deadlock risk is high (estimated 3–5 substantive deadlocks in 90 days across 2–4 sites with multiple discrepancy types). Each 14-day partial suspension removes one disputed function from operations (e.g., intake verification paused at one site, exit procedures paused, or equipment-identity adjudication paused) while continuous monitoring of other sites continues. This partial-suspension model preserves operational continuity and prevents brittle shutdowns; estimated impact is 2–3 weeks total Phase-One delay if all 5 deadlocks max the suspension period. Recommendation: pre-approve advisory-panel charter and independent-panel specialist roster as entry conditions, so convening is immediate. Age thresholds (14, 21, 28 days) are locked in bilateral memorandum before Phase One starts; disputes about threshold compliance are resolved by independent timekeeper (dedicated staff member from neutral facility, tracking bilateral clock). This removes the threshold itself from co-chair dispute. Public ledger annotation of every partial suspension creates political pressure for timely resolution and provides audit trail for the final verdict.

Question 5 - What is the protocol for live challenge exercises (unreported arrival, substituted equipment, inaccurate records, delayed access, disputed identity, vendor refusal, reluctant operator), and who will design, schedule, execute and score them to ensure independence and credibility to both governments?

Assumptions: Assumption: An independent Exercise Authority (mixed-nationality staff, 5–8 personnel, funded from USD 500M testing envelope) designs, schedules and scores all exercises without input from co-chairs or participating inspectors until execution. Each country's red team may nominate challenge types but cannot control selection or timing. Target exercise load: 3–4 exercises per month per site (9–12 total per month across 2–4 sites), aiming for 6–8 replicates per event type across all sites in 90 days (45–60 total exercises). Scoring is by independent video, witness and cryptographic attestation; no retroactive claims of staging or manipulation are credible. Events are run in staging, spare-inventory, maintenance or expansion areas, without interrupting active computation. A pilot exercise (Month 2 = 2026-12-08) tests all seven event types once at a test facility (not a production site) to validate detection procedures before Phase One.

Assessments: Title: Safety & Risk Management Exercise Credibility Description: Blind-challenge exercise design, independence and detection-rate validation under realistic operational conditions. Details: Exercise credibility is the sole basis for Phase One detection evidence; no continuous monitoring or other detection mechanisms exist. Risk of detection-rate ambiguity is high if sample size is <5 per event type (insufficient statistical power); 6–8 replicates per type per site over 90 days provides 50–80 total data points, supporting detection rates at ±10–15% confidence interval (95% CL). Each exercise is fully scripted before execution: scenario description, success criteria (detected within N hours), expected inspector actions, witness assignments. Scenario secrecy is essential: if inspectors know a challenge is scheduled, they adjust behavior, rendering detection rates unrepresentative. Pilot exercise (Month 2 = 2026-12-08) validates that exercises can run without production disruption; operators must grant access to staging/spare areas and tolerate instrumented equipment moves that replicate real scenarios. If operators refuse pilot-exercise cooperation, Phase One site selection fails. Recommended independence measure: Exercise Authority reports to neither co-chair; findings are published to both simultaneously, with any co-chair contest requiring a formal double-key challenge (rare, documented, logged). Exercises are the only direct detection evidence; verdict thresholds must be pre-registered and applied mechanically to results, not negotiated post-hoc.

Question 6 - How will environmental and workload protection (bounded inspection zones, filtered evidence, vendor-supervised testing fallbacks, clean-room procedures) be implemented so that inspectors cannot see or retain sensitive network topology, model weights, customer data or unrelated infrastructure?

Assumptions: Assumption: Inspector Information Firewall Doctrine compartmentalizes knowledge by role and site, with post-rotation debriefs and monitored cooling-off periods before reassignment. Implementation: sealed observation-and-report model where inspectors hold only filtered evidence packages; raw observations are retained in site custody for audited review only. Filters remove IP addresses (hashed), network paths (redacted), maintenance-provider identities (blinded), model weights, customer lists and security architecture details. Filters are co-designed by both sides' teams and audited by an independent certifier at Month 1.5 (2026-11-23) and monthly thereafter. Vendor refusal fallback ladder: vendor-supervised testing → filtered evidence → accredited independent examiners → clean-room procedures → validated attestations. If a vendor refuses all rungs, equipment is classed unverifiable. Access to raw evidence is granted only under dual escort in a joint secure reading room, with no copying or retention allowed.

Assessments: Title: Environmental Impact Data Protection Description: Evidence filtering, information barriers and vendor-refusal fallback procedures to protect sensitive technology and infrastructure. Details: Filtering adds latency (2–3 days per evidence package prepared and certified) but is essential to prevent IP leakage. Risk: if filters are too aggressive, event-relevant detail is removed, raising unverifiable-equipment counts by 10–15% and pushing adjudication load above inspectorate capacity. Mitigation: independent filter auditor validates that filters preserve all event-relevant data (timestamps, equipment identifiers, arrival/departure records, maintenance logs) while removing unrelated details. Filter disputes (counterpart claims key evidence is hidden) are resolved by dual-escort secure-room access, adding 3–5 days per dispute but preserving trust in filtering process. Vendor-refusal fallback ladder is stress-tested during pilot exercise (Month 2 = 2026-12-08): attempt vendor-supervised testing on a real piece of equipment and validate that evidence sufficiency can be demonstrated despite vendor restrictions. Estimated vendor-refusal incidents: 2–4 per 90 days (critical vendors refusing reporting or escort duties). Each fallback consumes 8–12 weeks (clean-room exam or independent-examiner validation), so multiple simultaneous vendor refusals can stall site preparation. Mitigation: pre-stage one accredited independent-examiner team per country by Month 0 (2026-10-08), funded from USD 500M testing envelope, so fallback procedures can be activated immediately if vendor refuses.

Question 7 - What are the success criteria and Stop conditions for Phase One, and how will the Go/Modify/Stop verdict be determined from exercise detection rates, false positives and negatives, unverifiable-equipment counts, and parity metrics when statistical power is thin (estimated 6–8 trials per event type)?

Assumptions: Assumption: Verdict thresholds are pre-registered before Phase One exercises begin and locked in bilateral memorandum. Provisional thresholds (marked 'TBD' with validation path): detection rate ≥70% for planned events (unreported arrival, substitution), ≥50% for unplanned (vendor refusal, reluctant operator); false-positive rate ≤10%; unverifiable-equipment share ≤5%; reciprocal-access parity ≥85%; maximum unresolved-discrepancy age ≤21 days at Phase One conclusion. Stop triggers: asymmetric inspector access, material unverifiable equipment (>5–10%), evidence ledger divergence without resolution, one country shielding an operator, or funding withholding. Outcomes: ≥80% of threshold targets → Go; 50–80% → Modify; <50% → Stop. Thin sample size (6–8 per event type) is acknowledged; confidence intervals are ±10–15% (95% CL), and thresholds are validated post-hoc against pilot-exercise data (Month 2 = 2026-12-08) before being locked.

Assessments: Title: Stakeholder Involvement Verdict Credibility Description: Pre-registered thresholds, statistical rigor acknowledgment and bilateral confidence-building in Phase One outcomes. Details: Thresholds must be locked before first Phase One exercise (Month 3 = 2027-01-08) to prevent post-hoc bargaining. Thin data (6–8 trials per type) is normal for a proof-of-concept test; stating this openly (provisional, confidence-interval ranges) is critical to bilateral credibility. Pilot-exercise validation (Month 2 = 2026-12-08) refines thresholds: if pilot detection rate for unreported arrival is 85% (vs. assumed 70%), threshold can be recalibrated to 75% as a more realistic target. Ambiguous outcome zones (65–80% detection rate) are handled by default Modify trigger, avoiding false Go claims on marginal results. Stop conditions are binary and objective (asymmetric access parity score <85%, unverifiable-equipment count >10% of declared items, ledger divergence unresolved >28 days, explicit government shielding of operator found in adjudication, either government withholds appropriated funding). Go requires <5 open discrepancies at conclusion and ≥70% detection rates across all event types. Verdict scoring is done by independent auditor with both co-chairs present; results are published unclassified (detection rates, thresholds met or missed, Go/Modify/Stop conclusion) so legislatures and public see objective outcome. This design frontiers the fact that Phase One covers only monitored changes at participating declared sites; it does not estimate total computing capacity, verify workloads, or prove absence of hidden facilities.

Question 8 - How will the replicated tamper-evident ledger with independently verifiable national copies be synchronized across the US–China border, with immediate local event recording, bounded counterpart synchronization and cryptographic attestation that resists undetected tampering?

Assumptions: Assumption: Ledger architecture is replicated: each country hosts its own national copy in a secure, audited facility (or in the neutral facility with dual-custody key material). Events are recorded locally at each site with timestamps and witness signatures, immediately entered into the national ledger copy (latency <1 hour). Synchronized digests (cryptographic hashes of recorded events) are exchanged between national copies every N hours (proposed bound: 1-hour interval for routine events, with escalation triggers at 30 minutes). Divergence (a discrepancy recorded in one copy but not the other) is detected by failed digest match and escalates to double-key co-chair review and adjudication. Key custody is dual-hold (each country holds non-reconstructable share of signing keys; both shares required for ledger entry signing or attestation validation) or mirrored (each country's independent signing hierarchy, cross-certified through audited exchange). A lost or contested signing key triggers key-recovery ceremonies, which stall ledger entries for 8–24 hours pending both countries' agreement on key revocation and new-key generation.

Assessments: Title: Operational Systems Ledger Architecture Description: Replicated tamper-evident ledger, event recording, synchronization bounds and key custody procedures. Details: Ledger integrity is foundational to all evidence and adjudication. Critical risks: (1) synchronization latency >1 hour creates windows for undetected local tampering (mitigation: escalation triggers at 30 min, redundant digest verification); (2) ledger divergence (missing event in one copy) requires 2–7 days to resolve through double-key adjudication (mitigation: automated divergence detection, immediate co-chair notification, pre-approved resolution procedures); (3) key loss or compromise blocks ledger entries for 8–24 hours (mitigation: key-recovery ceremonies at Months 1.5 and 5 = 2026-11-23, 2027-03-08 with full rehearsal, deputy key-custody officers, pre-approved key-revocation procedures). Estimated ledger-divergence incidents: 10–15 in 90 days if synchronization latency is 4+ hours and event volume is 5–10 per day per site. Each incident adds 2–7 days to evidence validity. Recommended synchronization architecture: (a) local recorder at each site (hardware module, tamper-sealed) stores events with cryptographic timestamp and witness signature; (b) periodic batch sync (hourly) of signed digests to both national copies via monitored network; (c) any digest mismatch triggers automatic dual-ledger audit and co-chair escalation within 4 hours; (d) secondary asynchronous audit trail for events exceeding the 1-hour sync bound, re-syncing when connectivity is restored, with ledger flag marking delayed sync. Key custody: pre-stage dual-key ceremonies at Months 1.5 and 5 (2026-11-23, 2027-03-08); both countries' key officers present in person; keys never transmitted digitally across border. Estimated ledger-hosting operational cost: USD 20–30M (within USD 1.25B ledger-and-attestation envelope).

Distill Assumptions

  • Phase One 90-day operational test begins only after entry-condition completion: bilateral instrument signature, appropriations, domestic authority, site selection, inspector approval, vendor participation, covered-equipment schedule.
  • Budget is USD 5 billion, split 50/50 (USD 2.5 billion per country); domestic operator compensation charged to each government's contribution.
  • Budget allocated to seven envelopes: USD 1.25B ledger/attestation/communications; USD 1B site preparation/operator compensation; USD 750M inspectors/personnel/training; USD 750M facilities/cybersecurity/counterintelligence; USD 500M testing/exercises/red teams; USD 250M legal/auditing; USD 500M contingency.
  • Governance uses equal national co-chairs and double-key authorization; no casting vote; deadlock, impaired-confidence and automatic-suspension procedures predefined.
  • Mission is verification of declared-equipment changes only; no estimates of total computing capacity, workload verification, model-weight inspection, or hidden-facility detection.
  • Matched set: estimated 2–4 paired sites (4–8 total); reciprocal-access parity validated as entry condition; asymmetric access excludes sites.
  • Mirrored inspectorates estimated at 144–216 personnel per country; 24/7 shifts; minimum 4–6 inspectors per site per shift; 20% surge buffer; 30% leave coverage.
  • Inspector recruitment begins Month -3; vetting and clearances Month -1; training Month -1 to Month 2 (2026-12-08); deployment target Month 2.5 (2026-12-23).
  • Inspector Information Firewall: compartmentalized by role and site, with post-rotation debriefs and cooling-off periods before reassignment.
  • Layered evidence rule is confidential, rotating, designed by accountable specialists from both sides; validated against blind-exercise outcomes.
  • No single evidence source is decisive; evidence includes attestation, physical inspection, customs/shipment records, identifiers, maintenance logs, infrastructure changes, witnessed movement.
  • Vendor Refusal Fallback Ladder: vendor-supervised testing → filtered evidence → accredited independent examiners → clean-room procedures → validated attestations.
  • Blind-challenge exercises cover seven event types: unreported arrival, substituted equipment, inaccurate records, delayed access, disputed identity, vendor refusal, reluctant operator.
  • Exercise Authority (mixed-nationality, independent, 5–8 personnel) designs, schedules, scores all exercises; each country's red team tests what it doubts most.
  • Pilot exercise Month 2 (2026-12-08) tests all seven event types once at non-production facility; full Phase One target is 6–8 replicates per event type (45–60 total exercises).
  • Verdict thresholds are pre-registered, marked provisional or TBD with validation path; locked before first Phase One exercise.
  • Provisional thresholds: detection rate ≥70% planned events, ≥50% unplanned; false-positive rate ≤10%; unverifiable equipment ≤5%; reciprocal-access parity ≥85%; unresolved discrepancies ≤21 days.
  • Go/Modify/Stop: ≥80% thresholds met → Go; 50–80% → Modify; <50% → Stop.
  • Stop triggers: asymmetric inspector access, material unverifiable equipment (>5–10%), ledger divergence without resolution, government shielding of operator, funding withholding.
  • Replicated ledger with independent national copies; events recorded locally within 1 hour; digest synchronization every 1 hour; divergence escalates to co-chair review.
  • Key custody is dual-hold (non-reconstructable shares) or mirrored (independent hierarchies, cross-certified); lost key stalls entries 8–24 hours pending recovery.

Review Assumptions

Domain of the expert reviewer

Bilateral Arms-Control Verification & International Governance

Domain-specific considerations

  • Double-key governance without casting vote under asymmetric trust and strategic ambiguity
  • Detection credibility and statistical rigor under thin operational data (90-day window, 6–8 event samples per type)
  • Reciprocal transparency versus protection of frontier computing IP and unrelated infrastructure
  • Operational feasibility of 24/7 mirrored inspectorates across adversary borders under full counterintelligence exposure
  • Transition from Phase One proof-of-concept to Phase Two commitment without credible interim verdict

Issue 1 - Entry Conditions Stalling: Bilateral Instrument, Site Selection and Vendor Participation Gates May Consume Months-3 to Months 4, Compressing Phase One Timeline and Invalidating 90-Day Test Window

Phase One clock starts only after six sequential gates: signed bilateral instrument, appropriations, domestic authority, matched-site selection, inspector approval, vendor participation, and covered-equipment schedule. Each gate has veto points and no parallel-track acceleration is proposed. Entry-condition delays compound: site-selection disputes (asymmetric access, mismatched staging capacity) can stall the Matched Site Selection Doctrine for 6–8 weeks; vendor-participation deadlock (critical vendor refusing reporting or escort) forces fallback-ladder negotiations, consuming another 4–6 weeks. Estimated total entry-condition timeline: 12–16 weeks. If completion slips to Month 4 (2027-02-08), Phase One operationally runs Months 4–7 (2027-02-08 to 2027-05-08), not Months 3–6 (2027-01-08 to 2027-04-08), compressing by 4 weeks. Thin detection statistics worsen: 6–8 event replicates per type become 4–5, reducing statistical power and widening confidence intervals from ±10–15% to ±15–20% (95% CL). Final verdict thresholds become even more ambiguous, and Stop credibility weakens.

Recommendation: Establish pre-Phase-One entry-condition task force with binding timelines and external escalation authority. Set hard deadlines: bilateral instrument signature Month 0.5 (2026-10-23); domestic authority Month 1 (2026-11-08); site nominations Month 1 (2026-11-08); site-selection audit completion Month 1.5 (2026-11-23); inspector selections Month 2 (2026-12-08); vendor participation agreements Month 2.5 (2026-12-23); schedule adoption Month 3 (2027-01-08). Conduct site-selection and vendor-participation negotiations in parallel (not sequentially) starting Month -1 (before Phase One entry conditions are finalized). Pre-identify 4–6 candidate sites per country by Month -2; vendor outreach begins Month -2 (written commitments required by Month 1 = 2026-11-08). If any gate slips >2 weeks, activate emergency co-chair summit and publish public timeline of delay. Reserve USD 50–100M (5–10% of contingency) for compressed negotiation timelines. If entry conditions cannot complete by Month 3 (2027-01-08), publicly announce scope reduction (fewer matched sites, shorter test window from 90 to 60 days) rather than stretching the timeline, preserving statistical defensibility.

Sensitivity: Entry-condition delay impact ranges: Baseline Phase One start Month 3 (2027-01-08), 90-day test duration, 45–60 total exercises, 6–8 replicates per event type, confidence intervals ±10–15% (95% CL). Scenario 1: 4-week delay (Month 4 = 2027-02-08 start) → test runs 60 days, 30–40 exercises, 4–5 replicates per type, confidence intervals widen to ±15–20%, final verdict becomes ambiguous (Go/Modify/Stop boundary shifts by 5–10 percentage points). Scenario 2: 8-week delay (Month 5 = 2027-03-08 start) → test runs 32 days (Phase One window ends), insufficient operational time for even pilot exercises, Phase One becomes infeasible, contingency consumed by delay costs (estimated USD 100–200M), supplemental appropriations required (political veto risk). Scenario 3: 12-week delay (Month 4.5 = 2027-02-23 start) → sunk entry-condition costs estimated USD 300–500M (5–10% of total budget), Phase One reduced to 45 days, test ceases to be a credible proof-of-concept.

Issue 2 - Evidence Ambiguity Under Equal Co-Chairs Deadlock: Rotating Confidential Evidence-Weighting Rule Cannot Be Validated Before Phase One Starts, Creating Post-Hoc Dispute Risk Over Rule Legitimacy and False-Positive/Negative Rates

The design specifies that the Layered Evidence Weighting Model uses a confidential, rotating combination rule (which evidence categories must be corroborated) set by accountable specialists and validated only post-hoc against blind-exercise outcomes. The rule is locked before Phase One (Month 3 = 2027-01-08) but its accuracy is unknown. If the rule is too strict (requires corroboration from 4+ evidence layers), false-positive rates surge to 20–30%, unverifiable-equipment counts spike, and adjudication load exceeds inspectorate capacity (estimated 10–15 cases per month, vs. 50+ generated). If too loose, gaming becomes possible: an operator or government can learn which evidence categories weigh most by watching adjudication patterns and engineer evidence to pass the rule. A third risk: the rule itself becomes a contested finding. If results show, for example, 18% false-positive rate but the bilateral instrument called for ≤10%, both governments can claim the other gamed rule-setting. Disputes over rule validity are unresolvable within the double-key framework (no tie-breaker, no appeal to external authority), so the evidence basis for the entire verdict becomes suspect.

Recommendation: Publish the confidential evidence-weighting rule in versioned escrow locked by both co-chairs by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23), three months before first Phase One exercises. Conduct a pilot-validation exercise at Month 2 (2026-12-08) using historical equipment-change records from participating sites (estimated 100–200 past events per site). Apply the proposed rule to historical records, calculate identity-confidence outputs, and compare against known ground truth (what equipment was actually present) from operator records or maintenance logs. Target pilot results: false-positive rate within ±3% of threshold (e.g., if threshold is ≤10%, pilot should produce 7–13%), false-negative rate <5%. If pilot shows material miscalibration (e.g., 25% false positives vs. 10% target), adjust the rule and re-validate with a second cohort of historical events before Phase One begins. Maintain a versioned rule-change log: every amendment is double-key approved and timestamped; every evidentiary output shows which rule-version was applied. This prevents retroactive reclassification of findings. Document rule-validation uncertainty explicitly in final verdict: if confidence intervals for detection rates include the Go/Modify/Stop thresholds (e.g., detection rate 68±12%, threshold 70%), default verdict is Modify, not Go.

Sensitivity: Evidence-weighting rule miscalibration impact: Baseline proposed rule targets 10% false positives, 5% false negatives over 45–60 Phase One exercises. Scenario 1: Rule too strict (actual false-positive rate 20–25% vs. 10% target) → 10–15 unverifiable-equipment findings per 90 days, adjudication load becomes unsustainable, 30–50% of discrepancies remain unresolved at Phase One conclusion, Go verdict impossible. Scenario 2: Rule too loose (gaming possible) → 50% likelihood either government contests rule legitimacy, rule-validity dispute consumes 4–8 weeks of co-chair negotiation, verdict delayed or invalidated. Scenario 3: Rule validated post-hoc only (no pilot validation) → false-positive rate unknown until Month 6 (2027-04-08) (mid-Phase-One), corrective action impossible, contingency consumed by unanticipated adjudication costs (estimated USD 50–100M additional), Phase One credibility compromised.

Issue 3 - Thin Detection Statistics and Ambiguous Verdict Thresholds: 6–8 Trials Per Event Type Over 90 Days Yields ±10–15% Confidence Intervals; Final Go/Modify/Stop Decision May Fall in Ambiguous Zone (50–80% Thresholds Met) Where Multiple Verdicts Are Defensible

Phase One success rests entirely on blind-challenge exercise detection rates (no continuous monitoring, no other detection mechanisms). With 45–60 total exercises across 2–4 matched sites over 90 days targeting 6–8 replicates per event type per site, each event type has only 12–32 total data points. This sample size supports detection-rate estimates at 95% confidence with ±10–15% intervals (e.g., 'detection rate 72±12%' for unreported-arrival events). Pre-registered verdict thresholds (proposed: detection rate ≥70% for planned events, ≥50% for unplanned) place the threshold at or near the confidence-interval boundary. If actual detection rates fall in the 60–80% zone, the estimate is statistically ambiguous: Go (if best estimate is 75%), Modify (if best estimate is 68%) and Stop (if conservative bound is 58%) are all defensible readings of the same data. The plan proposes a default Modify if results fall in 50–80% band, but this default is itself arbitrary and becomes a negotiation target. Additionally, if either country suspects the other gamed exercise design (scheduled reported arrivals to pass as unreported, selected easy-to-detect substitutions), the entire exercise data becomes contested, and no verdict is possible without a trust-breaking investigation.

Recommendation: Pre-register verdict thresholds before the first Phase One exercise (Month 2.5 = 2026-12-23) in a joint bilateral memorandum locked by both co-chairs. Thresholds must include explicit confidence-interval bands, not point estimates: e.g., 'Go threshold: detection rate for planned events ≥75% at 90% confidence (lower bound); Modify threshold: 55–75%; Stop threshold: <55% at 90% confidence (upper bound).' Mark all thresholds 'provisional, validated against pilot-exercise data.' Conduct pilot exercise at Month 2 (2026-12-08) running all seven event types once at a non-production test facility; score against draft thresholds and document any threshold adjustments required. Publish pilot results (declassified: detection rates per type, false-positive/negative rates, unverifiable counts) to both governments by Month 2.5 (2026-12-23); lock final thresholds by Month 3 (2027-01-08). At Phase One conclusion (Month 9 = 2027-07-08), score results using pre-registered mechanical rules (not judgment calls): if lower bound of confidence interval exceeds Go threshold, verdict is Go; if upper bound falls below Stop threshold, verdict is Stop; otherwise Modify. Publish unclassified verdict summary (detection rates, confidence intervals, thresholds, verdict logic) so legislatures and media see objective outcome. If thresholds fall in ambiguous zone, explicitly state that Modify commits both countries to Phase Two with credible transition criteria (not subjective reassessment).
