Sensitivity: Verdict-threshold ambiguity impact: Baseline 6–8 replicates per event type, detection rate estimate 70±12% (95% CL), Go threshold ≥70%, Modify 50–70%, Stop <50%. Scenario 1: Actual detection rate 72±13% (confidence intervals widen due to higher variance than expected) → all three verdicts remain defensible, 50% likelihood of co-chair disagreement on verdict interpretation, final decision requires political negotiation (stalling risk 2–4 weeks). Scenario 2: Sample size compressed by entry-condition delay (4–5 replicates per type instead of 6–8) → confidence intervals widen to ±18–22%, ambiguous zone expands to 45–85%, Go becomes indefensible statistically, Modify or Stop become default, proof-of-concept verdict weakened. Scenario 3: One country contests exercise integrity (claims other side gamed scenarios) → entire detection-rate dataset becomes subject to forensic adjudication (4–6 weeks), delayed verdict, Phase One conclusion passes without credible Go decision.

Review conclusion

The Consortium is an unprecedented bilateral US–China verification mechanism of very high complexity and political risk. Three critical missing assumptions create cascading vulnerabilities: (1) Entry-condition gates lack explicit deadlines and parallel-track acceleration, risking 4–8 week slippage that compresses Phase One from 90 to 45–60 days, degrading statistical credibility; (2) the confidential evidence-weighting rule is locked without pre-validation against historical data, risking material miscalibration (false-positive rates 20–30% vs. 10% target) that paralyzes adjudication; (3) verdict thresholds are pre-registered but statistical confidence intervals are so wide (±10–15%) that Go/Modify/Stop boundaries become ambiguous, requiring political negotiation to resolve, undermining the technical credibility goal. Mitigation priorities: (A) Lock entry-condition deadlines and activate parallel negotiation tracks (site selection and vendor participation simultaneous, not sequential) by Month -1 (before Phase One formally begins), front-loading fixed costs to confirm budget realism by Month 1 (2026-11-08); (B) conduct mandatory pilot-validation exercise (Month 2 = 2026-12-08) of the evidence-weighting rule against 100–200 historical events per site, with adjustment and re-validation before Phase One exercises begin, documenting rule-change justification; (C) publish verdict thresholds with explicit confidence-interval bands (not point estimates) and mechanical scoring rules (lower bound → Go, upper bound → Stop, ambiguous zone → Modify default) locked by Month 3 (2027-01-08), with unclassified verdict scoring and rationale at conclusion. These three actions reduce stalling risk, evidence disputes and political renegotiation of verdicts, improving Phase One credibility as a proof-of-concept.

Governance Audit

Audit - Corruption Risks

  • Inspectors from each country deployed to the other's datacenters could be pressured by their own government to conduct unauthorized intelligence collection, bypassing the Information Firewall Doctrine and compromising equipment identity findings with concealed observations or biased reporting.
  • Equipment vendors or site operators could bribe inspectors or co-chair staff to misclassify equipment identity, falsify maintenance records, or suppress discrepancies in the ledger, leveraging the high-value frontier computing stakes and competitive sensitivity.
  • A national government could instruct its co-chair representative to systematically block adjudication of discrepancies at the counterpart's site (exploiting the double-key no-casting-vote rule) to shield its own operators from suspension, creating systematic bias in findings.
  • Critical vendors could offer side payments or preferential maintenance contracts to inspectors' home governments in exchange for favorable fallback-ladder rulings when reporting duties are refused, converting vendor-refusal procedures into a patronage gate.
  • Dual-custody key material could be exploited: one country's key-custody officer, under duress or incentive, could leak or compromise the non-reconstructable share held by the other, enabling tampering with ledger entries and attestation validity without detection.
  • Accredited independent examiners (third-country nationals) hired for vendor-refusal fallback procedures could be co-opted by either government or by vendors to produce favorable (or unfavorable) findings, compromising the chain of evidence when operators resist direct inspection.

Audit - Misallocation Risks

  • Envelope mapping misuse: Domestic operator compensation charged to each country's USD 2.5 billion contribution could be inflated or misdirected (e.g., paying non-participating operators, inflating per-site costs beyond the USD 167 million ceiling per facility) without itemized reconciliation, consuming site-preparation budget that should cover physical infrastructure.
  • Personnel double-billing: Full-time inspectors, specialists and surge-pool staff could be paid from both the personnel envelope (USD 750 million) and from domestic operator-compensation budgets, or could be re-tasked to domestic counterintelligence duties while drawing Consortium salaries, inflating effective headcount without actual deployment.
  • Contingency scope creep: The USD 500 million contingency could be drawn for non-emergency costs (e.g., routine personnel turnover, standard shift-relief coverage, office supplies) instead of reserved for entry-condition delays or mid-test crises, prematurely exhausting the buffer before Phase One conclusion.
  • Neutral-facility cost overrun: Construction and staffing of the joint secure facility (Geneva or Singapore) could exceed the secure-facilities envelope without competitive bidding or cost controls, consuming shared funding meant for cybersecurity and counterintelligence infrastructure.
  • Ledger and attestation infrastructure gold-plating: The USD 1.25 billion ledger-attestation-communications envelope could be spent on redundant or over-engineered systems (e.g., multiple hardware custody modules, excessive encryption layers) that exceed Phase One operational needs, reducing funds available for exercise testing or adjudication staffing.
  • Exercise and red-team budget leakage: The USD 500 million testing envelope could fund overly elaborate or repeated exercises, independent-examiner teams with excessive staffing, or extended red-team deployments beyond the 90-day Phase One window, delaying detection results or inflating per-exercise costs.

Audit - Procedures

  • Monthly independent envelope reconciliation (100 percent sampling of invoices and supporting documents) mapped against the seven-envelope budget allocation, with unclassified summaries published by the 25th of each following month; escalation at 2 percent variance; quarterly external audit sign-off by an independent auditor cleared by both countries.
  • Quarterly ledger-synchronization audit: sample five percent of recorded events across all sites, verify that each event appears in both national ledger copies within the one-hour synchronization bound, and reconcile any divergence within 72 hours; publish the audit exception count and resolution time in the monthly KPI dashboard.
  • Quarterly contingency-burn rate review (Months 3, 6, 9 = 2027-01-08, 2027-04-08, 2027-07-08): validate actual spending against the compression reserve (USD 50–100 million) and free contingency (USD 400–450 million); trigger co-chair briefing if cumulative draws exceed 30 percent, scope-reduction planning at 50 percent, joint budget review at 75 percent.
  • Biannual evidence-rule audit (Months 4.5, 8 = 2027-02-23, 2027-06-08): apply the locked evidence-weighting rule to a random sample of 20–30 adjudicated discrepancies from the prior period; verify that the rule's false-positive and false-negative rates remain within the calibrated band (±3 percentage points of target); flag any drift as a rule-adjustment candidate for post-Phase-One review.
  • Annual key-custody ceremony audit (conducted at Months 1, 4, 8 = 2026-11-08, 2027-02-08, 2027-06-08 during Phase One): verify that both countries' key-custody officers were present, that dual shares were generated in joint ceremony, and that no share was held unilaterally; audit the key-recovery procedures and test time-to-recovery against the 8–24 hour standard.
  • Post-Phase-One final audit (Month 9.5 = 2027-07-23): independent external auditor scores all five verdict criteria (detection rate, false positives, unverifiable equipment, parity, discrepancy age) against pre-registered thresholds; publishes unclassified audit opinion on Go/Modify/Stop decision logic; includes forensic sample of 10–15 exercise records and 5–10 discrepancy cases to confirm scoring integrity.

Audit - Transparency Measures

  • Weekly KPI dashboard (published to both co-chairs, bilingual) tracking: detection rate by event type, false-positive count, unverifiable-equipment count, reciprocal-access parity score, ledger-divergence incidents (count and resolution time), unresolved-discrepancy age distribution (percent >14 days, >21 days, >28 days), funding timeliness (tranche deposits, days elapsed since each release), contingency burn rate (percent of USD 500 million drawn), and audit exceptions; provide narrative interpretation of each metric.
  • Monthly unclassified summary of audit findings and envelope reconciliation (25th of each month), distributed to both parliaments and published on a joint bilateral website, showing total spending year-to-date per envelope, percentage of budget consumed, and any reconciliation exceptions without sensitive operational details.
  • Published adjudication case log (updated weekly, unclassified summary): count of open discrepancies by type and age cohort (0–7 days, 7–14 days, 14–21 days, 21–28 days, >28 days); count of cases resolved per week; partial-suspension events with timestamps and rationale; editorial narrative of systemic deadlock patterns if three or more suspensions occur in a month.
  • Pre-registration document (locked Month 5.5 = 2027-03-23): bilateral memorandum co-signed by both co-chairs containing the evidence-weighting rule (versioned and confidential, but the fact of locking is public), verdict thresholds with confidence-interval bands, deadlock procedures, and suspension triggers; published in full text (unclassified summary) on the bilateral website.
  • Bilateral monthly legislature briefing (unclassified, 15–20 minute oral or written summary): progress against entry-gate timeline, Phase One operational status (personnel deployment, exercise execution rate), detection results to date (binned by event type, without revealing scenario details), unresolved discrepancy count and age, and any funding or major-operational incidents; delivered jointly by both co-chairs or their designated representatives.
  • Final Phase One verdict scoreboard (published within 5 days of Month 9 = 2027-07-08 clock conclusion, unclassified): detection rates achieved per event type with 95 percent confidence intervals, false-positive rate and confidence interval, unverifiable-equipment count and share, reciprocal-access parity score, maximum unresolved-discrepancy age, count of hard-stop triggers invoked, Go/Modify/Stop decision with explicit reference to which thresholds were met or missed, and external auditor sign-off on scoring logic.

Internal Governance Bodies

1. Co-Chair Steering Board

Rationale for Inclusion: The Consortium is a bilateral US–China national-security program governed by equal national co-chairs with double-key authorization for budgets, protocol changes, site findings and sanctions. The plan explicitly forbids a single Project Sponsor, investor board or casting vote. This body provides strategic oversight, deadlock resolution and the final Go/Modify/Stop decision. It is essential to operationalize equal governance without stalling or brittle suspensions.

Responsibilities:

  • Strategic direction and bilateral consensus on mission phases, scope changes and major milestones
  • Double-key authorization of budgets (tranches), protocol amendments, and evidence-rule versioning
  • Approval of entry-condition gates and matched-pair selections before Phase One begins
  • Deadlock escalation: convening the Adjudication Panel and advisory technical board when co-chairs cannot resolve disputed findings or procedural disputes within 14 days
  • Go/Modify/Stop verdict decision at Phase One conclusion, scored mechanically against pre-registered thresholds
  • Partial-suspension triggers: authorizing the pause of a single disputed function when deadlock exceeds 14 days, without full program shutdown
  • Tranche release authorization synchronized between both countries; withholding decision if funding conditions (14-day escalation, 30-day Stop) are triggered
  • Emergency summit convening within 5 days if any entry-condition gate slips over 2 weeks

Initial Setup Actions:

  • Establish bilateral Charter and Terms of Reference signed by both governments, locking deadlock procedures, partial-suspension rules and threshold-locking timeline
  • Designate each country's co-chair representative (senior diplomat or national-security official) and appoint a co-chair office staff of 4–6 (1 chief of staff, 1 deputy per country, shared executive assistant)
  • Pre-approve the roster of the Adjudication Panel (3 technical specialists per country) and the advisory technical board for deadlock referral
  • Lock entry-condition roadmap with explicit 2-week slip triggers and emergency-summit procedures
  • Schedule weekly steering-board meetings (Mondays, 2 hours, bilingual) and monthly co-chair summit (3 hours, in-person at neutral facility or video conference)
  • Establish the KPI dashboard process: weekly bilingual dashboard, monthly unclassified legislature briefing

Membership:

  • US national co-chair (senior diplomat or national-security official, full-time equivalent)
  • Chinese national co-chair (senior diplomat or national-security official, full-time equivalent)
  • US chief of staff to co-chair (1 FTE)
  • Chinese chief of staff to co-chair (1 FTE)
  • US executive staff (1 deputy chief of staff, 1 shared operations coordinator per co-chair)
  • Chinese executive staff (1 deputy chief of staff, 1 shared operations coordinator per co-chair)

Decision Rights: Double-key authorization (both co-chairs must agree) required for: budgets over USD 50M in any single tranche or envelope, protocol amendments to evidence rule, site-finding sanctions (equipment classified unverifiable), partial-suspension orders, and Go/Modify/Stop verdict. Operational decisions under USD 50M per co-chair's authority independently (finance officer sign-off). Entry-gate certification and final verdict are joint decisions only. Tie-breaker: if deadlock on a Go/Modify/Stop verdict persists past 7 days, verdict defaults to Modify (not Go). If deadlock on a withholding decision persists past 30 days total co-chair impasse, both countries remain funded (status quo; no unilateral withholding allowed).

Decision Mechanism: Consensus-seeking: co-chairs meet weekly to pre-align. When consensus cannot be reached within 3 business days, formal double-key ballot by recorded vote. No casting vote by either co-chair or by an external party. For verdicts and deadlock escalations, the Adjudication Panel provides an advisory recommendation within 5 days of referral; co-chairs have 3 days to accept, override with published rationale, or escalate to emergency summit. Partial suspension can proceed unilaterally by the co-chair requesting it (no joint approval required); the suspension order is logged and both co-chairs are notified immediately, triggering a mandatory co-chair call within 2 hours.

Meeting Cadence: Weekly steering meetings (Mondays, 2 hours, bilingual video conference or in-person at neutral facility). Monthly in-person co-chair summit (3 hours, at neutral facility). Emergency summits convened within 5 days of any 2-week entry-condition slip, key-custody incident, ledger divergence, or unresolved deadlock exceeding 35 days. During Phase One (Months 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08), daily co-chair briefings (15 minutes) on KPI dashboard metrics.

Typical Agenda Items:

  • KPI dashboard review (weekly): detection rates, false positives, unverifiable equipment, parity, discrepancy age, ledger-divergence incidents, funding timeliness, contingency burn rate, audit exceptions
  • Entry-condition milestone tracking (Months 0–5 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-03-08.5): signed instrument, appropriations, access authority, site selection, inspector approval, vendor participation, schedule adoption; escalation of any slips over 2 weeks
  • Deadlock escalations and Adjudication Panel referrals (as needed): disputes that inspectors or operational teams cannot resolve within 10 days
  • Partial-suspension orders and impaired-confidence triggers (as needed): documentation of disputes exceeding 14–28 day thresholds by case type
  • Tranche releases and budget contingency status (every Month 2, 4, 6, 8 = 2026-12-08, 2027-02-08, 2027-04-08, 2027-06-08 = quarterly plus go/no-go gates): authorization of synchronized tranches, review of contingency burn, escalation of overruns
  • Phase One verdict preparation (Months 8–9 = 2027-06-08 to 2027-07-08): exercise results compilation, threshold scoring, confidence-interval analysis, preliminary Go/Modify/Stop assessment
  • Go/Modify/Stop verdict and final decision (Month 9.5 = 2027-07-23): mechanical scoring against locked thresholds, independent auditor sign-off, public verdict release

Escalation Path: Deadlocked co-chair decisions escalate to the Adjudication Panel (technical recommendation within 5 days) and then back to co-chairs for final decision. If co-chair deadlock persists >35 days (including Adjudication Panel advisory time), the issue escalates to an emergency summit convened within 5 days by the Program Risk Officer, with authority to recommend scope reduction, supplemental appropriations, or formal Stop condition. For verdicts, the final decision is a mechanical co-chair application of pre-registered thresholds (no second-level appeal, but both co-chairs must formally confirm the scoring). For withholding of funding, the 30-day escalation threshold automatically triggers Stop condition without further co-chair negotiation.

2. Program Operations and Site Delivery

Rationale for Inclusion: Phase One requires operational execution of entry-condition sequencing, site preparation, inspectorate deployment and daily verification activities at 2–4 matched pairs across two countries. A dedicated operational-management team reports to the co-chairs and manages day-to-day decisions (below USD 50M threshold), operational-risk mitigation, personnel scheduling, logistics and vendor coordination. This separates strategic oversight from operational execution and avoids overloading the steering board with tactical details.

Responsibilities:

  • Entry-condition task force leadership: coordinate bilateral roadmap (Months 0–5 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-03-08.5), manage milestone tracking, parallel negotiation tracks (site selection, vendor participation), and escalation procedures for 2-week gate slips
  • Site-selection and matched-pair validation: lead reciprocal-access audits (Months 0–1 = 2026-10-08 to 2026-11-08), document functional equivalence (staging, lift capacity, 24-hour access), resolve asymmetric-access disputes, and certify co-chair approval of final matched-pair roster
  • Inspectorate recruitment, vetting, training and deployment: manage simultaneous recruitment (Month -3 start, concurrent with entry gates), security-clearance processing (Months -1 to 4), joint training academy (Months -1 to 5), shift scheduling and leave rotations (4 months on-site, 2 months off-site, staggered cohorts), surge-pool mobilization and retention-bonus administration
  • Vendor and operator liaison: secure written vendor-participation commitments by Month 2 (2026-12-08), conduct operator-compliance workshops at each site, establish baseline access expectations (4-hour staging access, 48-hour exercise notice), document refusal triggers and fallback-ladder sequencing, and manage vendor-refusal incidents in real-time
  • Personnel cost tracking and payroll administration: manage USD 750M personnel envelope (distributed per country's contribution), track FTE deployment vs. budgeted headcount, monitor retention and turnover, submit monthly reconciliation to independent auditors, and flag overages requiring contingency draw
  • Logistical and facilities coordination: staff liaison offices at each participating site (5–8 personnel per country total), manage 24/7 shift coverage, coordinate with operators for exercise windows and staging access, arrange transport and secure storage of evidence packages, oversee neutral-facility operations (staffing, security, ledger hosting)
  • Operational-risk dashboard and mitigation: track leading indicators (entry-gate burn-down, vendor-refusal count, inspectorate-fill rate, discrepancy-age distribution, ledger-divergence incidents, contingency-burn rate), escalate risks >2 standard deviations from target to co-chairs within 48 hours, recommend scope adjustments or accelerated timelines in response to cumulative cascade risk

Initial Setup Actions:

  • Establish the Program Operations Center as a joint entity staffed by operational leads from each country (1 US Program Director, 1 Chinese Program Director, co-located at neutral facility or connected by secure video) with direct reporting to co-chairs
  • Publish the entry-condition roadmap by Month 0 (2026-10-08) with explicit deadlines, parallel-track assignments (site selection, vendor engagement, recruitment, vetting), and 2-week slip escalation thresholds
  • Activate the entry-condition task force by Month -1 with bilingual coordinators for each gate (legal/diplomatic track, site-selection track, vendor-engagement track, personnel track)
  • Conduct bilateral site-selection workshop by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23) to identify 4–6 candidate facilities per country and establish reciprocal-access audit criteria
  • Begin inspector recruitment concurrently with entry-gate negotiations (Month -3, before formal clock) to compress timeline and reduce deployment gaps
  • Establish the Vendor Liaison Office (5 personnel per country: legal, compliance, technical, logistics, adjudication) by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23) to negotiate vendor-participation agreements and document refusal triggers
  • Schedule the training academy facility, curriculum development and instructor certification (Months -1 to 0) so first cohort training begins Month 1 (2026-11-08)

Membership:

  • US Program Director (FTE operational lead, reports to US co-chair)
  • Chinese Program Director (FTE operational lead, reports to Chinese co-chair)
  • Entry-Condition Task Force Lead (shared bilingual coordinator, 1 per country)
  • Site-Selection Lead (1 per country, leads reciprocal-access audits and asset documentation)
  • Vendor Liaison Officer (5 per country: legal, compliance, technical, logistics, adjudication liaison)
  • Inspectorate Deployment Officer (1 per country, manages recruitment, vetting, training, shift scheduling and leave rotations)
  • Finance Officer (1 per country, tracks personnel costs, envelope reconciliation, contingency draws)
  • Logistical Coordinator (1 per country, manages site operations, transport, evidence custody, neutral-facility staffing)
  • Operational-Risk Officer (1 per country, co-reports to co-chairs and Program Directors, tracks leading indicators and escalates cascade risks)

Decision Rights: Operational decisions within approved budgets (single-envelope authority up to USD 50M per decision, contingency draws up to USD 10M per incident), personnel deployments and shift scheduling per established guidance, vendor-fallback-ladder sequencing and timing (with co-chair notification), site-access baselines and exercise-window coordination, and operational-risk escalations to co-chairs. Decisions requiring double-key co-chair approval: protocol amendments affecting inspectorate conduct, site-access restrictions, major cost overruns (>10% of an envelope), and entry-gate certification. Decisions escalated to co-chairs: vendor refusals affecting site eligibility, inspectorate staffing shortfalls exceeding 15%, and contingency-burn rate exceeding 30%.

Decision Mechanism: Daily Program Operations Center standup (bilateral video, 15 minutes) to review KPI dashboard and day-to-day issues. Operational decisions by Program Director consensus; if disagreement occurs, escalate to co-chairs within 4 hours. Personnel and shift scheduling by Deployment Officer with monthly auditor reconciliation. Vendor escalations decided by Vendor Liaison Officer in consultation with the counterpart country's liaison (majority of the 10-person office suffices; consensus preferred). Contingency-draw requests require Program Director sign-off and independent auditor concurrence before disbursement. Operational-risk cascades (3+ metrics >2 standard deviations) trigger an automated co-chair alert by the Risk Officer.

Meeting Cadence: Daily Program Operations standup (15 minutes, bilingual, 0800 UTC). Bi-weekly Program Directors' synoptic review (2 hours, deep-dive into entry-gate burn-down, inspectorate fill, vendor-refusal status, discrepancy age distribution, contingency burn). Weekly Vendor Liaison coordination call (1 hour, all 10 officers). Monthly full-program operational review with co-chairs (2 hours, prepare for steering-board meeting). Ad-hoc emergency calls as needed (within 4 hours of any 2-week gate slip or operational-risk cascade).

Typical Agenda Items:

  • Entry-gate milestone tracking: signed instrument status, appropriations progress, access-authority enactment, site-selection audit progress, inspector-approval status, vendor-participation registry updates, covered-equipment-schedule finalization
  • Site-selection and reciprocal-access audit: candidate-site documentation, functional-equivalence scoring, access-parity validation, audit exception resolution, matched-pair approval readiness
  • Inspectorate deployment status: recruitment pipeline (# nominated, # in vetting, # cleared, # trained, # deployed), fill rate per cohort, leave-rotation scheduling, surge-pool mobilization, retention-bonus tracking
  • Vendor-refusal incidents: fallback-ladder sequencing, independent-examiner availability, filter-certification status, evidence-package preparation timelines, unresolvable refusals (site eligibility impact)
  • Personnel costs and payroll: monthly actuals vs. budget per country, FTE tracking (deployed vs. planned), contingency draws and approvals, reconciliation for independent auditors
  • Logistical and facilities coordination: neutral-facility readiness (staffing, security, ledger hosting, key-custody ceremony prep), site-level operations (shift coverage, exercise-window scheduling, staging-area access), evidence-package custody and transport
  • Operational-risk dashboard: entry-condition slip tracking, vendor-refusal count and resolution time, inspectorate-fill rate, discrepancy-age distribution, ledger-divergence incidents, contingency-burn status, audit-exception count; escalate any metric >2 standard deviations

Escalation Path: Operational decisions (<USD 50M, routine personnel/logistics) resolved by Program Directors and functional leads. Decisions >USD 50M or affecting entry-gate certification escalate to co-chairs within 4 hours. Vendor refusals or staffing shortfalls >15% escalate immediately. Contingency draws >USD 10M require co-chair and auditor approval. Any gate slipping >2 weeks triggers emergency-summit convening within 5 days. Cascade-risk alerts (3+ metrics >2 standard deviations) escalate to co-chairs via Risk Officer immediately, with recommended scope reductions or timeline adjustments.

3. Evidence and Verification Committee

Rationale for Inclusion: The Consortium's core mission is credible, reciprocal verification of declared-equipment changes. This requires specialized oversight of evidence standards, equipment-identity confidence rules, vendor-refusal fallback procedures, and detection-rate calibration. The plan explicitly specifies that no single evidence source is decisive and that evidence rules must be confidential, rotating, and validated against blind-exercise outcomes. This committee integrates technical expertise from both countries, manages the layered-evidence rule and its validation, oversees the Exercise Authority, and ensures detection results are defensible to both governments.

Responsibilities:

  • Design, versioning and validation of the Layered Evidence Weighting Model: establish the confidential combination rule specifying how attestation, physical inspection, customs records, identifiers, maintenance logs, infrastructure changes and witnessed movement combine into equipment-identity confidence ratings; ensure no single source is decisive
  • Evidence-rule calibration and pilot validation: apply the draft rule to 100–200 historical equipment-change records per participating site (Month 4.5 = 2027-02-23 through Month 5.5 = 2027-03-23); document false-positive and false-negative rates; adjust the rule if pilot results deviate >5 percentage points from target (false positives 10% ±3); lock the final rule by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23)
  • Covered-Equipment Schedule maintenance: keep the confidential, versioned technical schedule technology-neutral; manage amendments at fixed review points (Months 3, 6, 9 = 2027-01-08, 2027-04-08, 2027-07-08); ensure each version is double-key approved and timestamped; prevent the schedule from lapsing into a product list
  • Vendor-refusal fallback-ladder implementation: oversee the sequence (vendor-supervised testing → filtered evidence → independent examiners → clean-room → validated attestation); manage pre-staged accredited independent-examiner teams (1 per country, 5–8 specialists); coordinate with operators and vendors when refusals occur; document the disposition of each refusal and the evidence sufficiency of each fallback rung
  • Oversight of the Exercise Authority: establish the mixed-nationality independent Exercise Authority (8 core staff); approve exercise scenarios and success criteria before execution (without disclosing scenarios to inspectors); verify that exercises are scored independently and that results are logged with witness attestations and cryptographic timestamps; ensure exercise load meets the target (54 exercises in 90 days, 6–8 replicates per event type)
  • Detection-rate analysis and adjudication of exercise disputes: compile exercise results as they occur (weekly during Phase One); calculate detection rates per event type with 95% confidence intervals; flag any event type falling significantly below target (e.g., <50% for unplanned); recommend investigation if a single site's detection rate diverges >15% from the pooled rate (asymmetric access or operator resistance suspected)
  • False-positive and unverifiable-equipment root-cause analysis: when a false positive is identified (inspector reported a discrepancy, but investigation cleared it) or when unverifiable-equipment counts surge, convene a technical review to determine whether the evidence rule, operator records or inspector procedures require adjustment
  • Reciprocal-access parity assessment: monitor whether each side's inspectorate achieves equivalent detection rates and staging-area access; calculate a parity score (target ≥85%); flag asymmetric access or operator resistance that compromises parity

Initial Setup Actions:

  • Establish the Committee co-chairs (1 senior technical officer per country) and recruit specialist members: technical/attestation (2 per country), cryptography/key custody (1 per country), equipment identifiers and maintenance records (1 per country), vendor-relation specialists (1 per country), red-team representatives (1 per country)
  • Publish the draft Layered Evidence Weighting Model by Month 4.5 (2027-02-23) in a versioned escrow jointly approved by both co-chairs; mark it confidential but lock both countries' agreement on the approach
  • Conduct the pilot-validation exercise at a non-production test facility by Month 5 (2027-03-08), applying the rule to all seven event types once and documenting detection procedures and scoring consistency
  • Perform historical-record validation (Month 4.5 = 2027-02-23 to Month 5.5 = 2027-03-23) by applying the draft rule to 100–200 past equipment-change records per site; document false-positive and false-negative rates; if calibration is off, revise and re-validate with a second cohort
  • Lock the final evidence rule and covered-equipment schedule by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23) with bilateral co-chair double-key approval; publish a declassified summary (rule principles, but not specific weighting values) to both legislatures
  • Establish the Exercise Authority structure and charter by Month 3 (2027-01-08); recruit mixed-nationality staff (8 core, funded from testing envelope); pre-stage accredited independent-examiner teams (1 per country, 5–8 specialists) funded from testing envelope by Month 4 (2027-02-08)
  • Develop exercise-scenario templates and scoring rubrics by Month 4 (2027-02-08); pre-register all scenarios before first Phase One exercise (Month 6 = 2027-04-08) without disclosing to inspectors

Membership:

  • US Evidence and Verification Committee co-chair (senior technical officer, FTE)
  • Chinese Evidence and Verification Committee co-chair (senior technical officer, FTE)
  • US technical/attestation specialists (2 FTE)
  • Chinese technical/attestation specialists (2 FTE)
  • US cryptography/key-custody officer (1 FTE, liaison to Root-of-Trust Key Custody Architecture team)
  • Chinese cryptography/key-custody officer (1 FTE, liaison to Root-of-Trust Key Custody Architecture team)
  • US equipment-identifier and maintenance-records specialist (1 FTE)
  • Chinese equipment-identifier and maintenance-records specialist (1 FTE)
  • US vendor-relation specialist (1 FTE, liaison to vendor-liaison office)
  • Chinese vendor-relation specialist (1 FTE, liaison to vendor-liaison office)
  • US red-team representative (1 FTE, liaison to blind-challenge exercise design)
  • Chinese red-team representative (1 FTE, liaison to blind-challenge exercise design)
  • Exercise Authority Director (mixed-nationality, reports to committee co-chairs, 1 FTE + 7 staff per country split)
  • Independent filter-auditor liaison (1 FTE, third-country national, reports to committee, validates disclosure-tier filters monthly)

Decision Rights: Committee co-chairs jointly approve the evidence-weighting rule, covered-equipment schedule, exercise scenarios and scoring rubrics, and the disposition of vendor refusals that affect site eligibility. Exercise Authority has full autonomy to design, schedule and score exercises without co-chair input until after execution; co-chairs can contest results through a formal double-key challenge (rare, documented). Detection-rate analysis is technical; if results fall clearly outside thresholds (e.g., <50% for unplanned), the committee recommends investigation but does not retroactively change thresholds. False-positive and unverifiable-equipment root-cause reviews are internal committee work; findings are reported to co-chairs but do not alter locked thresholds (adjustments deferred to post-Phase-One). Parity-score calculations are mechanical; asymmetric access flagged for co-chair escalation if score falls below 85% or a single site's detection rate diverges >15% from pooled.

Decision Mechanism: Consensus-seeking at bilateral co-chair level; drafts developed by specialist working groups and reviewed by full committee. For the evidence rule, a working group (2 technical specialists per country) drafts the rule, the committee debates it, and both co-chairs must approve in writing before it is locked. For exercise scenarios, the Exercise Authority proposes scenarios in writing; the committee reviews for scenario coverage and independence (no co-chair or inspector input until execution); both co-chairs formally acknowledge receipt but may not comment. Detection-rate calculations are automated from logged exercise results; threshold scoring is mechanical (no judgment call). If a technical dispute arises (e.g., whether a false positive is valid), the committee convenes a sub-group for technical investigation and reports findings to co-chairs without recommendation; co-chairs decide whether to re-investigate or accept findings.

Meeting Cadence: Bi-weekly Evidence Committee meetings (2 hours, bilateral, deep-dive on rule calibration, pilot data, schedule amendments, vendor-refusal fallback status). Weekly Exercise Authority status updates (1 hour, exercise load, detection rates to date, incident reports). Monthly parity-score and reciprocal-access review (1 hour, during Phase One). During Phase One (Months 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08), daily exercise-result compilation and incident log (automated, reviewed by co-chairs).

Typical Agenda Items:

  • Evidence-rule development and validation: draft rule review, pilot-exercise results, historical-record calibration, false-positive and false-negative rate analysis, adjustment justification if calibration drifts >3 points
  • Covered-equipment schedule maintenance: amendment proposals, technology-neutrality review, version control and effective-date timing, scope disputes (e.g., should new hardware generations be added mid-test)
  • Vendor-refusal fallback-ladder implementation: refusal incidents and disposition (vendor-supervised testing, filtered evidence, independent examiners, clean-room, attestation), evidence sufficiency per rung, unresolvable refusals and site-eligibility impact
  • Exercise Authority oversight: scenario development and pre-registration, exercise load tracking (target 6 per month per site = 54 total), detection-rate compilation per event type and per site, incident reports (production disruptions, access delays, equipment substitution scenarios failed to detect)
  • False-positive and unverifiable-equipment root-cause analysis: investigation findings, evidence-rule adjustment recommendations (if any), inspector-procedure feedback, operator-record quality issues
  • Reciprocal-access parity assessment: parity score (target ≥85%), per-site detection rates, asymmetric access flagged, operator-compliance baseline violations, recommendation for co-chair escalation if asymmetry suspected

Escalation Path: Technical disputes on evidence rules or exercise scoring escalate from the committee to the Adjudication Panel (technical recommendation within 5 days). If the panel recommendation is contested by a co-chair, the issue escalates to the co-chairs for final decision via the steering board. Vendor-refusal dispositions that affect site eligibility escalate to co-chairs immediately. Asymmetric access (parity score <85% or single-site detection divergence >15%) escalates to co-chairs for investigation and possible site-selection remediation. False-positive surges or unverifiable-equipment counts exceeding thresholds escalate for possible evidence-rule re-calibration post-Phase-One (not mid-test changes to locked rule).

4. Compliance and Audit Committee

Rationale for Inclusion: The plan requires rigorous fiscal accountability and auditing: every USD expense must map to one of seven budget envelopes; 100% of invoices are sampled by independent auditors; monthly envelope reconciliation and contingency-burn tracking; quarterly external audit sign-off. Additionally, the plan identifies multiple compliance risks: corruption, misallocation, envelope scope creep, operator-compensation inflation, and double-billing. The plan also specifies mandatory transparency: weekly KPI dashboard, monthly unclassified auditor findings, monthly legislature briefings. A dedicated Compliance and Audit Committee operates independently from the co-chairs and Program Operations to maintain audit integrity and compliance credibility.

Responsibilities:

  • Envelope mapping and allocation governance: maintain the seven-envelope budget map (ledger/attestation/communications 1,250M; site prep/operator compensation 1,000M; personnel/training/translation 750M; secure facilities/cyber/counterintelligence 750M; testing/challenge/red teams 500M; legal/auditing 250M; contingency/surge 500M); classify every expense against an envelope; enforce maximum per-envelope spending (120% triggers supplemental-appropriation review); track per-country allocations (50/50 split, each 2,500M)
  • Monthly independent envelope reconciliation: sample 100% of invoices and supporting documents submitted by both countries (consolidated by category: personnel, site prep, testing, facilities, legal); verify proper envelope classification; flag exceptions (>2% variance = re-check, >5% = co-chair escalation); publish unclassified monthly summary (total spend per envelope, % of budget consumed, reconciliation exceptions) by the 25th of each following month
  • Contingency-burn tracking and escalation: monitor cumulative contingency draws against the USD 500M pool; trigger co-chair briefing at 30% spent (USD 150M), scope-reduction planning at 50% (USD 250M), joint budget review with external audit at 75% (USD 375M); maintain separate tracking of compression reserve (USD 50–100M, earmarked for entry-condition delays) vs. free contingency (USD 400–450M, for Phase-One operations)
  • Quarterly budget actuals-vs-plan review: compile actuals through the end of the prior quarter; calculate variance per envelope and per country; identify overruns requiring contingency or supplemental appropriation; recommend scope reductions if free contingency approaches exhaustion
  • Auditor coordination and independence assurance: recruit and vet independent auditors (third-country nationals, security-cleared by both countries) before Month 0 (2026-10-08); establish auditor charter guaranteeing independence and preventing interference by co-chairs or Program Ops; manage auditor schedule (monthly reconciliation sampling, quarterly external sign-off, final Phase-One audit at Month 9.5 = 2027-07-23)
  • Personnel cost tracking and FTE reconciliation: collect monthly payroll and staffing data from both countries; verify FTE counts against planned headcount (180 per country target); flag turnover rates >5% monthly or <80% deployment rate; reconcile personnel costs within the USD 750M envelope; track retention-bonus spending against the budgeted 2–3% (USD 15–22.5M)
  • Ledger-synchronization and key-custody audit: quarterly review of ledger divergences (sample 5% of recorded events, verify appearance in both national copies within 1-hour sync bound); audit key-custody ceremonies (verify both countries' officers present, dual shares generated jointly, no unilateral hold); test key-recovery procedures against 8–24 hour standard
  • Public transparency and reporting: publish weekly KPI dashboard (bilingual) to both co-chairs tracking detection rates, false positives, unverifiable equipment, parity, discrepancy age, ledger-divergence incidents, funding timeliness, contingency burn, audit exceptions; monthly unclassified auditor findings and envelope summary (25th of each month); monthly unclassified legislature briefing (bilingual, 15–20 minutes, co-signed by both co-chairs); final Phase-One audit report and verdict scoreboard (within 5 days of Month 9 = 2027-07-08 clock conclusion)
  • Compliance investigations and violations reporting: identify personnel, financial or procedural violations (unauthorized evidence handling, envelope misallocation, unauthorized vendor communications); escalate to co-chairs within 48 hours with investigation summary and recommended remediation; document all violations and remediation in the public ledger as events

Initial Setup Actions:

  • Establish the Compliance and Audit Committee co-chairs (1 senior audit or finance official per country, reporting independently to co-chairs and ministries of finance) and recruit supporting staff: budget analysts (2 per country), envelope auditors (1 per country), FTE/payroll specialists (1 per country), transparency officer (1 shared, bilingual)
  • Publish the Compliance and Audit Charter by Month -1 (2026-09-08, before Phase One starts) specifying auditor independence, escalation procedures, violation-reporting protocols and public transparency measures; sign jointly by both co-chairs
  • Identify and recruit independent third-country auditors by Month -2 (2026-08-08); require biography review, security-clearance coordination and signed independence statement from each auditor; finalize auditor roster by Month 0 (2026-10-08)
  • Establish the envelope-mapping protocol and budget-tracking system by Month 0 (2026-10-08): define invoice-submission requirements (envelope category, supporting docs, country and cost center), monthly reconciliation procedures, exception-reporting thresholds, and automated alerts when an envelope approaches 110% or 120% of plan
  • Design the KPI dashboard and monthly reporting templates by Month 0 (2026-10-08) with input from co-chairs, Program Ops, Evidence Committee and counterintelligence offices; establish bilingual formats and distribution procedures
  • Conduct a compliance-baseline audit of Months -1 and 0 (2026-09-08 to 2026-10-08) spending before Phase One, reconcile major cost categories and confirm that baseline auditor procedures work before the 90-day test begins
  • Brief both countries' legislatures on compliance and audit procedures (Month 1 = 2026-11-08) as part of the monthly transparency-briefing series

Membership:

  • US Compliance and Audit Committee co-chair (senior finance or audit official, FTE, reports to US finance ministry and co-chair)
  • Chinese Compliance and Audit Committee co-chair (senior finance or audit official, FTE, reports to Chinese finance ministry and co-chair)
  • US budget analyst (2 FTE, track invoices and envelope reconciliation)
  • Chinese budget analyst (2 FTE, track invoices and envelope reconciliation)
  • US envelope auditor (1 FTE, specialize in one or two high-risk envelopes like site prep, testing, facilities)
  • Chinese envelope auditor (1 FTE, specialize in one or two high-risk envelopes)
  • US FTE and payroll specialist (1 FTE, track personnel costs, headcount, turnover, retention bonuses)
  • Chinese FTE and payroll specialist (1 FTE)
  • Shared transparency officer (1 FTE, bilingual, prepares KPI dashboard and public monthly summaries)
  • Independent external auditors (3–5 total, third-country nationals, 1–2 FTE each, security-cleared, hired on contract for the duration of Phase One through Month 9.5 = 2027-07-23)

Decision Rights: Committee co-chairs jointly approve budget amendments, contingency draws over USD 10M, and audit procedures. Budget analysts classify invoices and flag exceptions; co-chairs review exceptions >2% variance. Envelope auditors recommend reallocation or contingency draw if an envelope approaches overage; co-chairs authorize draws. Payroll specialist verifies FTE and cost reconciliation monthly; co-chairs approve or dispute. Transparency officer compiles and publishes reports on a fixed schedule (no editorial discretion; formats set in advance). Independent auditors operate under a charter that prohibits co-chair interference; auditors sign off on invoice sampling results and final verdict scoreboard independently. Violations identified by auditors are escalated to co-chairs immediately but reported publicly in the ledger within 48 hours (no suppression).

Decision Mechanism: Consensus-seeking at co-chair level for budget decisions. Automated invoice classification by category; exceptions reviewed by envelope auditors and escalated if variance exceeds threshold. Contingency-draw requests require both the requesting country's program director and the committee co-chair to sign off, plus auditor review and sign-off before disbursement. Quarterly actuals-vs-plan reviews conducted by bilateral working group (budget analyst + auditor from each country) with findings presented to committee co-chairs for decision on scope reductions or supplemental-appropriation requests. KPI dashboard compiled automatically from ledger and operational databases; no judgment call. Monthly legislature briefings scripted and approved in advance by both co-chairs (no ad-hoc commentary). Violations flagged by auditors trigger a co-chair conference call within 4 hours; investigation and remediation decision within 48 hours, with findings documented in the public ledger.

Meeting Cadence: Weekly budget status call (1 hour, budget analysts from both countries, review invoice submissions and flag exceptions). Bi-weekly Compliance Committee meeting (2 hours, full committee, deep-dive on envelope reconciliation, contingency burn, auditor findings, compliance incidents). Monthly KPI dashboard review with co-chairs (1 hour, part of steering-board meeting agenda). Quarterly external-auditor coordination (1 hour, independent auditors present findings, committee co-chairs discuss next-quarter audit plan). Contingency-burn escalation calls at 30%, 50% and 75% thresholds (emergency 1-hour co-chair + committee call). Monthly legislature briefings (15–20 minutes, co-signed by both co-chairs, delivered jointly).

Typical Agenda Items:

  • Monthly envelope reconciliation: invoices submitted, classification accuracy, exceptions flagged (>2% variance), explanations and corrective actions, cumulative spend per envelope vs. plan, per-country allocations check (50/50 parity)
  • Contingency-burn tracking: draws authorized and paid in prior month, cumulative draws against 500M total, percentage of compression reserve vs. free contingency spent, forecast through Phase One conclusion, escalation triggered (30%, 50%, 75%)
  • Personnel cost and FTE tracking: monthly payroll actuals, FTE deployed vs. planned (target 180 per country), turnover rate and resignation reasons (if >5% monthly, investigate retention issues), retention-bonus spending (2–3% of 750M)
  • Quarterly actuals-vs-plan review: variance per envelope (target <5%), causes of overruns, reductions possible in later quarters, supplemental-appropriation needed (if overrun >120% of envelope), free contingency remaining forecast
  • Ledger-synchronization and key-custody audit: divergence incidents (count and resolution time), key-custody ceremony attendance and dual-share generation, key-recovery test results, audit exceptions (if any)
  • Independent auditor coordination: monthly invoice-sampling results (% exceptions, re-check rate), quarterly external-audit scope and timeline, final Phase-One audit plan (Month 8 = 2027-06-08 prep)
  • Compliance violations and remediation: unauthorized evidence handling, envelope misallocation, vendor-communication breaches, personnel-conduct violations; investigation findings, recommended remediation, public ledger entry documenting incident and resolution
  • KPI dashboard metrics: detection rates, false positives, unverifiable equipment, parity, discrepancy age, ledger-divergence incidents, funding timeliness, contingency burn, audit exceptions; escalate any metric >2 standard deviations

Escalation Path: Invoice exceptions >5% variance escalate to co-chairs for decision on reclassification or contingency draw. Contingency draws >USD 10M require co-chair approval plus auditor concurrence before disbursement. Overruns >110% of an envelope trigger co-chair briefing; >120% requires supplemental-appropriation request (veto point). Compliance violations escalate immediately (within 48 hours) to co-chairs; investigation and remediation decision within 48 hours, with ledger documentation. Auditor disagreement with co-chair budget decision escalates to the independent auditor panel (3–5 auditors vote on final sign-off; majority rule, auditors do not veto but publish dissent if any). Major audit findings (e.g., systematic envelope misallocation, personnel double-billing) published in the monthly legislature briefing and the final Phase-One audit report (no suppression).

5. Counterintelligence Oversight Board

Rationale for Inclusion: Inspectors from each country are deployed to the other country's datacenters for extended periods (24/7 shifts, 4-month rotations), creating significant counterintelligence exposure and incentive for each side to conduct unauthorized intelligence collection or to suspect the other of doing so. The plan identifies this as a high-risk area (Estimated 40–60% chance of at least one breach attempt during a 90-day test; 30–40 day timeline to political withdrawal if a breach is discovered). The plan specifies Inspector Information Firewall Doctrine (compartmentalized knowledge, post-rotation debriefs, monitored cooling-off periods) but requires a dedicated oversight body to enforce compliance, adjudicate suspected breaches and prevent a single incident from derailing the entire mechanism. This board reports to co-chairs and operates with classified authority to investigate and sanction violations.

Responsibilities:

  • Inspector vetting and continuous security review: coordinate baseline and periodic security clearance reviews (polygraph or equivalent) for all deployed inspectors (estimated 360 total, 180 per country) before deployment and at 4-month rotation intervals; maintain confidential security profiles; recommend removal of any inspector flagged as at-risk; approve security-cleared status for each rotation cohort
  • Information-barrier enforcement: oversee implementation of the compartmentalized inspector knowledge model (isolated by role and site, post-rotation debriefs, monitored cooling-off periods before reassignment); conduct quarterly spot-check audits of inspector communications (secure on-site channels only, no personal phones) and compliance documentation; flag unauthorized access to sensitive areas or data
  • Breach investigation and adjudication: receive breach allegations (from co-chairs, other inspectors, operator security, partner counterintelligence agencies); conduct expedited investigation (48-hour fact-finding, 72-hour recommendation to co-chairs, 7-day remediation decision); determine whether breach is substantiated and whether the inspector should be removed, recalled or sanctions applied
  • Personnel rotation and cooling-off procedures: manage the 4-month on-site, 2-month off-site rotation schedule to ensure continuous, staggered coverage without requiring any inspector to stay deployed >4 months; enforce mandatory debriefs upon return from assignment; coordinate cooling-off periods (recommended 3–6 weeks off-site) before reassignment to other duties or other sites; track cooling-off compliance and exceptions
  • Counterintelligence risk assessment and briefing: assess counterintelligence threats to the program (assessed foreign-intelligence targeting, identified collection attempts, known espionage methods); brief inspectors on threat awareness and reporting requirements during training (Months -1 to 5 = 2026-09-08 to 2027-03-08); provide on-site security briefings for each rotation cohort; track reported suspicious activity and investigation outcomes
  • Interagency liaison and threat reporting: coordinate with national counterintelligence agencies of both countries on identified threats or investigation results; share threat intelligence bilaterally within the Board (classified, restricted compartment); report to co-chairs any evidence of systematic collection attempts or intelligence-service targeting; recommend program adjustments if counterintelligence posture requires strengthening
  • Sanctions and personnel removal: recommend sanctions for confirmed breaches (removal from program, criminal referral, diplomatic notification if a foreign intelligence service is involved); enforce mandatory removal if an inspector is found to be conducting unauthorized collection or if counterintelligence agencies assess an unacceptable risk; coordinate with home-country governments on personnel consequences
  • Public transparency within security constraints: maintain a confidential breach-incident log (shared with co-chairs) tracking all investigations opened, outcomes and personnel actions; publish a quarterly unclassified summary of breach-investigation activity (e.g., 'X investigations opened, Y substantiated, Z personnel removed') to establish public confidence that breaches are being monitored and adjudicated

Initial Setup Actions:

  • Establish the Counterintelligence Oversight Board by Month -1 (2026-09-08) with 3 senior counterintelligence officers per country (6 total), each representing their national counterintelligence service; appoint a board chair (rotating annual chair, starting with US or mutual agreement) and executive secretary (1 bilingual FTE reporting to both co-chairs)
  • Develop inspector vetting and security-review procedures by Month -1 (2026-09-08): establish baseline security-clearance requirements (national-security background check, polygraph or equivalent, compartment-specific clearance for classified evidence); schedule reviews at deployment and at each 4-month rotation interval; coordinate with national clearance authorities for pre-approval
  • Draft the Information Firewall Doctrine enforcement procedures by Month -1 (2026-09-08): define compartmentalization rules (isolated by role, site, assignment duration), post-rotation debrief requirements (3–6 hours per inspector, conducted by neutral party), cooling-off periods (3–6 weeks off-site before reassignment), communication-security protocols (on-site secure channels only, monitored logging), and audit procedures (quarterly spot-checks of compliance documentation)
  • Establish breach-investigation procedures by Month -1 (2026-09-08): define allegation-intake process (any co-chair or inspector can report), triage criteria (substantive allegations only, frivolous complaints not investigated), fact-finding teams (mixed-nationality, 2 senior officers per country), evidence-collection procedures, recommendation-drafting, and co-chair adjudication process (7-day timeline)
  • Design personnel rotation schedule and cooling-off tracking by Month 0 (2026-10-08): establish 4-month on-site, 2-month off-site rotations staggered so 80–90% of each shift is always covered; create cooling-off tracking system to ensure every returning inspector completes mandatory cooling-off before reassignment
  • Brief inspectors and Counterintelligence Threat Awareness Training during training academy (Months -1 to 5 = 2026-09-08 to 2027-03-08): cover threat landscape, reporting requirements, unauthorized-collection penalties, compartmentation rules, cooling-off procedures, and secure communication protocols; document training completion for each inspector before deployment
  • Coordinate with national counterintelligence agencies (Month -1 to Month 0 = 2026-10-08 to 2026-10-08): establish liaison procedures, intelligence-sharing protocols (classified, bilateral only), and threat-briefing schedule; clarify how program-level breaches are reported vs. escalated to foreign-intelligence reporting channels

Membership:

  • US Counterintelligence Oversight Board member (3 senior counterintelligence officers from US federal agency, representing counterintelligence, security and interagency liaison functions, 1–2 FTE shared across the three)
  • Chinese Counterintelligence Oversight Board member (3 senior counterintelligence officers from Chinese national security authority, 1–2 FTE shared across the three)
  • Board chair (rotating annual chair, chair officer is 1 of the 6 members, holds explicit chair authority)
  • Executive secretary (1 bilingual FTE, not a voting member, reports to both co-chairs, maintains breach-incident log and schedules Board meetings)

Decision Rights: The Board jointly (all 6 members present) adjudicates breach investigations and makes recommendations to co-chairs on personnel removal, sanctions or program adjustments. Vetting approval (clearance sign-off for each rotation cohort) is delegated to each country's representatives (3 members per country can clear their own personnel; counterpart country does not veto but receives notification). Threat briefings and classified intelligence are compartmented (no dissemination outside the Board without explicit co-chair authorization). Breach-incident log is classified; quarterly unclassified summary published by Board consensus. Personnel removal recommendations require Board consensus; if disagreement (unlikely, but if both sides' representatives split), the issue escalates to co-chairs for final decision. Interagency liaison activities (threat sharing with national agencies) conducted by each country's representatives independently but with notification to Board chair.

Decision Mechanism: Breach allegations received and triaged by Board executive secretary; substantive allegations convene a fact-finding team (2 senior officers per country) for 48-hour investigation. Investigation team compiles evidence, interviews relevant personnel (inspector, co-workers, operator security contacts), and prepares a confidential report. Full Board (all 6 members) convenes within 72 hours of investigation completion to review findings and make a recommendation to co-chairs: substantiated breach (recommend removal), unsubstantiated (no action), partially substantiated (recommend monitoring or conditional reassignment), or insufficient evidence (file and monitor). Vetting decisions are mechanical: each country's clearance authority certifies its personnel; counterpart receives notification. Threat briefings and intelligence sharing occur through established liaison channels; Board chair ensures all members are informed of significant threats. Cooling-off compliance tracked by a shared database; quarterly audit verifies all inspectors completed required cooling-off before reassignment.

Meeting Cadence: Monthly Counterintelligence Oversight Board meeting (classified, 2 hours, full Board review of breach investigations, vetting status, threat briefings, cooling-off compliance). Emergency Board calls (within 24 hours) if a breach allegation is received or if a significant counterintelligence threat is identified. Quarterly unclassified summary preparation (1 hour working session before public release). Interagency liaison coordination calls (bilateral, each country's representatives, monthly, classified, 1 hour).

Typical Agenda Items:

  • Breach allegations and investigations: status of open investigations (count, age, expected completion date), completed investigations (substantiation outcome, recommended sanctions, personnel actions), breaches identified and remediated in prior months
  • Personnel vetting and clearance: rotation cohorts in vetting (% cleared, % pending), security-review results (any flags, repeat-reviewer issues), personnel removed or flagged as at-risk, clearance denials and appeals if any
  • Information-barrier compliance: spot-check audit results (communications-protocol compliance, compartmentation violations, unauthorized access attempts), inspector self-reporting of alleged policy violations, cooling-off completion tracking (% on-site personnel who completed cooling-off before reassignment)
  • Counterintelligence threat assessment: current threat landscape (foreign-intelligence targeting identified, collection-method assessments, specific-threat briefings per site or inspector category), briefing delivery to inspectors and program staff
  • Personnel rotation and cooling-off: cohort schedule (% deployed, % in cooling-off, % available for reassignment), anomalies (any inspector exceeding 4-month deployment, cooling-off waivers requested), staffing impact on continuous-coverage targets
  • Interagency liaison and intelligence sharing: threat intelligence received, shared with Board, and disseminated to co-chairs; coordination with national counterintelligence authorities on program-related investigations

Escalation Path: Breach allegations that appear substantiated escalate from Board to co-chairs immediately (within 24 hours of investigation completion) with a recommendation for personnel removal or sanctions. If co-chairs disagree on the appropriate remedy (rare), the issue escalates to emergency co-chair summit within 5 days. Vetting denials or security-clearance challenges escalate from the Board to the respective country's clearance authority for administrative appeal; the Board defers to national clearance decisions but can recommend retesting or reassignment conditions. Major counterintelligence threats (evidence of systematic foreign-intelligence targeting or collection attempts) escalate from the Board to co-chairs immediately and may trigger program-adjustment recommendations (e.g., revised compartmentation rules, additional security protocols). Recurring breaches or systematic policy violations escalate to a formal program-security review with co-chairs and the Compliance and Audit Committee.

6. Root-of-Trust Key Custody Architecture

Rationale for Inclusion: The Consortium's core infrastructure is a replicated, tamper-evident ledger with independently verifiable national copies. Every entry is signed and timestamped. Validated cryptographic attestations underpin equipment-identity confidence. The integrity of these systems depends entirely on the security of signing keys. The plan specifies dual-hold keys (non-reconstructable shares, both required to sign) to enforce the double-key governance principle. Key-custody ceremonies, key-recovery procedures and breach response are critical to operations. A compromise of key material would allow tampering with ledger entries and invalidating entire classes of evidence. This body is responsible for designing, implementing, securing and recovering key material, and for adjudicating key-custody disputes.

Responsibilities:

  • Key-generation ceremonies and dual-share procedures: design secure ceremony procedures generating dual-hold (non-reconstructable shares) signing keys at a neutral secure facility; ensure both countries' key-custody officers are present and witness each generation; distribute shares immediately to secure custody (one share per country's secure facility, physically isolated); document each ceremony with a signed attestation from both officers and an independent witness; conduct key-generation ceremonies at Months 1, 4 and 8 (2026-11-08, 2027-02-08, 2027-06-08) with rehearsal at Month -1 (2026-09-08)
  • Key-share custody and physical security: manage physical custody of non-reconstructable key shares (one per country) at secure facilities meeting classified-information standards; restrict access to authorized key-custody officers only (principal + deputy per country, total 4 personnel); implement two-person rule (both officers present for any access to key material); conduct monthly physical-security audits (verified custody, no unauthorized access, environmental controls functioning); document all key-access events in an access log
  • Key-recovery procedures and lost-key response: establish an automated key-recovery procedure if a signing key is lost, compromised or contested: both countries' key-custody officers convene within 4 hours; conduct a 48-hour investigation (verify the loss, assess tampering scope, reconstruct any affected ledger entries from backup); issue a joint revocation attestation signed by both countries; generate a new signing key in a routine ceremony (within 24 hours of revocation); apply the new key to all entries after the revocation timestamp; estimate recovery time: 8–24 hours depending on scope and backup-restoration complexity
  • Key-rotation and lifecycle management: rotate signing keys on a defined schedule (proposed: annual rotation, or after 1 million signatures, whichever is first, TBD) to limit the exposure window if a key is compromised mid-lifecycle; conduct each rotation in a ceremony with both key-custody officers present; archive retired keys in a secure, isolated vault with dual access control; maintain a version history of all active and archived keys with generation date, rotation date, retirement date and compromise status
  • Cross-certification and ledger verification: if using mirrored independent signing hierarchies (alternative to dual-hold), establish a cross-certification process where each country's root key is independently validated by the other country's key-custody officer; periodically (monthly) both countries compare their key registries to verify no divergence; validate a sample of ledger entries (5–10 per week) by verifying cryptographic signatures against the published key registries
  • Key-compromise investigation and remediation: if a key is suspected compromised (unauthorized signing, suspected theft or coercion of a key-custody officer), convene an emergency investigation (2 officers from each country) within 2 hours; assess the scope (which entries may have been tampered with), gather digital and physical evidence, and determine whether the compromise is confirmed or unsubstantiated; if confirmed, execute key revocation and recovery procedures immediately; if unsubstantiated, document findings and monitor for recurrence
  • Audit and compliance: maintain a key-custody audit log (all ceremonies, all accesses, all rotations, all recoveries) accessible to independent auditors monthly; quarterly auditor review of key-custody procedures against the design (verify two-person rule, access-log integrity, ceremony documentation, backup-restore procedures); annual formal audit of the full key-lifecycle including archive storage and retention
  • Training and deputy-capability maintenance: conduct annual training for all key-custody personnel (principal + deputy per country) on ceremony procedures, emergency response, evidence collection and recovery procedures; require all deputies to participate in at least one ceremony per year (by rotation with principals) to maintain capability if principal is unavailable; test the full key-recovery procedure annually (at Month 8 = 2027-06-08 during Phase One) with a simulated loss scenario

Initial Setup Actions:

  • Establish the Root-of-Trust Key Custody Architecture team by Month -1 (2026-09-08): designate 1 principal key-custody officer and 1 deputy per country (4 total); recruit from national cryptography or information-security agencies; require background checks and compartmentalized security clearance for classified cryptographic material
  • Design key-generation and key-recovery procedures by Month -1 (2026-09-08): document all ceremony steps, material flows, access controls, physical security requirements, witness roles and sign-off procedures; prepare draft procedures in English and Mandarin; circulate for peer review by cryptographic experts from both countries; finalize procedures by Month 0 (2026-10-08)
  • Identify and prepare the neutral secure facility for key-custody operations by Month -1 (2026-09-08): ensure the facility has hardware-security modules (HSMs) or equivalent for key generation, an offline secure workspace for ceremony execution, dual-custody safe or vault for key-share storage, and audit-log capability; conduct a security dry-run at Month 0 (2026-10-08) and full operational test at Month 1.5 (2026-11-23)
  • Conduct the first key-generation ceremony at Month 1 (2026-11-08) (or Month 1.5 = 2026-11-23 if facility readiness slips): both key-custody officers present, dual shares generated, distributed to secure storage in each country, ceremony documented with signed attestation
  • Prepare backup-and-restore procedures for ledger recovery (if needed for key-loss recovery) by Month 0 (2026-10-08): establish daily encrypted backups of both national ledger copies at geographically separated secure locations; test restore time (target <2 hours) and verify integrity of restored entries; coordinate with the Ledger Synchronization team on backup procedures
  • Document the key-custody audit trail and access-log procedures by Month -1 (2026-09-08): design a tamper-evident access log (hardware-enforced if possible) recording all key-access events with timestamp, accessing officer, purpose and outcome; ensure the log cannot be modified retroactively; test log integrity quarterly
  • Train all key-custody officers by Month 0 (2026-10-08): hands-on training on ceremony execution, emergency procedures, evidence collection, and recovery procedures; require all four officers to sign off on understanding and capability; observe one officer executing a full ceremony from memory (without reference) before deployment

Membership:

  • US principal key-custody officer (senior cryptography or information-security officer, 1 FTE, represents US national security authority)
  • US deputy key-custody officer (1 FTE, fully trained and capable to substitute for principal, required to participate in ceremonies annually)
  • Chinese principal key-custody officer (senior cryptography or information-security officer, 1 FTE, represents Chinese national security authority)
  • Chinese deputy key-custody officer (1 FTE, fully trained and capable to substitute for principal, required to participate in ceremonies annually)
  • Neutral independent witness (1 FTE, third-country national or independent security professional, observes all key-generation ceremonies and signs attestation; recruited by Month -1 = 2026-09-08)

Decision Rights: Key-generation ceremony execution requires both principal key-custody officers (or principal + deputy if principal unavailable, with advance authorization from co-chairs). Key-rotation decisions are made annually by the key-custody team and approved by co-chairs in advance (locked schedule, no ad-hoc rotation). Key-recovery procedures are triggered automatically by detecting a lost or compromised key (no co-chair pre-approval needed, but co-chairs are notified immediately). Key-compromise investigation decisions are made by the full four-person key-custody team (both countries represented); if there is disagreement on whether a compromise is confirmed, the issue escalates to co-chairs for final determination. Audit procedures are set by the independent auditors (audit scope and frequency); key-custody team provides access and documentation.

Decision Mechanism: Key-generation ceremonies are strictly procedural and scripted; decisions are binary (ceremony execution checklist: all steps completed, both officers present, independent witness present, shares generated and distributed, ceremony documented). Key-recovery is triggered by technical detection (key rejected by signing hardware, ledger-entry signature fails validation, or key-custody officer reports loss or suspected compromise); initiation is automatic (no decision-gate), but investigation of the cause and scope is conducted by the four-person team. Key-compromise assessment uses a four-step decision tree: (1) Is the potential compromise confirmed by technical evidence (unauthorized signatures) or by human report (officer coercion)? (2) If unconfirmed, what investigation will resolve it (2-hour technical audit, interviews)? (3) If confirmed, what is the scope (which ledger entries are affected)? (4) Proceed with key revocation and recovery. Disagreement among the four officers on whether a compromise is confirmed escalates to co-chairs (rare; most cases are clear-cut: either signatures fail verification or they don't).

Meeting Cadence: Monthly key-custody status review (1 hour, all four officers + independent auditor liaison, review access logs, ceremony schedule, upcoming rotations, and quarterly audit findings). Quarterly key-audit review (1 hour, with independent auditors, examine ceremony documentation, access-log integrity, backup-restore procedures). Annual training and testing (4 hours, all officers, simulated key-loss recovery, ceremony rehearsal, written exam on procedures). Emergency response calls (within 2 hours of suspected key loss or compromise).

Typical Agenda Items:

  • Monthly key-custody operations: access-log review (all key-access events since prior month, no unauthorized access), upcoming ceremony schedule (next rotation date, facility readiness), key-version inventory (active keys, retired keys in archive, lifecycle status), and any incidents or near-misses since prior month
  • Quarterly key-audit findings: independent auditor's assessment of ceremony documentation, access-control compliance, physical-security audits, and backup-restore procedure effectiveness; recommendations for procedural updates if any
  • Annual key-rotation ceremony planning: schedule next annual rotation (proposed timing, facility readiness, both officers' availability), review updated procedures if any changes are made, coordinate with ledger team on transition procedures (old key retired, new key activated)
  • Key-recovery and incident response: if any key loss or compromise occurs, emergency investigation findings, scope assessment, remediation timeline, and post-incident follow-up (how will this be prevented in future)
  • Training and capability maintenance: annual refresher training agenda, all officers' certification status, deputy-officer participation in last ceremony, any identified training gaps

Escalation Path: Suspected key loss or compromise escalates immediately (within 2 hours) to co-chairs with a status report and preliminary assessment. If recovery procedures are needed, the key-custody team executes them without waiting for co-chair authorization (emergency procedures already pre-approved). If there is disagreement among the four officers on whether a compromise is confirmed, the issue escalates to co-chairs for decision on whether to proceed with revocation (risk: false revocation stalls ledger for 8–24 hours; risk: failure to revoke allows tampering to continue). Key-recovery time exceeding 24 hours (backup restore slow, multiple entries affected) escalates to co-chairs with a status briefing and expected completion time.

Governance Implementation Plan

1. Senior leadership from both governments formally designate their national co-chair representatives (senior diplomat or national-security official, full-time equivalent) and appoint co-chair office staff (chief of staff, deputy, shared executive assistant per country). Execute and sign the bilateral Charter and Terms of Reference locking deadlock procedures, partial-suspension rules, threshold-locking timeline, and emergency-summit procedures.

Responsible Body/Role: Project Sponsor (Senior US and Chinese national-security leadership, pre-existing authority prior to any committee formation)

Suggested Timeframe: Month 0 (2026-10-08) to Month 0.5 (2026-10-23)

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Bilateral Charter and Terms of Reference signed by both governments
  • Named co-chair representatives and office staff (US and Chinese)
  • Charter locked deadlock procedures, partial-suspension rules, and emergency-summit procedures

Dependencies:

  • Project start authorized by both governments
  • Senior leadership commitment to bilateral governance

Schedule monthly in-person co-chair summits at the neutral facility (site selection OPEN; decide by Month 1 = 2026-11-08).

Target false-positive rate 7-13% (10% target +/- 3 points); false-negative rate <5%.
