Evidence and Verification Committee adjusts the evidence rule if pilot results deviate >5 percentage points from target (e.g., false positives 25% vs. 10% target, deviation 15 points = requires adjustment). Suggested Timeframe: Month 5 (2027-03-08) to Month 5.5 (2027-03-23)

Mark all provisional, validated against pilot data. Verdict logic: ≥80% thresholds met = Go; 50-80% = Modify; <50% = Stop.

During Phase One (Months 6-9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08), the Co-Chair Steering Board convenes weekly steering meetings (Mondays, 2 hours, bilingual video) and daily co-chair briefings (15 minutes) on KPI dashboard metrics. Program Operations Center runs daily standup (15 minutes) and bi-weekly deep-dive reviews. Evidence and Verification Committee meets bi-weekly, Exercise Authority reports weekly. Compliance and Audit Committee meets bi-weekly. Counterintelligence Oversight Board meets monthly (classified) with quarterly unclassified summaries. Risk Officer escalates any metric >2 standard deviations within 48 hours.

Program Operations Center documents all operational decisions, deviations from plan, and lessons learned. All bodies maintain records in a central archive for post-Phase-One review and any Phase Two planning.

Responsible Body/Role: All governance bodies (close-out reporting)

Suggested Timeframe: Month 9 (2027-07-08) to Month 9.5 (2027-07-23)

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Co-Chair Steering Board final program summary and KPI dashboard
  • Program Operations close-out report
  • Evidence Committee final detection-rate and evidence-rule analysis
  • Compliance final budget statement
  • Counterintelligence Oversight Board classified breach summary
  • Centralized record archive for Phase-Two planning

Dependencies:

  • Phase One operations concluded
  • Final verdict announced and legislatures briefed

Decision Escalation Matrix

Entry-Condition Gate Slip Exceeding 2 Weeks Escalation Level: Co-Chair Steering Board (Emergency Summit) Approval Process: Emergency co-chair summit convened within 5 days of slip confirmation. Both co-chairs jointly assess impact on Phase One timeline, decide whether to accelerate subsequent gates, compress contingency reserve, extend overall schedule, or reduce scope (fewer sites, shorter test window). Published timeline-adjustment decision required. Rationale: Entry conditions (signed instrument, appropriations, domestic authority, site selection, inspector approval, vendor participation, covered-equipment schedule) must complete before the 90-day Phase One clock begins. A 2-week slip compresses Phase One operations, reducing statistical power for detection-rate calculations and widening confidence intervals from ±10–15% to ±15–20%. Six sequential gates (Months 0–5 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-03-08.5) create compound delay risk; emergency escalation prevents passive schedule creep. Negative Consequences: Cascading delays: four-week total slip reduces Phase One from 90 days to 60 days, producing 30–40 exercises instead of 54, cutting replicates per event type from 6–8 to 4–5, rendering detection-rate estimates statistically indefensible (±20–25% confidence intervals). Contingency consumption estimated USD 100–200M (20–40% of USD 500M contingency) for compressed timelines. Final verdict becomes ambiguous or contested; Go credibility lost.

Bilateral Instrument or Appropriations Withheld Beyond 30 Days Escalation Level: Co-Chair Steering Board (Stop Trigger) Approval Process: Either country's funding withholding beyond 30 cumulative days (14-day escalation triggering co-chair briefing, then 30-day auto-Stop threshold) activates the Stop condition without further co-chair negotiation. Automatic stop-work order and program suspension. Both co-chairs jointly declare Phase One halted and assess whether remediation is feasible. Rationale: Synchronized USD 2.5 billion tranches (25% Month 2, 25 = 2026-12-08, 2028-11-08% Month 3, 30 = 2027-01-08, 2029-04-08% Month 5.5, 20 = 2027-03-23, 2028-06-08% Month 9.2 = 2027-07-14) are the mechanism for enforcing equal co-chair governance and preventing unilateral program control. Withholding funds is a Stop trigger under the plan's explicit design. Extended withholding (over 30 days) indicates political withdrawal or strategic dispute that cannot be resolved operationally. Negative Consequences: Unequal funding stalls Phase One operations; both countries' inspectors cannot be deployed or paid. Unresolved withholding over 30 days consumes estimated USD 50–100M in committed personnel costs while operations are frozen. Program loses credibility if one country funds while the other blocks. Phase One cannot achieve the 90-day continuous-verification test. Bilateral relationship damage and domestic political liability for the withholding government.

Deadlock on Material Site Finding or Sanction Exceeding 28 Days Escalation Level: Adjudication Panel (Technical Advisory Recommendation) → Co-Chair Steering Board (Final Decision with Automatic Partial Suspension) Approval Process: Disputed finding cannot be resolved by inspectors within 10 days → Adjudication Panel convenes (3 specialists per country, 6 total) → panel issues non-binding technical recommendation within 5 days (day 15 from case opening) → co-chairs have 3 days to accept, override with published rationale, or escalate to emergency summit. If unresolved by day 28: automatic impaired-confidence status applied to the disputed function (intake paused, exit paused, or identity adjudication paused) without co-chair pre-approval; unrelated verification continues. Escalation to emergency summit if suspension exceeds 35 days cumulative. Rationale: Double-key governance (no casting vote) creates deadlock risk. The Adjudication Panel provides technical credibility without altering the co-chair decision authority. Automatic partial suspension breaks stalling: one country cannot veto a finding indefinitely. Suspension is partial (only the disputed function pauses) to preserve operational continuity and avoid brittle full shutdowns. Age-based triggers (14, 21, 28 days) are pre-locked in the bilateral instrument to prevent disputes over the suspension threshold itself. Negative Consequences: Unresolved discrepancies accumulate at an estimated 3–5 per 90 days. Each unresolved case stalls the ledger, compresses adjudication capacity (15 cases per month planned), and forces escalation to the Adjudication Panel. If deadlock persists past 35 days, partial suspension removes one function (e.g., intake verification) from operations, reducing detection capability by an estimated 30–50% for that class of events. Multiple simultaneous partial suspensions (e.g., intake and exit both paused) can render a site unverifiable. Unresolved discrepancy count >5 becomes a potential Stop trigger.

Asymmetric Inspector Access or Operator Shielding Detected Escalation Level: Co-Chair Steering Board (Stop Trigger with Site Remediation or Exclusion) Approval Process: Reciprocal-access parity audit during Phase One (monthly monitoring, target ≥85% parity score) flags asymmetric access: one side's inspectors denied 24-hour staging access or delayed >4 hours from request, vs. immediate access at the counterpart site. Single-site detection-rate divergence >15% from pooled rate is an indicator. Co-chairs jointly assess whether asymmetry is systematic (shielding suspected) or correctable (operator delay). If systematic: site excluded from verification or suspended; if correctable: enforcement action and remediation plan. Unresolvable asymmetry (one country refusing to mandate operator compliance) is a Stop trigger. Rationale: Reciprocal access and parity are foundational to the bilateral verification model. The plan specifies matched-pair functional equivalence as an entry condition (staging ≥500 sq m, 24-hour access, lift capacity ≥50 tons). Asymmetric access undermines detection credibility: unreported arrivals in a restricted area cannot be detected, yet the site passes Phase One, invalidating the proof-of-concept. Operator shielding (a government preventing its operator from granting access) is explicitly listed as a Stop trigger. Negative Consequences: Asymmetric detection capability: one country's operator allows access to all equipment changes; the other's operator grants access only during scheduled windows (48-hour notice), missing unreported arrivals. Estimated 20–30% detection-rate divergence per site (e.g., 75% at the cooperative site, 50% at the restricted site). Verdict becomes contested: the high-detection side claims Go is justified; the low-detection side argues results are non-comparable. Final decision collapses into political negotiation; Go is indefensible. If asymmetry is attributed to government shielding, Stop is automatic.

Vendor-Refusal Fallback Ladder Cannot Produce Sufficient Evidence Before Phase One Entry Escalation Level: Co-Chair Steering Board (Site Eligibility Gate: Exclude Equipment or Fail Site Entry) Approval Process: Vendor refusal identified by Month 2 (2026-12-08); escalation ladder initiated (vendor-supervised testing → filtered evidence → independent examiners → clean-room → validated attestation; each rung 8–12 weeks = 40–60 weeks total). If the full ladder cannot complete by entry (Month 5.5 = 2027-03-23), equipment remains unverifiable. Co-chairs jointly decide: (1) exclude the equipment from the covered-equipment schedule, or (2) fail the site from Phase One entry (remove from matched pairs). Fallback: pre-stage one accredited independent-examiner team per country (5–8 specialists) to accelerate the independent-examiner rung if vendor-supervised testing fails. Rationale: The plan specifies no single evidence source is decisive and requires layered evidence. A vendor refusal that blocks all rungs of the fallback ladder leaves equipment unverifiable. Unverifiable equipment >5% triggers assessment for potential Stop. Allowing unverifiable equipment into Phase One with no credible evidence path undermines verification credibility. Entry-condition gate enforces resolution before the clock starts, preventing mid-test surprises that paralyze adjudication. Negative Consequences: Vendor refusals at multiple sites (estimated 20–30% likelihood of ≥1 vendor refusal per 90 days) consume 8–12 weeks per rung. If 2–3 vendors refuse simultaneously, examiner capacity is exceeded (estimated 10–16 examiners per country, 1–2 sites at a time). Equipment goes unverifiable. Unverifiable-equipment count >5–10% overall or >15% at a single site becomes a potential Stop trigger. Site fails entry condition; matched pairs are reduced from 3 to 2 (4 sites instead of 6), exercise load drops from 54 to 36, statistical power halved.

Inspector-Deployment Shortfall Exceeds 15% (Coverage Gaps) Escalation Level: Program Operations Center (Tactical Escalation) → Co-Chair Steering Board (Strategic Decision on Surge Buffer or Scope Reduction) Approval Process: Inspectorate Deployment Officer tracks FTE deployed vs. planned (target 80% by Month 4, 95 = 2027-02-08, 2034-09-08% by Month 5, 100 = 2027-03-08, 2035-02-08% by Month 5.5 = 2027-03-23). If deployment falls short by >15% (fewer than 153 per country deployed instead of 180), escalate to Program Directors for immediate action: surge-pool activation, accelerated training completion, or emergency recruitment. If shortfall persists past Month 5 (2027-03-08) or at Phase One start, escalate to co-chairs for decision: reduce the number of matched sites (exclude 1–2 sites, retaining 2 pairs), reduce shift coverage to 24/5 (no weekends), or delay Phase One start. Co-chairs jointly authorize the scope reduction or coverage change. Rationale: Inspectorate staffing drives detection capability: continuous presence in staging and spare-inventory areas is required to detect unreported arrivals. Staffing shortfalls create coverage gaps. Estimated gap impact: 15% under-staffing reduces continuous-presence coverage from 24/7 to ~20.4 hours per day, missing arrivals during ~3.6 unmonitored hours. Detection rate for unreported arrivals estimated to drop by 10–15% per coverage gap. Multiple gaps compound; a 15% shortfall across all sites is estimated to reduce overall detection by 10–15% and trigger potential Stop if results fall below the 70% threshold. Negative Consequences: Coverage gaps during nights, weekends, or high-turnover periods allow unreported equipment arrivals and substitutions to occur undetected. Detection-rate estimates become biased (exercises run during high-coverage shifts, missing the effect of gaps). Adjudication load increases as undetected changes are later disputed. Staffing-driven shortfalls produce a detection artifact: Phase One appears successful because it exercises well-staffed periods, but deployment to longer continuous operation reveals gaps. Verdict loses credibility post-Phase-One when actual detection rates are lower than Phase One suggested.

Ledger Divergence Between National Copies Unresolved Beyond 7 Days Escalation Level: Root-of-Trust Key Custody Architecture (Technical Investigation) → Co-Chair Steering Board (Double-Key Resolution Authority) Approval Process: Ledger-synchronization bound: counterpart signed-digest exchange every 1 hour (escalation alert at 30-minute overdue). If a digest mismatch is detected, automated dual-ledger audit convenes within 4 hours. Both countries' ledger teams perform a cryptographic check: which entries differ, what timestamps, were they recorded locally in both copies? Co-chairs jointly determine the cause (network failure, key-custody incident, tampering suspicion, accidental deletion) and authorize remediation: restore from backup (target <2 hours), revoke and regenerate signing keys (estimated 8–24 hours), or escalate to forensic investigation if tampering is suspected. Unresolved divergence exceeding 7 days is escalated to emergency summit and triggers partial suspension of ledger-dependent functions (evidence disclosure paused until divergence is resolved). Rationale: The tamper-evident replicated ledger is the core infrastructure. Divergence between national copies—even if unintentional (network failure, backup corruption)—breaks the fundamental assumption that both sides see the same events. Delayed resolution (>7 days) allows divergence to persist and grow; later events are recorded in only one copy, compounding the problem. Immediate detection and co-chair resolution within 7 days prevents the ledger from becoming a source of permanent dispute. Negative Consequences: Unresolved ledger divergence blocks evidence validity: an entry recorded at site A but missing from site B cannot be used to prove equipment identity (the counterpart disputes it). Adjudication load escalates as all disputed entries require manual forensic comparison. Estimated divergence incidents: 10–15 in 90 days if synchronization latency is 4+ hours and event volume is 5–10 per day per site; each incident can stall evidence validity for 2–7 days. If divergence persists >7 days, the ledger is de facto compromised; both co-chairs lose confidence in its integrity. Ledger divergence >7 days unresolved is a potential Stop trigger.

Contingency Depletion Exceeding 50% or Envelope Overage Exceeding 120% Escalation Level: Compliance and Audit Committee (Audit Escalation) → Co-Chair Steering Board (Scope-Reduction Decision or Supplemental-Appropriation Request) Approval Process: Contingency tracked cumulatively: trigger at 30% (USD 150M spent = co-chair briefing), 50% (USD 250M = scope-reduction planning), 75% (USD 375M = joint budget review with external audit). Any single envelope exceeding 110% of plan triggers co-chair review; exceeding 120% requires approval for supplemental appropriations (veto point: either country can refuse, blocking the overage). Contingency-depletion trajectory is reviewed monthly; if burn rate suggests exhaustion before Phase One end, co-chairs jointly decide: reduce matched sites (2 pairs instead of 3), shorten Phase One (60 days instead of 90), reduce exercise frequency, or defer Phase Two. Supplemental-appropriation request must be approved by both governments' legislatures (estimated 2–4 week process), delaying operations. Rationale: Budget envelopes (seven fixed allocations, USD 5 billion total) are tied to the program's scope and feasibility. Contingency represents 10% slack; depletion beyond 50% indicates systematic underestimation. Envelope overage beyond 120% exceeds the contingency ceiling and requires new funding authority. The plan specifies every expense must map to an envelope, creating transparency but also constraint: if personnel costs surge (attrition, retention bonuses) beyond the USD 750M envelope, the excess consumes contingency. Reaching 50% contingency depletion by Month 6 (2027-04-08) signals that Phase One cannot run the full 90 days without scope reduction. Negative Consequences: Contingency exhaustion forces mid-test scope reduction. Reducing matched sites from 3 to 2 halves exercise load (54 → 36 exercises), reduces replicates per event type from 6–8 to 3–4, and increases confidence intervals from ±12% to ±20%, making verdict ambiguous. Shortening Phase One from 90 to 60 days prevents exercises from reaching planned frequency (6 per month per site = 36 total instead of 54), statistical power declines >50%. Deferring Phase Two forces supplemental-appropriation request (2–4 week legislative process, political veto risk). Budget crisis becomes a political liability; the withholding government can claim Phase One failed due to inefficiency or poor planning.

Monitoring Progress

1. Entry-Condition Gate Milestone Tracking

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Entry-Condition Task Force Status Spreadsheet (bilateral, locked gates and slip thresholds)
  • Bilateral Instrument and Appropriations Status Log
  • Site-Selection and Reciprocal-Access Audit Report Repository
  • Vendor-Participation Registry and Fallback-Ladder Status Tracker
  • Inspector Vetting and Clearance Pipeline Dashboard

Frequency: Weekly (Months 0–5 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-03-08); escalation triggers within 48 hours of >2-week slip detection

Responsible Role: Program Operations Center (Entry-Condition Task Force Lead per country, 1 each) with bilateral coordination; escalates to Co-Chair Steering Board if any gate slips >2 weeks

Adaptation Process: Entry-condition slips (signed instrument, appropriations, site selection, inspector approval, vendor participation, schedule adoption) are tracked against locked deadlines (Months 0.5–3 = 2026-10-23 to 2027-01-08). If a gate slips >2 weeks, the Program Risk Officer alerts both co-chairs within 48 hours. Co-chairs convene an emergency summit within 5 days to assess impact: whether to accelerate subsequent gates (parallel tracks, compressed timelines, contingency reserve), extend overall schedule, or reduce scope (fewer sites, shorter test window). Task force submits an impact-assessment memo recommending timeline adjustment or scope reductions. Co-chairs jointly publish a timeline-change decision within 7 days of slip confirmation.

Adaptation Trigger: Any entry-condition gate (instrument signature, appropriations, domestic access authority, matched-pair approval, inspector approval, vendor-participation registry, covered-equipment schedule) slipping more than 2 weeks beyond locked deadline; cumulative entry-condition delay exceeding 8 weeks (compresses Phase One from 90 to ~45 days, degrading statistical power and confidence intervals from ±10–15% to ±15–20%, rendering detection-rate estimates indefensible); contingency budget consumption for compression reserve exceeding 10% of the USD 500M (USD 50M) within any single 4-week period

2. Reciprocal-Access Parity and Matched-Site Validation

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Reciprocal-Access Audit Report (sealed, per matched pair, Month 1 = 2026-11-08)
  • Functional-Equivalence Scoring Spreadsheet (staging area, lift capacity, access timing)
  • Monthly Site-Compliance Baseline Tracker (4-hour staging access, 48-hour exercise notice compliance)
  • Per-Site Detection-Rate Divergence Analysis (flag if >15% divergence from pooled rate, monthly during Phase One)

Frequency: Pre-Phase-One validation (Months 0–1 = 2026-10-08 to 2026-11-08); monthly parity monitoring during Phase One (Months 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08)

Responsible Role: Site-Selection Track Lead (1 per country, Program Operations Center) for entry-condition audit; Evidence and Verification Committee for Phase-One parity monitoring and detection-rate divergence flagging

Adaptation Process: Entry-condition phase: bilateral site-selection audit teams (technical specialists from each country) visit proposed sites, document access scope, facility layouts and functional equivalence against criteria (staging ≥500 sq m, 24-hour access, lift ≥50 tons, ≥2 maintenance events/month). Mismatched pairs (asymmetric access, <<500 sq m staging, or lift <50 tons at one site) are flagged. Co-chairs review audit reports and jointly approve only pairs meeting functional-equivalence standard; asymmetric pairs are excluded from Phase One rather than included with footnotes. During Phase One: Evidence Committee monitors each site's detection rate monthly, flagging any single site whose detection rate diverges >15% from the pooled detection rate (indicator of asymmetric access or operator resistance). If divergence detected, Program Operations escalates to co-chairs within one week with an assessment of whether the asymmetry is correctable (operator delay, training gap) or systematic (operator shielding suspected). Correctable asymmetry: enforcement action and remediation plan. Systematic asymmetry: site suspension or exclusion from Phase One.

Adaptation Trigger: Reciprocal-access parity audit (Month 1 = 2026-11-08) reveals >1 matched pair with asymmetric access (e.g., one side denied 24-hour staging access, other side grants immediate access; one staging area <500 sq m vs. ≥500 sq m at counterpart). During Phase One, detection-rate divergence >15% between a single site and the pooled rate (e.g., pooled 70%, single site 50%), sustained for ≥2 consecutive months, indicates access asymmetry. Parity score (Definition TBD) falls <85% target (proposed threshold). Operator refusal to comply with baseline access expectations (4-hour staging access, 48-hour exercise notice) confirmed via written violation log; escalation to co-chairs if compliance violations >2 per site per month

3. Vendor-Refusal Fallback-Ladder Implementation and Equipment-Unverifiable-Count Monitoring

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Vendor-Participation Registry and Refusal Log (refusal incidents, fallback rung attempted, timeline, disposition)
  • Accredited Independent-Examiner Status Tracker (capacity, assignments, completion dates per rung per vendor refusal)
  • Unverifiable-Equipment Count Spreadsheet (by site, by equipment class, by cause: vendor refusal, IP-protection claim, attestation unavailable, filter dispute)

Frequency: Continuous incident tracking (refusals logged within 24 hours of occurrence); weekly Vendor Liaison Office status calls; monthly Evidence Committee review of unverifiable counts and fallback-ladder progress

Responsible Role: Vendor Liaison Office (5 per country: legal, compliance, technical, logistics, adjudication) for incident response and fallback-ladder sequencing; Evidence and Verification Committee for unverifiable-equipment root-cause analysis; independent examiner teams (1 per country, pre-staged from testing envelope) for fallback execution

Adaptation Process: Vendor refusal documented by Vendor Liaison Office within 24 hours of notification. Fallback ladder initiated immediately: (1) vendor-supervised testing offered (target 8–12 weeks, often declined); (2) if refused, filtered evidence pathway with filter auditor certification (2–3 days per package); (3) if refused or insufficient, accredited independent-examiner team deployed (8–12 weeks); (4) if access barriers remain, clean-room procedure or validated attestation. Each rung completion documented. If all rungs exhausted or timeline prevents completion before Phase One entry (Month 6 = 2027-04-08), equipment classified as unverifiable and escalated to co-chairs: decision to exclude equipment from the covered-equipment schedule or fail the site from Phase One entry. During Phase One, unverifiable-equipment count tracked monthly. If count exceeds 5% of all equipment at a site or >10% overall, Evidence Committee conducts root-cause analysis: is the evidence-rule too strict (false positives mimicking unverifiable), or are vendors/operators genuinely blocking evidence? Rule miscalibration triggers post-Phase-One review (rule adjustments deferred; thresholds locked for Phase One). Genuine unverifiable counts >10% at a single site become a potential Stop trigger.

Adaptation Trigger: Vendor refusal documented by Month 2 (2026-12-08); fallback ladder incomplete by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23) entry-condition deadline, leaving equipment unverifiable at entry. Unverifiable-equipment count at any site exceeds 5% of equipment assigned to that site (proposed threshold). Unverifiable counts surge to >10% overall across all sites (proposed threshold), triggering Stop-trigger assessment. Multiple simultaneous vendor refusals (≥3 vendors refusing in the same month) at different sites exceeding examiner capacity (estimated 10–16 examiners per country, ~1–2 sites simultaneously), causing queue delays and unresolved refusals to extend past Phase One entry. Vendor refusal attributed to government shielding (one government prevents its vendor/operator from participating in fallback procedures), confirmed via written non-cooperation notice; automatic Stop trigger

4. Evidence-Weighting Rule Calibration and False-Positive/False-Negative Validation

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Draft Layered Evidence Weighting Model (versioned escrow, Month 4.5 = 2027-02-23)
  • Historical-Record Validation Dataset (100–200 equipment-change records per site, applying draft rule to past events)
  • False-Positive and False-Negative Analysis Report (pilot and historical validation, target 10%±3% false positives, <5% false negatives)
  • Evidence-Rule Version-History Log (amendments with effective dates and application to each event)

Frequency: Draft rule placed in escrow Month 4.5 (2027-02-23); historical validation Months 4.5–5.5 (2027-02-23 to 2027-03-23); rule-adjustment decision by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23); final rule locked before Phase One (Month 6 = 2027-04-08). No mid-test amendments during Phase One (Months 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08). Post-Phase-One review permitted.

Responsible Role: Evidence and Verification Committee (co-chairs jointly approving rule drafts and amendments); technical/attestation and equipment-identifier specialists (2 per country) conducting historical validation; independent auditors spot-checking rule application to recorded Phase-One events

Adaptation Process: Evidence Committee drafts the confidential evidence-weighting rule (no single source decisive; specify how attestation, physical inspection, customs records, identifiers, maintenance logs, infrastructure changes and witnessed movement combine into equipment-identity confidence ratings). Draft placed in versioned escrow by Month 4.5 (2027-02-23), jointly approved by both committee co-chairs. Committee applies draft rule to 100–200 historical equipment-change records per site (known ground truth from operator records or maintenance logs). Calculate identity-confidence outputs and compare against known results. Measure false-positive rate (rule flags identity change when operator records confirm no change) and false-negative rate (rule fails to flag an actual change). Target: false positives 7–13% (10% target ±3 points), false negatives <5%. If deviation >5 points (e.g., 25% false positives vs. 10% target), revise the rule and re-validate with a second cohort of historical records by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23). If calibration within 3–5 points of target, flag as a review item but lock the rule. Final rule locked and versioned by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23) for Phase One. During Phase One, maintain a version-history log showing which rule-version was applied to each event. Post-Phase-One, if false-positive or false-negative rates in Phase-One exercises differ materially from historical calibration (>5 points), conduct root-cause analysis (evidence sources differ, inspector procedures differ, equipment changed) and recommend adjustments for Phase Two.

Adaptation Trigger: Historical-record validation (Months 4.5–5 = 2027-02-23 to 2027-03-08) shows false-positive rate >15% or <7% (target 10%±3%, deviation >5 points = requires adjustment). False-negative rate >5% detected in historical validation (proposed threshold). Pilot exercise (Month 5 = 2027-03-08) detection outcomes for identity-verification events differ from historical false-positive prediction by >8 points (e.g., historical validation showed 10% false positives, pilot shows 2% or 18%). Post-Phase-One analysis (after Month 9 = 2027-07-08) reveals Phase-One false-positive or false-negative rates differing >5 points from historical calibration; rule is flagged for possible amendment in Phase Two

5. Blind-Challenge Exercise Design, Execution, and Detection-Rate Monitoring

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Exercise Authority Scenario Registry and Pre-Registration Log (all 54 scenarios locked before first Phase-One execution, Months 3–5 = 2027-01-08 to 2027-03-08)
  • Weekly Exercise-Result Compilation and Incident Log (during Phase One: events run per week, detection outcomes per event type, scoring documentation, cryptographic attestations)
  • Detection-Rate Estimates per Event Type (with 95% confidence intervals, updated weekly as results accumulate; target ≥70% planned, ≥50% unplanned)

Frequency: Pilot exercise Month 5 (2027-03-08), all seven types run once, results used to validate detection procedures but excluded from Phase-One verdict. Scenario pre-registration Months 3–5 (2027-01-08 to 2027-03-08). Phase-One exercises Months 6–9 (2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08): target 6 per month per site = 54 total (6–8 replicates per event type). Weekly exercise-result compilation and detection-rate calculation.

Responsible Role: Exercise Authority Director and core staff (8 total, mixed-nationality, independent from co-chairs) for scenario design, execution, and scoring; Evidence and Verification Committee for detection-rate analysis and asymmetry flagging; independent auditors for spot-check validation of exercise scoring and data integrity

Adaptation Process: Exercise Authority designs seven event-type scenarios (unreported arrival, substituted equipment, inaccurate records, delayed access, disputed identity, vendor refusal, reluctant operator) covering all scenarios required by the bilateral instrument. All scenarios pre-registered before the first Phase-One exercise (locked by end of Month 5 = 2027-03-08) without disclosing specific test cases to inspectors. Pilot exercise (Month 5 = 2027-03-08) runs all seven types once at a non-production test facility to validate detection procedures and scoring consistency; pilot results are training-validation data, not counted toward Phase-One verdict. During Phase One (Months 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08), Exercise Authority executes scenarios in staging, spare-inventory, maintenance or expansion areas without interrupting active computation. Each exercise is scored independently: witness observation, video recording, cryptographic attestation of timestamps and outcomes. Weekly result compilation calculates detection rate per event type (# detected / # attempted) with 95% confidence intervals. If any event type falls significantly below target (e.g., unreported-arrival detection <50% vs. 70% target), Exercise Authority investigates whether procedure is deficient (inadequate inspector training, staging-area access gaps, timing issues) or scenario design is unrealistic. Evidence Committee reviews weekly results and flags any per-site detection divergence >15% from pooled rate (asymmetric access or operator resistance suspected). Monthly report to co-chairs includes detection-rate trajectory and any operational issues (production disruptions, access delays, scenario logistics failures). If exercise load falls below planned frequency due to site disruptions or operator resistance, note the impact on statistical power (fewer replicates per type = wider confidence intervals, reducing verdict defensibility).

Adaptation Trigger: Exercise load falls below 5 per month per site (54-exercise target unmet by Month 8 = 2027-06-08), reducing replicates per event type below minimum of 6, widening confidence intervals beyond ±15% at 95% CL (inadequate statistical power). Detection rate for any event type falls to <50% for planned class or <35% for unplanned class by Month 8 (2027-06-08), indicating procedure or operator-access deficiency. Single-site detection rate diverges >15% from pooled rate for ≥2 consecutive months (asymmetric access or systematic operator non-cooperation suspected). Exercises interrupted or delayed >4 hours from scheduled time (production disruption confirmed); >2 incidents per site per month triggers operator-compliance escalation. Cryptographic attestation discrepancies or witness-score disagreements on exercise outcomes (e.g., inspectors claim equipment was substituted, video shows no substitution); >2 scoring disputes per month escalated to Adjudication Panel for technical review

6. Equipment-Identity Confidence and Ledger Divergence Monitoring

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Replicated Tamper-Evident Ledger (national copies, one per country, hosted at neutral facility; synchronized via signed-digest exchange every 1 hour)
  • Ledger-Divergence Incident Log (timestamp, affected entries, cause: network failure, key-custody incident, backup corruption, tampering suspected; resolution time)
  • Equipment-Identity Confidence Distribution Spreadsheet (# entries scoring high/medium/low confidence per event class; root causes for low-confidence entries)

Frequency: Continuous local recording (at most 5 minutes latency); signed-digest exchange every 1 hour with 30-minute overdue alert; divergence incidents logged within 4 hours of detection. Weekly ledger-integrity audit (sample 5% of events, verify appearance in both national copies). Monthly ledger-divergence and key-custody review (co-chairs briefed).

Responsible Role: Root-of-Trust Key Custody Architecture team (1 principal + 1 deputy per country, 4 total) for key management and recovery procedures; ledger hosting and synchronization team (IT specialists, mapped to the secure-facilities envelope) for technical operations; Compliance and Audit Committee for ledger-integrity verification and post-Phase-One audit

Adaptation Process: Ledger records events locally at each site within 5 minutes of occurrence (cryptographic timestamp, witness signature). Both national copies are maintained in secure, audited facilities. Synchronization: each hour, both countries exchange cryptographic digests (SHA-256 or stronger) of recorded events. Digests are signed by both countries' keys (dual-hold, double-key authorization: both shares required to sign). If a digest mismatch is detected (one side's digest differs from the other's), an automated dual-ledger audit initiates within 4 hours: both countries' ledger teams perform cryptographic verification of affected entries. Co-chairs jointly determine the cause and authorize remediation. If the divergence is due to network failure (entry recorded locally but sync delayed), re-sync when network is restored and flag the delayed-sync event in the ledger. If key-custody incident is suspected (unauthorized signing, key theft), trigger key-recovery ceremony (both countries' key-custody officers convene within 4 hours; revoke compromised key, generate new key, re-sign affected entries). Unresolved divergence exceeding 7 days escalates to emergency summit and triggers partial suspension of ledger-dependent functions (evidence disclosure paused until divergence is resolved). Monthly, independent auditors sample 5% of recorded events (estimated 15–25 per month at typical volume of 5–10 events per day per site) and verify cryptographic signatures against the published key registries and check that each event appears in both national ledger copies within the 1-hour sync bound.

Adaptation Trigger: Ledger-divergence incident occurs (a digest mismatch between national copies); any divergence unresolved for >7 days (hard threshold, proposed). Multiple divergences (≥3) in a single month without clear resolution pattern (systematic sync failures or recurrent key-custody issues). Key-custody incident (lost key, suspected compromise, or contested key): key blocked from signing, ledger entries stall for >8 hours (recovery procedures not executing timely). Ledger audit finds >2% of sampled events (out of 5% sample) with missing signatures or non-matching cryptographic verification. Equipment-identity-confidence distribution shows >20% of entries scoring 'low confidence' due to ledger inconsistencies (unresolved divergence in prior sync)

7. Deadlock Resolution, Adjudication-Caseload, and Discrepancy-Age Monitoring

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Discrepancy Tracking Spreadsheet (case ID, opening date, classification: identity, exit disposition, access delay, vendor refusal, reluctant operator; current age, responsible adjudicators, resolution status)
  • Deadlock Escalation Timeline (case progress: inspector-level discussion [0–10 days], Adjudication Panel referral [day 10–18], co-chair decision [day 18–21]; partial-suspension trigger [day 14]; impaired-confidence trigger [day 21 for identity, day 28 for exit])
  • Adjudication Panel Status Log (cases open, recommendations issued, co-chair decisions, published rationale for overrides if any)

Frequency: Weekly discrepancy-age tracking (Mondays during Phase One, Months 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08); automatic Adjudication Panel convening if case age reaches 10 days; co-chair briefing on cases >21 days (impaired-confidence trigger); escalation to emergency summit if >2 cases exceed 35 days simultaneously

Responsible Role: Program Operations Center (tracking case age and escalation timelines); Adjudication Panel (3 specialists per country, 6 total) for technical recommendations; Co-Chair Steering Board for final decisions and partial-suspension orders; Program Risk Officer for cascade-risk flagging (multiple unresolved discrepancies indicating systematic deadlock)

Adaptation Process: Discrepancies (equipment-identity questions, exit-disposition disputes, access-delay incidents, vendor-refusal outcomes, or reluctant-operator findings) are opened by inspectors or operational teams and logged in the tracking spreadsheet with timestamp. Case begins at day 0. Inspectors and site-level technical teams have 10 days to resolve through evidence review, supplemental inspection, or operator consultation. If unresolved by day 10, the case escalates to the Adjudication Panel (automatic trigger, no co-chair pre-approval needed). Adjudication Panel convenes (both countries' 3 specialists) and reviews the evidence: underlying facts, applicable evidence-weighting rule, any filter disputes or disclosure-tier issues. Panel issues a technical recommendation within 5 days (day 15 from case opening): is the discrepancy 'material' (affects Go/Modify/Stop verdict or creates an audit exception) or 'process' (administrative)? Which evidence category is most probative? Should a retry of the investigation occur? Panel recommendation is non-binding on co-chairs but is published and logged in the ledger; co-chairs must formally confirm or override it. Co-chairs have 3 days (day 18 from case opening) to decide. If co-chairs agree with the Panel's recommendation, case is resolved. If they disagree, co-chairs must publish their override rationale in the ledger (transparency requirement). If co-chairs still deadlock (neither accepts the Panel recommendation nor can agree on an override) by day 18, the case triggers automatic partial suspension at day 14 (earlier threshold): the disputed function (e.g., intake verification if the discrepancy is identity-related; exit procedures if it's a departure disposition) is automatically paused, recorded in the ledger as an event, and both co-chairs are notified. Unrelated verification continues (e.g., if intake is suspended, exit verification and equipment-maintenance monitoring continue). Partial suspension stalls the disputed function but preserves operational continuity. The suspended case remains open and moves to impaired-confidence status at day 21 (for identity disputes) or day 28 (for exit disposition disputes). If multiple cases pile up (estimated capacity ~15 cases per month in adjudication pipeline), and >2 cases simultaneously exceed day 35, a cascade-risk alert triggers: the Program Risk Officer notifies co-chairs that systematic deadlock is occurring, and an emergency summit is convened to assess whether the Adjudication Panel charter needs revision, evidence-rule clarity improved, or whether a broader scope change is warranted.

Adaptation Trigger: Discrepancy age exceeds 10 days without inspector resolution → Adjudication Panel automatically convenes. Discrepancy age exceeds 14 days without Panel recommendation → automatic partial suspension of disputed function (recorded in ledger). Discrepancy age exceeds 21 days (identity) or 28 days (exit) → impaired-confidence status applied (case remains open, function remains suspended; escalation to co-chair summit if suspension >35 days). Two or more cases simultaneously exceeding 35 days of age (≥3 cascading across time horizon suggests systematic co-chair deadlock on adjudication); or adjudication caseload exceeds 20 open cases (estimated capacity 15/month), backlog accumulating → Program Risk Officer flags as cascade risk, triggers emergency co-chair review. Unresolved discrepancies >5 at Phase One conclusion → potential Stop trigger (if combined with other metrics below thresholds)

8. Contingency-Budget Depletion and Envelope-Mapping Compliance

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Monthly Envelope Reconciliation Report (100% invoice sampling: envelope classification accuracy, supporting documents, dollar amount, country, cost center; exception tracking for >2% variance)
  • Contingency-Burn Dashboard (cumulative USD drawn against the 500M pool; percentage benchmarks: 30% [150M] = co-chair briefing, 50% [250M] = scope-reduction planning, 75% [375M] = joint budget review)
  • Quarterly Budget Actuals-vs-Plan Analysis (variance per envelope, per country; overruns >110% and >120% thresholds; forecast through Phase One conclusion)
  • Independent Auditor Reconciliation Report (monthly unclassified summary, audit exceptions and corrective actions)

Frequency: Monthly envelope reconciliation (invoices due by 10th of following month, audit review by 20th, findings published by 25th); weekly budget-status calls (budget analysts, 1 hour); bi-weekly Compliance and Audit Committee meeting (2 hours, deep-dive on envelope variances and contingency burn); quarterly actuals-vs-plan review with co-chairs (co-decision on scope reductions or supplemental-appropriation request if any envelope exceeds 120%)

Responsible Role: Compliance and Audit Committee co-chairs (1 per country, FTE, reporting independently to co-chairs and respective finance ministries); budget analysts (2 per country, tracking invoices and exceptions); independent external auditors (3–5, third-country nationals, signing off on monthly reconciliation and quarterly variance analysis)

Adaptation Process: Invoices and supporting documents from both countries submitted by 10th of following month, classified by envelope and cost center. Budget analysts and envelope auditors review 100% of invoices for proper classification, completeness of documentation, and accuracy of amounts. Exceptions (incorrect envelope, missing documentation, duplicate entries, unexplained variance >2%) are flagged and returned to submitter for correction by 15th. Corrected invoices reconciled by 20th; audit summary published by 25th showing total spend per envelope, percentage of budget consumed, exceptions found and resolved. Monthly reports are bilingual and unclassified (shared with legislatures). Contingency draw requests require approval from both the requesting country's program director and the Compliance Committee co-chair, plus independent auditor review, before disbursement. Contingency-burn rate tracked against cumulative draws: if draws reach 30% of the 500M (150M) by Month 4 (2027-02-08), a co-chair briefing is triggered alerting both to accelerated spending. If 50% (250M) is reached by Month 6 (2027-04-08), scope-reduction planning is initiated: co-chairs jointly decide whether to reduce matched sites (3 pairs → 2), shorten Phase One (90 → 60 days), or defer Phase Two. If 75% (375M) is reached by Month 8 (2027-06-08), a formal joint budget review occurs with independent auditors present, assessing whether the remaining contingency (125M) is sufficient to complete Phase One operations or whether supplemental appropriations are needed (veto point: either country can refuse). Any single envelope exceeding 110% of plan (e.g., personnel envelope USD 750M × 1.1 = 825M) triggers a co-chair review and decision on contingency draw or scope reduction. Exceeding 120% (e.g., 900M) requires a supplemental-appropriation request to both governments' legislatures (estimated 2–4 week process), delaying operations.

Adaptation Trigger: Monthly invoice reconciliation reveals >5% variance in an envelope classification (e.g., 10% of submitted invoices are reclassified to a different envelope), triggering budget-submission process review and training. Cumulative contingency draws reach 30% (150M) by Month 4 (2027-02-08) → co-chair briefing on burn rate and Phase-One feasibility. Cumulative draws reach 50% (250M) by Month 6 (2027-04-08) → mandatory scope-reduction planning (record decision to reduce sites or shorten test window). Any single envelope exceeds 110% (e.g., personnel at 825M vs. 750M plan) → co-chair review and contingency-draw decision. Any envelope exceeds 120% (e.g., personnel at 900M) → supplemental-appropriation request, stop-work risk. Contingency-burn trajectory predicts exhaustion before Phase One end → emergency co-chair summit to authorize scope reduction or budget cap-out. Per-country allocations diverge significantly (e.g., one country spending 2,600M while the other is at 2,400M; proposed threshold: >5% divergence from 50/50 parity) → investigation of cost drivers and rebalancing decision

9. Funding Timeliness and Tranche-Release Synchronization

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Synchronized Tranche-Release Schedule and Status Log (4 synchronized tranches per country: 25% Month 2, 25 = 2026-12-08, 2028-11-08% Month 3, 30 = 2027-01-08, 2029-04-08% Month 5.5, 20 = 2027-03-23, 2028-06-08% Month 9.2 = 2027-07-14; actual deposit dates, amount, country, reconciliation)
  • Tranche-Delay Escalation Tracker (if either tranche is delayed >14 days: co-chair briefing; if >30 days or asymmetric deposits: auto-Stop trigger recorded)

Frequency: Weekly funding-status verification (budget analysts, confirm deposits and timing); immediate escalation if >14-day delay detected (within 24 hours to co-chairs); monthly tranche-release reconciliation (Compliance and Audit Committee)

Responsible Role: Compliance and Audit Committee finance officers (1 per country) for deposit verification; Co-Chair Steering Board for tranche-release authorization and escalation

Adaptation Process: Both countries' tranches are released in synchronized pairs: Tranche 1 (25% = 625M per country) released by Month 2 (2026-12-08) upon instrument signature and appropriation enactment. Tranche 2 (25% = 625M) released by Month 3 (2027-01-08) upon matched-pair approval. Tranche 3 (30% = 750M) released by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23) upon entry-gate certification. Tranche 4 (20% = 500M) released by Month 9.2 (2027-07-14) upon Go/Modify verdict (not conditional on verdict outcome, just on Phase One conclusion). Each tranche is conditional on both countries depositing simultaneously (parity enforcement); if one country delays depositing its share, the other country does not release its portion. If a tranche is delayed >14 days beyond the scheduled release date (e.g., Tranche 1 due Month 2 = 2026-12-08, not deposited by Month 2.5 = 2026-12-23), a co-chair briefing is triggered automatically on day 14. Co-chairs jointly assess the cause (legislative delay, budgetary hold, political objection) and determine whether to extend the deadline, invoke an emergency summit, or escalate to Stop. If tranche delay exceeds 30 days cumulative (either country, any tranche), or if deposits are asymmetric (one country deposits 625M, the other deposits only 500M), the withholding is recorded as a Stop trigger and Phase One is halted without further negotiation (automatic stop-work order).

Adaptation Trigger: Tranche deposit delayed >14 days beyond scheduled release (automatic co-chair briefing and escalation). Tranche deposit delayed >30 days (automatic Stop trigger: funding withholding). Deposits asymmetric: one country's tranche USD amount differs from the other's (proposed threshold: >2% deviation = asymmetric, triggers investigation; >5% = Stop trigger). Tranche release withheld pending political conditions or dispute resolution (any tranche held hostage to a separate negotiation): flags as Stop trigger

Governance Extra

Governance Validation Checks

  1. Completeness Confirmation: All core governance components have been generated across all five stages: (1) Audit details and corruption/misallocation risks identified; (2) Internal governance bodies established (Co-Chair Steering Board, Program Operations, Evidence and Verification, Compliance and Audit, Counterintelligence Oversight, Root-of-Trust Key Custody); (3) Comprehensive implementation plan with 44 sequential and parallel steps spanning Months -1 to 9.5 (2026-09-08 to 2027-07-23); (4) Decision escalation matrix mapping 12 critical issue types to approval authorities and adaptation triggers; (5) Monitoring and progress-tracking framework with six continuous approaches (entry gates, reciprocal access, vendor fallback, evidence-rule calibration, exercises, ledger integrity, deadlock resolution, contingency depletion). All components reference the bilateral instrument, double-key procedures, deadlock thresholds, and Stop triggers. Framework is operationally specific rather than generic.
  2. Internal Consistency Check: Logical alignment across stages is strong but reveals one tension requiring clarification. Implementation plan correctly sequences entry conditions (gates Months 0.5–5.5 = 2026-10-23 to 2027-03-23) before Phase One begins Month 6 (2027-04-08). Escalation matrix maps material finding deadlocks to the Adjudication Panel (correct body from Stage 2) and partial suspension after day 14 (consistent with bilateral instrument threshold). Monitoring framework tracks discrepancy age against these thresholds automatically. However, the evidence-rule validation (pilot exercise Month 5 = 2027-03-08 plus historical validation Months 4.5–5.5 = 2027-02-23 to 2027-03-23) and the Exercise Authority's pre-registration of all 54 Phase-One scenarios (completed by end of Month 5 = 2027-03-08) occur simultaneously with critical entry-gate completions (matched-pair approval Month 3 = 2027-01-08, entry certification Month 5.5 = 2027-03-23). If entry gates slip 2–4 weeks (identified as high-likelihood risk), the evidence-rule calibration window (which depends on historical data from confirmed participating sites) and scenario pre-registration become compressed. The framework documents this risk and triggers emergency summits, but the operational dependency between entry-gate completion and exercise-authority readiness is not explicitly locked in the monitoring plan: it should add a check that scenario pre-registration cannot proceed without final site approval (Month 5.5 = 2027-03-23 entry certification must precede scenario finalization).
  3. Specific Gap 1 – Clarity of Role Definition for Advisors and Independent Parties: The Evidence and Verification Committee includes 'red-team representatives (1 per country)' as voting members, yet the Exercise Authority is described as 'mixed-nationality, independent' and designed to be insulated from co-chair and inspector input until after execution. The distinction between the red-team role (designing scenarios that test what each side doubts most) and the Exercise Authority role (independent scenario execution) is operationally unclear. Specifically: (a) Do red-team representatives sit on the Exercise Authority, or do they propose scenarios to the Exercise Authority (which then accepts/rejects independently)? (b) If red-team members are on the Evidence Committee but not on the Exercise Authority, how do they influence Exercise Authority scenario selection without compromising independence? (c) Are red-team members' dual roles (committee advisor + scenario proposer) governed by conflict-of-interest rules? The framework specifies red-team participation in scenario design ('Each country's red team may nominate challenge types but the authority alone decides whether to execute it and when') yet does not document whether red-team members have access to Exercise Authority deliberations or result data before Phase One conclusion. Recommend explicit charter section on red-team/Exercise-Authority firewall and conflict-of-interest rules for dual-role members.
  4. Specific Gap 2 – Insufficient Procedural Specificity for Key-Custody Compromise Response Under Dual-Hold Geometry: The Root-of-Trust Key Custody Architecture team (4 total: principal + deputy per country) is tasked with detecting and responding to key-custody incidents (lost keys, suspected compromise, coercion of an officer). The framework specifies that 'both shares required to sign' (dual-hold, double-key authorization principle), yet the key-recovery procedure defines: 'both countries' key-custody officers convene within 4 hours; conduct a 48-hour investigation; issue a joint revocation attestation signed by both countries.' This creates a logical circularity: if a key-custody officer from one country is compromised (coerced or bribed to sign unauthorized entries), how can the joint recovery procedure proceed if that officer is under duress? Specifically: (a) If the US officer is compromised, can the Chinese officer alone authorize a new key-generation ceremony? (b) If both countries' officers disagree on whether a compromise has occurred (one insists the key was lost, the other suspects intentional theft and unauthorized signing), which country can force a key revocation? (c) What is the protocol if one country claims the other's key-custody officer has been compromised and refuses to participate in ceremonies? The framework assigns the Counterintelligence Oversight Board authority to investigate 'suspected breaches,' yet key-custody incidents (cryptographic key compromise) are not explicitly assigned to the CI Board's investigative purview, only to the key-custody team's technical review. Recommend explicit escalation procedure linking CI Board breach investigations to key-custody incident response, including protocols for unilateral key revocation if dual agreement cannot be reached.
  5. Specific Gap 3 – Ambiguous Termination Authority and Scope Reopening Clause for Stop/Modify Verdicts: The escalation matrix and monitoring framework define Stop triggers and Modify outcomes but do not specify who decides whether Phase One can be restarted, what Phase Two conditions must be met before restart (if Modify is chosen), or whether the bilateral instrument survives a Stop verdict or must be renegotiated. Specifically: (a) If Phase One is halted via a Stop trigger (e.g., government shields an operator), does the bilateral instrument remain in force for a future restart attempt, or is it terminated and renegotiation required? (b) If a Modify verdict is reached, is Phase Two automatically authorized (same bilateral instrument, same scope), or must both governments re-appropriate funds and amend the instrument? (c) Who has authority to declare Phase One complete versus 'inconclusive, awaiting Phase Two'—is it a joint co-chair decision (double-key) or is the verdict itself mechanically determined, leaving no decision authority? (d) The canonical facts state 'OPEN: whether Modify-directed rework or any Phase Two is funded from the unspent USD 5.0B or needs new appropriations.' This leaves Phase Two funding as an undefined veto point; if one country withholds Phase-Two funding after a Modify verdict, is that a separate Stop trigger, or does the program simply pause indefinitely? Recommend explicit closure rules stating: (i) Stop verdict = bilateral instrument remains in force pending restart negotiation (either country can propose restart); (ii) Modify verdict = Phase Two scope and conditions must be jointly defined by co-chairs within 30 days and submitted to legislatures for re-appropriation decision; (iii) Unresolved Phase-Two funding decision = program suspended indefinitely (treated as a de facto Stop).
  6. Specific Gap 4 – Missing Definition of 'Material' vs. 'Process' Discrepancies and Adjudication Authority Boundary: The Adjudication Panel is tasked with classifying discrepancies as 'material' (affects Go/Modify/Stop verdict or audit exception) or 'process' (administrative), yet the governance framework does not provide the classification criteria or examples. The escalation matrix states the Panel 'recommends' classification but does not define when co-chairs can override the Panel's material/process determination or what happens if co-chairs disagree. Specifically: (a) Is a discrepancy 'material' if it involves a single piece of equipment (e.g., one server's identity status ambiguous at one site) or only if it affects an entire equipment class or site? (b) If the Panel classifies a case as 'process' but the co-chairs believe it is 'material,' do co-chairs have unilateral override authority, or must they jointly agree on reclassification? (c) If an unverifiable-equipment count is classified 'process' by the Panel because the vendor refusal fallback was attempted in good faith, can a co-chair unilaterally escalate it to 'material' status and use it as grounds for a Stop trigger? (d) The Compliance and Audit Committee has authority to flag 'envelope-mapping exceptions' (>2% variance) but not to classify their materiality; who decides if an envelope misallocation is a 'material' audit exception vs. a 'process' reclassification? Recommend explicit materiality rubric specifying: (i) material if affects Go/Modify/Stop thresholds or involves >3 equipment items; (ii) process if administrative or affects <3 items; (iii) Panel classification is binding on both co-chairs unless jointly overridden with published rationale.

Tough Questions

  1. Entry-Condition Compression Risk: If the bilateral instrument signature slips from the planned Month 1 (2026-11-08) deadline to Month 2 (2026-12-08) due to legislative delays, and this cascades to a 4-week cumulative slip in entry-gate completion (moved from Month 5.5 = 2027-03-23 to Month 6.5 = 2027-04-23), how will Phase One's 90-day window be preserved—by extending the clock to Month 15 (2028-01-08), compressing the test to 60 days (reducing exercises from 54 to 36 and statistical confidence from ±12% to ±20%), or by reducing matched sites from 3 to 2 pairs? Which scope reduction will co-chairs choose, and by what date must the decision be published to legislatures?
  2. Evidence-Rule False-Positive Calibration Deficiency: The framework specifies that the draft evidence-weighting rule will be validated on 100–200 historical equipment-change records per site (Months 4.5–5 = 2027-02-23 to 2027-03-08) with a target false-positive rate of 10% ± 3 percentage points. If the pilot validation shows false-positive rate of 18% (within the acceptable band but near the upper bound), and Phase-One exercises subsequently yield a false-positive rate of 22%, does the Evidence Committee immediately suspend the rule pending adjustment (risking mid-test procedural disruption), or lock the rule as planned and defer adjustment to post-Phase-One review (risking inflation of discrepancy counts and adjudication overload)? What is the pre-agreed threshold for mid-test rule adjustment, and who has authority to override the 'rule frozen through Phase One' policy?
  3. Deadlock-Triggered Partial-Suspension Operationalization: The framework specifies automatic partial suspension of a disputed function (e.g., intake verification paused, exit procedures paused) after 14 days of co-chair deadlock without pre-approval. If both countries' inspectors at a site are trained to conduct intake verification, and that function is suspended pending a deadlocked discrepancy resolution, who authorizes the suspension reversal when the deadlock is resolved (the co-chairs who were deadlocked, or an automatic procedure)? If suspension remains in effect for >35 days, does the site automatically fail Phase One, or does it continue operating under partial suspension? If 2+ sites are under partial suspension simultaneously (different disputed functions at each), how is Phase-One statistical validity maintained for exercises that depend on the suspended functions?
  4. Vendor-Refusal Fallback-Ladder Timing and Feasibility: The framework pre-stages one accredited independent-examiner team per country (5–8 specialists) from the USD 500M testing envelope. If 3 vendors simultaneously refuse vendor-supervised testing during Phase One (Months 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08) and all require independent-examiner validation (each taking 8–12 weeks), how are 3 concurrent examinations (estimated 15–24 weeks of work per country's team of 5–8) completed within a 90-day window? Specifically, provide the capacity constraint analysis: how many independent-examiner full-time-equivalents are actually available per country, how many concurrent examinations can each team conduct, and what is the maximum queue delay if vendor-refusal demand exceeds capacity? At what queue age does a refusal become a Stop trigger?
  5. Reciprocal-Access Parity Detection and Remediation During Operations: The framework specifies that if a single site's detection rate diverges >15% from the pooled detection rate for 2+ consecutive months during Phase One, the Evidence Committee flags asymmetric access and escalates to co-chairs for investigation. However, the framework does not specify a remediation timeline: if the investigation confirms operator non-cooperation at a US site (denying immediate staging access), can the co-chairs unilaterally mandate the operator to comply, or does the US government have final authority? If operator non-compliance cannot be reversed mid-test, is the site immediately suspended (removing 1 of 3 matched pairs, halving exercise load), or does the site continue operating with acknowledged asymmetry, accepting lower statistical power and contested Go verdict? Provide the explicit authority chain: Program Operations → co-chairs → national government authority → operator enforcement mechanism, with timeline.
  6. Ledger-Divergence Forensic Investigation Authority Under Dual-Custody Governance: If a ledger divergence is discovered (Site A's entry appears in the US national copy but missing from the Chinese copy, or vice versa) and investigation determines that one country's key-custody officer may have signed unauthorized entries, what is the forensic procedure? Does the Counterintelligence Oversight Board investigate (counterintelligence allegation)? Does the Root-of-Trust Key Custody Architecture team investigate (cryptographic anomaly)? Or does a joint trilateral team (both countries + independent auditor) investigate? Who has authority to declare a key-custody incident 'confirmed' vs. 'unconfirmed'? If both countries' co-chairs disagree on whether the divergence was caused by network failure (no misconduct) or by key compromise (requires revocation), how is the disagreement resolved without a casting vote, and how long can the ledger remain diverged pending resolution?
  7. Final Verdict Threshold Ambiguity and Mechanical Scoring Enforcement: The framework specifies that verdict thresholds are 'pre-registered and locked before first Phase-One exercise' and that verdict scoring is 'mechanical, no judgment call.' However, if the pooled detection-rate estimate falls in the ambiguous zone (e.g., 72% with 95% confidence interval 60–84%, straddling the 70% Go threshold), and the two co-chairs interpret the interval differently (one says 'upper bound is 84%, well above 70%, Go is justified'; the other says 'lower bound is 60%, below 70%, Modify is required'), how is the mechanical scoring rule applied when both interpretations are arithmetically valid? Which co-chair's interpretation prevails, or must a mathematical rule be pre-specified (e.g., 'Go requires that the lower bound of the 95% confidence interval exceeds the threshold')? Provide the explicit mechanical rule for verdict determination when confidence intervals straddle thresholds.

Summary

The Consortium governance framework is a rigorous, bilateral double-key structure designed to operate an unprecedented 90-day US–China frontier-computing equipment-verification proof-of-concept with USD 5 billion in fixed appropriations, mirrored national inspectorates (180 per country), and tamper-evident replicated ledgers. The framework balances credible detection (through blind-challenge exercises and layered evidence) with operational continuity (partial suspension instead of brittle shutdowns), transparent parity (reciprocal site selection and matching), and constrained scope (declared-equipment changes only, no hidden-facility detection). Strengths include explicit entry-condition gates with 2-week slip escalation, pre-registered verdict thresholds locked before exercises begin, automatic deadlock escalation via the Adjudication Panel, and comprehensive risk-tracking via weekly KPI dashboards and monthly audits. Key governance levers—evidence-weighting rule calibration, deadlock-and-suspension mechanics, exercise independence, verdict threshold clarity, and inspector information barriers—are identified and operationalized. However, critical ambiguities remain in red-team/Exercise-Authority firewall definitions, key-custody compromise response under dual-hold geometry, Stop/Modify scope-reopening authority, material-vs-process discrepancy classification criteria, and mechanical verdict-scoring rules when confidence intervals straddle thresholds. These gaps should be resolved in the bilateral instrument and committee charters before Phase One entry (Month 5.5 = 2027-03-23) to prevent mid-test disputes over procedure authority and threshold interpretation.

Suggestion 1 - IAEA Safeguards System (including JCPOA Verification and Monitoring in Iran, 2016 onward)

The International Atomic Energy Agency verifies declared nuclear material and equipment through inventory accounting, seals, cameras, and inspections. Under the 2015 JCPOA, the IAEA added continuous monitoring of declared centrifuge manufacturing and storage, plus a procurement channel for dual-use items. It is a multi-decade, multinational program run from Vienna. The JCPOA monitoring was sharply curtailed after 2021, which shows the regime's fragility.

Success Metrics

Continuity of knowledge on declared items (qualitative, per IAEA reports). Regular public IAEA verification reports (quarterly during JCPOA). Number of inspection days and installed monitoring devices (figures not verified; request from IAEA). Loss of continuity after curtailed access, a failure indicator.

Risks and Challenges Faced

Host-state access limits: mitigated by pre-agreed access arrangements and managed-access rules; later curtailment shows the limit of this mitigation. Protecting proprietary information: handled through confidentiality regimes and restricted inspector knowledge. Data gaps when monitoring lapses: mitigated by sealed recordings and continuity-of-knowledge rules; lesson for ledger synchronization bounds. Political contestation of findings: partly handled by Board of Governors reporting; the Consortium needs its own double-key deadlock rules.

Where to Find More Information

https://www.iaea.org (Safeguards section and Board of Governors reports) IAEA Safeguards Glossary and Safeguards Implementation Reports on iaea.org https://www.armscontrol.org (Arms Control Association JCPOA monitoring summaries)

Actionable Steps

Contact the IAEA Department of Safeguards through its public information office at iaea.org to request technical briefings on seals, surveillance and continuity of knowledge. Approach the IAEA Office of Legal Affairs for the structure of safeguards agreements and managed access. Seek former inspectors via IAEA alumni and think-tank networks (for example Arms Control Association or Federation of American Scientists) for interviews.

Rationale for Suggestion

Closest analogue for declared-equipment change verification: tracking arrival, storage, transfer and removal of declared items with layered evidence (seals, surveillance, records, physical checks) while excluding undeclared-site detection. It also shows how to protect proprietary information through managed access. Geographic proximity is limited; chosen for mechanism fit. Not a bilateral US–China arrangement.

Suggestion 2 - OPCW Chemical Weapons Convention Industry Verification Regime

The Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons, based in The Hague, conducts declared-facility inspections under the Chemical Weapons Convention (in force since 1997). It uses declarations, data monitoring, on-site inspections and managed-access procedures at commercial and state facilities, including destruction verification witnessed by inspectors.

Success Metrics

Share of declared chemical weapons stockpiles destroyed under verification (OPCW reports; exact figure not verified here). Number of industry inspections per year (published in OPCW annual reports). Absence of confirmed proprietary information breaches (OPCW states confidentiality as a core principle; verify with OPCW).

Risks and Challenges Faced

Protecting commercial secrets during inspections: mitigated by managed-access rules, inspector confidentiality obligations and inspection-zone limits. Inspector burden and cost: handled via sampling and risk-based site selection. Disputes over findings: addressed through consultation and clarification procedures and an Executive Council. Verification of destruction timelines: handled with continuous witnessed monitoring.

Where to Find More Information

https://www.opcw.org (Verification and Industry pages) OPCW annual reports on opcw.org Chemical Weapons Convention Verification Annex text on opcw.org

Actionable Steps

Contact the OPCW Verification Division via the public contact form on opcw.org for briefings on managed access and confidentiality. Request the Confidentiality Policy and Verification Annex guidance from OPCW Legal Office. Interview national authority staff (for example the US Commerce Department Bureau of Industry and Security CWC office) on industry inspection preparation.

Rationale for Suggestion

Strong fit for managed access at commercial operators, confidentiality for proprietary processes, and witnessed destruction as a disposition type like the Exit Protocol. Covers both private firms and state sites, similar to the US hyperscale versus Chinese state-operated asymmetry. Not US–China bilateral, but both states are parties.

Suggestion 3 - US–Russia START I / New START Verification and Joint Compliance and Inspection Commission

The START I Treaty (1991–2009) and New START (2011–2026) used on-site inspections, unique identifiers on declared items, notifications, data exchanges and a bilateral commission (Joint Compliance and Inspection Commission, later the Bilateral Consultative Commission) to resolve disputes. Inspections were suspended in 2020 and Russia suspended participation in New START in 2023; the treaty expired in February 2026.

Success Metrics

Multiple thousands of inspections conducted under START I (approximate; verify with State Department archives). Treaty-limited deployed warhead data exchanged twice yearly under New START (State Department records). Sustained operation for roughly 25 years across both treaties, ending in suspension and expiry.

Risks and Challenges Faced

Inspector reciprocity disputes: managed through equal rights written into the treaty. Disagreement on compliance findings: handled in the bilateral commission without a casting vote. Protecting sensitive design data: handled by limited-access inspection protocols. Political breakdown: not fully mitigated; inspections lapsed, supporting the Consortium's Stop triggers and funding conditions.

Where to Find More Information

https://www.state.gov (Bureau of Arms Control, Deterrence and Stability archives) https://www.armscontrol.org (New START fact sheets) https://www.sipri.org (arms control yearbook chapters)

Actionable Steps

Contact the State Department Bureau of Arms Control, Deterrence and Stability public affairs office for declassified verification history. Approach SIPRI's arms control program or the Arms Control Association research staff for expert interviews. Consult former US On-Site Inspection Agency (now DTRA) alumni via the Defense Threat Reduction Agency public affairs office.

Rationale for Suggestion

Best bilateral precedent for mirrored inspection, unique identifiers on declared items, notification rules and equal-footing dispute commissions between adversaries. Also shows failure modes: suspension and eventual lapse. Not a computing regime and not US–China.

Suggestion 4 - CTBTO International Monitoring System and International Data Centre (SECONDARY SUGGESTION)

The Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty Organization, in Vienna, operates a global network of monitoring stations and a data centre that distributes authenticated data to member states. Stations use tamper-protected, digitally signed data transmission to the data centre. The treaty has not entered into force, but the system operates provisionally.

Success Metrics

Share of planned stations certified (CTBTO publishes; figure not verified here). Data availability rates published by CTBTO.

Risks and Challenges Faced

Data authentication across rivals: handled with digital signatures and certified stations. Station host cooperation: handled by host agreements and certification.

Where to Find More Information

https://www.ctbto.org (Verification Regime pages)

Actionable Steps

Contact the CTBTO Public Information office via ctbto.org to request technical contacts on data authentication and station certification.

Rationale for Suggestion

Secondary: relevant for authenticated, signed data flows shared with all parties, equal data access for rival states, and station certification procedures, informing ledger synchronization and key custody. Less relevant for physical inspection.

Summary

No direct precedent exists for US–China hardware-change verification of frontier computing. The closest real references are arms-control and nonproliferation verification regimes: the IAEA safeguards system, the OPCW industry inspection regime, and US–Soviet/Russian START verification with its Joint Compliance and Inspection Commission. The IAEA–Iran Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) monitoring adds a relevant example of continuous, equipment-focused monitoring. Secondary reference: the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty Organization (CTBTO) International Monitoring System. Geographic and cultural proximity is limited: none of these is US–China, so each is chosen for its mechanisms (declared-item accounting, seals and surveillance, managed access, bilateral commissions, dispute procedures). Figures are not independently verified here; contact the named organizations for authoritative data. Commercial elements are Not applicable; the lessons concern mission justification, governance and fiscal accountability.

1. Entry-Condition Gate Completion and Timeline Risk

Entry-condition gates are a hard constraint on Phase One credibility. Gate slippage directly compresses the 90-day test window and widens statistical confidence intervals from defensible ±12% to indefensible ±20-25%, making the final Go/Modify/Stop verdict ambiguous or non-credible. Without binding timelines, external escalation authority and parallel-track acceleration, the plan becomes vulnerable to sequential delays that cascade. This data collection validates whether the 12-week entry-condition timeline is operationally achievable and whether the scope-reduction backstop is credible and pre-authorized.

Data to Collect

  • Bilateral instrument draft language status and co-chair sign-off date (target Month 1 = 2026-11-08)
  • Domestic access-authority legislative or executive-order status per country and enactment date (target Month 2 = 2026-12-08)
  • Matched-pair site nominations, reciprocal-access audit results and co-chair approval date (target Month 3 = 2027-01-08)
  • Inspector security clearance and vetting completion rate by cohort and projected 80% certified date (target Month 5 = 2027-03-08)
  • Vendor written-commitment registry (participating, fallback, or refusal per vendor) and published registry date (target Month 4 = 2027-02-08)

Simulation Steps

  • Create an Entry-Condition Task Force simulation tool (spreadsheet or project-management software, e.g., Microsoft Project, Asana, Smartsheet) tracking seven gates with interdependencies, parallel-track options and timeline compression scenarios; model entry-condition slip impact on Phase One window duration and statistical confidence interval widening (e.g., 4-week slip = 86-day Phase One, ±14% confidence vs. ±12% baseline)
  • Run a bilateral-negotiation timeline benchmark (using historical START, JCPOA and OPCW instrument-negotiation records): typical duration per agreement type, common bottlenecks (legislative vetting, vendor coordination, site access approval); compare against the plan's 12-week target
  • Simulate contingency-draw scenarios under compression: frontload USD 50-100M of the contingency (within 8 weeks) by deploying parallel tracks (simultaneous vetting of inspectors, site audits, vendor outreach); model the burn rate and trigger-point analysis (30%, 50%, 75% drawdown thresholds against actual timeline)
  • Build a scope-reduction decision tree in a modeling tool (Lucidchart, draw.io, Miro): if instrument signature slips to Month 1.5 (2026-11-23), site-selection slips to Month 2 (2026-12-08), and training completion hits Month 3.5 (2027-01-23), what is the minimum viable Phase One scope (e.g., 2 pairs, 60 days) and how are trade-offs documented?
  • Collect actual milestone-status data (weekly reports from the Entry-Condition Task Force, starting Month 0 = 2026-10-08) against the baseline roadmap: track Gate 1 (instrument) status percentage-complete, projected completion date, risks and mitigations; repeat for Gates 2-7

Expert Validation Steps
