  • Consult bilateral arms-control treaty negotiators (e.g., State Department Bureau of Arms Control, Deterrence and Stability; Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs treaty office) to validate the 12-week instrument-negotiation timeline against precedent (JCPOA took 2+ years; New START took 9 months formal negotiation plus 2 years from Agreed Framework; START I took 9 months); obtain expert judgment on which gates are historically fastest (domestic authority enactment vs. site selection vs. vendor agreement) and which typically slip
  • Engage a former OSCE inspector-deployment coordinator or equivalent (e.g., retired OSCE/ODIHR official) to validate inspector-vetting and training timelines: typical clearance turnaround (4-12 weeks), typical training-course duration before deployment (2-4 weeks), typical attrition rate during vetting (5-15%), contingency staffing buffer (minimum 20-30% of baseline); confirm whether 80% certification by Month 5 (2027-03-08) is achievable with parallel-cohort training
  • Obtain written commitment from both co-chairs' offices (via bilateral legal team) that the Entry-Condition Task Force will report weekly (every Monday, 09:00 CET) to both co-chairs and that any gate slipping >2 weeks will trigger an emergency summit within 5 days; secure approval for the scope-reduction decision authority (external escalation official or co-chair deputies) and the USD 50-100M compression reserve allocation
  • Have the bilateral legal team review the draft instrument language (deadlock procedures, suspension triggers, threshold lock-down clauses) for internal consistency and enforceability by Month 1 (2026-11-08); confirm that 'no amendment after any results known' language and 'automatic partial suspension' are unambiguous and do not contain procedural-exception loopholes
  • Conduct a formal procurement-readiness audit (e.g., through a third-country auditor or international organization) on neutral-facility site selection: confirm that Geneva or Singapore (the two candidates) can deliver an ISO 27001-certified, 1,000+ sq m facility by Month 3 (2027-01-08); verify hardening feasibility, staffing availability and host-country permits

Responsible Parties

  • Entry-Condition Task Force (co-chairs' offices, US and China); weekly reporting to co-chairs and bilateral legal team
  • Bilateral legal implementation team (3 attorneys per side) drafting instrument language and reviewing gate interdependencies
  • External escalation authority (named neutral third-country official or named co-chair deputies) with emergency-summit convening power and scope-reduction decision authority
  • Independent inspector-vetting and training coordinator (both countries' personnel officers) tracking recruitment and clearance pipeline
  • Joint facility-procurement team coordinating neutral-site selection and host-country negotiations

Assumptions

  • High: Bilateral instrument signature is feasible within 4 weeks (Month 0.5 = 2026-10-23) with parallel vetting and compressed legal review.
  • High: Site-selection reciprocal-access parity can be confirmed by Month 3 (2027-01-08) using pre-prepared audit templates and no fundamental asymmetry will block any of the 2-4 planned pairs.
  • Medium: Inspector recruitment and security vetting (300+ personnel, both countries) can achieve 80% certification by Month 5 (2027-03-08) using parallel-cohort training and concurrent vetting.
  • Medium: Vendor written-commitment registry will identify at least 3-4 major vendors willing to participate directly or via fallback procedures, allowing sufficient equipment coverage for a credible test.
  • Medium: Emergency scope-reduction authority (2 pairs, 60-day test) is pre-authorized and carries political acceptance in both countries as a backstop to prevent timeline extension beyond Month 5.5 (2027-03-23).

SMART Validation Objective

By Month 3 (2027-01-08), validate that at least 5 of the 7 entry-condition gates are met or are on track for completion by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23) (bilateral instrument signed, domestic authority enacted, matched pairs approved, 70%+ inspector clearances complete, vendor registry published); if cumulative slippage exceeds 4 weeks (any combination of gates), trigger the emergency scope-reduction decision (2 pairs, 60-day Phase One, finalized by Month 4 = 2027-02-08) so entry certification can occur by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23) without further compression.

Notes

  • The Entry-Condition Task Force is the critical governance hub for timeline discipline; without it, gates are managed independently and slippage compounds undetected.
  • The scope-reduction backstop (2 pairs, 60-day test) is politically contentious and must be pre-approved as a binding option, not a contingency negotiation, to prevent stalling at the decision point.
  • Compressed timelines (instrument in 4 weeks, site selection in 8 weeks total, vetting in 4 weeks) are unprecedented in bilateral arms-control agreements; historical data from JCPOA, New START and OPCW will anchor expert judgment on feasibility.
  • Inspector recruitment from Month 0 (2026-10-08) is front-loaded; later cohorts (Months 2-4 = 2026-12-08 to 2027-02-08) must not be contingent on Gate 1 (instrument) completion, or vetting bottlenecks will emerge.
  • External escalation authority must be named, pre-empowered and operationally independent; co-chairs cannot delegate to each other (double-key rule), so a neutral third party or explicitly authorized deputies must have binding authority.

2. Confidential Evidence-Weighting Rule Validation and Miscalibration Risk

The evidence-weighting rule is the technical foundation for equipment-identity confidence and discrepancy classification. Miscalibration (false-positive rate 20–30% instead of 10%) directly overloads the adjudication system (estimated capacity 15 cases/month vs. 30–50 cases/month at 20% false positives), causing discrepancies to age past automatic-suspension thresholds (days 14, 21, 28) and triggering cascading partial suspensions. Validation on historical records alone is insufficient because historical data reflect benign, cooperative operations; adversarial synthetic cases test whether the rule detects gaming by operators or vendors. This data collection validates the rule before Phase One exercises begin, ensuring adjudication capacity is not exhausted by miscalibration.

Data to Collect

  • Historical equipment-change record dataset (100–200 events per site covering 4–6 weeks of maintenance and customs records) with ground truth (known equipment identity, disposition, serial numbers) for pilot validation at Month 2 (2026-12-08)
  • Adversarial synthetic test-case library (20–30 scenarios per site mimicking operator gaming: misidentified serial, swapped headers, forged attestations, delayed access, omitted vendor signatures) and expected classification outputs from reference-panel expert judgment
  • Draft confidential evidence-weighting rule (locked in versioned escrow by Month 1.5 = 2026-11-23) specifying weights per evidence layer (attestation, physical inspection, customs records, identifiers, maintenance logs, infrastructure changes, witnessed movement) and decision logic (contradiction vs. accumulation)
  • Pilot-validation scorecard (false-positive rate, false-negative rate, unverifiable-equipment count, confidence-band outputs) comparing rule output to ground truth on historical records and synthetic scenarios
  • Rule-amendment decision log (if deviation >±5 points from target, document adjustment weights, re-validation cohort results and co-chair double-key approval timestamp)

Simulation Steps

  • Establish a Rule Validation Task Force (2–3 statisticians, 2–3 red-team members, 1–2 domain experts per country, USD 2–3M budget from the testing envelope) by Month 1 (2026-11-08) to design and manage the validation workflow
  • Extract 100–200 historical equipment-change records per site from each participating datacenter (via operator cooperation under confidentiality agreements) by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23): capture events spanning 4–6 weeks (e.g., arrival records, maintenance logs, customs clearance, equipment removal, serial-number documentation)
  • Use forensic-analysis software (e.g., R or Python with statistical packages) to apply the draft evidence rule to historical records and compute false-positive rate (classified as identity discrepancy when ground truth shows equipment matches), false-negative rate (missed discrepancies) and unverifiable-equipment count; document output distribution by evidence-layer combination
  • Design synthetic adversarial test cases (20–30 per site) using a scenario-generation tool (spreadsheet with case templates) or a red-team workshop: construct equipment records with deliberate mismatches (serial mismatch + matching maintenance = rule contradiction test; delayed access + missing attestation = evidence-insufficiency test) and document the expected classification that the rule should produce
  • Apply the rule to synthetic cases and measure detection rate (% of seeded adversarial cases correctly flagged as lower-confidence or discrepancy); document false-positive rate (benign cases misclassified as discrepancies) and false-negative rate (adversarial cases missed by the rule)
  • Create a calibration-confidence visualization tool (heat map or decision-tree diagram) showing rule output (confidence score or discrepancy flag) across a grid of evidence combinations (e.g., attestation + customs match but maintenance log missing = 65% confidence; no attestation + customs mismatch + identity dispute = 35% confidence) so both sides can audit whether thresholds are reasonable

Expert Validation Steps

  • Convene a Reference-Panel Workshop (Month 2 = 2026-12-08, 2 days, 3–4 senior evidence-assessment specialists per country, 1 independent foreign expert) to independently score each synthetic scenario (20–30 per country) without knowing the rule's output; document panel consensus on what confidence each scenario should receive ('this scenario shows equipment substitution with partial vendor attestation = should score 50–60% confidence, not 70%')
  • Compare Rule Output to Reference Panel: histogram of rule scores vs. panel scores for each scenario; if mean absolute error exceeds 10 percentage points (3+ scenarios substantially misprioritized), flag the rule as miscalibrated and recommend weight adjustment
  • Engage an independent statistician (from a neutral third country or academic institution, pre-approved by both co-chairs) to audit the pilot-validation methodology: confirm that the historical-records sample is representative, that synthetic cases are realistic, that false-positive and false-negative definitions are standardized, and that confidence intervals around the pilot rates are properly computed
  • Request formal sign-off from both evidence-rule owners (accountable specialists per the Layered Evidence Weighting Model) in the form of a 'Rule Calibration Confidence Memo' (classified, 2–3 pages) documenting: historical-validation dataset, pilot false-positive and false-negative rates, deviation from 10% false-positive target, adjustment justification (if adjusted), adversarial-scenario results, residual uncertainty, and a statement that the rule is fit-for-phase-one or requires further refinement
  • Have the bilateral legal implementation team review the rule for patent or intellectual-property ambiguity: confirm that the evidence-weighting logic does not inadvertently reveal either country's authentication procedures, security standards or proprietary processes; if sensitivity is discovered, apply legal confidentiality language to the rule escrow

Responsible Parties

  • Rule Validation Task Force (statisticians, red teams, domain experts, both countries); reporting to co-chairs by Month 2.5 (2026-12-23)
  • Evidence-rule owners (accountable specialists from both sides) providing final calibration sign-off
  • Reference-Panel Workshop facilitators and independent statistician conducting external audit
  • Bilateral legal team reviewing intellectual-property and confidentiality implications of the rule
  • Participating datacenter operators providing historical records under confidentiality agreements

Assumptions

  • Medium: Participating sites can extract 100–200 historical equipment-change records per site (4–6 weeks of logs) with documented ground truth (known correct identity and disposition) for comparison against rule output.
  • High: Synthetic adversarial test cases (20–30 per site) can be designed credibly using IAEA, OPCW and START precedent and will expose rule miscalibration if false-negative rate exceeds 15% on gaming scenarios.
  • High: Rule false-positive rate will cluster near the 10% target (7–13% at ±3 points tolerance); if deviation exceeds ±5 points, a second-cohort validation is feasible by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23) without delaying Phase One clock.
  • Medium: The Rule Validation Task Force and Reference Panel will have sufficient expertise and independence to produce credible calibration recommendations; both co-chairs will accept the panel's judgment (within published confidence limits) rather than reopening the rule post-validation.
  • Medium: The evidence-weighting rule does not inadvertently leak either country's authentication, identification or security procedures; legal confidentiality review will catch any sensitive technical details before the rule is locked.

SMART Validation Objective

By Month 2 (2026-12-08), complete historical-record and synthetic-scenario pilot testing and deliver a Calibration Confidence Memo signed by both evidence-rule owners confirming: (1) false-positive rate within 7–13% (10% ±3 points), (2) false-negative rate on adversarial cases under 15%, (3) no material discrepancy between rule output and reference-panel consensus (mean absolute error <10 percentage points), (4) rule is validated and fit-for-Phase-One or identified misalignments and adjustment plan. By Month 2.5 (2026-12-23), lock the rule version in bilateral escrow and publish a redacted rule-description summary (unclassified, confidentiality reviewed) to both co-chairs so final-decision procedures and verdict logic can be calibrated against the confirmed rule behavior.

Notes

  • Adversarial synthetic cases are essential and distinct from historical validation; historical records show cooperative operator behavior, while synthetic cases test operator gaming (equipment substitution, forged attestations, delayed access to obscure changes).
  • False-positive and false-negative rates must be separately tracked; a rule that has low false positives but high false negatives (misses real substitutions) is useless for detection credibility, even if adjudication load is manageable.
  • If the pilot reveals >±5 point deviation, the second-cohort adjustment and re-validation must complete by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23) to allow thresholds to be locked before Phase One clock (Month 6 = 2027-04-08). A three-week re-validation window (May 23–June 8) is tight but achievable with parallel processing.
  • The rule is confidential to prevent operators and vendors from gaming it by learning which evidence combinations carry the most weight; however, the rule must be transparent enough that both co-chairs, adjudication specialists and exercise designers understand its logic.
  • Once the rule is locked (Month 5.5 = 2027-03-23), no amendments are permitted during Phase One (Months 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08); if the rule is suspected of miscalibration during operations, the mitigation is adjudication surge staffing, not rule adjustment.

3. Verdict Threshold Bands and Mechanical Scoring Rule Lock-Down

Verdict thresholds define success and failure for the Consortium. Without pre-registered, mechanical scoring rules locked in the bilateral instrument, the final verdict becomes a political negotiation over confidence-interval interpretation, inviting delegitimization and post-hoc renegotiation. Statistical uncertainty (±12% pooled, ±32% per-type) is inherent in a 90-day test; the only way to preserve verdict credibility is to: (1) state thresholds as confidence-interval bands, (2) specify a mechanical rule for boundary cases, (3) lock the rule before any results are known, and (4) apply the rule mechanically at conclusion without co-chair discretion. This data collection validates that thresholds are realistic, mechanically consistent, and pre-authorized by both governments and legislatures.

Data to Collect

  • Proposed detection thresholds for five scoring criteria (planned-event detection, unplanned-event detection, false-positive rate, unverifiable-equipment share, reciprocal-access parity definition and measurement method) and supporting confidence-interval bands (90% CL for Go/Modify, 95% CL for Stop, or alternative confidence levels negotiated by co-chairs)
  • Statistical power analysis (actual binomial confidence intervals for n=8–16 per event type, pool n=54, p=0.7 baseline) confirming interval widths and ambiguity zones where threshold overlap occurs
  • Mechanical scoring rule (algorithm) specifying when lower confidence bound exceeds Go threshold (verdict = Go), upper bound falls below Stop threshold (verdict = Stop), or interval straddles a threshold (verdict = Modify by default)
  • Bilateral memorandum language (specimen draft by legal team) locking thresholds into binding procedural law; amendment-prevention language; and certification procedure requiring both co-chairs to initial the final-verdict report applying the mechanical rule
  • Unclassified summary of thresholds, confidence bands and mechanical scoring logic for legislative briefing (by Month 5.5 = 2027-03-23, before Phase One exercises begin)

Simulation Steps

  • Use statistical software (R, Python, MATLAB or Excel with binomial functions) to compute exact 90% and 95% confidence intervals for detection rates under the planned sample sizes: (a) n=8 per event type (single-pair, 3-month test at 1 per month): CI width approximately ±32% at 95%; (b) n=16 per planned-event class (e.g., unreported arrival + substitution combined): CI width approximately ±22% at 95%; (c) n=54 pooled (all 54 exercises): CI width approximately ±12% at 95%; document the intervals visually as bands on a probability graph showing where Go (≥70–75%), Modify (55–75%) and Stop (<55%) thresholds overlap
  • Generate a threshold-sensitivity matrix (spreadsheet with rows for observed detection rate 50–85%, columns for Go/Modify/Stop thresholds) and populate each cell with the verdict that the mechanical rule produces (lower bound exceeds Go? = Go; upper bound below Stop? = Stop; otherwise Modify) for all combinations; visualize as a heat map so co-chairs can see where ambiguity exists
  • Simulate Phase One outcomes under three scenarios: (A) actual detection 72% with ±12% interval [60–84%], (B) actual detection 65% with ±14% interval [51–79%], (C) actual detection 58% with ±16% interval [42–74%]; apply the proposed mechanical rule to each and show the verdict outcome; confirm that scenarios B and C yield Modify (not Go or Stop) due to interval ambiguity, so Modify is a defensible real outcome
  • Model the impact of parity criteria: if reciprocal-access parity cannot be measured or only one country's site achieves >85% parity (proposed threshold), show how that affects the overall 'at least 4 of 5 criteria met' Go gate; confirm whether parity is weighted equally to detection or weighted differently
  • Create a 'verdict-contingency playbook' (2-page decision tree) that co-chairs can consult during Phase One conclusion: IF detection is 68% ± 14%, THEN interval is [54%, 82%], which straddles all three thresholds, THEN mechanical rule defaults to Modify, THEN co-chairs ratify the verdict report applying the rule, THEN verdict is published as Modify within 5 days. No renegotiation path exists; the decision is mechanical.

Expert Validation Steps

  • Engage an independent statistician (from a neutral third country or academic institution, pre-approved by both co-chairs by Month 2 = 2026-12-08) to audit the confidence-interval calculations and the mechanical scoring rule: confirm that interval construction (binomial, Clopper-Pearson, or other method) is standard, that the choice of 90% vs. 95% CL is justified and symmetric (not favoring either outcome), and that the default-to-Modify rule is mathematically sound (i.e., there is no hidden asymmetry that favors Go or Stop).
  • Convene a bilateral Statistical Advisory Panel (3–4 independent statisticians from neutral countries) by Month 3 (2027-01-08) to review the pre-registered thresholds and mechanical rule and issue a 'Statistical Fitness Opinion' (classified, 2–3 pages): (1) are confidence intervals and thresholds compatible (i.e., will ambiguous zones occur), (2) is the default-to-Modify rule defensible, (3) do the thresholds change meaningfully if sample sizes differ (e.g., 4 per type vs. 8), and (4) what is the unspoken Type I and Type II error rate of this verdict procedure (i.e., how often will the procedure produce a Modify when detection truly warrants Go, or vice versa)?
  • Conduct a bilateral legal review (by the legal implementation team) to confirm that the mechanical scoring rule is embedded in the bilateral instrument as binding procedural law; that no escape clauses or 'good-faith renegotiation' language exist; and that both co-chairs' signature on the final-verdict report constitutes acceptance of the mechanical outcome, not a renegotiable judgment.
  • Brief both countries' legislatures (unclassified summary) by Month 5 (2027-03-08) on the pre-registered thresholds, confidence bands and mechanical scoring logic; solicit legislative feedback on acceptability of Go, Modify and Stop outcomes; flag any legislative concern that the Modify outcome is unsatisfying or that one government might pressure the co-chair to reject a Modify verdict as insufficiently strong. Record legislative positions so co-chairs know in advance whether domestic political acceptance is at risk.
  • Conduct a 'verdict-consensus stress test' (Month 5 = 2027-03-08, 2-hour virtual meeting with both co-chairs, co-chair deputies, legal advisors and independent statistician) in which hypothetical Phase One results (e.g., 68% detection with wide intervals) are presented and the mechanical rule is applied transparently; confirm that both co-chairs accept the Modify verdict as inevitable and will not attempt post-hoc renegotiation of thresholds or scoring logic.

Responsible Parties

  • Bilateral statistical committee (both co-chairs' offices, legal implementation team, independent statisticians) designing and locking thresholds by Month 2.5 (2026-12-23)
  • Independent statistician auditing confidence-interval calculations and mechanical rule (Month 2–3 = 2026-12-08 to 2027-01-08)
  • Bilateral Statistical Advisory Panel (3–4 neutral statisticians) reviewing thresholds and issuing fitness opinion (Month 3 = 2027-01-08)
  • Bilateral legal team embedding thresholds as binding procedural law in the bilateral instrument (Month 2 = 2026-12-08)
  • Legislative liaisons in both countries briefing parliaments and recording political feedback (Month 5 = 2027-03-08)

Assumptions

  • High: Confidence intervals for Phase One detection rates will be approximately ±12% pooled (n≈54, p=0.7) and ±32% per event type (n≈8); if sample sizes differ (e.g., 4 per type instead of 8), intervals widen and ambiguity zones expand but the mechanical rule still produces a defensible Modify outcome.
  • High: Both co-chairs will pre-commit (in writing, embedded in the bilateral instrument) to accepting a Modify verdict as a real outcome (not a placeholder for rework) and to applying the mechanical scoring rule without exception or post-hoc renegotiation.
  • Medium: The default-to-Modify rule (when confidence intervals straddle a threshold) will be politically acceptable to both countries' legislatures; if either legislature signals that Modify is unacceptable (e.g., demanding either Go or Stop), the bilateral instrument must be amended before Phase One to clarify the Modify outcome.
  • Medium: Independent statisticians will concur that the confidence-interval construction and mechanical rule are unbiased and mathematically sound; if the statistician disputes the rule (e.g., argues that the default-to-Modify logic favors one outcome), the rule must be adjusted before co-chair signature.
  • High: The mechanical scoring rule can be fully pre-registered and applied blindly at conclusion without requiring any post-hoc co-chair judgment about whether a specific result 'should' be interpreted differently; no provision for 'extraordinary circumstances' or 'waiver' of the mechanical rule exists.

SMART Validation Objective

By Month 2.5 (2026-12-23), produce and bilaterally sign a Verdict-Thresholds Memorandum specifying: (1) detection thresholds (Go ≥75% or ≥70% for planned class, Modify 55–75%, Stop <55%; unplanned Go ≥60%, Modify 40–60%, Stop <40%; false positives Modify ≤15%, Stop >15%; other criteria TBD); (2) confidence-interval bands (90% CL for Go/Modify boundaries, 95% for Stop or alternative negotiated); (3) mechanical scoring rule ('lower bound of interval exceeds Go = Go verdict; upper bound below Stop = Stop verdict; otherwise Modify'); (4) no-amendment clause ('thresholds locked and may not be amended after any Phase One exercise result is known'); (5) publication requirement ('unclassified summary of thresholds and mechanical rule published by Month 5.5 = 2027-03-23, before any Phase One exercises begin'). Lock the memorandum by bilateral signature (both co-chairs) no later than Month 2.5 (2026-12-23), a minimum of 3.5 weeks before the Phase One clock (Month 6 = 2027-04-08).

Notes

  • Thresholds are marked 'provisional' in the plan but must become 'locked' by Month 2.5 (2026-12-23); the term 'provisional' should be retired once the bilateral memorandum is signed, to eliminate ambiguity about whether renegotiation is possible.
  • The mechanical scoring rule is the linchpin of verdict credibility; without it, every ambiguous result (interval straddles a threshold) becomes a political argument. The rule must be algorithmic and non-discretionary.
  • The Modify outcome is often treated as unsatisfying (neither success nor failure), but in a thin-statistics setting (±12–32% confidence), Modify is the intellectually honest outcome when results are ambiguous; both legislatures must pre-commit to accepting Modify as real and actionable.
  • The bilateral Statistical Advisory Panel is a check on co-chair bias; if the panel finds the thresholds or rule to be biased or mathematically unsound, the rule must be adjusted before Phase One begins, even if that delays the clock.
  • Unclassified legislative briefing by Month 5 (2027-03-08) gives parliaments 4 weeks to object to the thresholds before exercises begin (Month 6 = 2027-04-08); objections trigger an emergency co-chair summit and potential rule revision, but the risk is managed before operations start.

4. Mirrored Inspectorate Deployment Staffing and Shift Coverage Validation

Mirrored inspectorate staffing and shift coverage directly enable detection of unreported arrivals, substitutions and other time-sensitive events. Inadequate or predictable shift coverage allows exercises to be gamed (red teams avoid high-coverage windows) and allows operators to obscure changes (scheduling maintenance during low-presence shifts). The staffing model choice (continuous, 2-shift, event-triggered) determines feasibility and cost within the USD 750M envelope and directly impacts detection rates for unreported-arrival and disputed-identity exercises. This data collection validates whether the baseline staffing model (described at a high level in the plan) can be operationalized, whether timelines for recruitment-to-certification are achievable, and whether shift coverage will actually support the exercise load and detection credibility claims.

Data to Collect

  • Confirmed staffing model choice: Continuous 3-shift (requires ~300+ per country), Two-shift 16-hour coverage (requires ~180 per country), or Event-triggered deployment (requires ~120 per country plus 30+ surge), with realistic per-country headcount and cost estimate mapped to the USD 750M personnel envelope
  • Inspector recruitment and security-vetting pipeline status by cohort: cohort 1 (Month -1 = 2026-09-08), cohort 2 (Month 0–1 = 2026-10-08 to 2026-11-08), cohort 3 (Month 1–2 = 2026-11-08 to 2026-12-08), final cohort (Month 2–3 = 2026-12-08 to 2027-01-08); percentage certified and ready-for-deployment by Month 5 (2027-03-08) and Month 5.5 (2027-03-23)
  • Shift schedule and rotation plan (4 months on-site, 2 months off-site, staggered cohorts) validated against leave-coverage rules (30% leave buffer); actual staffing available per shift per site per month during Phase One (Months 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08)
  • Inspector-hours-per-site dashboard (weekly tracking during Phase One): actual on-site hours per country per site per week, compared to baseline (target 12+ hours per week per country-team); detection-opportunity parity between paired sites (unreported-arrival test windows matched, substitution-exercise staging times accessible to both sides)
  • Retention-bonus budget (2–3% of USD 750M = USD 15–22.5M estimate) and reconciliation against actual personnel costs; attrition tracking (% of certified inspectors remaining deployed through Phase One conclusion)

Simulation Steps

  • Build a staffing-model calculator (spreadsheet or simulation tool) comparing three coverage scenarios: (A) Continuous 3-shift 24/7 (6 per shift × 3 shifts × 3 sites × 2 countries × 1.4 seven-day multiplier × 1.3 leave buffer = ~617 per country, exceeds USD 750M personnel envelope at ~USD 29M/month × 9.5 months = ~USD 276M per country, assumes full cost front-loaded); (B) Two-shift 16-hour (6 per shift × 2 shifts × 3 sites × 2 countries × 1.2 multiplier = ~288 per country, fits within envelope at ~USD 14M/month × 9.5 months = ~USD 133M per country); (C) Event-triggered with on-call response within 4 hours (baseline 120 per country + 30+ surge = 150, fits envelope at ~USD 10M/month × 9.5 months = ~USD 95M per country, but risky for unreported-arrival detection if exercises are timed to night hours)
  • Conduct a recruitment-timeline simulation (Project or Excel Gantt chart) showing recruitment pace (estimated 5–10 per week per country × 36 weeks = 180–360 candidates screened for ~150–200 positions), security-clearance turnaround (4–8 weeks per batch of 50), and training-cohort scheduling (12 days per cohort × 4 cohorts = 48 days of training delivery, parallel across months −1 to 3). Calculate the percentage certified by each milestone (50% by Month 2, 80 = 2026-12-08, 2033-06-08% by Month 5, 95 = 2027-03-08, 2034-09-08% by Month 5.5 = 2027-03-23).
  • Model shift coverage under a Rotation Scenario (4-month on-site, 2-month off-site, staggered): Cohort 1 (Months −1 to 3 on-site, Months 3–5 = 2027-01-08 to 2027-03-08 off-site), Cohort 2 (Months 1–5 = 2026-11-08 to 2027-03-08 on-site, Months 5–7 = 2027-03-08 to 2027-05-08 off-site), Cohort 3 (Months 3–7 = 2027-01-08 to 2027-05-08 on-site, Months 7–9 = 2027-05-08 to 2027-07-08 off-site), Cohort 4 (Months 5–9 = 2027-03-08 to 2027-07-08 on-site). Calculate minimum staffing present during Phase One (Months 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08): at least cohorts 2 and 3 fully present, cohort 4 ramping in, cohort 1 ramping out. Ensure minimum 4 per shift (2 per country) maintained throughout.
  • Simulate an unreported-arrival exercise injection scenario: assume an exercise is scheduled for Month 7 (2027-05-08) at site A, 'unreported arrival to staging area during day shift.' Map the presence schedule of both countries' inspectors to that week and confirm that full shift coverage exists; repeat for three different times of day (06:00, 14:00, 22:00) and three different shift-choice scenarios (continuous, 2-shift, event-triggered). Document the detection-opportunity parity between countries if shift patterns differ.
  • Create a retention-bonus allocation model: budget USD 15–22.5M across 300–360 inspectors × 12-month commitment = USD 42–75k per inspector per year (or ~USD 9.5–18k for 6-month Phase One + 6-month ramp-down). Map bonus payments to deployment milestones (10% at certification, 45% at Month 6 = 2027-04-08 Phase One start, 45% at Month 9 = 2027-07-08 conclusion) to incentivize completion.

Expert Validation Steps

  • Engage a multinational military personnel-operations expert (e.g., retired NATO or UN multilateral-force commander with experience staffing continuous-presence operations, e.g., Cyprus UNFICYP, Sinai MFO) to validate the staffing model against precedent: typical multipliers for continuous presence (1.5–2.0× for 7-day coverage), typical leave and illness rates (20–30%), typical attrition during deployment (5–8% per 6 months), and recommend adjustments to the plan's 1.4 multiplier or 30% leave buffer if they appear unrealistic.
  • Request a formal written commitment from both countries' Personnel Officers (or equivalent) by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23) confirming: (1) headcount allocation (whether continuous, 2-shift, or event-triggered is approved by their budgets), (2) recruitment and vetting timeline (can 80% certification be achieved by Month 5 = 2027-03-08?), (3) rotation and leave policies (will 4-month on-site/2-month off-site rotation be implemented), and (4) retention-bonus funding (is USD 15–22.5M available within the USD 750M envelope).
  • Conduct a security-vetting feasibility audit with both countries' CI offices: can 300+ personnel undergo baseline polygraph/equivalent vetting by Month 2 (2026-12-08)? What is typical vetting turnaround (4–8 weeks)? Are there pipeline bottlenecks (polygraph-examiner availability, CI-investigator capacity) that would delay clearances? Request mitigation strategies (e.g., pre-vetting before recruitment, concurrent vetting during training) and realistic completion-date estimates.
  • Engage an independent training-curriculum specialist (e.g., retired IAEA or OSCE inspector-training director) to validate that a 12-day training course (evidence collection 4 days, sealed observation 3 days, identity verification 3 days, exercises 2 days) is sufficient to produce 80% certification at the competency level needed for Phase One. Request recommendations on whether the curriculum should be extended or whether certification standards should be lowered to meet the timeline.
  • Obtain a formal written attestation from both participating datacenters (Operator Statements of Cooperation, by Month 5 = 2027-03-08) that they will provide: (1) uninterrupted staging-area access to inspectors during agreed shift windows (e.g., 6:00–22:00 for 2-shift model or 24/7 for continuous), (2) operator staff to support shift rotations and emergency coverage, (3) documented shift-schedule publication (so exercises cannot be gamed by timing to low-presence moments), and (4) confirmation that they will not unilaterally restrict access during Phase One except for documented emergencies (with notification to co-chairs within 4 hours and public ledger logging).

Responsible Parties

  • Both countries' Personnel Officers (or equivalent defense/foreign-ministry staffing authority) committing to headcount allocation and recruitment timeline
  • Bilateral Inspector Recruitment and Vetting Coordinator (dedicated staff, 2–3 per country) managing cohort pipeline and clearance status
  • Inspector Rotation and Leave Manager (1 per country, both reporting to co-chairs) tracking on-site presence and shift schedules weekly
  • Both countries' Counterintelligence and Security Offices approving vetting procedures and validating clearance timelines
  • Participating datacenters' Operations Leads providing shift-access commitments and operator-staffing allocations

Assumptions

  • High: The baseline staffing model (99 per country, Mirrored Shift Coverage Architecture choice 1: 'continuous presence in staging and spare-inventory areas') can achieve 80% on-site presence (78 per country) during Phase One with a 1.4 multiplier for 7-day coverage and 30% leave buffer.
  • High: Security-clearance vetting (baseline polygraph or equivalent) for 300+ personnel can complete by Month 2 (2026-12-08) using parallel-processing (concurrent with recruitment in months −3 to 1); if vetting is sequential or requires repeat polygraph rounds, the timeline slips and affects deployment readiness.
  • Medium: A 12-day training curriculum (delivered in parallel cohorts) can produce 80% of personnel at certification-ready level by Month 5 (2027-03-08); higher certification standards (e.g., requiring 20-day courses) would compress deployment timeline or reduce certified headcount below minimum-coverage thresholds.
  • Medium: Both countries will implement the stated rotation model (4 months on-site, 2 months off-site, staggered cohorts) and will not unilaterally recall inspectors or skip leave rotations due to operational pressures, which would erode the rotation model and breach leave-coverage rules.
  • Medium: Participating datacenters will publish their shift schedules in advance (by Month 6 = 2027-04-08) so red-team exercises cannot be timed to low-coverage windows, and will not use 'operational emergency' claims to restrict inspector access during exercises, except for genuine force-majeure events (documented and logged within 4 hours).

SMART Validation Objective

By Month 4 (2027-02-08), validate that: (1) staffing model choice (continuous 3-shift, 2-shift 16-hour, or event-triggered) is locked with both Personnel Officers' written commitment, (2) recruitment pace is on track (100+ of 300 inspectors screened, 50+ in vetting pipeline, attrition rate <5%), (3) security clearances are 50%+ complete by Month 2 (2026-12-08), (4) training cohorts 1–2 are completed and 50+ inspectors are certified by Month 4 (2027-02-08), targeting 80%+ certified by Month 5 (2027-03-08). By Month 5.5 (2027-03-23), confirm full staffing deployment (150–200 per country depending on model choice) is in place at all sites, shift schedules are published, and operator Statements of Cooperation are signed.

Notes

  • Continuous 3-shift coverage (600+ per country) exceeds the USD 750M personnel envelope and is labeled 'Aspirational' in the plan; 2-shift 16-hour coverage (180 per country) fits the envelope and is operationally sustainable based on UNFICYP and similar precedent.
  • The 1.4 multiplier for 7-day coverage is conservative; multinational operations typically use 1.5–2.0×; a 1.2× multiplier (higher on-site presence) would reduce total headcount but require tighter leave discipline and would increase burnout risk.
  • Recruitment and vetting for 300+ personnel in 4 months is unprecedented in arms-control mechanisms; IAEA inspector corps grew over decades; OPCW expanded more rapidly (1997–2005, ~100 inspectors) but with higher per-inspector onboarding cost. The plan requires aggressive parallel processing.
  • If 80% certification cannot be achieved by Month 5 (2027-03-08), the Phase One start must slip to Month 7 (2027-05-08) or later, compressing the test further. This drives the Entry-Condition Task Force urgency: staffing delays cascade directly to Phase One delays.
  • Shift-schedule publication prevents red teams from gaming exercises by timing injections to low-presence windows; however, publication also reveals shift gaps and vulnerability windows to potential adversaries (operators). The trade-off between transparency and operational security must be managed by bilateral agreement.

5. Bilateral Counterintelligence Vetting and Inspector Information-Firewall Enforcement

Inspector integrity is foundational to Phase One credibility. A single confirmed breach (espionage, unauthorized data retention, IP leakage) delegitimizes the entire mechanism and triggers bilateral withdrawal risk. The Counterintelligence Oversight Board is the governance structure that detects and adjudicates breaches transparently, with both countries represented and a neutral chair to prevent deadlock. Compartmentalization rules (sealed communication, cooling-off periods, debriefing protocols, no data retention) operationalize the Inspector Information Firewall Doctrine and limit an individual inspector's damage if they are later compromised by a foreign intelligence service. This data collection validates that CI vetting is operationally feasible, that the fast-track adjudication timeline is legally sound in both countries, and that compartmentalization rules are implementable without excessive burden on inspectors.

Data to Collect

  • Bilateral Counterintelligence Oversight Board charter (3 senior CI officers per country) and monthly classified meeting schedule (starting Month 0 = 2026-10-08, monthly every 2nd Tuesday, 14:00 CET)
  • Inspector baseline-vetting protocol and results (baseline polygraph or equivalent security-assessment completion rate and any anomalies or red flags by Month 2 = 2026-12-08); quarterly re-vetting schedule (starting Month 3 = 2027-01-08, every 3rd Friday)
  • Inspector compartmentalization and information-firewall procedures: debriefing protocol (4–6 hour session upon departure or reassignment, CI-led, focus on unusual access requests or data-retention), cooling-off period enforcement (14-day minimum between reassignments, logged), shift-scheduling compliance (no inspector >2 consecutive sites, 4-week minimum tenure per assignment)
  • Sealed on-site communication infrastructure (monitored encrypted phone only, no personal devices, 5-minute call limit per inspector per shift, call logs submitted weekly to CI Oversight Board); network architecture ensuring no inspector can access external networks or store retained data on equipment they can carry off-site
  • Monthly unclassified breach-count summary (suspected breaches opened, sustained breaches confirmed, false-positive allegations cleared, average investigation turnaround time, adjudication outcomes: recall, remediation, or clearance); adjudication log of 7-day fast-track procedure (case opened → 48-hour investigation → 72-hour recommendation → 7-day co-chair decision)

Simulation Steps

  • Model a breach-incident scenario using a decision-tree tool (Lucidchart, draw.io): Inspector A requests to carry a notebook with equipment serial numbers back to their home-country office. Flowchart triggers: (1) sealed communication protocol violation (personal note-taking outside the secured network), (2) data-retention concern (notebook could be lost or stolen), (3) investigation initiated (48 hours to determine intent and risk), (4) recommendation due (day 3: is this a breach or a process-understanding gap?), (5) co-chair decision (day 7: recall inspector, require remedial training, or clear). Document the roles and escalation path.
  • Build a personnel-security vetting tracker (spreadsheet or database) with fields: inspector ID, cohort, baseline-vetting date, baseline-result (pass/conditional/fail), quarterly-vetting date, re-vetting result, any red-flag details (unauthorized data retention, unauthorized access attempt, unusual travel, counterintelligence-contact allegation). Simulate monthly roll-up reports: 'X% of 300 inspectors passed baseline; Y% have completed Q1 re-vetting; Z% show concerning patterns.'
  • Model the compartmentalization-enforcement scenario: Inspector B rotates off-site after 4 months at Site A (unreported-arrival testing, identity-verification tasks). Debriefing protocol: (1) 4-hour CI-led session (focus: any unusual access requests? Any data retention outside the system?), (2) post-session cleanup: all notes, photos and recordings on CI-provided equipment are electronically wiped in the debriefing room under witness, (3) 14-day cooling-off period (no contact with Site A staff or other inspectors for 2 weeks), (4) if reassigned to Site C, must wait additional 14 days before assignment (total 28 days off-site).
  • Simulate the sealed-communication infrastructure using a network diagram tool: All on-site inspectors connect via a single monitored encrypted phone or radio channel (location: Site A inspector station, equipment: hardware appliance, operator: Site A CI liaison). Each inspector's call is logged with timestamp, duration, recipient (home-country CI office or co-chair), and subject-line (e.g., 'health incident requiring evacuation', 'equipment access question', 'shift-change coordination'). Calls exceeding 5 minutes are flagged for post-session review. Simulate a log: 'Tuesday 09:00–09:02 Inspector B calls home office (2 min): shift rotations'; 'Wednesday 14:30–14:35 Inspector C calls home office (5 min): incident report on equipment disruption.'
  • Model the monthly breach-count summary format: Table with rows for breach-incident category (data retention, unauthorized access, external communication, espionage allegation, false positive) and columns for 'suspected' (case opened), 'sustained' (breach confirmed by investigation), 'cleared' (investigation found no breach). Example row: 'Unauthorized data retention: 2 suspected, 1 sustained (remedial training assigned), 1 cleared (inspector was following protocol correctly, process clarification issued).' Publish unclassified version (count of cases, categories, outcomes) to both legislatures monthly (by Month 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08).

Expert Validation Steps

  • Engage a bilateral Counterintelligence Board Chair (pre-approved by both co-chairs, neutral third-country senior CI officer or retired, e.g., retired OSCE/CIO official) to chair the monthly Oversight Board meetings and to adjudicate any disputes over breach investigations or inspector clearances. The Chair's role is non-voting but carries weight: if both countries' CI officers disagree on whether an incident is a breach or a false positive, the Chair provides a tie-breaking recommendation (non-binding but published to co-chairs and logged).
  • Request formal certification from both countries' CI/security agencies (by Month 0.5 = 2026-10-23) that they accept the vetting protocol (baseline polygraph or equivalent, quarterly re-vetting, compartmentalization rules) and that they will comply with the fast-track 7-day adjudication timeline for breach cases. If either country's legal system does not permit the fast-track procedure (e.g., requires longer due-process periods), bilateral negotiation must resolve this constraint before Phase One.
  • Engage an independent polygraph examiner or security-assessment specialist (from a neutral third country, pre-approved and bonded by both co-chairs) to conduct the baseline vetting (Month 2 = 2026-12-08) and to oversee quarterly re-vetting (Months 3, 6, 9 = 2027-01-08, 2027-04-08, 2027-07-08). The examiner is contractually independent (not working for either government) and reports results simultaneously to both co-chairs.
  • Request both countries' legislative-oversight bodies (intelligence or defense committees) to confirm that the sealed on-site communication protocol (no personal phones, single monitored channel, 5-minute limit) is operationally acceptable and does not violate inspector privacy or due-process rights. If either legislature objects, alternative protocols must be negotiated (e.g., allow brief personal calls under monitoring, or allow personal phones with software-level recording enabled).
  • Conduct a mock breach-investigation scenario (Month 5 = 2027-03-08, 48-hour tabletop exercise) with both countries' CI officers, the Oversight Board Chair and legal counsel: present a simulated breach case (e.g., inspector attempts to retain notebook with serial numbers) and walk through the 7-day adjudication procedure; identify bottlenecks, clarify decision authority (can the Oversight Board recommend inspector recall, or only to co-chairs?), and document the agreed process before Phase One begins.

Responsible Parties

  • Bilateral Counterintelligence Oversight Board (3 senior CI officers per country, reporting jointly to co-chairs), chaired by a neutral third-country CI official
  • Independent polygraph examiner or security-assessment specialist (neutral third country, contracted and bonded)
  • Bilateral Inspector Compartmentalization and Firewall Enforcement Officer (1 per country, both reporting to the Oversight Board) managing on-site communication infrastructure, debriefing schedules and cooling-off enforcement
  • Both countries' CI and security agencies certifying vetting protocols and fast-track adjudication timelines
  • Both countries' legislative oversight bodies (intelligence or defense committees) confirming operational acceptability of sealed-communication and privacy constraints

Assumptions

  • High: Baseline polygraph or equivalent security vetting (300+ inspectors in 4 weeks, Month 2 = 2026-12-08) is feasible using parallel processing (multiple examiners, concurrent sessions); if vetting is sequential or requires multiple rounds, it will slip the timeline and delay deployment readiness.
  • High: Both countries' legal systems accept the 7-day breach-adjudication fast-track procedure (48-hour investigation, 72-hour recommendation, 7-day decision) and will not require longer due-process delays or judicial review before an inspector can be recalled or remediated.
  • Medium: Inspector compartmentalization rules (sealed communication, 14-day cooling-off, 4-week minimum tenure per site, no consecutive-site assignments) can be enforced without excessive burden on inspectors and without triggering labor-law or privacy-rights violations in either country.
  • Medium: The sealed on-site communication infrastructure (single monitored phone, 5-minute call limit) will not be perceived by either country's legislature as excessive surveillance of inspectors, and will be accepted as a security necessity for Phase One.
  • Medium: Both countries will pre-authorize the Bilateral Counterintelligence Oversight Board Chair (neutral third-country official) to issue tie-breaking recommendations in cases of disagreement between the two countries' CI officers, and will agree to publish all breach-case adjudication outcomes (unclassified summaries) to legislatures monthly.

SMART Validation Objective

By Month 2 (2026-12-08), complete baseline security vetting of 300+ inspectors and deliver a Baseline Vetting Report (classified) showing: (1) percentage cleared/conditional/failed by country, (2) any red-flag patterns or anomalies, (3) re-vetting schedule starting Month 3 (2027-01-08) (every 3rd Friday thereafter). By Month 0.5 (2026-10-23), obtain formal written certification from both countries' CI/security agencies confirming acceptance of vetting protocols and 7-day breach-adjudication timeline. By Month 5 (2027-03-08), conduct a mock breach-investigation tabletop and validate that the Oversight Board can resolve a simulated case within the 7-day target. Publish the first unclassified monthly breach-count summary at Month 6.5 (2027-04-23) during Phase One, showing 0 sustained breaches, Y suspected cases under investigation, and average investigation turnaround time meeting the 7-day target.

Notes

  • Baseline polygraph for 300+ inspectors in 4 weeks (50+ per week, or 10 per day if 5-day exams per week) requires 6–10 concurrent polygraph examiners; this is a significant procurement challenge if examiners are limited in both countries.
  • The fast-track 7-day breach-adjudication procedure is aggressive compared to typical security-incident responses (10–14 days); it requires both countries to pre-authorize expedited investigation procedures and to waive certain due-process requirements (e.g., extended legal discovery or inspector-counsel participation) for the duration of Phase One.
  • Compartmentalization via cooling-off periods (14 days off-site before reassignment, 4-week minimum per site, no consecutive-site assignments) reduces inspector mobility but increases retention burden (fewer available inspectors per cohort); carefully balance enforcement against staffing feasibility.
  • The sealed on-site communication (no personal phones, single monitored channel, 5-minute limit) is restrictive but operationally necessary to prevent data leakage; inspect-rate perception is important (privacy concerns, isolation, inability to contact family) and must be managed through pre-deployment briefing and mental-health support.
  • Monthly unclassified breach-count summaries build legislative confidence in the CI governance mechanism; publishing case outcomes (categories, investigation results) without naming individuals protects inspector privacy while demonstrating that breaches are detected and adjudicated transparently.

6. Bilateral Instrument Finalization and Double-Key Governance Operationalization

The bilateral instrument is the legal foundation for all governance procedures. Without a detailed, internally consistent instrument that locks procedures (deadlock clock, automatic suspension, threshold amendments) into binding law, co-chairs can later dispute what the rules were or claim procedural exceptions ('urgent national interest', 'procedural dispute', 'good-faith renegotiation') that circumvent the no-casting-vote and no-amendment principles. The instrument must specify: (1) what stops/starts the deadlock clock (no ambiguity), (2) consequences of clock thresholds (automatic partial suspension is not discretionary), (3) verdict thresholds as mechanical rules (not negotiable after results are known), (4) evidence-rule confidentiality and lock-down (no mid-Phase-One amendments). This data collection validates that the instrument is legally sound, operationally specific, internally consistent and ready for co-chair signature by Month 1 (2026-11-08).

Data to Collect

  • Draft bilateral instrument (estimated 80–120 pages, classified): full text covering mission, scope, governance (co-chairs, double-key procedures, no casting vote), entry conditions, seven budget envelopes and envelope-mapping rules, Phase One procedures (intake, ledger, exercises, adjudication), hard Stop triggers, deadlock clock and automatic-suspension procedures, neutral-facility status, inspector privileges and immunity, operator compensation terms, confidentiality and disclosure tiers, evidence-weighting rule lock-down language, verdict-threshold lock-down language, termination clauses
  • Internal-consistency audit results: do all major procedural clauses align (e.g., deadlock clock definition vs. partial-suspension trigger, threshold-amendment clause vs. 'no-waiver' rule, evidence-rule confidentiality vs. adjudication transparency)
  • Bilateral legal-implementation team sign-off and co-chair approval for signature (target Month 1 = 2026-11-08)
  • Specimen bilateral memoranda as annexes: (1) Verdict-Thresholds Memorandum (with mechanical scoring rule), (2) Rule-Calibration Confidence Memo (evidence-rule validation results), (3) Entry-Condition Roadmap (with binding milestone deadlines and emergency-summit triggers), (4) Key-Custody Charter (specifying dual-share ceremony procedures and recovery protocols)
  • Unclassified legislative summary (10–15 pages) of key procedural sections (deadlock, suspension, thresholds, evidence-rule lock-down, stop triggers) for briefing both countries' parliaments by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23), before Phase One exercises begin

Simulation Steps

  • Create an Instrument Dependency Matrix (spreadsheet or graph) mapping key clauses to each other: (1) Co-chair Authority (delegation, decision-making, no casting vote); (2) Deadlock Clock (definition, clock start/stop, timekeeper certification); (3) Automatic Partial Suspension (trigger at day 14, scope, logging); (4) Impaired-Confidence Status (trigger at day 21/28, legality, effect on verdict); (5) Evidence Rule (confidentiality, lock-down, no-amendment clause); (6) Verdict Thresholds (mechanical rule, no-negotiation clause); (7) Hard Stop Triggers (shielding, access asymmetry, ledger divergence). Color-code cells to identify dependencies: e.g., 'partial suspension depends on deadlock clock definition' (yellow), 'deadlock clock validity depends on timekeeper role definition' (orange), 'evidence rule's fitness depends on validation results' (red). Highlight circular or missing dependencies.
  • Draft instrument language (500–1,000 words per major clause) using arms-control treaty templates as reference (IAEA Safeguards Agreements, OPCW Verification Annex, New START Protocols): for each clause (co-chairs, deadlock, suspension, evidence rule, thresholds, stops), write model language showing procedural specifics, decision authority, clock mechanics, amendment restrictions and logging requirements. Examples: 'The Co-Chairs shall establish a Joint Deadlock Clock managed by an independent Timekeeper, commencing upon the recording of a discrepancy in the Ledger. The Clock shall advance hourly unless both Co-Chairs jointly approve a timestamped waiver logged in the Ledger, which shall not exceed 5 calendar days. Automatic partial suspension of the disputed function shall occur upon the Clock reaching 14 days without co-chair resolution.' This language is unambiguous and operationally specific.
  • Perform an internal-consistency sanity check: (1) Does the deadlock-clock language define what stops/starts the clock the same way in all clauses (deadlock, suspension, impaired-confidence)? (2) Does the evidence-rule confidentiality clause prevent public disclosure but allow judges/adjudicators to access the rule? (3) Do the verdict-threshold and mechanical-rule clauses align in what they define as Modify (both default to Modify when intervals straddle, or do they differ)? (4) Are there any escape hatches or 'good-faith renegotiation' clauses that let a co-chair defer a decision? Produce a 'Consistency Memo' (5–10 pages, unclassified) documenting gaps and recommended fixes.
  • Simulate a bilateral-signature scenario (Month 1 = 2026-11-08): assume the legal team completes the draft instrument by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23) and both co-chairs' offices begin legal review. Model a timeline: legal office review (5 days per side), legislative-coordination (3 days per side), co-chair sign-off meeting (1 day), signature ceremony (1 day). Identify any bottlenecks (domestic legislature requirement? Senate or parliament approval? Executive-only authority?). In the US, treaty signature typically requires Senate consent; in China, Standing Committee approval may be required. If a legislature approval gate exists, the instrument must be submitted 2–4 weeks before desired signature date. Model the realistic timeline: draft complete Month 0.5 (2026-10-23), submit for approval Month 0.75 (2026-10-31), approval Month 1.25 (2026-11-16), signature Month 1 (2026-11-08) is not achievable if legislature approval is required. Re-baseline the signature target to Month 2 (2026-12-08) or use executive authority if available.
  • Create a Specimen Specimen Bilateral-Signature Document Set (classified briefing packet for co-chairs at signature): (1) final instrument text (80–120 pages), (2) side-by-side comparison of key clauses (this version vs. draft), (3) Consistency Memo (identified gaps fixed), (4) Specimen Verdict-Thresholds Memorandum (with mechanical rule, unclassified), (5) Specimen Rule-Calibration Memo (evidence rule validation results, classified), (6) Legislative Summary (10–15 pages, unclassified) for parliamentary briefing post-signature. This allows co-chairs to understand the full package at signature.

Expert Validation Steps

  • Engage a bilateral legal implementation team (3 experienced arms-control attorneys per side, ideally with IAEA, OPCW or START treaty experience) by Month 0 (2026-10-08) to draft the instrument and conduct internal-consistency audits. Monthly deliverables: Month 0.5 (2026-10-23) = draft instrument; Month 1 (2026-11-08) = internal-consistency audit and fixes; Month 1.5 (2026-11-23) = final language for co-chair review.
  • Consult an independent instrument-compliance auditor (external to both governments, with treaty-law background, pre-approved by both co-chairs) to review the final instrument (Month 1.5 = 2026-11-23) for: (1) legal enforceability in both countries' domestic systems, (2) absence of loopholes or renegotiation clauses that could defeat the no-amendment principle, (3) clarity of deadlock and suspension procedures (no ambiguous terms like 'good faith' or 'urgent interest' that invite interpretation), and (4) consistency with precedent from IAEA, OPCW or UN agreements. Deliver a 'Legal Compliance Certificate' (classified, 2–3 pages) to co-chairs confirming fitness-for-purpose or identifying residual risks.
  • Request formal review and sign-off by both countries' foreign ministries or legal advisors (by Month 1 = 2026-11-08) confirming that the instrument text is acceptable and ready for co-chair signature. The sign-off explicitly confirms: (1) no hidden legal risks or domestic-law conflicts, (2) accepting that certain clauses (deadlock, suspension, threshold lock-down) are binding and non-amendable, (3) legislatures have been briefed and have no objection to proceeding.
  • If the instrument requires legislature approval (Senate in the US, Standing Committee in China, or parliament in other countries), submit the unclassified legislative summary (Month 0 = 2026-10-08) and the instrument (classified, if necessary) for expedited review, with a target decision by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23). If legislature approval will require 6+ weeks, negotiate a temporary executive authority or Memorandum of Understanding that allows Phase One to begin pending formal ratification.
  • Conduct a 'Bilateral Signature Readiness Review' (Month 0.75 = 2026-10-31, one-day meeting of co-chairs, legal advisors, bilateral legal implementation team, independent auditor) to: (1) confirm the instrument text is ready, (2) walk through the deadlock clock, suspension triggers and threshold-lock procedures so both co-chairs understand and accept the non-negotiable rules, (3) identify any last-minute concerns or requests for clarification, and (4) set the signature date and ceremony details (location, witnesses, public/classified status).

Responsible Parties

  • Bilateral legal implementation team (3 attorneys per side, both countries' foreign/defense ministry legal offices) drafting and revising the instrument
  • Independent instrument-compliance auditor (external, pre-approved, third country) auditing for legal enforceability and consistency
  • Both countries' legislative-liaison offices coordinating with parliaments for briefing and approval (if required)
  • Co-chairs and their chief legal advisors conducting final review and approving the instrument text for signature
  • Both co-chairs (by Month 1 = 2026-11-08) signing the instrument and witnessing the signature ceremony (public announcement)

Assumptions

  • High: The bilateral instrument can be drafted, reviewed and signed by Month 1 (2026-11-08) without requiring legislature approval beyond executive authority or a provisional Memorandum of Understanding; if parliament ratification is required, the timeline slips to Month 2 (2026-12-08) or later, compressing entry conditions.
  • High: The instrument text will be internally consistent (no circular dependencies, no conflicting clauses); an independent legal auditor will certify fitness-for-purpose before signature.
  • High: Both co-chairs will accept that certain instrument clauses (deadlock clock, automatic suspension, threshold lock-down, evidence-rule confidentiality) are binding and non-negotiable; the co-chairs will not later claim a 'good-faith' exception or request amendments during Phase One.
  • Medium: The specimen bilateral memoranda (Verdict-Thresholds, Rule-Calibration, Entry-Condition Roadmap, Key-Custody Charter) can be finalized as annexes to the instrument by Month 2.5 (2026-12-23) and will be enforceable as binding supplementary procedures under the main instrument.
  • Medium: The unclassified legislative summary will be accepted by both countries' parliaments as adequately informative without compromising confidential procedures or security details; parliaments will not demand additional transparency that conflicts with the need to keep evidence rules and key-custody procedures confidential.

SMART Validation Objective

By Month 1 (2026-11-08), complete and co-chair-sign a comprehensive bilateral instrument (80–120 pages, classified) with: (1) unambiguous deadlock clock and automatic-suspension procedures; (2) locked verdict thresholds with mechanical scoring rule; (3) evidence-rule confidentiality and no-amendment clauses; (4) hard Stop triggers and their legal consequences; (5) inspector privileges, immunity and CI-vetting authority; (6) operator compensation and neutral-facility status. By Month 1.5 (2026-11-23), obtain an independent Legal Compliance Certificate confirming the instrument is internally consistent and legally enforceable. By Month 5.5 (2027-03-23), publish an unclassified legislative summary to both parliaments so they understand the key procedures before Phase One exercises begin (Month 6 = 2027-04-08).

Notes

  • The bilateral instrument must be specific enough that a judge or arbiter can apply it mechanistically without discretion; vague terms like 'good faith', 'urgent interest' or 'exceptional circumstance' create escape hatches that defeat the no-amendment principle.
  • The instrument must specify what happens if a procedure fails: e.g., 'If the Timekeeper cannot certify the clock due to a system failure, both Co-Chairs shall agree within 24 hours on a proxy clock value (historical timestamp) or jointly declare the clock reset.' This removes ambiguity about what happens if procedures break.
  • The specimen bilateral memoranda (thresholds, rule calibration, entry-condition roadmap, key-custody procedures) are annexes to the main instrument, not stand-alone documents; they must be legally incorporated by reference ('Annex X' language in the main instrument) so they are binding.
  • If the instrument requires parliament ratification, negotiate a provisional implementation agreement (Memorandum of Understanding) that allows Phase One to begin under executive authority pending formal ratification; this protects the timeline from legislative delays.
  • The unclassified legislative summary must balance transparency (showing key procedures to parliaments) with confidentiality (not revealing evidence-rule details, key-custody procedures, or other sensitive methods); coordinate the summary with both countries' legal offices before publication.

7. Neutral Facility Procurement, Hardening and Operational Readiness

The neutral facility is a critical single-point-of-failure. If the facility is unavailable (due to host-country closure, security incident, or operational breakdown), the replicated ledger cannot synchronize, key ceremonies cannot occur, and the entire Consortium halts. The facility must be operationally ready by Month 3 (2027-01-08), with security certification complete and full operational dry-run done by Month 5 (2027-03-08), to allow a buffer before Phase One (Month 6 = 2027-04-08). This data collection validates that the facility site is identified, secured, staffed and operationally tested before the stakes are real.

Data to Collect

  • Neutral-facility site selection decision (Geneva or Singapore candidate, or alternative; site OPEN, decide by Month 1 = 2026-11-08) with host-country Memorandum of Understanding confirming site availability, access rights, immunity and dispute-resolution procedures
  • Facility hardening and security certification (ISO 27001, IAEA-equivalent physical security, Tempest-rated or equivalent electronic security) validation by independent auditor by Month 3 (2027-01-08)
  • Secure facility layout and operational-capability inventory: co-chair boardroom, secure reading room (for raw-evidence escort access), ledger-hosting center (dual-redundancy hardware, continuous backup), key-custody ceremony room (with fail-safe power and escape routes), inspector debriefing/cooling-off spaces, bilateral communications center (air-gapped network, monitored secure phone/video conference), staff offices (mixed-nationality, no single-person critical functions)
  • Facility staffing plan (15–20 full-time, mixed-nationality staff, bonded and cleared by both co-chairs) and operational procedures (24/7 staffed, dual-lock access controls, incident-response procedures, quarterly security re-audit)
  • Host-country agreement: customs procedures for inspectors transiting through the neutral facility, visa and diplomatic status (are facility staff considered diplomats or civilian contractors? What immunity applies?), liability and insurance provisions, dispute-resolution mechanisms (if either country claims the facility violates its sovereignty or if an incident occurs)

Simulation Steps

  • Create a Neutral-Facility Site Comparison Matrix (spreadsheet) comparing Geneva and Singapore (or other candidates) on: (1) Host-country willingness (diplomatic precedent: Geneva hosts IAEA, OPCW, UN; Singapore hosts regional agreements but fewer global arms-control precedents), (2) Lease/facility costs (estimated USD 100–200k/month for 1,000+ sq m, hardened), (3) Security-hardening feasibility (both are high-security, pro-transparency jurisdictions), (4) Access/travel for both countries' personnel (Geneva favors Europe; Singapore favors Asia-Pacific), (5) Staffing availability (both have multilingual, security-cleared personnel available), (6) Construction/hardening timeline (Geneva: existing facilities available, 8–12 weeks to harden; Singapore: similar or slightly faster). Score each factor on a 1–5 scale and tabulate; likely conclusion: Geneva is slower to negotiate (multiple organizations claiming space) but more precedent-rich; Singapore is faster and equally secure but less arms-control precedent.
  • Design the facility layout (floor plan or schematic diagram) allocating 1,000+ sq m across: (1) Co-Chair Boardroom (200 sq m, secure video conference, dual large-screen displays, secure phones, wall-mounted map of participating sites), (2) Secure Reading Room (150 sq m, 4 workstations with air-gapped monitors, dual-escort seating for counterpart teams, log sheet for evidence-access tracking, all documents scanned and retained on-site), (3) Ledger-Hosting Center (200 sq m, hardware servers for dual national ledger copies, UPS and generator backup, environmental controls, 24/7 staffed monitoring station, network monitoring appliances for digest-exchange and mismatch alerts), (4) Key-Custody Ceremony Room (100 sq m, air-gapped clean-room environment, dual locked safes for share storage, witness-observation stations, video recording equipment for ceremony documentation), (5) Inspector Debriefing/CI Spaces (150 sq m, 3–4 interview rooms with sound-proof walls, observation windows, secure document-handling area for wiping electronics), (6) Bilateral Communications Center (100 sq m, secure phone lines, video conference, encrypted network, air-gapped from public internet), (7) Staff Offices, break rooms, storage (remaining space).
  • Model a key-custody ceremony workflow using a BPMN (business process model and notation) diagram or flowchart: (1) Pre-ceremony (Day −1): both countries' key-custody officers, a neutral security officer and independent observers arrive at the facility, verify seals on the ceremony space, conduct a 2-hour briefing on procedures. (2) Ceremony (Day 0, 4 hours): both teams generate a random seed (coin flips, dice rolls), feed the seed into a hardware random-number generator, generate a master key from the output, split the key using Shamir's Secret Sharing (e.g., 2-of-2 shares), print the shares on cards, seal each share in a tamper-evident envelope, each country's officer carries their envelope to a dual-lock safe (both keys required to open). (3) Post-ceremony (Day +1): both officers sign a Certificate of Ceremony (witnessed and notarized), photographs of sealed envelopes are taken and retained by the neutral facility. (4) Recovery (if key is lost): both officers and independent auditor jointly open the safe, verify seals, regenerate the key from the shares (2-of-2 requires both shares), repeat ceremony to generate a new master key, retire the old key and issue a Key Retirement Certificate (logged in the ledger as an Event).
  • Simulate the facility's operational-availability scenario: Ledger Hosting Center is 24/7 staffed and continuously backs up both national ledger copies. An event occurs at Site A at 03:00 UTC (local time varies by country). Inspector records the event in the local ledger at 03:05 UTC. Facility's Ledger Operations Center checks the event at 04:00 UTC (hourly synchronization trigger), reads the local entry, computes a signed digest, sends the digest to both national ledgers via monitored secure network at 04:02 UTC. Both national ledgers receive the digest at 04:05 UTC, compute a hash of their local ledger copies, compare to the received digest; if match, acknowledge the synchronization; if mismatch, alert the Ledger Operations Center and both co-chairs within 4 hours (04:00 UTC + 4 hours = 08:00 UTC). This scenario assumes the facility is never offline and never fails to send digests on schedule.
  • Create a facility-staffing organization chart: Joint Facility Director (neutral third country, reports jointly to both co-chairs); Deputy Directors (1 per country, report to Director); Operational Staff: Ledger Manager (1), Key-Custody Coordinator (1), CI/Inspector Liaison (2), Communications/IT Officer (1), Administrator (3), Security/Physical Plant (4), Cleaning & Logistics (2). Total: ~16–20 staff. Model the weekly meeting schedule: Weekly operations briefing (Monday, 09:00 CET, Facility Director and both Deputy Directors), Monthly security re-audit (first Friday of month), Quarterly budget/staffing review (mid-month). This ensures dual-country oversight and prevents any single country from taking unilateral control of the facility.

Expert Validation Steps

  • Engage a bilateral facility-procurement team (1 diplomat per country, 1 facility-design expert, 1 security/hardening consultant) by Month 0 (2026-10-08) to identify candidate sites and negotiate host-country agreements. Deliverable: site nomination and MOU by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23); final site decision by Month 1 (2026-11-08).
  • Request a pre-audit by the host country's building inspector or equivalent (by Month 1.5 = 2026-11-23) to confirm the facility meets structural, fire, electrical and environmental standards for a secure facility. Request a security-certification audit (ISO 27001, Tempest or equivalent electronic-security standards) by Month 2 (2026-12-08), to be completed by Month 2.5 (2026-12-23).
  • Engage an independent facility-security expert (from a neutral third country, pre-approved by both co-chairs) to audit the hardening specifications and the completed facility by Month 3 (2027-01-08). Deliverable: Security Certification Report confirming that the facility meets international standards for secure communications, key custody, and classified-document handling, or identifying residual vulnerabilities with mitigations.
  • Request both countries' chief information-security officers to validate the ledger-hosting architecture (hardware redundancy, network isolation, synchronization procedures) and to approve the Technical Specifications for the Ledger Hosting Center by Month 2.5 (2026-12-23).
  • Conduct a full operational dry-run of the facility (Month 4.5 = 2027-02-23 to Month 5 = 2027-03-08): simulate a key-custody ceremony (generate test keys, split, store, verify recovery), test the ledger synchronization (mock events at a test site, transmit to the facility, verify both national copies receive the digest, detect and remediate a simulated divergence), test inspector debriefing (practice the 4-hour debriefing protocol with volunteer inspectors, time the process, identify bottlenecks). Produce a Facility Operational Readiness Report by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23) confirming zero critical gaps and <5 minor gaps (with mitigation plans) before Phase One begins.

Responsible Parties

  • Bilateral facility-procurement team (1 diplomat per country, facility-design expert, security consultant) coordinating site selection and host-country agreement
  • Host-country authorities (building inspector, foreign ministry, security agency) confirming site availability and issuing hardening permits
  • Independent facility-security expert (neutral third country, pre-approved) auditing hardening specifications and certifying the facility
  • Both countries' information-security officers validating ledger-hosting architecture and network isolation
  • Joint Facility Director and Deputy Directors (appointed by Month 3 = 2027-01-08) managing 24/7 operations and monthly security re-audits

Assumptions

  • High: Geneva or Singapore will commit to hosting the facility, granting diplomatic immunity/status to staff, and will not close or restrict the facility during Phase One operations.
  • High: The facility can be hardened (ISO 27001, Tempest or equivalent security standards) and operationally ready by Month 3 (2027-01-08), allowing a 2–3 month buffer before Phase One begins.
  • Medium: The key-custody ceremony (dual-share generation and storage) can be executed safely and reliably within the ceremony room's controlled environment, and key recovery (if a share is lost) can restore operational keys within 8–24 hours.
  • Medium: The ledger-hosting center can maintain continuous operation (24/7, with redundancy and backup power) and can synchronize both national ledgers at 1-hour intervals with <4-hour mismatch escalation throughout Phase One.
  • Medium: Mixed-nationality facility staffing (15–20 personnel, no single-person critical functions) can operate without either country gaining unilateral control or access to the other country's ledger copy or key shares.

SMART Validation Objective

By Month 1 (2026-11-08), identify and negotiate a bilateral MOU with the host country (Geneva or Singapore) confirming site availability and immunity status by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23). By Month 2.5 (2026-12-23), complete security-hardening certification (ISO 27001 or equivalent) and approve the Technical Specifications for the Ledger Hosting Center. By Month 3 (2027-01-08), occupy the facility and install all operational systems (ledger hardware, key-custody safe, secure reading room, video conference infrastructure). By Month 5.5 (2027-03-23), conduct a full operational dry-run (key-custody ceremony, ledger synchronization test, inspector debriefing simulation) and produce a Facility Operational Readiness Report confirming zero critical gaps. Approve the Joint Facility Director and Deputy Directors by Month 3 (2027-01-08) and ensure 24/7 staffing begins by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23).

Notes

  • Geneva has precedent (IAEA, OPCW are based there) but facility availability and diplomatic negotiation may be slow; Singapore is faster but less arms-control precedent. The bilateral procurement team must negotiate both sites in parallel and decide by Month 1 (2026-11-08) based on schedule risk.
  • The facility is not a secondary backup; both countries' ledger copies and key shares are held there. If the facility is compromised (infiltrated by an intelligence service, occupied by one country's military), both co-chairs lose evidence custody. Host-country political stability and security commitment are critical assumptions.
