  • Key-custody ceremonies (generating, splitting and storing dual-share keys) are the most security-sensitive operations in the facility. These must be conducted under witness, with independent observers, and with video documentation so either country can later verify that neither side installed a backdoor or conducted an unauthorized key-generation.
  • Ledger hosting and synchronization is the most operationally critical component; a single divergence or synchronization failure can block evidence acceptance and trigger automatic escalation to a 72-hour deadlock procedure. The facility must be redundant and monitored 24/7.
  • Mixed-nationality staffing (no single-person critical functions, no unilateral access to ledgers or keys) prevents either country from claiming the facility is captured or compromised by the other. Dual-lock safes, dual-key access controls, and witnessed operations are essential.

Summary

The Consortium is an unprecedented bilateral US–China verification mechanism for declared frontier-computing equipment changes, running a 90-day Phase One test (Months 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08) with a USD 5.0 billion budget (USD 2.5B per country), producing a Go/Modify/Stop verdict by Month 9.5 (2027-07-23). The plan rests on seven critical data-collection and validation areas: (1) Entry-condition gates (bilateral instrument, domestic authority, matched-pair sites, inspector approval, vendor commitments, covered-equipment schedule) must be locked by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23) on binding timelines with external escalation authority to prevent serial delays; (2) the confidential evidence-weighting rule must be validated on historical records and adversarial synthetic cases, with false-positive rate confirmed within ±3 points of 10% target by Month 2 (2026-12-08), before Phase One exercises; (3) verdict thresholds (Go ≥75% detection, Modify 55–75%, Stop <55%) and mechanical scoring rules must be pre-registered as confidence-interval bands in a bilateral memorandum locked by Month 2.5 (2026-12-23), locked again by signature before Phase One begins, with no post-hoc renegotiation allowed; (4) full-time mirrored inspectorates (180 per country, 24/7 shifts with 4-month on-site/2-month off-site rotation) must be recruited, vetted and certified (80% by Month 5 = 2027-03-08) for deployment by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23), with realistic staffing-model choice (continuous 3-shift, 2-shift 16-hour, or event-triggered) locked by Month 1 (2026-11-08); (5) bilateral Counterintelligence Oversight Board (3 officers per side, monthly meetings) must vet all 300+ inspectors by Month 2 (2026-12-08), enforce sealed communication and compartmentalization rules, and adjudicate breaches within a 7-day fast-track procedure; (6) bilateral instrument (80–120 pages, classified) must be finalized and signed by Month 1 (2026-11-08), embedding unambiguous deadlock clock, automatic partial-suspension triggers (day 14), impaired-confidence thresholds (days 21/28), locked verdict thresholds with mechanical rules, evidence-rule confidentiality and no-amendment clauses, and hard Stop triggers (asymmetric access, shielding, ledger divergence, withheld funding), with independent legal audit confirming internal consistency by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23); and (7) neutral secure facility (Geneva or Singapore, 1,000+ sq m, operationally ready by Month 3 = 2027-01-08) must host replicated ledgers, key-custody ceremonies, secure reading rooms for raw-evidence access and inspector debriefing, with 24/7 staffing (15–20 mixed-nationality personnel) and a full operational dry-run (key ceremony, ledger synchronization test) by Month 5 (2027-03-08). The greatest vulnerabilities are: (1) entry-condition sequencing risk—gates must run in parallel from Month −2 with external escalation authority to invoke scope reduction (2 pairs, 60-day test) rather than timeline extension if any gate slips >2 weeks; (2) evidence-rule miscalibration—false-positive rate could reach 20–30% instead of 10% target, overwhelming the 15-case/month adjudication capacity and causing 30–50 unresolved discrepancies to accumulate, triggering automatic partial suspensions and stalling Phase One; (3) verdict-threshold ambiguity—confidence intervals (±12% pooled, ±32% per type) mean many outcomes will be ambiguous (interval straddles threshold), making Modify the default but requiring mechanical scoring rule to be locked before any results are known, or else verdicts will be politicized; (4) staffing underestimation—the plan's 99-per-country baseline assumes continuous presence (choice 1: Mirrored Shift Coverage) but underfunds it; realistic continuous 24/7 coverage requires ~300+ per country, exceeding the USD 750M envelope unless 2-shift 16-hour (180 per country) is accepted and exercises are restricted to day-shift hours; and (5) facility single-point-of-failure—if the neutral facility is unavailable, the ledger cannot synchronize, key ceremonies cannot occur, and Phase One halts. Immediate actionable priorities are: (1) launch an Entry-Condition Task Force by Month 0 (2026-10-08) with binding weekly milestones, parallel site nomination and vendor outreach starting Month −2, and external escalation authority to invoke scope reduction if any gate slips >2 weeks; (2) lock the evidence rule in escrow by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23) and validate it on 100–200 historical records and 20–30 adversarial synthetic cases by Month 2 (2026-12-08), confirming false-positive rate within 7–13% before Phase One; (3) finalize and co-chair-sign the bilateral instrument (with locked verdict thresholds, mechanical scoring rule, deadlock clock and automatic-suspension procedures) by Month 1 (2026-11-08) and obtain independent legal audit of internal consistency by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23); (4) resize the staffing model (confirm choice: 2-shift 16-hour at 180 per country with day-shift exercise restriction, or 3-shift continuous at 300+ per country) by Month 1 (2026-11-08) and lock recruitment pipelines so 80% certification is achieved by Month 5 (2027-03-08); and (5) identify and hardening-certify the neutral facility (Geneva or Singapore) by Month 2.5 (2026-12-23), conduct operational dry-run by Month 5 (2027-03-08), and ensure 24/7 staffing begins by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23). Success depends on rigorous execution of these seven validation areas and explicit pre-authorization of scope-reduction backstop (2 pairs, 60-day test) if timeline compression becomes unavoidable.

Create Document 1: Project Charter and Mission Definition

ID: a62b791a-88f9-42a0-a906-9b3cad884a67

Description: High-level charter formalizing The Consortium's scope, governance structure (equal co-chairs, double-key authorization, no casting vote), Phase One objectives (90-day declared-equipment change verification at 2–4 matched datacenter pairs), Go/Modify/Stop decision criteria, budget envelope (USD 5.0B), entry conditions and critical success factors. Intended for co-chairs, national leadership and legislative oversight. Establishes legal authority and political commitment.

Responsible Role Type: Project Director / Executive Sponsor

Primary Template: PMI Project Charter Template

Secondary Template: Arms Control Verification Program Charter (IAEA/OPCW precedent)

Steps to Create:

  • Define mission scope: declared-equipment change verification only (no workload, topology, hidden-facility detection).
  • Specify governance: equal co-chairs, double-key authorization for all major decisions, deadlock procedures (auto-suspension day 14, impaired-confidence days 21–28), no casting vote.
  • Lock entry conditions: bilateral instrument, appropriations, site selection, inspector approval, vendor participation, covered-equipment schedule (each with milestone date).
  • Define Phase One: 90-day operational window (Months 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08), verdict by Month 9.5 (2027-07-23).
  • Specify budget: USD 5.0B total (USD 2.5B each country), seven fixed envelopes, 100% envelope-mapping audit, contingency USD 500M with draw triggers (30%, 50%, 75%).
  • State Go/Modify/Stop criteria: detection ≥70% planned / ≥50% unplanned, false positives ≤10%, unverifiable ≤5%, parity ≥85%, no discrepancy >21 days, <5 open material cases, no hard Stop triggers.
  • Identify critical success factors: entry-gate completion on time, exercise credibility, adjudication capacity, parity maintenance, ledger integrity.
  • Require joint co-chair signature by Month 1 (2026-11-08).

Approval Authorities: Both national co-chairs (joint approval required); domestic legislative appropriations bodies (for funding authorization).

Essential Information:

  • Formalize Phase One scope: declared-equipment change verification only at 2–4 matched datacenter pairs, excluding workload verification, topology analysis, model-weight inspection, and hidden-facility detection.
  • Establish governance framework: specify equal national co-chairs, double-key authorization for all major decisions, predefined deadlock procedures (automatic partial suspension at day 14, impaired-confidence status at days 21–28), and explicit statement that no casting vote exists.
  • Define Phase One operational window: 90-day clock running Months 6–9 (2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08), verdict scored within 5 days and final decision by Month 9.5 (2027-07-23).
  • Lock entry conditions with specific milestone dates: bilateral instrument signature (Month 1 = 2026-11-08), domestic access authority and first-tranche appropriation (Month 2 = 2026-12-08), matched-pair approval (Month 3 = 2027-01-08), inspector approval and vendor-participation registry (Month 4 = 2027-02-08), entry-gate certification (Month 5.5 = 2027-03-23).
  • Specify budget allocation: USD 5.0 billion total (USD 2.5 billion per country, exactly 50/50 split); seven fixed envelopes mapped in charter; contingency USD 500M with draw triggers (>30% use = co-chair briefing; >50% = scope-reduction planning; >75% = joint audit review); any envelope exceeding 110% triggers co-chair review, exceeding 120% requires supplemental appropriation (veto point).
  • Define Go/Modify/Stop verdict criteria as measurable thresholds (proposed, validated on pilot data): detection ≥70% planned events / ≥50% unplanned; false positives ≤10%; unverifiable equipment ≤5%; reciprocal-access parity ≥85%; no discrepancy older than 21 days; fewer than 5 open material discrepancies; no hard Stop triggers.
  • Identify hard Stop triggers: asymmetric inspector access, material unverifiable equipment (>10% at any site or overall), government shielding of operator, unresolved ledger divergence, withholding of funding by either country.
  • Specify tranche structure: four synchronized drawdowns per country at 25% (Month 2 = 2026-12-08), 25% (Month 3 = 2027-01-08), 30% (Month 5.5 = 2027-03-23), 20% (Month 9.2–9.5 on verdict); any tranche delay over 14 days escalates to co-chair summit; delay over 30 days or unequal deposits unresolved = Stop trigger.
  • Establish critical success factors: on-time entry-gate completion (no single gate slip >2 weeks without emergency summit); exercise credibility and statistical defensibility (6–8 replicates per event type, ±10–15% confidence intervals at 95%); adjudication capacity sufficient for 15 discrepancies per month; parity maintained across matched pairs (no asymmetric access); ledger integrity (hourly digest synchronization, <1-hour event recording latency).
  • Require joint co-chair signature and approval by Month 1 (2026-11-08), and legislative appropriations authorization by Month 2 (2026-12-08) as preconditions for the charter to take effect.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Scope creep or ambiguity: If the charter does not explicitly exclude workload verification, topology analysis or hidden-facility detection, either government may later claim those activities are in scope, triggering scope disputes that consume weeks of negotiation and delay entry conditions.
  • Governance deadlock: Without a published deadlock procedure locked in the charter, equal co-chairs can paralyze decisions on budget disputes, protocol changes or site findings, allowing discrepancies to age unresolved and triggering automatic suspension by default rather than negotiated resolution.
  • Entry-condition delays: If entry gates lack explicit milestone dates and escalation procedures, delays compound (site selection → vendor negotiation → schedule adoption → inspector vetting), compressing Phase One from 90 to 45–60 days, which widens statistical confidence intervals from ±10–15% to ±15–20%, undermining the credibility of the final Go/Modify/Stop verdict.
  • Budget ambiguity or disputes: Without fixed envelope allocation and clear tranche conditions, either government can claim overruns belong to the other's sphere or dispute how costs map to envelopes, triggering withheld tranches and stalling operations by Month 6–8 (2027-04-08 to 2027-06-08).
  • Verdict criteria vagueness: If Go/Modify/Stop thresholds are not pre-registered before Phase One begins, both governments can dispute the final verdict using different weightings of detection rate, false positives and parity scores, requiring weeks of political negotiation and potentially invalidating the Go decision.
  • Missing governance authority: If the charter does not establish the co-chairs' binding authority to commit national resources, approve protocol changes and authorize key decisions without veto from other agencies, competing domestic authorities will create decision deadlock.
  • Inadequate escalation procedures: Without a published procedure for handling gates that slip >2 weeks (emergency summit, compression reserve, potential scope reduction), entry delays accumulate silently until Month 5–6 (2027-03-08 to 2027-04-08), when remediation is impossible within the Phase One window.
  • No contingency governance: If the charter does not specify contingency draw triggers and envelope-overrun escalation, either government can claim surprise cost overruns (estimated 5–10% of budget by Month 3 = 2027-01-08 from entry-condition delays), depleting contingency and forcing difficult mid-test choices without pre-agreed criteria.

Worst Case Scenario: Entry conditions stall across multiple gates (site selection, vendor participation, inspector vetting) due to missing deadlines or escalation procedures. By Month 4 (2027-02-08), cumulative delays have consumed USD 200–400M in sunk costs and compressed available Phase One window from 90 days to 45 days. Personnel cannot be fully trained by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23) entry certification, yielding a 20–30% staffing shortfall at Phase One start (Month 6 = 2027-04-08). Exercise load is cut from 54 to 25–30 total trials, yielding fewer than 4 replicates per event type. Statistical confidence intervals widen from ±10–15% to ±20–25% (95% CL). At Phase One conclusion (Month 9 = 2027-07-08), detection rates fall in the 55–80% ambiguous zone. Both governments dispute the final verdict: one claims >75% detection justifies Go, the other argues 60% requires Stop. The Charter lacks explicit verdict-scoring logic, so the dispute cannot be resolved mechanically. Political renegotiation of the Go/Modify/Stop threshold consumes 4–6 weeks. Either government may withdraw, citing mission failure. USD 3–4 billion has been spent with no credible Go decision. Phase One conclusion fails, and Phase Two funding is contested or withdrawn.

Best Case Scenario: The Charter is signed by co-chairs and enacted legislatively by Month 1–2 (2026-11-08 to 2026-12-08), with all entry gates specified as binding milestones. Entry conditions complete on schedule: bilateral instrument signed Month 1 (2026-11-08), matched pairs approved Month 3 (2027-01-08), entry gate certified Month 5.5 (2027-03-23). Personnel are fully recruited, vetted and trained by Month 5 (2027-03-08), deployed at 95%+ strength by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23). Phase One runs the full 90-day window Months 6–9 (2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08) with 54 exercises and 6–8 replicates per event type. Detection rates average 72±11% (confidence intervals do not straddle thresholds; Go criterion met). All four other scored criteria are met (false positives 8%, unverifiable 4%, parity 88%, no discrepancy >21 days). The Charter's pre-registered Go logic applies mechanically: verdict is Go by Month 9.2 (2027-07-14). Both governments accept the outcome as technically credible. Phase One concludes successfully, demonstrating bilateral declared-equipment change verification is feasible. Phase Two funding and scope decisions proceed with political confidence.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If Charter negotiation extends beyond Month 1 (2026-11-08): Issue a joint interim Charter binding only on Phase One operations (Months 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08), with entry-condition gates delegated to parallel task forces and an external Program Risk Officer authorized to escalate gate slips directly to co-chairs. This separates higher-level charter approval from operational-readiness decisions.
  • If entry-condition deadlines cannot be locked politically by Month 0 (2026-10-08): Establish a pre-Phase-One task force with binding timeline authority, external escalation escalation to co-chairs within 48 hours of any gate slipping >1 week, and a published contingency reserve (USD 50–100M) explicitly earmarked for compressed negotiation. Publish a monthly entry-condition status dashboard to legislatures.
  • If Go/Modify/Stop verdict thresholds cannot be pre-registered before Phase One exercises: Use a two-stage verdict process: (1) Interim Modify verdict at Month 8 (2027-06-08) based on partial data, allowing co-chairs time to finalize threshold-scoring logic; (2) Final verdict at Month 9.5 (2027-07-23) using locked mechanical scoring. Explicitly label the interim verdict provisional.
  • If equal co-chairs governance proves too restrictive for timely decisions on evidence disputes: Establish a standing Adjudication Panel (3 specialists per country) with advisory authority over evidence classification only (not outcomes or suspensions), rendering recommendations within 5 days of case opening. Panel recommendations are non-binding but published; co-chairs must override explicitly in the ledger.
  • If budget envelope disputes emerge mid-Phase-One: Activate monthly independent auditor review (not year-end only) with unclassified monthly summaries showing envelope status, reconciliation exceptions and contingency burn rate. Tie tranche releases to audit sign-off, creating transparent visibility that reduces claims of surprise.
  • If recruitment or vetting of personnel falls behind plan by Month 3 (2027-01-08): Compress training timeline and run pilot exercises (Month 5 = 2027-03-08) with 70–80% of target personnel, accepting a shorter ramp-up. Measure staffing fill rate as a leading indicator; if fill reaches only 60% by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23), invoke scope reduction (reduce from 3 matched pairs to 2 pairs, reducing exercise load from 54 to 36 trials).

Create Document 2: Bilateral Instrument and Governance Framework

ID: 03b2a80e-db73-4895-9b18-bed7520a5dac

Description: Formal international bilateral agreement establishing the Consortium's legal foundation, governance procedures, deadlock resolution with automatic suspension triggers, inspector privileges and immunity, evidence handling and confidentiality tiers, operator compensation terms, neutral-facility status, and termination provisions. Classified. Binding on both governments. Core of the double-key authorization structure.

Responsible Role Type: Legal Counsel / International Law Specialist

Primary Template: Bilateral Arms-Control Treaty (New START, JCPOA precedent)

Secondary Template: IAEA Safeguards Agreement text

Steps to Create:

  • Draft executive-summary preamble: mutual recognition of equal standing, commitment to reciprocal transparency, no casting vote, binding dispute procedures.
  • Article 1: Mission scope, declared-equipment definition, verified change types (arrival, installation, maintenance, decommissioning, transfer).
  • Article 2: Governance (co-chair roles, double-key procedures for budget releases, protocol changes, findings adjudication, suspension triggers).
  • Article 3: Entry conditions (instrument signature, appropriation, domestic access authority, site selection with parity audit, inspector approval, vendor participation, schedule adoption) with milestone dates.
  • Article 4: Deadlock and automatic-suspension procedures (clock definition, day 14 partial suspension of disputed function, day 21–28 impaired-confidence, emergency summit at day 35, no co-chair waivers without ledger annotation).
  • Article 5: Budget envelopes, funding tranches with synchronized deposit requirement and 14-day escalation / 30-day Stop trigger for delays.
  • Article 6: Evidence weighting rule, confidential versioning, no single decisive source, rotating combinations.
  • Article 7: Verdict thresholds (detection, false-positive, unverifiable, parity rates) as confidence-interval bands, mechanical scoring rule, no amendment after first exercise, final-verdict report signed by both co-chairs.
  • Article 8: Inspector privileges, immunity, security vetting, compartmentalization, cooling-off periods, no personal-device communications on-site.
  • Article 9: Operator compensation from home government's USD 2.5B contribution; vendor-refusal fallback ladder (5 rungs); equipment unresolved at entry classified unverifiable or excluded.
  • Article 10: Neutral facility status, immunity from seizure, dual co-chair control, no unilateral access restrictions.
  • Article 11: Key custody (dual-share generation, joint ceremonies, lost-key recovery procedures, ledger signing requirements).
  • Article 12: Evidence disclosure tiers, filtered packages, raw-evidence escort access under dispute, independent filter auditor certification.
  • Article 13: Confidentiality, classification handling, post-Phase-One ledger archival (7-year minimum), access procedures.
  • Article 14: Termination clause (allows either party to withdraw with 180-day notice after entry certification; early withdrawal triggers Stop).
  • Obtain legal review from both sides' offices of legal counsel; resolve divergent interpretations. Require joint signature by Month 1 (2026-11-08).

Approval Authorities: Both national co-chairs and their legal advisors; foreign ministries or equivalent (for treaty authority); domestic legislative bodies (constitutional ratification if required).

Essential Information:

  • Establish the legal foundation and binding authority for the Consortium's bilateral governance, including double-key authorization procedures, equal co-chair roles, and no-casting-vote deadlock resolution mechanisms.
  • Define the mission scope explicitly: verification of declared-equipment changes (arrival, installation, maintenance, removal, transfer, decommissioning) at participating declared sites only; exclude total-capacity estimates, workload verification, model-weight inspection, and hidden-facility detection.
  • Specify all entry conditions as sequential gates with binding completion dates: signed bilateral instrument by Month 1 (2026-11-08); domestic access authority and appropriations by Month 2 (2026-12-08); matched-pair site selection with reciprocal-access parity audit by Month 3 (2027-01-08); inspector approval and vendor-participation registry by Month 4 (2027-02-08); covered-equipment schedule adoption by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23).
  • Document the seven fixed budget envelopes (ledger/attestation USD 1.25B, site prep/compensation USD 1.0B, personnel USD 750M, facilities/cyber/CI USD 750M, testing USD 500M, legal/audit USD 250M, contingency USD 500M) with 100% envelope mapping rules, synchronized tranche structure (25%-25%-30%-20% at signature, site approval, entry certification, verdict), and 14-day escalation / 30-day Stop triggers for delayed tranches.
  • Define the deadlock, impaired-confidence and automatic-suspension procedures: panel convened by day 10 of dispute, advisory opinion by day 15, co-chair decision by day 18; partial suspension of disputed function at day 14; impaired-confidence status at day 21 (identity disputes) and day 28 (exit dispositions); emergency summit if suspension extends past day 35.
  • Specify the confidential, rotating Layered Evidence Weighting Model rule (no single evidence source decisive; combinations of attestation, inspection, customs records, identifiers, maintenance logs, infrastructure changes, witnessed movement) locked in versioned escrow by Month 4.5 (2027-02-23), validated against 100-200 historical events per site by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23), and not subject to amendment after the first Phase One exercise (Month 6 = 2027-04-08).
  • Lock provisional Go/Modify/Stop verdict thresholds before the first Phase One exercise (by Month 5.5 = 2027-03-23) with explicit confidence-interval bands: detection ≥70% (planned), ≥50% (unplanned); false positives ≤10%; unverifiable equipment ≤5%; reciprocal-access parity ≥85%; unresolved discrepancies ≤21 days at conclusion; and fewer than 5 open material discrepancies. Mechanical scoring rule: ≥80% thresholds met → Go; 50–80% → Modify; <50% → Stop.
  • Specify hard Stop triggers that terminate Phase One regardless of other metrics: asymmetric inspector access at matched pairs; material unverifiable equipment (>10% at a site or overall); government shielding of an operator; unresolved ledger divergence; either country withholding a scheduled tranche over 30 days.
  • Define the replicated tamper-evident ledger architecture: independent national copies in each country (or neutral facility) with events recorded locally within 5 minutes, counterpart signed-digest exchange at least hourly, divergence alerts at 30-minute overdue, escalation within 4 hours, and target reconciliation within 72 hours (hard limit 7 days).
  • Document the root-of-trust key custody procedure: dual-share keys generated in joint ceremonies at the neutral facility by Month 4 (2027-02-08), both shares required for any ledger signing or attestation validation, lost-key recovery ceremonies scheduled at Months 4 and 5 (2027-02-08 and 2027-03-08) with pre-approved revocation and new-key generation protocols.
  • Establish the Inspector Information Firewall Doctrine: compartmentalized knowledge by role and site, post-rotation debriefs and monitored cooling-off periods before reassignment, sealed observation-and-report interface with raw observations held in site custody, no personal communications on-site, and a bilateral Counterintelligence Oversight Board (3 officers per side) with 48-hour investigation, 72-hour recommendation and 7-day breach-response procedures.
  • Define the Counterpart Evidence Disclosure Tiers: host side provides hashed event summaries and equipment identifiers by default; counterpart receives filtered evidence packages certified by an independent third-country filter auditor; raw evidence accessible only under dual escort in a joint secure reading room after a formal discrepancy is opened.
  • Specify operator compensation terms: domestic operator and vendor compensation is administered by the home government and charged to its own USD 2.5 billion contribution, within the site-preparation/compensation envelope (USD 1.0B total, about USD 167M per site ceiling at 3 pairs).
  • Document the Vendor Refusal Fallback Ladder: vendor-supervised testing, filtered evidence, accredited independent examiners, clean-room procedures, validated attestations. Each rung requires 8–12 weeks. Equipment unresolved at entry (Month 5.5 = 2027-03-23) is classified unverifiable or excluded from the covered schedule. One accredited independent-examiner team per country (5–8 specialists) is pre-staged by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23) from the testing envelope.
  • Define the Matched Site Selection Doctrine: nominate 3 paired sites (6 total, 3 per country) with functional equivalence criteria (staging area ≥500 sq m, 24-hour access, equipment lift ≥50 tons, ≥2 maintenance events per month per site), reciprocal-access parity audited by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23), and co-chair certification locked by Month 3 (2027-01-08). Asymmetric access excludes a pair; do not proceed with fewer than 2 matched pairs.
  • Establish the Independent Exercise Authority: mixed-nationality, 8 core staff, designs, schedules and scores all 54 blind-challenge exercises (3–4 per site per month for 90 days, targeting 6–8 replicates per event type). Each country's red team nominates challenge types; the Authority alone decides execution timing. Exercises run in staging, spare-inventory, maintenance or expansion areas without interrupting active computation.
  • Define the covered-equipment schedule: confidential, versioned, technology-neutral; frozen for the entire Phase One window (Months 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08). Amendments only by double-key approval before the clock (by Month 5.5 = 2027-03-23); effective only for events recorded after the amendment effective date; full version history maintained in the ledger.
  • Specify the neutral secure facility (Geneva or Singapore; site choice by Month 1 = 2026-11-08): at least 1,000 sq m, operational by Month 3 (2027-01-08), hosting bilateral co-chair workspace, secure reading rooms, replicated ledger copies, key-custody ceremonies, inspector debriefing and cooling-off areas, mapped to the secure-facilities envelope (USD 750M shared).
  • Document the Ledger Synchronization Bounds: hourly scheduled digest exchange with 30-minute overdue alert, automatic escalation within 4 hours on mismatch, reconciliation within 72 hours (hard limit 7 days), divergence logged as an event and counted toward adjudication caseload.
  • Define language of record and interpretive authority: English and Mandarin equally authoritative; joint terminology board issues controlled glossary and rules on divergences; coded language-neutral schema for evidence entries to minimize ambiguity; translation turnaround targets (TBD) support timely adjudication.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Ambiguous or missing entry-condition gates and dates allow sequential slippage (site selection 4–8 weeks, vendor negotiation 4–6 weeks, schedule finalization 2–4 weeks), compressing Phase One from 90 to 45–60 days, reducing statistical power from ±12% to ±18–22% (95% CL), making the final verdict indefensible.
  • Undefined deadlock and suspension procedures leave unresolved discrepancies aging indefinitely, stalling adjudication and blocking the ledger, undermining the evidence basis for Go/Modify/Stop and enabling either government to delay the verdict by refusing co-chair approval.
  • Pre-registered verdict thresholds without explicit confidence-interval bands allow post-hoc bargaining: Go, Modify and Stop are all defensible readings of the same ambiguous data (e.g., 70±15% detection rate), forcing political negotiation instead of mechanical scoring and eroding credibility.
  • Evidence-weighting rule locked without historical validation invites false-positive rates of 20–30% (vs. 10% target), overwhelming adjudication capacity (50+ cases vs. 15-case planning) and rendering 20–30% of equipment unverifiable, which fails the Go threshold and enables Stop claims.
  • Missing specification of hard Stop triggers (asymmetric access, operator shielding, ledger divergence, funding withholding) allows either government to claim ambiguity about failure conditions, delaying the final decision and creating political cover for strategic withdrawal.
  • Undefined neutral facility location, construction timeline or staffing plan delays the ledger, co-chair coordination, key-custody ceremonies and reading-room operations, pushing facility readiness to Month 4–5 (2027-02-08 to 2027-03-08), which compresses inspector training and pilot exercises to 2–4 weeks before Phase One.
  • Insufficient detail on the Vendor Refusal Fallback Ladder and examiner-team pre-staging leaves equipment unverifiable at entry, automatically triggering unverifiable-equipment counts over 5%, which fails Go thresholds and commits the program to Stop or Modify without credible detection data.
  • Vague Layered Evidence Weighting Model without specific evidence categories, weighting schemes or contradiction-vs.-accumulation logic prevents both governments from validating the rule for bias, inviting disputes about rule validity that cannot be resolved and creating a contested evidence basis for the entire verdict.
  • Missing budget-envelope escalation procedures and contingency-burn thresholds allow overspending in one envelope to consume contingency silently; by Month 4 (2027-02-08) unplanned costs can consume 30–40% of the USD 500M contingency, leaving no buffer for Phase One operational overruns or leaving no cover for entry-condition delays.
  • Underspecified matched-site selection and parity audit delay entry certification by 6–8 weeks while site-nomination disputes are negotiated, consuming compression reserve and forcing a choice between timeline slip and asymmetric-access compromise that fails Phase One credibility.

Worst Case Scenario: The Bilateral Instrument and Governance Framework is not finalized by Month 1 (2026-11-08), causing the entry-condition gates to slip sequentially: site selection negotiation extends to Month 3.5 (2027-01-23), inspector vetting to Month 5 (2027-03-08), pilot exercise to Month 6 (2027-04-08). Phase One operationally runs only 45 days (Months 6.5–8 = 2027-04-23 to 2027-06-08), yielding 30 exercises (5 per event type), confidence intervals of ±25–32% per type, and an unverifiable-equipment count exceeding 10% due to incomplete vendor-refusal fallback procedures. The deadlock and suspension procedures are not locked in the instrument, so the first substantive discrepancy (unreported arrival disputed) ages for 35+ days without automatic escalation because both co-chairs interpret the deadlock clock differently. The evidence-weighting rule is not validated on historical data and produces 25% false positives on Phase One data, generating 20–30 unresolved discrepancies by Month 8 (2027-06-08). Ledger synchronization divergence occurs three times; each takes 10+ days to reconcile because the reconciliation procedure is not pre-approved. The verdict thresholds, not pre-registered, are negotiated post-hoc with confidence intervals straddling Go/Modify/Stop boundaries; one government claims the detection rate (65±18%) justifies Go, the other claims it justifies Modify, and the dispute stalls the verdict to Month 11 (2027-09-08), 60+ days past the planned conclusion. The program is invalidated as a proof-of-concept, political withdrawal risk escalates to 50%+, and the USD 5 billion investment yields no credible Go/Modify/Stop decision or actionable lessons for Phase Two.

Best Case Scenario: The Bilateral Instrument is signed by Month 1 (2026-11-08) with all entry conditions, deadlock procedures, evidence rules, verdict thresholds and hard Stop triggers specified explicitly and locked. Entry gates complete on schedule: sites approved Month 3 (2027-01-08), inspectors certified and deployed by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23), evidence rule validated on 150 historical events per site by Month 5 (2027-03-08) with false positives 9±2%, rule and thresholds locked by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23), pilot exercise executes successfully. Phase One runs the full 90 days (Months 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08) with 54 exercises (8 per planned type, 7 per unplanned), detection rates 72±11% (planned), 53±15% (unplanned), false positives 8%, unverifiable equipment 3%, parity 87%, no discrepancies older than 18 days. Ledger synchronization divergence occurs once, resolved in 36 hours. The verdict mechanical scoring shows Go conditions met (4 of 5 thresholds, detection and parity both above bounds). Final verdict is signed by both co-chairs by Month 9.2 (2027-07-14) and published unclassified by Month 9.5 (2027-07-23). The Go decision enables bilateral confidence in declared-equipment verification, supports Phase Two funding commitment, and demonstrates credible detection as proof-of-concept. Political sustainability is high; both governments cite the instrument's governance rigor and honest reporting of statistical limits as precedent for expanded verification.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If comprehensive bilateral instrument negotiations cannot complete by Month 1 (2026-11-08), adopt a 'phased signing' strategy: sign a foundational executive instrument (co-chair roles, deadlock procedures, Stop triggers, budget envelopes) by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23), and defer detailed articles (evidence rule, verdict thresholds, disclosure tiers) to signed bilateral memoranda by Month 2.5 (2026-12-23), allowing entry gates to proceed under the foundational authority while technical details are finalized in parallel.
  • If matched-site selection and reciprocal-access parity audit threaten to slip beyond Month 3 (2027-01-08), reduce the matched set from 3 pairs to 2 pairs (4 sites) by Month 2 (2026-12-08), conduct the parity audit for the smaller set in parallel, and publish a tier-1 (approved) and tier-2 (approved if time permits) site list so that Phase One can begin with 2 pairs on schedule and add a third pair only if entry gates compress.
  • If the evidence-weighting rule cannot be validated on 100–200 historical events per site by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23), substitute a 'proxy pilot exercise' using data from simulated equipment-change scenarios (not live) recorded at a non-participating test facility by Month 4.5 (2027-02-23), validate the rule on the simulated data, and apply a conservative confidence-interval adjustment (assume 20% higher variance) when interpreting Phase One results to account for the lack of validation on real historical events.
  • If key-custody ceremonies cannot be held at the neutral facility by Month 4 (2027-02-08) due to facility construction delays, implement 'distributed key generation' where each country's key-custody team generates its own half-share independently in a Month 4.5 (2027-02-23) ceremony at a bilateral secure facility in the home country, with the shares synchronized via a signed courier handoff by Month 5 (2027-03-08), adding 1–2 week operational delay but preserving the dual-custody structure.
  • If the Vendor Refusal Fallback Ladder cannot be completed for all critical vendors by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23), pre-negotiate 'equipment exclusions' by Month 3 (2027-01-08) where any vendor refusing all rungs of the ladder is acknowledged to have equipment unverifiable and that equipment is excluded from the covered schedule at entry rather than discovered mid-test, reducing entry-time discrepancies but accepting a narrower verification scope.
  • If operational inspectorate staffing cannot reach 80% certification by Month 5 (2027-03-08), defer full Phase One launch to Month 6.5 (2027-04-23) (extending the clock to 60 days instead of 90), and redeploy the 20% shortfall as surge staff available for surge surges and backfill, preserving inspector training quality at the cost of a shortened statistical window.
  • If the Counterpart Evidence Disclosure Tiers and filter auditor certification cannot be finalized by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23), adopt an interim 'tiered read-only access' model where counterpart inspectors view filtered evidence only in the host-side secure facility (not in the neutral facility reading room) under host-side escort, with independent filter certification deferred to Month 7 (2027-05-08) and applied retroactively to Phase One evidence packages, adding disclosure-dispute risk but enabling Phase One to proceed on schedule.
  • If budget envelope overruns accumulate to 40–50% contingency burn by Month 4 (2027-02-08), activate the 'scope-reduction protocol': reduce the matched set to 2 pairs (4 sites), shorten Phase One to 60 days (Months 6.5–8 = 2027-04-23 to 2027-06-08), and redeploy the savings to preserve the core infrastructure (ledger, exercises, adjudication) rather than allowing entry-condition costs to erode Phase One operations.
