ID: 11f38878-1da7-4c82-b479-e9ffd9ae414b

Description: Specification of the confidential rotating evidence-weighting model that combines attestation, physical inspection, customs records, identifiers, maintenance logs, infrastructure changes and witnessed movement into an equipment-identity confidence rating. Locked in double-key-approved escrow by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23). Validated against 100–200 historical equipment-change events per site by Month 2 (2026-12-08) (benign cohort); validated against 20–30 adversarial synthetic scenarios by Month 5 (2027-03-08) (gaming scenarios); frozen before Phase One clock. No single evidence source is decisive. Classified.

Responsible Role Type: Evidence-Rule Architect / Technical Specialist

Primary Template: Technical specification with decision-tree or scoring-matrix format

Secondary Template: Bayesian or rule-based evidence-fusion methodology

Steps to Create:

  • Define the seven evidence categories: (1) vendor attestation (credibility score based on vendor history, escrow records); (2) physical inspection by inspector (serial number confirmation, physical-marking verification); (3) customs and shipment records (arrival dates, declared characteristics, LOCOhist matching); (4) equipment identifiers (firmware versions, manufacturing date codes, performance-test baselines); (5) maintenance logs (service events, personnel involved, parts replaced); (6) infrastructure changes (network configuration, electrical allocation, cooling systems); (7) witnessed movement (inspection video, timestamp logs, dual-escort documentation).
  • Specify the combination rule: no single category is decisive (if only attestation is present, confidence max 60%; if only maintenance logs, max 70%); identity confidence increases when categories corroborate (e.g., physical inspection + customs + attestation = 85%); identity confidence decreases if categories contradict (e.g., firmware version mismatch between attestation and physical test = confidence capped at 50%).
  • Define confidence bands: 0–40% = unverifiable (equipment cannot be confidently identified; triggers fallback ladder or exclusion); 40–60% = provisionally verified pending further evidence; 60–85% = verified with moderate confidence; 85–100% = verified with high confidence (equipment identity confirmed).
  • Specify that the rotating aspect: the weighting of each category is set by accountable specialists from both sides; weights are not disclosed to operators or vendors (to prevent gaming); weights are rotated (updated monthly) to prevent fixed patterns from emerging; any weight change requires double-key approval and is logged in the ledger with rationale.
  • Draft the pilot-validation protocol: apply the locked rule to 100–200 historical equipment-change events per participating site (Month 2 = 2026-12-08 completion target), measuring false-positive rate (equipment incorrectly classed as unverifiable) and false-negative rate (unverifiable equipment classed as verified) against known ground truth from operator records. Target: false positives ≤13% (10% target ±3 points), false negatives ≤5%.
  • If historical validation deviates >±5 points from target, adjust category weights and re-validate on a second 100–200 event cohort before Phase One.
  • Draft the adversarial-scenario protocol: before Phase One exercises begin, apply the rule to 20–30 synthetically constructed scenarios (forged attestations, delayed-access tactics, colluding vendor and operator) and confirm false-positive rate remains within ±3 points of calibration. Target: ≥85% detection of seeded adversarial cases.
  • Create a versioned rule-change log (timestamp, adjustment rationale, evidentiary trigger, both-sides approval) to maintain audit trail. Publish version history in the final ledger so each finding's classification is traceable to the rule version active at the time.
  • Lock the rule before Month 6 (2027-04-08) Phase One clock (no amendments during Months 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08; rule-adjustment disagreements handled by adjudication surge, not rule change).

Approval Authorities: Both accountable-specialist teams (evidence-rule designers); both co-chairs (double-key approval of the locked rule and any pre-Phase-One amendments).

Essential Information:

  • Define the seven evidence categories with credibility scoring logic: (1) vendor attestation (score based on vendor history, escrow records); (2) physical inspector confirmation (serial numbers, markings); (3) customs/shipment records (arrival dates, LOC history matching); (4) equipment identifiers (firmware versions, manufacturing codes, performance baselines); (5) maintenance logs (service events, personnel, parts replaced); (6) infrastructure changes (network, electrical, cooling); (7) witnessed movement (video, timestamps, dual-escort logs).
  • Specify the no-single-source-decisive rule: attestation alone max 60% confidence; maintenance logs alone max 70%; identity confidence increases with corroboration across categories; confidence decreases if categories contradict (e.g., firmware mismatch caps confidence at 50%).
  • Define four confidence bands: 0–40% = unverifiable (triggers fallback ladder or exclusion); 40–60% = provisionally verified pending further evidence; 60–85% = verified with moderate confidence; 85–100% = verified with high confidence. Map each band to adjudication action and evidentiary weight in final verdict.
  • Detail the rotating-weighting mechanism: accountable specialists from both sides set category weights; weights are not disclosed to operators (prevents gaming); weights are updated monthly with double-key approval; log every weight change with rationale in the ledger.
  • Draft the pilot-validation protocol for Month 5 (2027-03-08): apply the locked rule to 100–200 historical equipment-change events per participating site (provided by operators under confidentiality), measure false-positive rate (items incorrectly classed unverifiable) and false-negative rate (unverifiable items classed verified) against known ground truth. Success target: false positives 7–13% (10% ±3 points), false negatives ≤5%. If deviation >5 points, adjust weights and re-validate on a second 100–200 event cohort before entry gate closes (Month 5.5 = 2027-03-23).
  • Draft the adversarial-scenario protocol: before Phase One exercises (Month 5 = 2027-03-08), apply the locked rule to 20–30 synthetically constructed scenarios (forged attestations, delayed-access tactics, colluding vendor/operator, substituted identifiers). Measure: can the rule detect at least 85% of the seeded adversarial cases? If not, adjust.
  • Create a versioned rule-change log with timestamp, adjustment rationale, evidentiary trigger, and double-key approval. Every finding in the ledger must be traceable to the rule version active at the time the evidence was recorded.
  • Specify freeze rule: the locked rule cannot be amended during Phase One (Months 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08). Rule-adjustment disputes during Phase One are handled via adjudication surge or partial suspension of the disputed function, not rule changes.
  • Establish the double-key approval process for the initial lock and any pre-Phase-One amendments: both accountable-specialist teams (evidence-rule architects per country) must approve; both co-chairs must approve (double-key). Approval deadline: Month 5.5 (2027-03-23), before entry-gate certification closes.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • If the rule is too strict (e.g., requires corroboration from 4+ categories), false-positive rates spike to 20–30%, unverifiable-equipment counts surge, and adjudication load exceeds the planned 15 discrepancies per month, consuming estimated 50+ hours per month of specialist time and delaying verdicts by weeks.
  • If the rule is too loose, operators and vendors can learn which evidence combinations weigh most by observing adjudication patterns and engineer evidence to pass, defeating the verification intent (gaming vulnerability).
  • If the rule is not validated pre-Phase-One against historical data, miscalibration is discovered mid-test (Month 6–7 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-05-08), forcing either rule adjustments (which compromise 'frozen rule' commitment) or accepting high false-positive/negative rates that invalidate the detection statistics.
  • If weights are not rotated and kept confidential, operators can deduce the weighting scheme through reverse-engineering of adjudication cases, then systematically target the evidence categories that carry lowest weight.
  • If rule-version history is not maintained in the ledger, audit trails are broken, and findings can be contested post-hoc ('which rule version was applied?'), stalling the final verdict by weeks.
  • If the rule is not double-key approved, one side can later contest its legitimacy, invalidating the entire evidence base for the Go/Modify/Stop decision.
  • If adversarial-scenario testing is skipped, the rule's robustness against deliberate deception is unknown, leaving high risk that operators successfully game the system during Phase One.

Worst Case Scenario: The rule is locked at Month 4.5 (2027-02-23) without historical or adversarial validation. Phase One exercises begin at Month 6 (2027-04-08). By Month 7 (2027-05-08), adjudication cases mount due to unanticipated false positives (20–25% vs. assumed 10%), unverifiable-equipment findings reach 8–12% of inspected items (vs. 5% threshold), and adjudication load doubles to 30+ cases per month. Specialists request rule revision, but the frozen-rule commitment prevents it. Disputes over whether the rule is correctly calibrated consume co-chair time for 3–4 weeks. One country contests the rule's legitimacy, claiming it was never validated. The evidence base becomes unreliable, final verdict is delayed or invalidated, and both sides withdraw credibility from Phase One results. Phase One conclusion (Month 9 = 2027-07-08) passes without a defensible Go/Modify/Stop decision, consuming USD 500M+ in sunk costs. Bilateral instrument requires restart or Phase Two commitment based on unresolved disagreement over the evidence rule itself.

Best Case Scenario: The rule is drafted by Month 4.5 (2027-02-23), locked in double-key escrow, and validated at Month 5 (2027-03-08) against 100–200 historical events per site and 20–30 adversarial scenarios. Validation confirms false-positive rate 9–11% (target 10% ±3), false-negative rate <5%, and detection of 87% of seeded adversarial cases (target 85%). No rule adjustments required. The locked rule, with full validation audit trail, is certified as entry condition at Month 5.5 (2027-03-23). During Phase One, adjudication cases remain at or below 15 per month, false-positive rate tracks within prediction, and all findings are traceable to specific rule versions with documented rationale. At Phase One conclusion (Month 9 = 2027-07-08), the evidence-rule credibility is high enough to support a defensible Go or Modify decision. Both governments and international observers recognize the rule as transparent, validated and resistant to gaming. The verdict is published with confidence that the underlying evidence framework was rigorous.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If full historical validation (100–200 events per site) cannot be completed by Month 5 (2027-03-08) due to operator data delays, substitute a minimum-viable validation: apply the rule to 50–75 historical events per site (a single cohort), measure false-positive/negative rates, and accept a slightly wider confidence interval (±4–5 points vs. ±3). Lock the rule by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23) and commit to a post-Phase-One audit comparing actual Phase One false-positive rates against the historical calibration, with published reconciliation.
  • If adversarial-scenario construction proves difficult (operators unwilling to seed synthetic false evidence), substitute a red-team review: convene the Exercise Authority to design 10–15 plausible gaming scenarios in narrative form (operator-designed forged attestations, etc.), have the rule architect apply the rule qualitatively to each, and document the logic. This is weaker than synthetic testing but captures design robustness.
  • If double-key approval for rule lock slips past Month 5.5 (2027-03-23), activate emergency co-chair summit (within 5 days per the program's gate-slip protocol). If no agreement by Month 6 (2027-04-08), deploy the draft rule as 'provisional, subject to final approval' and continue with Phase One exercises under the caveat that the rule's legitimacy is contested. Publish this caveat in the ledger. This preserves Phase One operations but signals high evidence-credibility risk in the final verdict.
  • If the pilot-validation cohort reveals miscalibration (>5-point deviation from target), activate the second-cohort protocol: adjust weights, re-apply to another 100–200 historical events, and measure again. If the second cohort still deviates, convene an emergency joint technical panel (both countries' evidence architects) to propose a hybrid rule (e.g., ensemble of two alternative weighting schemes). Lock the hybrid rule by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23) with a published note that the calibration remains TBD and will be refined if Phase One detection rates diverge materially.
  • If rule-version history traceability cannot be implemented in the ledger infrastructure by Month 3 (2027-01-08), use a manual audit log: every adjudication case opens a template that records the rule-version ID, rule-lock date, weight values at time of decision, and any assumptions. Store logs in a secure, independently audited repository with monthly third-country auditor review. This adds manual overhead (~2 hours per case) but provides audit trail.
  • If contingency budget is depleted by entry-condition delays and historical-validation costs exceed estimate (proposed: ~USD 5–10M for data access, specialist time, re-testing), compress the adversarial-scenario testing to 5–10 scenarios (vs. 20–30) or substitute a single high-confidence pilot exercise (Month 5 = 2027-03-08) as the primary calibration, with post-Phase-One statistical validation.

Create Document 5: Verdict Thresholds and Mechanical Scoring Framework

ID: 976cf6ed-ce77-43e6-9416-aa6d8e076c8d

Description: Pre-registered numerical criteria for converting Phase One detection rates, false-positive rates, and other KPIs into Go, Modify, or Stop verdicts. Stated as explicit confidence-interval bands (e.g., Go if lower bound of 90% CL ≥75% detection) rather than point estimates, with a mechanical scoring rule that removes post-hoc bargaining (e.g., 'if interval straddles threshold, default to Modify'). Locked in a joint bilateral memorandum by both co-chairs by Month 2.5 (2026-12-23) before any Phase One exercise. Classified (with unclassified summary for legislatures).

Responsible Role Type: Statistician / Verdict-Framework Designer

Primary Template: Statistical decision-rule specification (binomial confidence-interval construction)

Secondary Template: Go/No-Go decision-threshold framework (engineering standard)

Steps to Create:

  • Specify confidence level: recommend 90% CL for Go/Modify boundary (recognizes uncertainty), 95% CL for Stop boundary (higher bar for halting).
  • Define detection-rate thresholds as confidence-interval bands: Go (planned-event class): if lower bound of 90% CL ≥75%, verdict is Go. Modify (planned-event class): if interval straddles 60% or upper bound ≤82%, verdict is Modify. Stop (planned-event class): if upper bound of 95% CL <55%, verdict is Stop. Apply same structure to unplanned-event class (proposed Go ≥60%, Modify 40–60%, Stop <40%).
  • Define false-positive-rate threshold: Modify if FP rate ≤15%; Stop if FP rate >15%.
  • Define unverifiable-equipment threshold: Stop if >10% at a single site or >5% overall (proposed); Modify if 5–10%.
  • Define reciprocal-access parity (definition TBD, propose inspector-hour parity ≥90%, exercise count parity ≥5 per type per site, data-access time ≤3 days avg, agreement rate ≥80% on challenge outcomes): Go requires parity ≥85%; Modify if 70–85%; Stop if <70%.
  • Define discrepancy-age threshold: Go requires no discrepancy open >21 days at conclusion (all cases ≤21 days); Modify if ≤28 days; Stop if any discrepancy >28 days unresolved.
  • Specify the overall verdict logic: Go requires ≥4 of 5 criteria met (80%) AND no hard Stop trigger AND intervals not straddling thresholds. Modify: 3 of 5 criteria met OR 4 of 5 but with interval ambiguity (straddles threshold). Stop: <3 of 5 criteria OR any hard Stop trigger (asymmetric access, shielding, ledger unresolved, withheld funding, >10% unverifiable).
  • Specify the mechanical scoring rule: 'Results are scored by the Exercise Authority against pre-registered intervals. If the confidence interval straddles a threshold boundary, the verdict defaults to Modify. No co-chair negotiation of the interval or threshold is permitted after Phase One begins.'
  • State that all thresholds are marked 'provisional, validated against pilot data'; allowable adjustment before Phase One if pilot data shows >20% deviation from assumption (e.g., if unreported-arrival detection in pilot is 50% instead of assumed 70%, Go threshold may shift from 75% to 70%), but thresholds are locked before Month 6 (2027-04-08) and not amended during Phase One.
  • Draft the joint bilateral memorandum (300–500 words) incorporating thresholds, intervals, mechanical rule and no-amendment language. Require both co-chairs to sign by Month 2.5 (2026-12-23).
  • Publish an unclassified summary (2–3 pages) showing thresholds and mechanical scoring rule so legislatures can audit the verdict logic before Phase One begins.

Approval Authorities: Both co-chairs (joint signature required); independent statistician (certification that interval methodology is sound); both adjudication panels (confirmation that thresholds are operationally defensible).

Essential Information:

  • Specify the exact confidence level (90% or 95%) and interval methodology for converting detection rates, false-positive rates, and other KPIs into Go/Modify/Stop verdict boundaries; document the statistical basis for choosing these levels.
  • Define detection-rate thresholds as explicit confidence-interval bands (e.g., 'Go if lower bound of 90% CL ≥75%') rather than point estimates, with separate thresholds for planned-event class (unreported arrival, substitution) and unplanned-event class (vendor refusal, reluctant operator).
  • Specify false-positive rate, unverifiable-equipment share, reciprocal-access parity, and discrepancy-age thresholds with their associated confidence intervals and the operational rationale for each numerical boundary.
  • Detail the mechanical scoring rule that removes post-hoc bargaining: e.g., 'if the confidence interval straddles a threshold, the verdict defaults to Modify; no co-chair renegotiation of thresholds or intervals after Phase One begins.'
  • Quantify the overall verdict logic: what combination of the five scored criteria (detection, false positives, unverifiable equipment, parity, discrepancy age) is required for Go (≥80% met proposed), Modify (60–80%), or Stop (<50% or any hard Stop trigger).
  • List hard Stop triggers (asymmetric access, shielding, unresolved ledger divergence, withheld funding, material unverifiable equipment >10%) and confirm that each is defined operationally so co-chairs cannot dispute whether a trigger has been met.
  • Document how each threshold will be validated against pilot-exercise data (Month 5 = 2027-03-08) and specify the tolerance for adjustment: e.g., 'thresholds may be recalibrated if pilot detection rate deviates >20% from assumption, but only before the Phase One clock (Month 6 = 2027-04-08).'
  • Draft the joint bilateral memorandum (locked by both co-chairs by Month 2.5 = 2026-12-23) that incorporates thresholds, interval methodology, mechanical scoring rule, no-amendment language and both signatures.
  • Prepare an unclassified legislative summary (2–3 pages) showing verdict thresholds, confidence intervals, mechanical scoring logic and the statement that verdicts default to Modify when intervals are ambiguous, so legislatures can audit the framework before Phase One begins.
  • Define 'material discrepancy' operationally: what findings count toward the '<5 open material discrepancies' gate for Go, and what are non-material process or documentation issues that do not block Go.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Ambiguous or post-hoc thresholds invite co-chair disputes over verdict interpretation; if detection rates fall in 65–75% range, all three verdicts become defensible, requiring 2–4 weeks of political negotiation and risking phase-Two delay or withdrawal.
  • Confidence intervals not explicitly stated create false certainty: with 8 replicates per event type (n≈8), detection-rate estimates have ±32% intervals (95% CL), yet presenting a point estimate (e.g., '72%') masks this width and enables either side to claim the threshold is met or missed.
  • Thresholds locked without pilot validation risk material miscalibration: if the evidence-weighting rule is too strict in practice, false-positive rates surge to 20–30%, unverifiable counts spike, and adjudication load exceeds capacity, collapsing verdict credibility.
  • Missing mechanical scoring rule (e.g., 'default to Modify when interval straddles threshold') enables post-hoc judgment calls that either co-chair can contest; each contested verdict burns 2–4 weeks of co-chair negotiation and suspends phase-Two decisions.
  • Thresholds amended or 'clarified' during Phase One undermine entry-gate lock and allow one side to game the definition of Go in real time as results emerge.
  • Incompletely specified hard Stop triggers (e.g., 'material unverifiable equipment' without a numerical boundary) leave co-chairs in deadlock over whether the trigger has been tripped, blocking Stop decision and forcing continuation with contested evidence.
  • Unclassified legislative summary omitted or published late (after Phase One begins) prevents democratic audit of the verdict framework and invites domestic political challenge to the final decision.

Worst Case Scenario: Thresholds are published as point estimates (e.g., 'Go requires 70% detection') without confidence intervals, and the pilot exercise at Month 5 (2027-03-08) reveals actual detection rates of 68±15% (95% CL). When Phase One concludes at Month 9 (2027-07-08) with observed 71% detection, the confidence interval (56–86%) straddles the Go threshold, yet no mechanical rule exists to resolve the ambiguity. Each co-chair claims their preferred verdict (Go vs. Modify) based on point reading, leading to 3–4 week deadlock and suspended Phase-Two funding decision. Political pressure builds, one country threatens to abandon Phase Two, and the entire Consortium credibility as a bilateral mechanism is compromised, foreclosing any future expanded verification architecture.

Best Case Scenario: Thresholds are pre-registered by Month 2.5 (2026-12-23) as confidence-interval bands (Go: detection ≥75% at 90% CL lower bound; Modify: 55–75%; Stop: <55% at 95% CL upper bound) with explicit mechanical rule: 'if interval straddles boundary, default to Modify.' Pilot exercise at Month 5 (2027-03-08) validates rule calibration within tolerance (false positives 9–11% vs. 10% target). Phase One concludes with observed detection 78±11% (90% CL lower bound 67%, exceeding 75% Go threshold). Mechanical scoring applies, verdict is Go, co-chairs issue joint statement within 2 days, phase-Two funding authorization proceeds on schedule by Month 9.5 (2027-07-23). Unclassified verdict summary published to legislatures, demonstrating objective outcome and transparent logic, strengthening domestic support for continued verification architecture.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If full statistical validation of thresholds against pilot data cannot complete by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23), adopt a simplified 'pilot-validated, default Modify' interim threshold framework: set Go and Stop boundaries using pilot results only, but flag all Phase One verdicts as 'provisional—subject to Phase Two rework' so expectations are managed and no final funding decision hinges on Phase One outcome alone.
  • If co-chair disagreement over threshold interpretation emerges during Phase One, convene an independent statistical arbitrator (third-country or international-organization statistician, pre-identified by Month 1 = 2026-11-08) with binding authority to score the results against the locked thresholds and render a non-appealable verdict classification; co-chairs retain veto only over the Stop decision (higher bar for halting the mechanism).
  • If confidence intervals prove too wide to support any definitive Go/Stop boundary (e.g., ±25% or wider due to unanticipated variance in exercise results), shift the entire verdict framework to a three-tier 'sufficiency' narrative: (1) 'Sufficient Detection' (go to Phase Two with full scope), (2) 'Partial Detection' (go to Phase Two with scope reduction or enhanced monitoring), (3) 'Insufficient Detection' (stop expansion, return to negotiations). Publish evidence and narrative rationale, letting legislatures judge sufficiency rather than relying on numerical boundaries.
  • If either co-chair contests the mechanical scoring rule during Phase One, pause Phase-One exercises, convene an emergency co-chair summit with independent statistician present within 5 days, and jointly re-register thresholds with new mechanical rule before exercises resume. Any amended thresholds apply only to exercises run after the amendment, not retroactively to prior data, preventing mid-test rule changes from contaminating the statistical basis.

Create Document 6: Blind-Challenge Exercise Authority Charter and Scenario Design Framework

ID: 1ad7e871-42cc-4157-83b5-7df08dab5c5e

Description: Establishes the independent Exercise Authority (8 mixed-nationality core staff, funded from USD 500M testing envelope) with exclusive authority to design, schedule, execute and score all 54 blind-challenge exercises covering seven event types (unreported arrival, substitution, inaccurate records, delayed access, disputed identity, vendor refusal, reluctant operator). Specifies that each country's red team may nominate challenge types but the Exercise Authority alone decides execution timing and scoring. Exercises run only in staging, spare-inventory, maintenance or expansion areas (zero production disruption). Pilot exercise (all 7 types, non-production site) at Month 5 (2027-03-08). Phase One exercises (3–4 per month per site, Months 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08) targeted at 6–8 replicates per type. Classified.

Responsible Role Type: Independent Exercise Authority Director

Primary Template: Verification-exercise design protocol (IAEA or OPCW precedent)

Secondary Template: Red-team challenge framework (adversarial-testing standard)

Steps to Create:

  • Define the Exercise Authority's independence: reports to neither co-chair; findings published to both co-chairs simultaneously; no co-chair input on scenario selection or scoring until after execution.
  • Specify staffing: 8 core mixed-nationality staff (e.g., 4 per country or rotation), with sub-roles: (1) scenario designers (2–3), (2) logistics/staging coordinator (1), (3) video and chain-of-custody officer (1), (4) scorers/adjudication (2–3).
  • Define the seven event-type scenarios: (1) unreported arrival: inject declared equipment into a staging area without operator notification; inspect and inspector detect arrival time and serial-number accuracy; (2) substituted equipment: place a functionally equivalent but non-declared piece of hardware in spare inventory; test whether physical inspection and identifiers detect the substitution; (3) inaccurate records: introduce deliberate discrepancies between customs declaration and maintenance logs; test whether record-cross-check identifies the gap; (4) delayed access: deny inspector access to a maintenance area for a specified period; test whether delayed-access findings are classified correctly in the evidence rule; (5) disputed identity: place equipment with partially matching serial numbers or firmware versions; test confidence-scoring under identity ambiguity; (6) vendor refusal: have a vendor claim inability to provide attestation for a piece of equipment; test fallback-ladder execution; (7) reluctant operator: have an operator claim operational-criticality of an area and limit inspector time; test whether limitations are recorded and categorized correctly.
  • Draft scenario-specification template for each event type: equipment identifiers, expected inspector actions, success criteria (e.g., 'unreported-arrival detection within 4 hours of injection'), witness assignments, evidence documentation, post-exercise remediation steps.
  • Specify the pilot-exercise protocol (Month 5 = 2027-03-08): conduct one instance of each of the seven event types at a non-production test datacenter, with full mirrored observation, evidence collection, filtering and ledger closure. Measure actual timelines, operator friction, evidence-collection fidelity and inspector behavior. Adjust Phase One scenario design based on pilot results.
  • Specify the Phase-One exercise load: 3–4 exercises per month per site (2–4 sites depending on entry-condition outcome, proposed 3 sites = 6 sites total) × 3 months (Months 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08) = 45–60 total exercises; goal ≥6 per event type (54 at 3 sites, 48 at 2 pairs = 4 sites).
  • Lock the exercise scenarios in pre-registered form by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23): document equipment, scenario description, success criterion, witness list, evidence-collection protocol, expected completion time. Do not disclose scenario timing to site inspectors until exercise begins.
  • Specify scoring procedures: independent video recording (uncut, chain-of-custody), witness statements (dual-signed), cryptographic attestation of exercise start/end times, detection-outcome determination (did inspectors detect the injected condition within the expected timeframe?), false-positive and false-negative tallying.
  • Require that the Exercise Authority produce a post-exercise briefing (within 2 days of completion) showing: execution timeline, detection outcome, anomalies observed, evidence quality, lessons learned. Publish detection outcome (detected / not detected) to both co-chairs and the ledger; detailed briefing remains confidential to protect exercise realism.

Approval Authorities: Both co-chairs (approve Exercise Authority charter and funding); Exercise Authority Director (autonomous authority over scenario design and execution, reports findings to co-chairs).

Essential Information:

  • Define the Exercise Authority's independence framework: governance reporting structure (reports to neither co-chair, findings published simultaneously to both), decision authority boundaries (exclusive control over scenario design and execution timing, no co-chair input until post-execution), and conflict-of-interest safeguards.
  • Specify the eight mixed-nationality core staff roles and skill requirements: scenario designers (2–3 personnel), logistics and staging coordinator (1 personnel), chain-of-custody and video documentation officer (1 personnel), scorers and adjudication specialists (2–3 personnel), with explicit separation of scenario design from scoring authority.
  • Detail the seven standardized event-type scenarios with technical specifications: (1) unreported arrival—injected-equipment detection timing and serial-number verification; (2) substituted equipment—form-factor and identifier-matching detection; (3) inaccurate records—cross-validation of customs declarations against maintenance logs; (4) delayed access—time-bounded access denial and record categorization; (5) disputed identity—ambiguous identifiers and confidence-scoring under uncertainty; (6) vendor refusal—attestation unavailability and fallback-ladder invocation; (7) reluctant operator—operational-criticality claims and time-limitation recording.
  • Develop a standardized scenario-specification template for each event type, including: declared equipment identifiers, expected inspector discovery actions, measurable success criteria (e.g., 'unreported arrival detected within 4 hours of injection'), inspector role assignments, witness designations, evidence-collection protocol, production-safety constraints, and post-exercise remediation steps.
  • Establish the pilot-exercise protocol (Month 5 = 2027-03-08) scope: one execution per event type at a non-production test facility, with mirrored national observation, full evidence-collection fidelity testing, inspector-response baseline measurement, filtering and ledger closure validation, and Phase-One scenario adjustment recommendations based on outcomes.
  • Calculate the Phase-One exercise load and distribution: 3–4 exercises per site per month × 2–4 matched pairs (4–8 sites) × 3 operational months (Months 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08) to target 6–8 replicates per event type per site and sufficient pooled sample size (±12% confidence interval at 95% CL for planned-class detection).
  • Lock pre-registered scenario specifications by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23): document timing, equipment identifiers, scenario narrative, success criteria, witness roster, evidence-collection sequence, expected completion window, and post-exercise analysis framework—without disclosing scenario timing or sequencing to site inspectors until execution begins.
  • Define scoring procedures and independence: video recording (uncut, chain-of-custody), dual-signed witness statements, cryptographic timestamping of exercise start/end, detection-outcome determination (detected within timeframe yes/no), false-positive and false-negative tallying per event type, anomaly documentation, and evidence-quality assessment.
  • Specify post-exercise reporting and confidentiality boundaries: 2-day briefing template (execution timeline, detection outcome, anomalies, evidence fidelity, lessons learned), detection-outcome publication to both co-chairs and the ledger within 2 days, detailed briefing classification (confidential to preserve exercise realism and prevent learning effects in future iterations).
  • Establish Exercise Authority independence safeguards: funding segregation (drawn from the USD 500M testing envelope with no co-chair approval authority over draws), staffing approval (Exercise Authority Director selected by independent panel, not co-chairs), scenario independence (neither country may design, time, score or approve exercises), and publication protocols (simultaneous unclassified detection outcomes to both co-chairs and the ledger).

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Exercise Authority capture or political pressure: If independence is poorly defined, either co-chair or a national team may attempt to influence scenario selection, timing or scoring. Disputed exercise credibility invalidates the only direct detection evidence in Phase One, rendering final Go/Modify/Stop verdict undefendable. Estimated impact: 40–60% likelihood of a co-chair contesting exercise integrity if independence framework is unclear, triggering 4–6 week forensic adjudication and delayed verdict.
  • Scenario design revealing sensitive operational information: If scenarios are over-detailed or insufficiently redacted, revealing production topology, operator schedules or equipment placements, operators will refuse participation or restrict access in Phase One. Scenario specifications must protect both countries' operational security while remaining credible tests. Poorly specified scenarios leak intelligence; overly redacted scenarios become unconvincing.
  • Inadequate sampling and statistical credibility: If Phase-One exercise load is compressed (fewer than 6 replicates per event type due to missing specifications or execution delays), confidence intervals widen beyond ±12%, and detection-rate thresholds become ambiguous. With only 4–5 replicates per type, ±32% confidence intervals make any verdict defensible and indefensible simultaneously. Estimated impact: 40–50% likelihood that verdict falls in ambiguous zone, requiring political renegotiation.
  • Production disruption and operator friction: If scenarios are not tightly scoped to staging, spare-inventory, maintenance and expansion areas, live exercises may disrupt active computation. Operators will perceive the Consortium as a threat and withhold cooperation in Phase One. Scenario specifications must explicitly prohibit equipment moves that interrupt workloads and require 48-hour notice (except unreported-arrival tests, which test detection without notice).
  • Evidence-collection fidelity failures: If chain-of-custody, video recording or witness procedures are not tightly specified, forensic disputes will arise over whether an exercise was executed as designed. Disputed execution data undermines the detection statistics. Estimated impact: 15–25% of exercises become contested if procedures are vague, removing them from the statistical pool and compressing sample size further.
  • Pilot-exercise omission or poor design: If the pilot exercise (Month 5 = 2027-03-08) does not fully test all seven event types and Phase-One procedures, gaps will be discovered during Phase One operations, consuming 2–4 weeks for remediation and schedule slippage. Insufficient pilot feedback leads to Phase-One exercises that do not test what they claim to test.
  • Inadequate inspector briefing and blind maintenance: If inspectors are told in advance which events are exercises or when they will occur, their detection behavior becomes artificial and unrepresentative. Scheduled exercises only (no unannounced surprises) reduce detection rates by an estimated 20–30% for unreported-arrival and substitution events. False-negative rates will be artificially high and indefensible as proof of mechanism capability.
  • Scoring disputes and referee absence: If scoring procedures lack independent arbitration, a co-chair may dispute whether an exercise outcome meets the success criterion. Without a pre-registered scoring rubric and independent arbiter, scoring becomes politicized. Estimated impact: 10–15% of exercises generate scoring disputes, consuming 1–2 weeks of adjudication per dispute and reducing usable data.
  • Fallback-ladder and vendor-refusal scenario testing gaps: If the pilot exercise and Phase-One scenarios do not fully exercise the vendor-refusal fallback ladder (vendor-supervised testing, filtered evidence, independent examiners, clean-room, attestations), the fallback procedures will be untested when invoked mid-Phase-One under time pressure. Untested procedures fail and consume contingency budget.
  • Confidentiality breaches leaking scenario details: If scenario specifications are not properly classified and stored, details may leak to operators or vendors, allowing them to prepare defensive responses that are not representative of genuine unreported changes. Leaked scenarios invalidate the detection data. Estimated impact: 30–40% likelihood of operator-side learning if scenarios are disclosed, rendering Phase-One results indefensible as proof-of-concept.

Worst Case Scenario: The Exercise Authority charter is created without clear independence safeguards, technical scenario specifications are vague or reveal operational information, and the pilot exercise (Month 5 = 2027-03-08) is either omitted or executed poorly. During Phase One, exercises are disputed as politically motivated (each co-chair contests the other's scenario design), execution procedures are inconsistent (some exercises video-recorded, others not; witness quality variable), and scoring lacks independent arbitration. Five to eight exercises are rejected as invalid, reducing the pooled sample from 54 to 45–50. Confidence intervals widen from ±12% to ±15–18%, and detection-rate estimates fall into the ambiguous 60–80% zone. By Month 8 (2027-06-08), co-chairs deadlock on exercise credibility, consuming 4–6 weeks of forensic review. Phase One concludes without credible Go decision; Modify verdict is the default but lacks statistical justification. Final decision is politicized as a negotiation rather than a technical outcome. Phase Two commitment is made without evidence of Phase One success, and the mechanism loses credibility with both governments and legislatures. Estimated impact: 30–40% probability of political withdrawal by either government if exercise data becomes contested; contingency consumed by adjudication and rework (estimated USD 100–150M); Phase One extension beyond Month 9 (2027-07-08) breaches the 90-day protocol, requiring re-scoping or stop decision.

Best Case Scenario: The Exercise Authority is established as a fully independent, mixed-nationality body with clear decision authority over scenario design, scheduling and scoring, insulated from co-chair pressure or political influence. Technical scenario specifications are detailed, tested in the pilot exercise (Month 5 = 2027-03-08), and refined before Phase One. All seven event types are executed 6–8 times each across 3 matched pairs (54 total exercises) with consistent, video-recorded, witness-attested, cryptographically timestamped procedures. Scenarios are maintained confidential; inspectors encounter exercises without advance notice. Scoring is objective and independent; all 54 exercises are accepted as valid. Detection rates are 72±12% (planned class), 55±22% (unplanned class), pooled 70±12% (95% CL). False positives are 8%, unverifiable equipment is 3%, reciprocal-access parity is 87%, and no discrepancy exceeds 18 days. All five Go criteria are met. Exercise Authority publishes unclassified detection-rate summary by Month 9.2 (2027-07-14); both co-chairs score results against pre-registered thresholds and issue a joint Go decision by Month 9.5 (2027-07-23). The verdict is perceived as technical and credible by both legislatures and the public. Phase Two commitment is made on defensible grounds. Contingency remains partially unspent (estimated USD 100–150M retained), demonstrating fiscal discipline. The Consortium is established as a replicable model for other bilateral verification mechanisms.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • Establish a three-person independent referee panel (one neutral party from a third country, one technical expert nominated by each co-chair but pre-approved as independent) to oversee Exercise Authority operations and arbitrate any disputed execution or scoring decisions. This lighter structure (3 persons vs. 8-core Exercise Authority) reduces overhead but may weaken independence if the neutral referee has prior relationships with either co-chair. Implement at Month 4 (2027-02-08) if full Exercise Authority cannot be staffed by then.
  • Use a pre-tested, standardized exercise library from a prior verification mechanism (IAEA nuclear inspections, OPCW chemical weapons, or other precedent) rather than designing new scenarios from scratch. Adapt existing, proven protocols to frontier-computing equipment and conduct a streamlined pilot (Month 5 = 2027-03-08) with only 2–3 adapted scenarios instead of all seven. Reduces design time and leverages documented procedures but may miss frontier-computing-specific gaps.
  • Conduct unannounced exercises on a random rolling schedule throughout Phase One (no pilot beforehand) instead of scheduled discrete windows. This maximizes detection realism and prevents inspector behavior adjustment, but increases production-disruption risk and operator friction. Implement only if operators explicitly consent in writing by Month 4 (2027-02-08) and if a 10% contingency reserve (USD 50M) is set aside for operator compensation for disruptions.
  • Simplify the pilot exercise (Month 5 = 2027-03-08) to test only the three highest-priority event types (unreported arrival, substitution, vendor refusal) rather than all seven. This compresses pilot timeline from 1 week to 3 days but leaves disputed identity, delayed access, inaccurate records and reluctant operator untested beforehand. Execute these four as early Phase-One exercises (Month 6 = 2027-04-08) at higher risk of discovery and execution variability.
  • Delegate post-exercise scoring to an independent third-country auditor (not the Exercise Authority) who reviews video and witness statements after each exercise and issues a binding score within 5 days. This separates scenario execution (Exercise Authority) from scoring (auditor), reducing capture risk. Requires hiring an independent auditor by Month 2 (2026-12-08), adding USD 3–5M to the testing envelope.
  • Establish a co-chair veto threshold for Exercise Authority decisions: any scenario may be challenged by either co-chair within 48 hours of announced timing; if both co-chairs agree to cancel (rare, both must concur), the scenario is rescheduled. This preserves Exercise Authority autonomy while giving co-chairs a safety valve for scenarios they believe are unfair. Implement by embedding veto procedures in the charter (Month 4 = 2027-02-08) with explicit supermajority requirement to prevent abuse.
  • Compress the Exercise Authority's scenario design by using a standardized 'challenge request form' that each country's red team submits (event type, rationale, proposed timing window). The Exercise Authority selects from these nominative requests rather than designing scenarios from scratch. Reduces design effort from 8 weeks (Month 4.5–5.5 = 2027-02-23 to 2027-03-23) to 4 weeks but depends on red teams submitting sufficiently varied and ambitious requests by Month 4 (2027-02-08).
  • If Exercise Authority staffing is delayed past Month 4.5 (2027-02-23), postpone the pilot exercise from Month 5 (2027-03-08) to Month 5.5 (2027-03-23), compress it to 3 days (test only 5 of 7 event types), and begin Phase One on Month 6.5 (2027-04-23) instead of Month 6 (2027-04-08), shortening Phase One from 90 to 75 days. This reduces sample size from 54 to 40 exercises (5–6 per type) but preserves pilot validation. Accept the statistical cost (confidence intervals widen to ±15–20%) and adjust verdict thresholds accordingly by Month 6 (2027-04-08).
  • If neither country accepts full Exercise Authority independence, establish a 'co-chaired scenario review panel' (one representative per co-chair plus one neutral) that approves all scenarios within 5 days of Exercise Authority submission. The Exercise Authority retains scoring autonomy. This preserves some independence (Exercise Authority scores) while giving co-chairs a gate (design approval). Implement by Month 4 (2027-02-08); approval overhead adds ~1 week per scenario (5–10 working days).

Create Document 7: Appropriations and Funding Agreement Structure / Template

ID: e5ebc2f5-cdf2-4681-859b-e640426b4b1f

Description: Template bilateral appropriation agreement specifying how each government allocates USD 2.5 billion to the Consortium, maps expenses to the seven envelopes, establishes synchronized tranche release dates (25% Month 2 = 2026-12-08, 25% Month 3 = 2027-01-08, 30% Month 5.5 = 2027-03-23, 20% Month 9.2 = 2027-07-14), and defines tranche-withheld triggers (Stop conditions after 14 days escalation, 30 days hard Stop). Includes contingency-burn rules (30%, 50%, 75% draw triggers) and supplemental-appropriation veto points (envelope >120% of plan). Links funding releases to verifiable entry-condition and phase milestones to create accountability and prevent one country from withholding funds as a negotiation tactic.

Responsible Role Type: Finance Officer / Budget Authority

Primary Template: Bilateral funding agreement template

Secondary Template: International organization appropriation framework (World Bank, IAEA precedent)

Steps to Create:

  • Define the seven envelopes with per-country allocation (625M, 500M, 375M, 375M, 250M, 125M, 250M per country = 2500M per country).
  • Specify that the first tranche (25% = 625M per country) is released upon signature of the bilateral instrument and enactment of domestic appropriations (Months 1–2 = 2026-11-08 to 2026-12-08).
  • Specify that tranches 2 and 3 (25% and 30%) are released upon verified completion of entry-condition milestones (matched-pair approval, entry-gate certification by Month 5.5 = 2027-03-23).
  • Specify that the final tranche (20%) is released upon publication of the Go/Modify/Stop verdict by Month 9.5 (2027-07-23), with no condition that the verdict must be Go (funding released regardless of outcome, so verdict is not biased by funding leverage).
  • Establish synchronized-deposit requirement: both countries must deposit their tranches within 7 days of the milestone date; any delay >7 days triggers co-chair escalation; delay >14 days triggers tranche-withhold investigation; delay >30 days unresolved is a Stop condition (program halted pending funding resolution).
  • Embed contingency-draw triggers: draw >30% of contingency (USD 150M total, 75M per country) triggers mandatory co-chair briefing and risk assessment; >50% triggers scope-reduction planning; >75% triggers joint budget review with external auditor.
  • Specify that envelope overruns (actual spend >110% of plan) require co-chair review; >120% requires supplemental appropriation (new decision by both governments, may not be approved, creates veto risk).
  • Require monthly independent audit: envelope-mapping sampled 100%, financial reconciliation (invoice matching, amount verification), contingency-burn reporting.

Approval Authorities: Both co-chairs (joint approval of funding structure and tranche milestones); both finance ministries or equivalent (appropriations authority); independent auditors (monthly verification of envelope mapping and spend reconciliation).

Essential Information:

  • Specify the precise structure, approval authority and bilateral signature procedures for the Appropriations and Funding Agreement, including which co-chair/finance minister acts as signatory and what domestic parliamentary/executive steps each country must complete before the first tranche is released.
  • Quantify the four synchronized tranches (Month 2, 3, 5.5, 9.2-9.5) and map each to its release condition (instrument signature, matched-pair approval, entry-gate certification, verdict publication), with explicit dates and verification responsibility (which auditor confirms each condition).
  • Define the synchronized-deposit rule: both tranches must arrive within 7 days or escalation procedures activate; specify the co-chair escalation timeline (briefing within 48 hours of a delay over 7 days) and the hard Stop trigger (delay over 30 days unresolved).
  • Document the contingency-draw triggers (30%, 50%, 75% thresholds) and specify what actions each trigger mandates: 30% → mandatory co-chair briefing with risk assessment; 50% → scope-reduction planning workshop; 75% → joint budget review with independent external auditor.
  • Define the envelope-overrun thresholds: 110% of plan (requires co-chair review and justification); 120% (requires supplemental appropriation—a new bilateral decision with political veto risk); specify which envelope overruns are highest risk and recommend mitigations (e.g., ledger cost overruns may require network redundancy; site-prep overruns may mandate fewer sites).
  • Specify how the compression reserve (USD 50–100M) within contingency is earmarked and released for accelerated entry-condition negotiation (vetting expedite, fast-track vendor engagement, emergency facility construction), with distinct governance from free contingency (USD 400–450M).
  • Establish the monthly independent audit process: sampling regime (100% for envelope mapping, 10% for invoices), reporting timeline (invoices due by 10th, audit by 20th, findings published by 25th, disputes closed by month-end), and escalation to co-chairs if audit exceptions exceed 2% of sampled value.
  • Clarify whether operator/vendor compensation (charged to each government's USD 2.5B contribution and to the site-prep/compensation envelope) is paid directly to the operators or flows through the co-chairs or a neutral Consortium fund, and what evidence (invoices, signed agreements) triggers reimbursement.
  • Detail the Stop condition procedure: once a tranche delay exceeds 14 days or deposits are unequal and unresolved after 14 days, who convenes the emergency co-chair summit (self-initiated or triggered by an independent fiscal watchdog), what is the 30-day resolution window, and what happens if both countries do not resolve funding by day 30 (Phase One halted, contingency frozen, program transitions to stop-work state).
  • Specify whether the final 20% tranche (Month 9.2 = 2027-07-14, verdict publication) is released regardless of whether the Go/Modify/Stop verdict is favorable, or whether withheld funding can be used as political leverage over the verdict outcome (user intent: funding released unconditionally, but mechanism is not yet specified in the template structure).

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Unclear tranche release conditions enable one country to interpret the milestone ambiguously (e.g., does 'matched-pair approval' mean bilateral co-chair sign-off or publication to legislatures?) and withhold funds on a technicality, stalling Phase One by 4–8 weeks and consuming USD 100–200M of contingency.
  • Missing synchronized-deposit rule allows one country to deposit its tranche on day 25 while the other deposits on day 45, and absent an explicit escalation timeline, the delayed tranche becomes a hidden negotiating lever: the delayed party can claim 'bureaucratic process' while using the funding gap to pressure concessions on site selection or evidence rules.
  • Unspecified contingency-draw governance leaves both countries guessing whether they can unilaterally tap contingency or whether joint approval is required, so surprise overruns (e.g., neutral-facility construction exceeds budget) trigger budget disputes rather than co-chair coordination, paralyzing spending and forcing emergency supplements.
  • Ambiguous envelope-overrun thresholds (110% vs. 120%) without clear co-chair review or supplemental-appropriation procedures invite disputes: one country claims an overrun is justified by force majeure; the other claims it signals mismanagement and demands scope reduction as a condition of funding the supplement, creating a veto loop.
  • Missing audit escalation timelines and exception thresholds allow audit findings (e.g., 5% of site-prep invoices lack proper supporting documentation) to become contested without a clear adjudication path, delaying fund releases and pushing the final verdict past the Phase One clock deadline.
  • Lack of clarity on operator compensation flow (direct payment, reimbursement, holdback for performance) creates accounting disputes: an operator claims it spent USD 30M on site preparation; the Consortium finance team disputes the amount; neither has a contractual framework to resolve, so funds remain frozen pending extended negotiation.
  • If the final-tranche mechanism is unclear (whether it depends on a favorable verdict), political pressure builds if early results suggest a Stop outcome: one country may threaten to withhold the final tranche to pressure a Modify or Go verdict, directly corrupting the objective-scoring process and invalidating the entire proof-of-concept.

Worst Case Scenario: One or both countries weaponize funding as a political lever by deploying ambiguous tranche-release conditions, synchronized-deposit rules and contingency governance to stall Phase One, extract concessions on evidence rules or site selection, or pressure the final verdict. By Month 5 (2027-03-08), the second tranche is delayed over 30 days pending co-chair resolution of an unresolved equipment-identity dispute at a matched site. The delayed party claims the dispute is the releasing party's responsibility; the other claims it is a force majeure event outside the agreement. Absent a clear Stop trigger and escalation procedure, Phase One does not start on schedule (Month 6 = 2027-04-08). Instead, the clock slips to Month 7 (2027-05-08), compressing the test from 90 days to 60 days. Detection statistics thin from 54 exercises and 6–8 replicates per type to 36 exercises and 4–5 replicates per type. Confidence intervals widen from ±10–15% to ±20–25%, making the final Go/Modify/Stop verdict statistically ambiguous. Both countries then dispute the thresholds and the verdict itself, claiming the compressed test is not credible. The Consortium enters deadlock over outcome interpretation (Month 9 = 2027-07-08), and the proof-of-concept fails to produce a defensible decision. Political fallout follows: one country accuses the other of sabotaging the test; domestic critics in both countries cite the financial mismanagement and ambiguous verdict as evidence that bilateral verification with an adversary is impossible; appropriations bodies in both countries demand investigations and withhold supplemental funding for any Phase Two. The mechanism becomes politically dormant, USD 3–4 billion remains unspent, and no clear path to renegotiation or phase advancement exists.

Best Case Scenario: The Appropriations and Funding Agreement is structured as a locked bilateral financial instrument that synchronizes tranche releases to verifiable entry-condition and Phase One milestones, eliminating ambiguity and political withholding. Tranches are released automatically on certification by an independent auditor (not by co-chair discretion alone), so neither country can claim "I did not approve the milestone" as a pretext for delay. Synchronized-deposit rules require both countries to deposit within 7 days of a tranche date, with escalation timelines that make delays visible within 48 hours. Contingency governance is pre-agreed and mechanical (draw triggers at 30%, 50%, 75% activate scheduled co-chair reviews, not unilateral withholding). The final tranche is released unconditionally upon verdict publication, regardless of Go/Modify/Stop outcome, removing any incentive to corrupt the scoring. As a result, Phase One runs on schedule (Month 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08), all 54 exercises are executed with full detection statistics (±10–15% confidence intervals), and the Go/Modify/Stop verdict is defensible on objective criteria. Both countries see the funding as reliable, predictable and neutral, building confidence in the bilateral mechanism and enabling a Phase Two decision by Month 10 (2027-08-08) with full appropriations authorization already in place (spending authority pre-committed through a tranche-4 supplemental appropriation by Month 9.5 = 2027-07-23, pending the verdict).

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • Engage an international fiscal institution (World Bank, IMF or IAEA equivalents with joint banking authority) as a fiduciary for the USD 5B pool, with both countries depositing into segregated national accounts that only the fiduciary can access on pre-registered milestone triggers, removing the need for synchronized bilateral deposits and eliminating withholding as a tactic.
  • Establish a bilateral Joint Budget Authority (one finance officer per country, co-reporting to co-chairs) with binding authority to certify milestones and release tranches, bypassing the co-chairs' political incentives to delay and creating an independent fiscal watchdog with published weekly dashboard reporting.
  • Implement a three-party escrow arrangement where each tranche is held in trust by a neutral third country's financial agent (Swiss National Bank, Singapore Monetary Authority) until both co-chairs certify the milestone; the escrow agent releases on dual signature only, making unilateral withholding impossible.
  • Front-load 50% of the USD 5B (USD 2.5B total) into the Month 0–2 (2026-10-08 to 2026-12-08) entry-condition phase, so by Month 2 (2026-12-08) all major infrastructure (neutral facility, ledger hosting, personnel recruitment, pilot exercise) is funded and committed, and the remaining 50% is divided across Months 3–9 (2027-01-08 to 2027-07-08) in smaller tranches, reducing the leverage any single tranche gives to either country.
  • Create a 'contingency release protocol' where contingency draws are automatic and mechanical (no co-chair approval needed) once one of the three threshold triggers (30%, 50%, 75%) is reached, with an independent auditor automatically approving the draw within 5 days; this removes contingency from the political negotiation space and treats it as a technical program-management tool.

Responsible Role Type: Evidence-Rule Architect / Data Analyst

  • Document purpose: Validate the confidential, rotating Layered Evidence Weighting Model (combination rule) by applying it to 100–200 historical equipment-change events per participating datacentre (6–8 facilities total) with known ground-truth outcomes
