  • Evidence inputs: attestation records, physical inspection notes, customs/shipment records, equipment identifiers, maintenance logs, infrastructure-change timestamps, and witnessed-movement records for each historical event
  • Scoring procedure: apply the locked evidence-weighting rule to each historical event, generate an equipment-identity confidence rating, and compare against ground truth to calculate false-positive rate (incorrect identity conclusion despite true facts), false-negative rate (missed identity discrepancy despite evidence), and unverifiable count (cases where confidence falls below the decision threshold)
  • Calibration targets: pilot false-positive rate 7–13% (10% target ±3 percentage points); false-negative rate <5%; unverifiable share <10%
  • Required output: summary table showing actual vs. target false-positive/negative rates per event type and per site, with identified miscalibrations flagged for rule adjustment before Phase One begins
  • Validation timeline: historical data collection by Month 5 (2027-03-08), pilot analysis complete by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23), rule locked by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23)
  • Scope clarification: records must cover equipment arrivals, installations, maintenance events, and departures; exclude workload, model-weight, or hidden-facility data

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Incomplete or inaccurate ground-truth data (missing dates, serial-number mismatches, or incorrect maintenance-log entries) renders the validation unreliable; rule adjustments based on flawed data propagate miscalibration into Phase One, creating false-positive or false-negative surge during actual operations
  • Evidence-package gaps (e.g., attestation records exist but customs data missing for 30% of events) bias the rule validation, making it appear more or less strict than it actually is when applied to Phase One data with complete evidence sets
  • Ground-truth ambiguity (e.g., maintenance events where it is unclear whether an equipment swap occurred) inflates the unverifiable count during validation and obscures the rule's true discrimination ability
  • Late delivery or compartmentalization delays (data held by operators, vendors, or governments with slow release) compress the 2–3 week analysis window, forcing rushed or incomplete validation that discovers miscalibration only after Phase One begins
  • Rule miscalibration undetected before Phase One: if actual false-positive rate is 20–25% vs. 10% target, Phase One unverifiable-equipment findings surge (10–15 cases per month), overwhelming the 15-case adjudication capacity and stalling discrepancy resolution by Month 6.5–7 (2027-04-23 to 2027-05-08), delaying the final verdict
  • If false-negative rate exceeds 5%, Phase One misses substituted or anomalous equipment, undermining detection credibility and rendering the Go verdict indefensible statistically

Worst Case Scenario: Historical equipment-change records are unavailable or incomplete (operators refuse access citing confidentiality, or data spans only 6 months instead of 12–24), forcing the Consortium to skip pilot validation and lock the evidence-weighting rule without calibration against ground truth. Phase One operations then uncover the rule's miscalibration: false-positive rate reaches 25–30%, generating 15–20 unverifiable-equipment findings per month, exceeding adjudication capacity and stalling discrepancy resolution. By Month 7 (2027-05-08), the ledger accumulates 45–60 unresolved discrepancies, all or many aged over 21 days, triggering automatic impaired-confidence status at multiple sites and shifting the verdict toward Stop. Either government contests the rule's legitimacy, demanding rule adjustment mid-test (double-key deadlock), or the final detection-rate dataset becomes too contaminated by false positives to support any credible Go decision. Phase One concludes with a forced Stop verdict, contingency depleted by USD 100–150M in unanticipated adjudication and legal costs, and both governments withdrawing to reassess the Consortium model, invalidating the proof-of-concept.

Best Case Scenario: Historical equipment-change records are obtained from all participating datacentres within 4 weeks (by Month 5.25 = 2027-03-16), covering 120–200 events per site with complete evidence packages and clear ground-truth status (operator attestation of what actually arrived, installed, left). The Consortium's Evidence-Rule Architect team applies the confidential rule to the historical cohort, generating false-positive rate 10±2% and false-negative rate 2–3%, both within target bands. No material miscalibration is detected; confidence intervals for calibration error are narrow (±1–2 percentage points). Rule is certified and locked by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23) with published (classified) validation summary. Phase One operations apply the validated rule from Month 6 (2027-04-08) onward, generating false-positive and false-negative rates in the expected 8–12% and 2–4% ranges respectively. Unverifiable-equipment count stays below 5%, adjudication load averages 12–14 cases per month (within 15-case capacity), and discrepancy resolution tracks within target (max age 18–20 days). Detection rates for planned events reach 72–78%, exceeding the 70% Go threshold; parity metrics exceed 85%. Final Go decision is statistically credible, contingency draw stays below 20% (USD 100M), and Phase One verdict is accepted by both governments as a foundation for potential Phase Two or broader verification.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If historical records are unavailable or fragmented, use a synthetic validation cohort: design 50–100 realistic equipment-change scenarios (with seeded true/false/ambiguous identity status) and run them through recorded procedures at one participating datacentre as a 'shadow exercise' (offline, not live) by Month 4.5 (2027-02-23), applying the rule to generate false-positive and false-negative outputs. This is slower and less realistic than historical validation but provides numerical calibration if historical data cannot be accessed
  • Conduct a compressed pilot exercise (Month 5 = 2027-03-08) at a non-production test facility, running all seven event types once with the rule applied live, and use detected vs. actual outcomes to estimate false-positive and false-negative rates with confidence intervals. If results show >5% miscalibration, adjust the rule and schedule a second pilot cohort (if time permits by Month 5.25 = 2027-03-16); otherwise, lock the rule with a 'provisional, validated on pilot data' caveat and increase Phase One monitoring frequency for early miscalibration detection
  • If rule validation cannot be completed before Phase One clock start (Month 6 = 2027-04-08), apply the rule with explicit uncertainty flags: mark every identity-confidence output with a 'preliminary' label and reserve right to retroactively adjust scoring if post-hoc validation in Month 7–8 (2027-05-08 to 2027-06-08) reveals systematic bias; document and publish all adjustments with rationale. This delays final verdict (Month 9.5 = 2027-07-23 becomes Month 10 = 2027-08-08) but preserves credibility by flagging provisional status
  • Establish a standing Evidence-Rule Review Panel (3 specialists per country) empowered to issue interim rule adjustments during Phase One if operational false-positive or false-negative rates exceed calibration targets by >3 percentage points (e.g., observed 13% false positives vs. 10% calibrated); amendments apply only to events recorded after the amendment effective date, preserving comparability of prior events. This adds agility but requires daily monitoring and runs counter to the freeze-the-rule principle; use only if baseline validation is severely miscalibrated (>5 percentage points)
  • If neither historical nor synthetic validation is feasible, substitute an expert-panel review: convene 2 senior inspectors per country plus an independent external specialist, and have them review a sample of 30–50 actual Phase One events (after they occur, by Month 6.5 = 2027-04-23) to estimate false-positive and false-negative rates empirically. Use Month 6.5–7 (2027-04-23 to 2027-05-08) results to make a single rule adjustment effective for Month 7+ events (Month 7 = 2027-05-08 onward), with all prior Month 6 (2027-04-08) events scored under the unadjusted rule. This preserves the integrity of early Phase One data while allowing mid-test calibration correction

Find Document 3: US and Chinese National Laws and Regulations on Equipment Import/Export, Customs Procedures, and Datacenters Security

ID: f0c33d83-6b4e-4b61-bf38-e745ed9a21b1

Description: Relevant legal texts governing equipment arrival/departure from participating datacenters: import/export regulations, customs procedures, export-control classifications (if applicable to frontier computing), datacenters' domestic access authority (government authority to compel operator participation in inspections), and sanctions or IP-protection rules. Used to establish the domestic access-authority entry condition and to understand the legal basis for inspector access and operator cooperation. Sourced from national legislative assemblies, customs agencies, and commerce ministries.

Recency Requirement: Current laws in effect for 2026–2027 (i.e., binding at the time of Phase One execution); any pending legislative changes must be mapped (e.g., if new export controls are expected, they are flagged for impact on the covered-equipment schedule).

Responsible Role Type: Legal Counsel / International Trade Specialist

Steps to Find:

  • US laws: search Congress.gov for current Export Administration Regulations (EAR), International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR), customs statutes (19 USC), and any datacenters-specific security regulations.
  • Chinese regulations: request text of relevant laws from the Ministry of Commerce, General Administration of Customs, and any sector-specific regulations (e.g., telecommunications infrastructure security law).
  • International context: review WTO schedules, bilateral trade agreements, and sanctions regimes that might affect equipment movements.

Access Difficulty: Easy—national laws are publicly available through legislative websites, government agency publications, and legal databases. Declassified trade agreements are publicly listed. Mitigation: assign legal counsel to compile and annotate the relevant statutes by Month 1 (2026-11-08).

Essential Information:

  • Identify the current (2026–2027) US export-control regimes governing frontier computing equipment: Export Administration Regulations (EAR), International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR), classified equipment restrictions, and any sector-specific datacenters-security statutes that authorize government access to private facilities for inspection.
  • Identify the current Chinese laws and regulations governing equipment import/export, customs procedures, telecommunications infrastructure security, and government authority to compel state-operated or state-approved datacenters to participate in international inspections without advance notice.
  • Map bilateral trade-agreement schedules (WTO, any bilateral instrument) that define import/export tariffs, prohibited items, or sanctions regimes affecting frontier-computing equipment movements between US and China during the test window (Months 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08).
  • Document the domestic legal authority by which each country can compel its datacenters operators (public or private) to grant inspector access, permit evidence collection, and comply with containment and confidentiality requirements without operator veto.
  • Identify any pending legislative changes or new export controls expected during Months 0–9 (2026-10-08 to 2027-07-08) that would affect the covered-equipment schedule or equipment movement permissions (e.g., new semiconductor restrictions, telecommunications bans).
  • Define the legal status and procedures for equipment transfer between participating sites (e.g., whether transfers require customs clearance, licensing or special authorization under import/export regimes).
  • Establish the legal and liability framework for equipment damage, loss or substitution during international transit or during inspection procedures, including indemnification and insurance requirements.
  • Quantify the legal constraints on inspector access duration, frequency, and scope (e.g., whether US operators can limit inspector hours to business days, whether Chinese sites must grant 24/7 access under domestic law).

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Incomplete or outdated export-control information causes equipment to be wrongly classified as prohibited or verifiable, excluding it from the covered-equipment schedule (unverifiable equipment surges above the 5% Stop threshold) or requiring late schedule amendments that undermine Phase One comparability.
  • Misinterpretation of Chinese domestic legal authority leads to operator resistance or government-mandated limits on inspector access (e.g., no nighttime access, 72-hour notice required), creating asymmetric access that fails the reciprocal-parity entry condition.
  • Missing or vague legal basis for compulsory operator participation allows a US or Chinese operator to contest inspector mandates or demand compensation beyond the budgeted envelope, stalling site preparation or forcing scope reduction.
  • Unidentified pending legislation (new sanctions, export-control expansions) takes effect during Phase One operations and retroactively prohibits equipment movements or inspections, invalidating scheduled exercises or forcing ledger corrections (ledger divergence risk).
  • Ambiguous customs procedures for inter-site equipment transfers cause delays or logistical disputes over whether transfers count as 'departures' requiring closure or 'internal moves' avoiding departure procedures, creating unresolved discrepancies and adjudication overload.
  • Inadequate liability and indemnification language leaves either country or operator vulnerable to claims if equipment is damaged during inspection, triggering payment disputes that consume contingency budget and create operator resistance.
  • Failure to map sanctions regimes allows prohibited equipment or vendors to be listed on the covered-equipment schedule, requiring late removal and schedule amendments that undermine credibility.

Worst Case Scenario: A critical export-control restriction or sanctions listing takes effect during Phase One (e.g., new US semiconductor controls effective Month 8 = 2027-06-08, or Chinese equipment ban) and retroactively affects equipment already being verified, forcing ledger corrections, schedule amendments and legal disputes over whether exercises remain valid. Simultaneously, a US operator successfully argues under commercial law that inspectors lack authority to access proprietary areas without operator consent, and China invokes national-security restrictions on foreign inspector duration, creating asymmetric access that invalidates reciprocal-parity metrics and triggers the Stop condition. Contingency is exhausted by legal disputes and operator compensation claims. Phase One verdict becomes uncertifiable due to legal uncertainty about which equipment was actually verifiable, and the program is forced to extend past Month 9 (2027-07-08) or issue a Stop decision without credible evidence that Go was infeasible (political failure, estimated 40–50% likelihood of international incident or public disclosure of disputes).

Best Case Scenario: Current US and Chinese laws unambiguously establish government authority to compel operator participation and grant inspector access to participating datacenters (24/7 for US sites, with Chinese sites' 24-hour accessibility established by domestic statute rather than negotiation). Export controls and sanctions regimes are stable through Month 9 (2027-07-08) with no retroactive changes. A bilateral legal memorandum clarifies that equipment transfers between participating sites are treated as internal moves within the monitored system and do not trigger customs or export-control procedures, simplifying logistics and reducing unresolved discrepancies. Operator liability is clearly allocated (each government indemnifies its own operator for inspection-related damage), eliminating compensation disputes. Legal counsel can certify by Month 1 (2026-11-08) that the covered-equipment schedule is aligned with current law, and any new controls identified by Month 3 (2027-01-08) allow sufficient lead time for schedule amendment before the Phase One clock (Month 6 = 2027-04-08) starts. No legal disputes arise during Phase One, adjudication load remains at 15 cases per month, and the final verdict is unchallenged on legal grounds.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If current Chinese domestic law does not explicitly grant authority for government mandate of operator participation, initiate emergency diplomatic negotiations (Months 0–1 = 2026-10-08 to 2026-11-08) to secure a bilateral supplementary agreement or executive order that grants equivalent legal force. Timeline: agreement drafted by Month 1 (2026-11-08), enacted by Month 2 (2026-12-08), with contingency allocation of USD 10–20M for negotiation support and legal counsel.
  • If pending export-control legislation is expected during Months 0–9 (2026-10-08 to 2027-07-08), request advance notice from the US Department of Commerce and China's Ministry of Commerce by Month -1 (before Phase One planning). If a control change is confirmed, proactively amend the provisional covered-equipment schedule at Month 4.5 (2027-02-23) before the Phase One clock to reflect new restrictions; classify affected equipment as unverifiable at entry rather than discovering the change mid-test.
  • If a US operator refuses 24/7 inspector access citing commercial harm, substitute a government-operated or state-controlled facility (e.g., a US Department of Energy datacenters complex) that has statutory access authority, rather than extending negotiation with the private operator. Substitute candidate sites pre-identified by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23) to avoid re-triggering site-selection deadlock.
  • If equipment-transfer procedures are ambiguous, establish a bilateral interpretation in the provisional covered-equipment schedule or in a joint protocol signed by Month 4 (2027-02-08) that explicitly classifies transfers between participating sites as 'internal monitored moves' exempt from customs procedures, with the ledger entry serving as the official departure/arrival record. This avoids retroactive disputes.
  • If operator liability for inspection-related damage cannot be resolved, establish a joint Operator Indemnification Fund (funded from the USD 1B site-preparation envelope, estimated allocation USD 20–30M) that covers all participating operators equally, removing per-operator negotiation. Each country contributes USD 10–15M to the fund by Month 2 (2026-12-08), before site preparation.
  • If sanctions regimes are complex or changing, engage a specialized trade-law firm (external cost estimated USD 1–2M from the legal envelope) to conduct a quarterly sanctions-and-export-control audit during Phase One (Months 6, 8 = 2027-04-08, 2027-06-08), publishing unclassified advisories to co-chairs about new restrictions. Preventive identification avoids mid-test legal surprises.
  • If US or Chinese operator access restrictions are discovered during pre-clock site selection but cannot be resolved by Month 5 (2027-03-08), exclude that site and substitute from the pre-identified candidate pool, reducing the matched-pair count to 2 pairs (4 sites) rather than 3 pairs (6 sites). Contingency adjustment: exercise load reduces from 54 to 36, sample sizes per event type drop to 4–6 (below the minimum 6), statistical confidence widens to ±32–40% (95% CL), but site selection is preserved within the entry-condition timeline.
