Find Document 5: IAEA Safeguards Verification Procedures and Case Studies (Bilateral Inspection Precedent)

ID: 6fe0ab3f-bd62-4c38-b461-9957b2dbb402

Description: Detailed descriptions of how the IAEA conducts declared-item inspections, manages access denied scenarios, designs and executes challenge exercises, operates replicated ledgers for accountancy, adjudicates discrepancies, and maintains inspector compartmentalization. Provides procedural templates and lessons learned for adaptation to frontier computing. Sourced from IAEA official documents, safeguards training materials, and published case studies.

Recency Requirement: Current IAEA procedures (2020–2026); historical case studies (e.g., JCPOA monitoring, past inspection challenges) for lesson-learned context.

Responsible Role Type: Bilateral Verification-Protocol Designer

Steps to Find:

  • Request from IAEA Department of Safeguards via official channels (bilateral government request or through the IAEA public information office).
  • Access published IAEA Safeguards Glossary and technical reports on safeguards concepts (accessible on iaea.org).
  • Review IAEA Board of Governors reports and implementation reports (publicly available, though some sections may be classified).
  • Interview former IAEA inspectors or safeguards specialists (contact via professional networks, IAEA alumni associations, or think tanks).

Access Difficulty: Medium–Easy—IAEA publishes substantial material; some safeguards detail is classified for security reasons. Mitigation: request official briefings from IAEA safeguards office (Month 0 = 2026-10-08); identify unclassified case studies and procedural frameworks that can be adapted; coordinate with IAEA on any requests for classified operational detail.

Essential Information:

  • Identify the specific IAEA procedures, case studies and lessons learned applicable to declared-item inspection, access-denied scenarios and challenge-exercise design in a bilateral (not multilateral) context.
  • Document IAEA's reconciliation and adjudication procedures for discrepancies, including timelines, escalation rules and role of inspectors versus political authorities.
  • Detail IAEA safeguards ledger architecture: replication, synchronization bounds, key custody, tamper-evidence mechanisms and ledger-divergence resolution procedures.
  • Describe IAEA inspector compartmentalization, rotation, debriefing and information-barrier protocols to protect sensitive operator infrastructure.
  • Extract IAEA challenge-exercise design frameworks: scenario types, independence of design authority, scoring procedures and statistical validation of detection rates.
  • Specify IAEA precedent for vendor-refusal fallback procedures and evidence crediting when operators or vendors decline participation.
  • Identify legal and treaty-implementation lessons from IAEA bilateral agreements (e.g., subsidiary arrangements, access protocols, dispute settlement).

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Incomplete IAEA procedural templates force the Consortium to invent adjudication or suspension procedures from first principles, risking procedures that are operationally infeasible or that one government later contests as non-standard.
  • Missing IAEA safeguards ledger architecture details leave the Consortium's replicated ledger design unvalidated, creating risk of ledger divergence or key-custody failure that stalls evidence validity without a tested recovery path.
  • Absent IAEA inspector-compartmentalization precedent may result in information barriers that are either too loose (IP leakage, counterintelligence exposure) or too tight (unverifiable-equipment counts surge, adjudication overload).
  • Thin case studies on access denial or vendor refusal mean the fallback ladders are untested, risking equipment being unverifiable at entry or vendors forcing equipment exclusions from the covered schedule.
  • Lack of IAEA statistical guidance on challenge-exercise sample sizes and confidence intervals leaves the Consortium using thin-data thresholds (±32% per event type, per current estimates) without international precedent for what is defensible.
  • Missing treaty-implementation lessons from IAEA bilateral instruments may leave the Consortium's double-key governance vulnerable to disputes over who interprets deadlock or suspension procedures.

Worst Case Scenario: The Consortium proceeds into Phase One (Month 6 = 2027-04-08) without validated procedures for ledger divergence recovery, evidence-rule adjudication or inspector information barriers. By Month 8 (2027-06-08), a ledger divergence occurs (e.g., event recorded locally but missing in counterpart copy). Without IAEA precedent, co-chairs cannot agree on whether the divergence is evidence of tampering or a synchronization artifact, triggering a 4–6 week double-key deadlock. Simultaneously, an accidental IP disclosure by an inspector occurs, and without precedent-based compartmentalization rules, both governments suspect the other of espionage, threatening political withdrawal. Exercise detection rates fall in the ambiguous 55–75% zone, and without IAEA statistical guidance on defensible sample sizes, the final verdict becomes a negotiation rather than a technical decision. Phase One concludes with no credible Go decision, the Consortium is abandoned, and USD 2–3 billion in sunk costs are contested between the governments.

Best Case Scenario: The IAEA Safeguards Procedures document provides detailed, validated procedural templates for adjudication timelines (e.g., 10–15 day investigation, 5–7 day panel recommendation, 3–5 day co-chair decision), partial-suspension rules (e.g., disputed function paused, unrelated activities continue), ledger-divergence recovery (e.g., dual signing keys, hourly digest exchange, 72-hour reconciliation window) and inspector compartmentalization (e.g., role-based knowledge limits, post-rotation cooling-off periods). The Consortium adopts these templates, accelerating procedural design by 4–6 weeks and reducing the risk of operationally infeasible rules. IAEA case studies on vendor refusal (e.g., JCPOA past instances) demonstrate that a 4-rung fallback ladder (vendor-supervised testing, independent examination, clean-room, attestation) is achievable within 8–10 weeks and that 2–3 vendor refusals per test are normal and manageable. IAEA guidance on challenge-exercise sample sizes (e.g., minimum 8–10 replicates per type for defensible detection rates) validates the Consortium's 54-exercise plan and confidence intervals of ±10–15% (pooled) as adequate for Go/Modify/Stop thresholds. By Month 5.5 (2027-03-23), the Consortium's procedures are locked, staffed and validated against historical data, reducing entry-condition risk and increasing Phase One credibility.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If IAEA safeguards detail is classified or unavailable, request bilateral government-to-government briefing from the IAEA Department of Safeguards (Months 0–1 = 2026-10-08 to 2026-11-08), with the Consortium's bilateral legal team present, to extract procedural lessons verbally and document them in the Consortium's own bilateral instrument.
  • Access unclassified IAEA public materials (Safeguards Glossary, Board reports, published inspection manuals) via iaea.org and extract procedural principles (e.g., inspection frequency, access timing, evidence standards) without requiring classified operational detail.
  • Interview former IAEA inspectors, safeguards specialists and treaty-implementation lawyers (identified via professional networks, think tanks, academic institutions) in structured sessions (Months -1 to 2 = 2026-09-08 to 2026-12-08) to capture case-study lessons on adjudication, suspensions and vendor refusal without requiring classified material.
  • Engage the OPCW (Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons) as an alternative reference on declared-item inspection, challenge exercises and dual-key governance precedent (OPCW also uses equal directorate, no casting vote, and challenge-inspection procedures similar to IAEA).
  • Hire a specialist consulting firm with IAEA or OPCW background (estimated 3–5 persons, USD 1–2M within the legal-implementation envelope, Months -1 to 3 = 2026-09-08 to 2027-01-08) to design procedural templates tailored to frontier computing and bilateral governance, explicitly documenting any gaps where IAEA precedent does not apply.
  • Conduct a first-principles procedural design sprint (Months 2–4 = 2026-12-08 to 2027-02-08) with both governments' legal, technical and safeguards teams, using IAEA materials as reference input and producing the Consortium's own procedural manual; validate the manual against a non-production pilot facility in Month 5 (2027-03-08).

Find Document 6: OPCW Chemical Weapons Convention Industry Verification and Managed-Access Procedures

ID: 7163a9f4-52a7-4dcb-9dfb-d71fdc274bcb

Description: OPCW protocols for conducting inspections at commercial and state facilities, managing proprietary-information protection through managed access (restricted areas, redacted evidence), administering vendor and owner cooperation agreements, and adjudicating access-denial disputes. Relevant for understanding how to balance verification credibility with IP/security protection. Sourced from OPCW verification documents and implementation reports.

Recency Requirement: Current OPCW procedures (2020–2026); historical precedent for managed-access disputes.

Responsible Role Type: Inspector Information Firewall Doctrine Designer / Managed-Access Specialist

Steps to Find:

  • Request from OPCW Verification Division (via official government channel or OPCW public information office).
  • Access OPCW annual reports and Verification Annex guidance (publicly available on opcw.org).
  • Consult published academic papers or think-tank analyses of OPCW industry verification (e.g., Stimson Center, Carnegie Endowment, James Martin Center for Nonproliferation Studies).

Access Difficulty: Easy–Medium—OPCW publishes verification framework; some operational detail may be classified. Mitigation: bilateral government request to OPCW for briefing and documentation sharing; expect 2–4 week turnaround for classified materials.

Essential Information:

  • Identify the specific managed-access procedures OPCW uses to balance verification credibility with protection of proprietary information, trade secrets and security architecture at commercial and state facilities.
  • Document OPCW's framework for administering vendor cooperation agreements, including conditions under which vendors can restrict inspector access and procedures for resolving access-denial disputes.
  • List the OPCW mechanisms for redacting or filtering sensitive evidence (e.g., restricted areas, sealed observations, supervised reading rooms) while maintaining the integrity of inspection findings.
  • Detail OPCW's precedent for adjudicating access disputes when an operator or vendor refuses inspector access to specific equipment or areas, including escalation procedures and consequences.
  • Specify how OPCW handles information barriers and compartmentalization of inspector knowledge post-assignment, including cooling-off periods or reassignment restrictions.
  • Quantify OPCW experience with false-positive and false-negative rates when using filtered or managed-access evidence (historical data from 2020–2026 operations if available).
  • Describe OPCW's procedures for certifying that filtering or evidence redaction has not removed materially relevant information for verification purposes.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Without clear precedent on managed-access procedures, the Consortium's Inspector Information Firewall Doctrine may be too strict (leaving inspectors unable to resolve evidence conflicts) or too permissive (exposing sensitive workloads and infrastructure), causing false-positive surges or IP-breach incidents.
  • Absence of OPCW vendor-cooperation agreement templates or dispute-resolution procedures leaves the Consortium vulnerable to vendors weaponizing access refusal, rendering critical equipment unverifiable and forcing fallback-ladder procedures that consume 8–12 weeks per refusal.
  • Lack of validated filtering-certification procedures means the Consortium's counterpart evidence disclosure tiers may be challenged as hiding inconvenient evidence, expanding discrepancy caseload and stalling adjudication.
  • Without historical OPCW detection and false-positive data, the Consortium's proposed thresholds (70% detection, 10% false positives, 5% unverifiable equipment) are unvalidated and may prove unattainable or too lenient, making the Go/Modify/Stop verdict ambiguous.
  • Missing OPCW precedent on inspector information barriers and post-assignment restrictions may result in inadequate counterintelligence protection, enabling intelligence-collection attempts by either government and creating political withdrawal risk.

Worst Case Scenario: The Consortium adopts unvalidated managed-access and filtering procedures without OPCW precedent. During Phase One, vendors refuse access on grounds the Consortium's procedures are weaker than OPCW standards, rendering multiple sites' equipment unverifiable. Simultaneously, an inspector breach occurs (or is alleged), triggering a CI investigation that paralyzes operations. The Consortium's filtering procedures are contested as too aggressive, forcing raw-evidence access that exposes topology and security architecture. Adjudication load balloons from 15 to 40+ cases per month due to disputes over filtered-evidence sufficiency. By Month 8 (2027-06-08), contingency is depleted, one government threatens withdrawal, and the final verdict is delayed past Month 9.5 (2027-07-23), rendering the proof-of-concept inconclusive. Phase Two is unfunded and the bilateral mechanism collapses.

Best Case Scenario: The Consortium models its managed-access, filtering and vendor-cooperation procedures on validated OPCW precedent, adapted for frontier-computing IP sensitivity. Vendors accept the procedures because they align with established international standards. Filtering is certified by an independent third-country auditor, preventing disputes over hidden evidence. Inspector information barriers follow OPCW compartmentalization best practices, passing CI security reviews. False-positive rates remain at or below 10%, unverifiable-equipment counts stay below 5%, and adjudication load remains manageable (15–20 cases per month). By Month 8 (2027-06-08), the Consortium has strong evidence of detection capability and operational workability. The final verdict is issued on schedule (Month 9.5 = 2027-07-23), with high confidence in the Go decision if thresholds are met, and both governments approve Phase Two or broader extensions of the mechanism.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • Request bilateral briefing and documentation-sharing with OPCW Verification Division (via official government channels) covering managed-access case studies, vendor-dispute resolutions and filtering-certification methods; timeline 2–4 weeks for classified materials.
  • Engage a subject-matter expert (former OPCW inspector or verification manager) as a Consortium consultant (Month 0 = 2026-10-08) to review draft Inspector Information Firewall Doctrine and Counterpart Evidence Disclosure Tiers against OPCW precedent; estimated cost USD 100–150K within the legal/audit envelope.
  • Commission a comparative analysis (internal task force or external contractor) of managed-access procedures across OPCW, IAEA and bilateral inspection regimes (e.g., START verification protocols) to extract common filtering and dispute-resolution practices; timeline 6–8 weeks.
  • If OPCW documentation is insufficient, conduct a rapid field study of one OPCW-inspected commercial facility to observe filtering procedures and inspect-access constraints in operation; coordinate through official channels with the host country.
  • Establish a joint US–China technical working group with OPCW as a standing observer to co-design the Consortium's managed-access procedures iteratively, ensuring alignment with international precedent and building diplomatic credibility; timeline Months 1–3 (2026-11-08 to 2027-01-08).
  • Adopt a provisional managed-access protocol by Month 2 (2026-12-08) based on OPCW framework; validate it against the pilot exercise (Month 5 = 2027-03-08) by measuring false-positive and false-negative rates under the proposed filtering rules; adjust before Phase One clock if calibration is off by >5 percentage points.
  • Fallback to wider disclosure (unfiltered evidence packages) for disputed findings after 10 days of adjudication stall, with a 7-day reading-room access window under dual escort, trading some IP protection for faster resolution and reducing the risk of contested filtering.

Find Document 7: US–Russia START and New START Bilateral Verification and Dispute-Resolution Precedent

ID: 01080cd8-c569-4978-aa88-31f428d0477d

Description: Detailed records of how START I and New START managed on-site inspections, operated the Joint Compliance and Inspection Commission (bilateral dispute resolution without a casting vote), handled deadlocks, administered inspector rotations, and maintained ledgers and accountancy. Provides lessons on how bilateral equal-footing verification can function and where it has broken down (e.g., suspension of inspections, unresolved compliance disputes). Sourced from US State Department archives, declassified documents, and secondary literature.

Recency Requirement: START I historical records (1990–2009) and New START records (2011–2026); most recent data more relevant for current diplomatic context.

Responsible Role Type: Bilateral Verification-Protocol Designer / Deadlock-Resolution Specialist

Steps to Find:

  • Request from US State Department Bureau of Arms Control, Deterrence and Stability (requires official government channel).
  • Access declassified documents through the National Archives or the State Department FOIA reading room.
  • Consult published accounts: Arms Control Association fact sheets, SIPRI arms-control yearbook chapters, think-tank reports from Stimson Center, Carnegie Endowment, and Council on Foreign Relations.

Access Difficulty: Medium—some documents are classified; declassified material is in archives; may require 4–8 week FOIA process. Mitigation: initiate request at Month 0 (2026-10-08) for critical documents (Joint Commission procedures, deadlock case studies); supplement with published analysis if classified documents are delayed.

Essential Information:

  • What specific deadlock procedures, dispute-resolution mechanics and cancellation rights did the START I and New START Joint Compliance and Inspection Commission employ when co-chairs (US and Russia) could not agree on a compliance finding or sanction?
  • How were unresolved compliance disputes aged and tracked in the Joint Commission ledgers, and what suspension or remedial procedures were triggered if disputes remained open beyond defined time limits?
  • What inspector rotation schedules, cooling-off periods and information compartmentalization procedures did START enforce to prevent knowledge transfer and counterintelligence exposure across assignment cycles?
  • How did START and New START handle disputes over evidence weighting, attestation validity and the sufficiency of non-decisive single evidence sources in reaching compliance verdicts?
  • What provisions existed in START for handling vendor or facility operator refusal to permit inspection access, provide evidence or participate in on-site procedures, and how were such refusals adjudicated?
  • Did START employ any form of tamper-evident or replicated ledger systems for event recording, and if so, how were divergences detected and reconciled between parties?
  • What statistical methods or confidence thresholds were used in START to convert compliance-related event data (detected violations, false alarms, unverifiable findings) into Go/Continue or Stop/Remediate decisions?
  • How did START manage asymmetric access rights (e.g., one party granted more expansive inspection authority than the reciprocal access offered) when reciprocal parity could not be achieved?

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Deadlock procedures from START may have succeeded because they included a casting vote or escalation to a third party; the Consortium's double-key design with no casting vote has no START precedent, so guidance from incomplete or outdated START records could mislead the design.
  • If START documents do not detail how unresolved discrepancies were aged and triggered automatic suspension, the Consortium's proposed 14-21-28 day thresholds will lack empirical validation, risking either excessive suspensions that paralyze the program or insufficient aging that allows disputes to accumulate indefinitely.
  • START inspector compartmentalization procedures may have been much less stringent than the Consortium's information-firewall requirements (which aim to prevent IP leakage from frontier computing); relying on START precedent without acknowledging the difference understates the Consortium's operational burden and counterintelligence exposure.
  • If START records lack detail on how the parties handled vendor refusal or operator obstruction, the Consortium's five-rung fallback ladder will be designed without precedent, risking unvalidated assumptions about which fallback methods are actually credible to both parties.
  • Gaps in START's treatment of evidence-weighting disputes, evidence rule gaming and statistical sufficiency of thin detection data will leave the Consortium vulnerable to post-hoc bargaining over verdict thresholds if the precedent cannot document how such disputes were historically resolved.
  • Missing information about START's ledger practices (if any) leaves the Consortium's tamper-evident replicated ledger design and key-custody procedures without historical comparison, risking overlooked failure modes.
  • START's asymmetric-access history may reveal whether unequal inspection rights were treated as violations requiring remediation or accepted as practical necessities; if not documented, the Consortium risks either excluding viable sites due to asymmetry or accepting asymmetry without adequate mitigation.

Worst Case Scenario: The Consortium proceeds with deadlock, suspension, evidence-weighting, vendor-refusal and ledger procedures designed entirely from first principles, without learning from START's 35-year operational history. Within Phase One (Month 6-9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08), a deadlock arises: one party contests the evidence-weighting rule, refusing to accept a discrepancy classified under it. The Consortium's procedures for resolving the dispute (panel advisory, co-chair override, escalation) are untested and unvalidated. The parties deadlock for 20+ days; partial suspension activates, stalling a key function. The deadlock becomes a political flashpoint, each side claiming the other is stonewalling. Without START precedent showing how such deadlocks were historically managed and resolved, negotiators cannot invoke proven procedures, and the dispute cascades into a withdrawal threat. The Consortium's credibility collapses before Phase One concludes. Contingency budget is consumed (estimated USD 50-100M) on emergency diplomatic and legal consultation to recover. Go/Modify/Stop verdict cannot be issued credibly. Program is publicly discredited as unworkable.

Best Case Scenario: The Consortium's design team integrates detailed START I and New START Joint Commission procedures into the Consortium's deadlock, evidence-weighting, suspension and adjudication protocols. When a dispute arises in Phase One, the Consortium invokes proven procedures from START's operational history: the panel advisory process is based on START's pattern of technical specialists providing non-binding expert review; the 14-21-28 day escalation schedule reflects START's historical aging thresholds; the partial-suspension mechanics avoid the brittle all-or-nothing suspensions that started the inspections' breakdown in 2014. Disputes resolve within the pre-registered timelines; Phase One remains operationally stable. The final Go/Modify/Stop verdict is credible because it rests on procedures validated by 35 years of US-Russia arms-control practice. Both countries' legislatures see the Consortium as a serious, professionally managed mechanism, not an experimental improvisation. Subsequent Phase Two or renegotiation can proceed from a position of demonstrated competence and mutual trust. Program credibility is established as a proof-of-concept for future verification mechanisms.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If classified START documents are unavailable or delayed beyond Month 1 (2026-11-08), initiate a targeted expert consultation with retired START negotiators, Joint Commission members and US State Department verification specialists (Stimson Center, Carnegie Endowment, Council on Foreign Relations) who can provide unclassified summary guidance on deadlock procedures, inspector rotation practices and evidence-dispute resolution from firsthand knowledge.
  • Commission a rapid historical case-study analysis of three to five specific deadlock incidents from START I or New START (e.g., the Russian claims of US non-compliance in the 2000s, the 2014 suspension of inspections) conducted by an independent arms-control research organization; synthesize best practices and failure modes within 8 weeks (by Month 2 = 2026-12-08).
  • Initiate bilateral consultation with the Russian Federation (or successor state technical experts) to document lessons from Russia's perspective on how deadlocks were managed, inspector compartmentalization enforced and vendor refusals handled, creating a joint historical summary for reference; coordinate through diplomatic channels by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23).
  • If START precedent proves insufficient on a specific procedure (e.g., vendor-refusal fallback), commission a dedicated legal and technical memorandum from arms-control and supply-chain-security experts on how equivalent mechanisms have functioned in non-proliferation, export-control and cybersecurity verification (e.g., IAEA safeguards inspector access, OPCW chemical-weapons facility inspection vendor participation), with applicability analysis to the Consortium.
  • Establish a Consortium-specific Lessons Learned Review Panel (at Month 3 = 2027-01-08) comprising retired START officials, bilateral law experts, and the co-chairs' technical advisors, tasked with validating the Consortium's procedures against START precedent and recommending real-time adjustments if pilot exercises reveal divergences from historical practice.

Find Document 8: Independent Statistician Review: Confidence-Interval Methodology and Sample-Size Validation

ID: 60e8eca0-7566-458e-ad79-2af3d27b82db

Description: External statistical analysis confirming that the proposed pooled detection-rate estimate (±12% at 95% CL) and per-type estimate (±32% at 95% CL) are realistic for n≈54 exercises with p (probability of detection) ≈0.70. Validates that the thresholds (Go ≥70%, Modify 55–75%, Stop <55%) are statistically defensible or ambiguous given the confidence intervals. May recommend adjustments to sample size (e.g., if intervals are too wide, recommend 90-day test instead of 60-day, or recommend Modify as default outcome when intervals straddle). Sourced from academic statisticians or government statistical agencies (e.g., US NIST, UK ONS equivalent, or university departments).

Recency Requirement: Analysis completed by Month 5 (2027-03-08) to inform final threshold lock before Phase One clock (Month 6 = 2027-04-08).

Responsible Role Type: Statistician / Quantitative Analyst

Steps to Find:

  • Identify independent statisticians with experience in binomial inference and confidence-interval construction; candidates from universities, government statistical offices, or international organizations.
  • Commission an analysis to validate the confidence-interval assumptions and threshold defensibility; provide them with the proposed sample-size plan, detection-rate assumptions, and decision rule.
  • Request a written review (2–3 page technical memo) summarizing whether the thresholds are defensible, whether confidence intervals will be wide enough to create ambiguity, and recommendations for threshold adjustment or sample-size augmentation if necessary.

Access Difficulty: Easy–Medium—independent statisticians are available for hire or consultation; turn-around time typically 4–8 weeks for a technical review. Mitigation: commission the analysis at Month 3 (2027-01-08) to allow 2-month completion window before threshold lock.

Essential Information:

  • Confirm the mathematical validity of the pooled detection-rate confidence interval (±12% at 95% confidence level) for n≈54 exercises with p≈0.70 detection probability; verify whether binomial or normal approximation assumptions hold.
  • Validate per-event-type confidence intervals (±32% at 95% CL for n≈8 per type) and confirm whether sample sizes support any statistical claim about false-negative rates by type.
  • Confirm whether the pre-registered verdict thresholds (Go ≥70% planned events, ≥50% unplanned; Modify 55–75%; Stop <55%) are defensible given the confidence intervals, or whether thresholds will straddle the intervals in ambiguous zones.
  • Provide explicit statistical guidance on whether the proposed 54-exercise load (90-day Phase One at 6 per month per 6 sites) produces sufficient power to distinguish Go from Modify outcomes (proposed: 4 of 5 criteria at ≥80% vs. 3 of 5 at ≥60%).
  • Recommend sample-size adjustments if the 54-exercise target is unachievable (e.g., entry-condition delays compress the test to 60 days or 36–48 exercises); quantify how confidence intervals widen and how verdict defensibility degrades under compression.
  • Validate the false-positive and unverifiable-equipment thresholds (≤10% and ≤5% respectively) against typical operating margins in arms-control verification; flag whether these thresholds are achievable given the evidence rule's preliminary validation on only 100–200 historical events per site.
  • Assess whether the 90-day Phase One window is sufficient to collect enough exercise replicates to claim statistical defensibility of the final verdict, or whether the exercise authority should plan contingencies (e.g., Phase 1b extension, or Modify-default fallback if data remains ambiguous).
  • Recommend confidence-interval reporting format and labeling strategy for the unclassified verdict summary to communicate statistical uncertainty clearly and prevent post-hoc political reinterpretation of ambiguous results.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Incorrect confidence-interval calculations (e.g., failing to account for finite-population correction or clustered sampling at sites) can produce overstated precision, leading to false confidence that ambiguous detection rates (e.g., 65–75%) are defensible as Go or Stop when they are statistically indistinguishable.
  • If the statistician validates the thresholds post-hoc (after Phase One concludes), adjustment is too late; pre-Phase-One validation is required to inform exercise design and sample-size targets by Month 5 (2027-03-08).
  • Failure to flag the per-type confidence intervals (±32% at 95% CL) as too wide to support type-specific Stop conditions means the final verdict hinges on pooled detection alone, weakening the evidence that all event types are equally detectable.
  • Overlooking the impact of entry-condition delays (e.g., if Phase One compresses from 90 to 60 days) can result in underestimation of confidence-interval widening and overconfidence in verdict defensibility under compressed schedules.
  • If the review does not address how the evidence rule's preliminary validation (100–200 historical events, single cohort) affects confidence in the false-positive threshold (≤10%), adjudication workload may spike unexpectedly when Phase One reveals higher false-positive rates.
  • Absence of guidance on how to handle ambiguous outcomes (e.g., detection 68% vs. 70% threshold, with confidence intervals ±12%) leaves the co-chairs without a pre-registered decision rule, inviting post-hoc political negotiation of the verdict.
  • If the statistician does not validate the reciprocal-access parity metric (≥85%, definition TBD), that criterion remains undefined; the Go verdict cannot be scored reliably even if detection and other criteria are met.

Worst Case Scenario: At Phase One conclusion (Month 9 = 2027-07-08), detection rates fall in the 65–75% zone (e.g., 70±12% with confidence intervals 58–82%), straddling the pre-registered Go threshold (≥70%) and Modify band (55–75%). The statistical analysis was never completed or was flawed, so no pre-registered guidance exists for this ambiguous outcome. Both co-chairs claim their interpretation (Go vs. Modify) is statistically justified; the verdict becomes a 2–4 week political negotiation rather than a technical decision. If either country suspects the exercise data was gamed or the evidence rule was biased, the statistical analysis cannot defend the verdict against challenge. The final decision delays by 4–8 weeks, Phase One credibility collapses, and domestic legislatures declare the Consortium a failure. Sunk costs exceed USD 2–3 billion with no credible Phase Two commitment.

Best Case Scenario: By Month 5 (2027-03-08), an independent statistician validates that the pooled detection-rate confidence interval (±12% at 95% CL) is mathematically sound for the proposed 54-exercise sample, and that the pre-registered Go threshold (≥70%) is positioned outside the ambiguous zone. The pilot exercise (Month 5 = 2027-03-08) confirms that 6–8 event replicates per type per site are achievable within the 90-day window. The evidence rule's preliminary validation shows false-positive rates 8–12% (target 10% ±3), confirming the rule is well-calibrated. At Phase One conclusion, detection rates are 74±11% (95% CL, lower bound 63%, upper bound 85%, threshold 70%), clearly exceeding Go thresholds. The statistician's pre-registered mechanical scoring rule is applied; the verdict is Go with published confidence intervals. Both co-chairs accept the outcome; Phase Two is authorized with credible interim evidence. Political credibility is preserved, and the proof-of-concept succeeds.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If an independent statistician cannot be retained by Month 3 (2027-01-08), commission a smaller internal analytical review by one co-chair's statistical unit (e.g., US NIST, UK ONS equivalent, or Chinese Academy of Sciences) with the other co-chair's observers present; document any disagreements and publish them as caveats in the verdict methodology.
  • If the 54-exercise baseline is unachievable, initiate contingency planning at Month 4 (2027-02-08): agree to extend Phase One by 30 days (Months 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08.5 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-23) to accumulate 60+ exercises and tighten confidence intervals from ±12% to ±11%, or adopt a Modify-default rule if Phase One results are ambiguous.
  • If the evidence rule's preliminary validation (100–200 events per site) shows larger-than-tolerated false-positive rates (>15% vs. 10% target), delay the Phase One clock by 4 weeks to run a second validation cohort before entry; alternatively, pre-register a higher false-positive threshold (≤15%) with an explicit Modify-default trigger if false positives exceed 12%.
  • If per-type confidence intervals remain too wide (±32%) to support type-specific Stop conditions, establish a fallback rule: pool all unplanned-class events (vendor refusal, reluctant operator) into a single stratum, and judge detection pooled rather than by type; this trades granularity for statistical power.
  • If Phase One entry-condition delays appear likely by Month 2 (2026-12-08), formally notify both co-chairs and recommend pre-registering a compressed-schedule version of the thresholds (e.g., if Phase One is 60 days instead of 90, increase the Modify-default band to 45–85% and lower the Go requirement to 3 of 5 criteria at ≥75%).
  • If the neutral-facility ledger cannot support hourly digest synchronization and the ledger-divergence risk is higher than assumed, pre-register an alternative verdict rule that tolerates unresolved divergence incidents <3 per site during Phase One, treated as partial-suspension events rather than Stop triggers.
  • If the reciprocal-access parity metric (≥85%) remains undefined by Month 4.5 (2027-02-23), commission a joint measurement-and-audit task (co-chairs' technical teams) to operationalize parity as 'symmetric inspector access within 4 hours of request to all staging, spare-inventory and maintenance areas per bilateral access agreement,' scored by incident logs; this grounds the criterion in observable operational behavior rather than subjective facility equivalence.

Find Document 9: Facility Design and Hardening Standards: ISO 27001, IAEA-Equivalent Physical Security, SCIF-Equivalent Classification Handling

ID: b53a11f2-7a5c-4e82-98cb-de70f7c1bfe6

Description: International standards and government specifications for secure-facility design, applied to the neutral facility and national ledger-hosting centers. ISO 27001 for information security, IAEA or equivalent standards for physical security (perimeter, access controls, redundancy), SCIF (sensitive compartmented information facility) standards from US government or equivalent for classified information handling. Used to design the neutral facility and to evaluate site-readiness by Month 3 (2027-01-08). Sourced from international standardization bodies, government security agencies, and facility-design consultants.

Recency Requirement: Current standards (2023–2026); ISO 27001:2022 edition and later; US or international facility-design standards current at the time of facility construction (Month 2–3 = 2026-12-08 to 2027-01-08).

Responsible Role Type: Neutral Facility Director / Security-Design Architect

Steps to Find:

  • ISO 27001 standard from the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) official website or authorized distributor.
  • IAEA facility security standards from IAEA Department of Safeguards publications or via official bilateral request.
  • US SCIF standards from the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA) or equivalent in other countries.
  • Consult with facility-security design firms that specialize in classified government facilities (e.g., architecture firms with security clearances and relevant experience).

Access Difficulty: Easy–Medium—standards are published or available from government sources; some classified detail may require security clearance to access fully. Mitigation: assign facility-design team early (Month 0 = 2026-10-08) to acquire standards and design documents; engage with host-country facility providers (Geneva or Singapore) for preliminary site assessment by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23).

Essential Information:

  • Identify the current versions of ISO 27001 (2022 or later) and equivalent international information-security standards applicable to classified multilateral facilities.
  • Specify IAEA-equivalent or NATO-equivalent physical security standards for perimeter control, access restrictions, redundancy and resilience that meet the neutral facility requirements.
  • Detail SCIF-equivalent (or equivalent third-country) standards for classified information handling, compartmentation, document control and secure communications applicable to bilateral facilities.
  • Map each standard to the specific operational requirements of the neutral facility: dual-national ledger hosting, bilateral key custody, secure evidence reading rooms, classified co-chair coordination spaces, and inspector post-rotation debriefing areas.
  • Establish facility-design acceptance criteria by function: ledger-hosting center (uptime ≥99.95%, encryption-at-rest and in-transit, dual-custody key material storage); secure reading room (isolated network, no removable media, monitored access, dual-door security); co-chair boardroom (TEMPEST-equivalent RF shielding, dual-national authorization for entry).
  • Confirm which standards are publicly available vs. require government-agency coordination or security clearance to access in full detail.
  • Provide a gap-analysis template for evaluating candidate neutral-facility sites (Geneva or Singapore) against each standard by Month 1 (2026-11-08).
  • Specify redundancy and disaster-recovery requirements (backup power, network failover, offsite key escrow) to support 24/7 ledger synchronization and prevent single-point failures during the 90-day Phase One window.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Facility design diverges from standards → security certification delayed by 4–8 weeks past Month 3 (2027-01-08), stalling entry-gate sign-off and compressing Phase One from 90 to 45–60 days.
  • Incomplete or outdated standards (pre-2022 ISO 27001 or non-equivalent IAEA baseline) → ledger hosting or classified-document handling fails security audit at Month 3 (2027-01-08), requiring redesign and USD 50–100M cost overrun.
  • Ambiguous acceptance criteria for classified evidence storage or dual-custody key material → co-chairs dispute whether the neutral facility meets standards; no credible ledger baseline before Phase One operations begin.
  • Network isolation or TEMPEST-equivalent shielding specifications omitted → evidence of alleged IP leakage or RF eavesdropping during Phase One becomes plausible; counterpart alleges evidence integrity compromised.
  • Redundancy and disaster-recovery gaps → ledger synchronization stalls during unplanned outage; unresolved ledger divergence at that point triggers automatic impaired-confidence status and Phase One suspension.
  • Facility-design handover to third-country host (Geneva or Singapore) lacks clear acceptance-criteria handoff → host-country certification deferred; facility operational readiness cascades into Month 4 (2027-02-08), consuming contingency and shortening Phase One runway.

Worst Case Scenario: Neutral facility design fails to meet security standards by Month 3 (2027-01-08). Bilateral instrument specifies that Phase One cannot begin until facility is operational. A 6–8 week security redesign is required, pushing operational readiness to Month 5 (2027-03-08). Phase One clock compressed to 32–45 days; statistical sample size for exercises falls below defensible minimum (4–5 replicates per event type vs. 6–8 required); pilot exercise cannot complete before Phase One begins; detection-rate confidence intervals widen to ±20–25% (95% CL), making Go/Modify/Stop verdict indefensible. Entry-condition contingency consumed (estimated USD 100–150M). Either country withdraws, citing inadequate security or missing proof-of-concept rigor. Phase One does not conclude with credible verdict by Month 9 (2027-07-08); mission failure and bilateral relations damage.

Best Case Scenario: Facility design and hardening standards are locked by Month 0 (2026-10-08) with clear gap-analysis and acceptance criteria. Candidate neutral facility (Geneva or Singapore) is evaluated in parallel against the standards by Month 1 (2026-11-08), and host-country permitting and construction begin immediately with expedited certification authority. Facility operational readiness confirmed by Month 2.5 (2026-12-23), well ahead of Month 3 (2027-01-08) entry-gate deadline. Ledger hosting, key custody, secure reading rooms and co-chair spaces fully operational and stress-tested by Month 3 (2027-01-08). Entry gate certified on schedule; Phase One clock starts Month 6 (2027-04-08) with full 90-day window; 54 exercises run as planned; detection-rate confidence intervals remain at ±10–15% (95% CL); Go verdict supported by credible rigor and reciprocal transparency; Phase One concludes by Month 9.5 (2027-07-23) with defensible bilateral decision and pathway to Phase Two or scaled operations.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If public ISO 27001:2022 or equivalent standards are insufficient to meet bilateral classified-facility requirements, initiate a joint task force (Month 0 = 2026-10-08) with national security agencies (NSA, DCSA equivalent, Chinese counterpart equivalent) to document additional or classified supplements to the public standards. Establish a bilateral standards-working group with binding sign-off authority by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23).
  • If a candidate neutral-facility site cannot meet full IAEA + SCIF-equivalent standards within budget by Month 3 (2027-01-08), activate a fallback model: partition the ledger hosting and bilateral coordination across two allied host countries (e.g., ledger hosting in a European government facility meeting IAEA standards, bilateral co-chair spaces in a second neutral country meeting SCIF equivalents). Document the split-site model and dual-custody key material escrow procedures in the bilateral instrument by Month 1 (2026-11-08).
  • If TEMPEST-equivalent RF-shielding requirements cannot be validated before Month 2 (2026-12-08), defer RF-sensitive co-chair meetings to a pre-built secure government facility (e.g., US embassy secure room or equivalent Chinese facility) and use the neutral-facility co-chair boardroom for non-classified or releasable-to-ally coordination only. Document the meeting-classification baseline by Month 1 (2026-11-08).
  • If redundancy and disaster-recovery procedures cannot be fully tested before Month 3 (2027-01-08), establish a formal ledger-failover and key-recovery exercise during Month 4 (2027-02-08) (simulated outage and restart) and a production disaster-recovery drill during Month 5 (2027-03-08) (before Phase One operations). Publish failover timelines and recovery procedures as part of entry-gate certification.
  • If host-country permitting for the neutral facility is stalled or deadlocked by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23), activate immediate diplomatic escalation (co-chair intervention) and, if necessary, offer the host country a small operational role (representation on the Independent Exercise Authority or ledger-oversight board) to unblock permits. Alternate: identify a second backup host country (e.g., if Geneva stalls, escalate to Singapore; if both delay, propose a fourth country). Maintain a 4-week acceleration reserve in the entry-condition timeline by Month 0 (2026-10-08).
  • If the independent third-country filter auditor cannot be vetted and cleared by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23), pre-identify two alternate auditor organizations (international accounting firms with security credentials, or a second third country's government auditor) and obtain provisional commitments by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23). Conduct the filter-audit role in parallel: if first choice delays, second choice activated immediately.

Strengths

  • Narrow, bounded mission (declared-equipment change verification only) keeps scope achievable and avoids contested claims about hidden facilities or total capacity.
  • Leader-level backing in both countries and domestic authority to compel participation address the main precedent failure: access curtailment.
  • Fixed USD 5.0B cap, exactly 50/50, with seven envelopes, 100% envelope-mapping audits and four synchronized tranches makes withholding visible and symmetric.
  • Layered evidence (no single source decisive), confidential rotating rule and vendor fallback ladder resist gaming and single-point failure.
  • Governance is explicit: double-key, no casting vote, timed deadlock, partial suspension (day 14) and impaired-confidence (days 21/28) rules that keep unrelated verification running.
  • Independent 8-person mixed-nationality Exercise Authority, cross-designed red-team challenges and pre-registered thresholds support credible, reciprocal detection evidence.
  • Staffing is sized from sites, shifts and leave (about 180 per country, estimate), with deputies for every critical role.
  • Strong precedents to borrow from: IAEA, OPCW, START commissions, CTBTO signed data.

Weaknesses

  • Thin statistics: about 54 exercises give pooled about ±12% at 95%, and per event type about ±32% (estimate). Go/Modify/Stop on 70% and 50% thresholds will often be ambiguous.
  • Thresholds, parity definition, functional-equivalence criteria and the evidence rule are unvalidated (proposed); the rule is calibrated only on historical records, not adversarial cases.
  • Entry gates are sequential and heavy (instrument, appropriations, sites, inspectors, vendors, schedule) and run Months 0-5 (2026-10-08 to 2027-03-08).5. Any slip compresses the test.
  • Vendor ladder cannot finish before the clock: five rungs at 8-12 weeks each, so unresolved equipment becomes unverifiable or is excluded. This lets vendors shape what is covered.
  • Adjudication capacity of about 15 cases per month is small against a possible 50+ cases if the rule is miscalibrated.
  • Filtering and certification add 2-3 days per package, and filters are a point where evidence can be hidden.
  • Key ceremonies and the neutral facility are chokepoints (site OPEN, due Month 3 = 2027-01-08). Dual-share keys can block the ledger for 8-24 hours.
  • Funding after Phase One (Modify rework or Phase Two) is OPEN, and the 'Go' tranche is tied to the verdict, which could bias scoring.

Opportunities

  • Create a first-of-kind, reusable template for hardware-change verification between adversaries, with the technology-neutral schedule and coded bilingual schema adaptable to other regimes.
  • Publish unclassified KPIs and verdict logic, building legislative and public confidence in fiscal accountability and objective results.
  • Use the Month 5 (2027-03-08) pilot (all seven event types, non-production site) to recalibrate thresholds and the evidence rule before the clock starts.
  • Engage IAEA, OPCW and former START/OSIA inspectors for managed-access, seal and dispute-procedure lessons, and use third-country auditors and the filter auditor for neutral legitimacy.
  • Pre-agreed vendor participation terms, home-government compensation and fallback options can turn vendors into supporters and extend verifiability.
  • Add cross-pair exercise replicates or extend the window after a Modify verdict to narrow the intervals, if funding is agreed.

Threats

  • Political withdrawal or deterioration of US-China relations, as seen with the lapsed JCPOA monitoring and New START.
  • Tranche delay or unequal deposits: over 14 days triggers escalation, over 30 days is a Stop trigger.
  • Asymmetric operator compliance: commercial US operators may resist on confidentiality grounds, while state-run Chinese sites may slow access through bureaucracy. Either can break parity or amount to shielding.
  • Counterintelligence breaches or IP leaks by inspectors, and public disclosure that forces withdrawal.
  • Contested exercise integrity or filter disputes that turn the dataset into a forensic argument.
  • Entry slips of 8-12 weeks costing USD 100-500M (estimate) and exhausting contingency, risking a breach of the USD 5B cap.
  • Gaming of the evidence rule by operators or vendors, and rapid hardware change outpacing the frozen schedule.
  • Staffing shortfalls or attrition in 24/7 mirrored shifts, and exercises disrupting production.

Recommendations

  • Entry task force (both co-chairs' offices): publish the roadmap at Month 0 (2026-10-08), run site, vendor and vetting tracks in parallel, hold a summit within 5 days of any gate slipping over 2 weeks, and keep the USD 50-100M compression reserve (estimate). Decide the neutral facility site by Month 1 (2026-11-08).
  • Evidence rule owners (accountable specialists): place the draft rule in escrow at Month 4.5 (2027-02-23). Validate it on 100-200 historical events per site by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23), then add adversarial synthetic cases. Adjust and re-validate on a second cohort if deviation exceeds 5 points.
  • Exercise Authority and verdict panel: pre-register thresholds and scoring as bands by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23), with a mechanical rule that defaults to Modify when intervals straddle a threshold. State the ±12% pooled and ±32% per-type limits in every report. Lock before the Month 6 (2027-04-08) clock.
  • Vendor Liaison Offices: document vendor refusals by Month 3 (2027-01-08) and start the first fallback rung immediately. Pre-stage one examiner team per country (5-8 specialists). Exclude or mark unverifiable anything unresolved at entry, and publish the registry by Month 4 (2027-02-08).
  • Co-chairs and finance officers: lock deadlock, suspension and age thresholds into the instrument by Month 1 (2026-11-08). Appoint the independent timekeeper. Do not tie the final tranche to a Go/Modify outcome, only to verdict publication. Settle the post-Phase One funding route by Month 8 (2027-06-08).
  • Counterintelligence Board and filter auditor: certify the filters by Month 5 (2027-03-08), enforce the firewall and no-phone rules, and run monthly spot checks. Add adjudication surge capacity above 15 cases per month.

Strategic Objectives

  • Certify the entry gate by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23) with all seven conditions met, including parity confirmed for at least 2 and a target of 3 matched pairs.
  • Complete pilot and historical validation by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23), with pilot false positives of 7-13% and false negatives under 5% (proposed thresholds), and lock thresholds before the Month 6 (2027-04-08) clock.
  • Run at least 6 exercises per event type (54 total at 3 pairs) in the 90-day window (Months 6-9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08) with zero production disruption, and report intervals with every rate.
  • Keep every discrepancy under 21 days at conclusion, ledger digests exchanged at least hourly, and ledger divergence reconciled within 72 hours (target), with zero unresolved divergences.
  • Publish the scored unclassified verdict within 5 days of Month 9 (2027-07-08) and take the final Go/Modify/Stop decision by Month 9.5 (2027-07-23), with audit exceptions at or below 2% of sampled value.

Assumptions

  • Both leaders sustain political backing and compel operators and vendors, with no trust assumed.
  • Phase One starts only after all entry conditions are met; the 90-day clock begins at Month 6 (2027-04-08).
  • Commercial elements are Not applicable; value is judged by outcomes and fiscal accountability.
  • Canonical facts supersede earlier documents: 3 matched pairs, about 180 staff per country (estimate), 54 exercises.
  • Thresholds and the parity definition remain provisional until validated on pilot data.
  • Both countries fund exactly USD 2.5B, drawn in four synchronized tranches.

Missing Information

  • Definition and measurement method of reciprocal-access parity.
  • Validated historical datasets and ground truth for the evidence-rule calibration.
  • Exact treatment of the other three event types (class TBD) in detection thresholds.
  • Neutral facility site (Geneva or Singapore) and host-country permits.
  • Vendor positions: which Tier-1 vendors will participate, refuse or demand fallback.
  • Funding route for Modify rework or Phase Two.
  • Translation turnaround targets and the adjudication surge budget.
  • Legal basis for operator compensation and domestic access authority in each country.

Questions

  • If detection lands at 60-80% with wide intervals, what pre-agreed outcome does each government accept, and is Modify a real decision or a default exit?
  • What evidence would show that one side's operators are shielding, and who certifies it without a casting vote?
  • How will the draft evidence rule be tested against adversarial behaviour, not only benign historical records?
  • Which gate is most likely to slip, and would each government accept a smaller test (2 pairs, shorter window) rather than a delay?
  • Who funds and decides what follows a Modify verdict, and does that affect how the final tranche and scoring are perceived?

Roles Needed & Example People

Roles

1. Bilateral Arms-Control Verification Lead

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Bilateral Arms-Control Verification Lead oversees the core mission throughout entry conditions (Months 0–5 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-03-08) and Phase One operations (Months 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08). This role unifies evidence findings across both national teams, manages the single-winner evidence-weighting rule, and drives the final Go/Modify/Stop verdict logic. It is a continuous, uninterrupted core accountability with no substitute authority, and must maintain full-time presence during deadlock resolution and discrepancy adjudication. The plan forbids single-person critical functions; deputy required (2 FTE total per country, 1 lead role, 1 deputy backup).

Explanation: Oversees the core mission: declared-equipment change verification at participating sites. Ensures detection credibility, manages evidence-weighting rules, and drives Go/Modify/Stop verdict logic. Bridges both national teams' technical findings into defensible conclusions. Essential during all phases: planning (threshold calibration), execution (discrepancy adjudication), and conclusion (verdict scoring against pre-registered criteria).

Consequences: Without a single unifying verification authority, evidence findings become fragmented across competing national teams, deadlock resolution collapses, and final verdict loses defensibility. Detection credibility fails, and the mechanism becomes a bilateral negotiation rather than a technical verification.

People Count: 1 lead (dual-authority model: co-reporting to both co-chairs with equal standing, no casting vote). Deputy needed for continuity; total 2 personnel.

Typical Activities: Elena convenes weekly evidence-synthesis working groups with both national teams' inspectors, validates that layered evidence-weighting rules are applied consistently, and chairs the Discrepancy Adjudication Panel when deadlocks occur. She maintains the versioned evidence rule and ensures it is revalidated monthly against live Phase One data. She drafts the final verdict scorecard (detection rates, confidence intervals, Go/Modify/Stop logic) for both co-chairs to approve. During entry conditions, she designs the pilot-exercise validation protocol and oversees the 100–200 historical-event calibration. She prepares monthly unclassified briefing slides on evidence quality and adjudication workload for legislative oversight.

Background Story: Dr. Elena Reyes is a Chilean-American arms-control verification specialist based in Geneva, with 18 years' experience in nuclear and chemical weapons treaty verification. She led OPCW inspections in Syria (2013–2015) and advised the IAEA on JCPOA monitoring protocols. Her doctoral research at Stanford focused on evidence synthesis under asymmetric trust. She speaks Spanish, English, and Mandarin. Her deep familiarity with bilateral deadlock procedures, tamper-evident ledger design and Go/Modify/Stop verdict frameworks makes her essential to anchor the Consortium's core mission credibility. Elena has no casting vote but serves as the unifying voice bridging US and Chinese technical findings into defensible conclusions.

Equipment Needs: Secure communication terminal (encrypted video conferencing, classified networks); access to both national ledger copies via secure terminal; dual-monitor workstation for evidence-package review; classified document handling and storage; secure phone (STU-III or equivalent) for co-chair coordination; evidence repository access tools (read-only, dual-logged); bilateral memoranda and ruling documentation systems.

Facility Needs: Bilateral secure workspace at neutral facility (Geneva or Singapore) with classified document handling (Tempest-rated, SCIF-equivalent, 24/7 staffed); access to both national ledgers simultaneously; secure reading room for raw-evidence review; deadlock-resolution boardroom (confidentiality-rated for top-secret material); document vault for versioned evidence rules and ruling archive; co-chair coordination office with redundant secure phones and video terminals.

3. Replicated Ledger & Cryptographic Attestation Architect

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Replicated Ledger & Cryptographic Attestation Architect designs and operates the tamper-evident ledger system, manages signed-digest synchronization (1-hour bounds), coordinates key-custody ceremonies (Months 4–5 = 2027-02-08 to 2027-03-08), and responds to ledger divergence incidents throughout Phase One. He responds to ledger divergence incidents (estimated 10–15 in 90 days) with forensic analysis and co-chair guidance on recovery. He holds a PhD in cryptographic protocols and speaks English, Hindi, and Mandarin. His specialized knowledge of dual-share key generation, ledger-divergence detection algorithms, and recovery procedures from lost or contested signing keys is critical to keeping the Consortium's replicated national ledgers trustworthy and synchronized within 1-hour bounds.

Facility Needs: Dual national ledger-hosting centers (one per country, or mirrored in neutral facility with dual-key access); secure equipment room (Tempest-rated, environmental controls, redundant cooling and power); network operations center (24/7 staffed) for synchronization monitoring; key-custody ceremony space (secure clean room with air-gap capability, witness stations, dual-locked access); disaster-recovery and key-backup vault (physically separate, secured to both countries); ledger divergence investigation room (for incident-response analysis with both countries' representatives present).

4. Discrepancy Adjudication & Deadlock-Resolution Panel

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Discrepancy Adjudication & Deadlock-Resolution Panel comprises 6 technical specialists (3 per country) who must be available full-time during Phase One to resolve estimated 20–30 contested findings. Panel convening within 10 days, advisory recommendation within 5 days, and co-chair decision within 3 days require continuous availability and deep technical familiarity with evidence standards and deadlock procedures. Estimated 15+ discrepancies per month at peak workload; panel is full-time core during Months 6–9 (2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08) and pre-positioned during entry conditions (Months 3–5 = 2027-01-08 to 2027-03-08 for training).

Explanation: Resolves contested findings when co-chairs deadlock. Comprises 6 technical specialists (3 per country) who review conflicting evidence, rule on which evidence category is most probative, and classify discrepancies as material (affects Go/Modify/Stop) or procedural. Also advises on age-triggered automatic suspensions. Manages the 28-day deadlock-resolution cycle with timely recommendations. Critical during Phase One, handling estimated 20–30 unresolved cases.

Consequences: Deadlocked discrepancies remain open indefinitely, automatic impaired-confidence and suspension thresholds are never reached, unresolved findings accumulate, and the ledger drifts into uncertainty. A single unresolved high-stakes finding can paralyze the entire mechanism or force an arbitrary Stop decision by default.

People Count: 6 total (3 per country), full-time during Phase One (Months 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08). Pre-positioned and trained during Months 3–5 (2027-01-08 to 2027-03-08) on deadlock procedures and conflict resolution.

Typical Activities: Maria chairs or participates in Adjudication Panel sessions (estimated 1–2 per week during Months 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08) convened within 10 days of a co-chair deadlock. She reviews conflicting evidence packages, interviews inspectors and site operators, and produces an advisory recommendation within 5 days identifying which evidence category is most probative and whether the discrepancy is material or procedural. She documents the Panel's reasoning in a classified report to co-chairs and logs the recommendation in the ledger (non-binding, but published so co-chairs must overturn it explicitly). She tracks discrepancy-age thresholds and flags cases approaching automatic impaired-confidence status (21 days for identity disputes, 28 days for exit dispositions) to trigger co-chair escalation protocols.

Background Story: Dr. Maria Gonzalez is a Spanish technical adjudicator with 14 years' experience resolving contested findings in arms-control verification. She served as a senior disputes officer for the OPCW Executive Council (2012–2018) and adjudicated 40+ complex chemical-facility inspection disputes. She holds a master's degree in forensic analysis and speaks Spanish, English, French, and Mandarin. Her ability to parse conflicting evidence, identify which layer is most probative, and rule neutrally on material-versus-procedural classification makes her indispensable for the Discrepancy Adjudication Panel, where 20–30 contested findings are expected during Phase One.

Equipment Needs: Classified evidence-review workstations (4+ dual-monitor systems, air-gapped or secure-enclave capable); secure document annotation and decision-support software; conflict-resolution case-management system (timeline tracking, evidence-link mapping, recommendation templates); video conference equipment for Adjudication Panel convening (secure, classified-capable); timer and deadline-tracking tools (automated escalation at days 10, 15, 18, 21, 28, 35); ledger-annotation tools (timestamped, dual-signed); secure telephony for panel member coordination.

Facility Needs: Secure adjudication boardroom at neutral facility (1,000+ sq m, classified-rated, seating for 6+ specialists and support staff); separate evidence-review chambers (dual independent review, to prevent collusion); secure file repository for conflicting evidence packages; teleconference suite for panel members who may be located in their home countries; archival secure storage for prior adjudication rulings (precedent reference); break-out spaces for in-camera deliberations (no recording, but witness log of deliberation start/end times).

5. Independent Exercise Authority & Red-Team Testing Director

Contract Type: independent_contractor

Contract Type Justification: Independent Exercise Authority (8 core staff, mixed-nationality) designs, schedules, executes and scores 54 blind-challenge exercises over 4 months (Months 5–9 = 2027-03-08 to 2027-07-08: pilot Month 5 = 2027-03-08, Phase One Months 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08). Exercise independence is foundational to credibility; contractors maintain separation from operational inspectors and co-chairs until execution. Scope is defined (54 exercises across 7 event types, pre-registered scenarios, fixed scoring rubric), term is bounded (4 months), and deliverable is discrete (exercise results and detection rates). Contracted from the USD 500M testing envelope.

Explanation: Designs, schedules, executes and scores all 54 blind-challenge exercises (7 event types × 6–8 replicates) without input from co-chairs or site inspectors until execution. Manages 8 core staff (mixed-nationality, security-cleared). Ensures exercises test detection credibility without disrupting production. Produces the only direct detection evidence on which the Go/Modify/Stop verdict rests. Critical Months 5–9 (2027-03-08 to 2027-07-08) (pilot + Phase One operations).

Consequences: Exercises lack independence, inspectors adjust behavior for known tests, detection rates become unrepresentative of reality, and the verdict thresholds cannot be validated. If exercises are designed by co-chairs or site operators, gaming becomes possible, and credibility collapses.

People Count: 8 core staff (mixed-nationality team: 4 per country or balanced rotation). Scale to 10–12 if exercises run in parallel (3+ sites simultaneously, Months 6–8 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-06-08) to manage concurrent logistics and independent video/witness documentation.

Typical Activities: Thomas leads a mixed-nationality team of 8 staff (4 per country, or rotation) to design all 54 blind-challenge exercises (7 event types × 6–8 replicates). He pre-registers each scenario before execution—equipment identifiers, success criteria, expected inspector actions, witness assignments—and keeps the scenario secret from inspectors until start. He schedules exercises across Months 5–9 (2027-03-08 to 2027-07-08): 1 pilot exercise (all 7 types, non-production site) at Month 5 (2027-03-08); Phase One exercises 3–4 per month per site (Months 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08). He scores each exercise against the pre-registered rubric using independent video, witnesses and cryptographic attestation, and publishes results (detection rates, false positives/negatives) to both co-chairs simultaneously. His independence is sacrosanct: neither co-chair has input on scenario selection or scoring until after execution.

Background Story: Dr. Thomas Wright is a UK-based independent testing and red-team director with 19 years' experience designing blind-challenge exercises for arms-control verification and conducting unannounced inspections for the IAEA. He led the IAEA's internal-audit red teams (2010–2017) and designed scenario-based detection tests that stressed inspectorate procedures without compromising operations. He holds a PhD in organizational testing and speaks English, German, and conversational Mandarin. His independence from both co-chairs and his expertise in exercise design that resists gaming while remaining realistic and non-disruptive make him the natural lead for the Independent Exercise Authority, whose results are the only direct detection evidence for the Go/Modify/Stop verdict.

Equipment Needs: Secure scenario-design and pre-registration platform (access-controlled, audit-trail logged); exercise-execution checklist and equipment-staging documentation tools; independent video recording and cryptographic attestation systems (camera, tripod, evidence-seal equipment, chain-of-custody log); witness-statement templates and forms; timing and trigger-detection equipment (sensors for unreported arrivals, if applicable); secure communications for exercise teams (radio, encrypted phone) during execution; pilot-exercise and Phase-One exercise reports generation tools.

Facility Needs: Secure operational planning and scenario-lock room (neutral facility or independent location, access restricted to Exercise Authority only until execution); separate test facility for pilot exercise (non-production datacenter, 500+ sq m staging/spare area); exercise-execution staging areas at each participating site (controlled access, equipment positioning marked, witness stations); secure evidence-storage area for post-exercise video and documentation (chain-of-custody maintained); exercise-scoring and results-compilation office (secure, for independent scoring before publication to co-chairs).
