She holds an MBA in supply-chain management and speaks English, Hindi, and conversational Mandarin. Her proven ability to secure written vendor commitments, negotiate fallback procedures and pre-stage accredited independent-examiner teams makes her critical to unlocking vendor participation before Phase One and managing the vendor-refusal fallback ladder if critical vendors refuse.

Equipment Needs: Vendor-management database (contact tracking, commitment status, fallback-ladder activation log); vendor-communication templates and confidentiality-agreement document management; covered-equipment schedule versioning and configuration-management tools (locked, with double-key amendment controls); accredited-examiner team roster and scheduling system; fallback-procedure activation checklist (vendor-supervised testing, independent-examiner coordination, clean-room booking); supply-chain documentation and attestation-verification tools.

Facility Needs: Vendor Liaison Office (US and China, estimated 300 sq m each, or joint satellite office at neutral facility); secure vendor-communication center (for sensitive discussions with critical vendors, classified-capable); accredited-examiner pre-staging facility or secure briefing room (coordinate equipment lists, inspect certifications, store sealed examination kits); clean-room procedures documentation and training space (if clean-room procedures are selected, coordinate with participating sites); equipment-schedule version-control and amendment-approval workspace (dual-access terminals for co-chair sign-off on schedule changes).

8. Joint Finance, Envelope Reconciliation & Contingency-Management Officer

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Joint Finance, Envelope Reconciliation & Contingency-Management Officer administers USD 5 billion budget across seven envelopes, reconciles actuals monthly (100% envelope mapping), manages contingency burn triggers (>30%, >50%, >75%), processes synchronized tranches (4 releases over 9.5 months), and escalates Stop conditions for funding withholds >30 days. This role runs continuously from Month 0 (2026-10-08) through Month 9.5 (2027-07-23) and cannot pause. Weekly dashboard reporting, monthly reconciliation and tranche processing require sustained presence. Contingency-draw decisions are time-sensitive. No single-person functions rule requires FTE lead plus deputy backup (2 per country).

Explanation: Administers the USD 5 billion budget split 50/50 (USD 2.5 billion per country), maps all expenses to the seven fixed envelopes, reconciles monthly actuals against budgets, and manages contingency burn. Tracks USD 625 million per country per envelope monthly. Provides weekly contingency-burn dashboard to co-chairs, escalates breaches (>30%, >50%, >75% of contingency drawn), and triggers Stop condition if either country withholds a tranche >30 days. Ensures 100% envelope-mapping audit compliance. Active throughout entry conditions and Phase One.

Consequences: Budget discipline collapses, overruns are discovered too late to correct, contingency is depleted without co-chair knowledge, one country withholds a tranche claiming mis-allocation, and Phase One stops mid-operation due to funding freeze. The mechanism loses fiscal accountability and trust.

People Count: 1 finance lead per country + 1 accountant/auditor coordinator per country = 4 full-time (2 per country). Deputy backup required (no single-person critical functions); total 6–8 personnel to handle parallel tranche processing, dispute adjudication, and envelope reallocation decisions.

Typical Activities: Michael administers the USD 2.5 billion per-country contributions across seven fixed envelopes (ledger, site prep, personnel, facilities, testing, legal, contingency). He processes synchronized tranches (Month 2 = 2026-12-08 first tranche 25%, Month 3 = 2027-01-08 second tranche 25%, Month 5.5 = 2027-03-23 third tranche 30%, Month 9.2 = 2027-07-14 final tranche 20%) with dual-signature authority. He reconciles actual spending against budgets monthly (100% envelope-sample audit), produces a weekly contingency-burn dashboard (current draw %, burn rate per month, projected depletion date), and escalates breaches (>30%, >50%, >75% of contingency drawn). He flags envelope overruns (>110% triggers co-chair review; >120% requires supplemental appropriations). He tracks funding-withhold delays (>14 days escalates; >30 days unresolved is a Stop trigger). He produces unclassified monthly financial summaries for legislative oversight.

Background Story: Mr. Michael Chen is a US public financial manager with 17 years' experience administering large international appropriations and envelope-based budgeting for multilateral arms-control programs. He managed the USD 2 billion OPCW destruction-operations budget (2009–2015) and designed the financial-governance structure for multinational confidence-building initiatives. He holds an MBA in public administration and speaks English, Mandarin, and conversational French. His discipline in 100% envelope mapping, timely tranche releases, contingency-burn tracking and Stop-condition enforcement makes him irreplaceable for keeping the Consortium's USD 5 billion budget honest and preventing mid-test funding crises.

Equipment Needs: Financial-management and budget-tracking software (envelope-mapped, real-time actuals vs. budget, multi-country currency handling); invoice and expense-documentation database (100% sampled audit trail); contingency-burn monitoring and dashboard tools (daily updates, escalation triggers at 30%, 50%, 75%); tranche-processing and payment-authorization systems (dual-signature workflows, dual-key payment approvals); personnel-cost allocation (FTE tracking, loaded-cost calculation); audit-readiness reporting tools (unclassified summaries, ledger exports).

Facility Needs: Joint Finance and Budget Authority office (US, China, and neutral facility liaison, estimated 400 sq m total); secure financial-data center with redundant systems (for budget databases, invoice records, contingency tracking); banking and payment infrastructure (authorized to receive and disburse USD 2.5B per country); audit-ready secure repository (for invoices, supporting documentation, audit reports); weekly dashboard-generation and co-chair briefing workspace (secure terminal access, classified budget summaries); contingency-draw decision room (for emergency budget re-allocation or scope-reduction decisions).

Omissions

1. Unclear Deputy and Succession Authority for Bilateral Co-Chairs

The plan specifies equal national co-chairs with double-key authorization and no casting vote, but does not define who assumes authority if a co-chair is incapacitated, retires, or is replaced mid-Phase-One. Absence of a clear succession rule creates a governance gap that could paralyze decision-making during critical deadlock resolution, key-custody ceremonies, or emergency funding decisions. A co-chair illness or political replacement without a pre-named deputy leaves adjudication and tranche releases unresolved.

Recommendation: Require both governments to name a deputy co-chair and a tertiary successor (chain of 3 per country) before the bilateral instrument is signed (Month 1 = 2026-11-08). Deputy co-chairs attend all double-key meetings and stand in during absences; succession is automatic upon the primary's incapacity or resignation. Deputies must have same security clearance and authority level as principals. Document succession procedures in the bilateral memorandum locked at entry-gate certification (Month 5.5 = 2027-03-23).

2. No Defined Escalation Path for Vendor Fallback Disputes

The vendor-refusal fallback ladder (vendor-supervised testing, filtered evidence, independent examiners, clean-room, validated attestation) establishes five rungs, but does not specify who decides whether a vendor's refusal justifies moving to the next rung or escalating the classification to 'unverifiable.' If the national teams disagree on whether a vendor's objection is legitimate, the dispute enters the general deadlock mechanism, consuming 28+ days by default. For time-sensitive vendor responses (vendors often demand quick decisions), the general deadlock timeline is too slow.

Recommendation: Establish a Vendor-Dispute Fast-Track Panel (1 specialist per country, pre-positioned by Month 2 = 2026-12-08, reporting to the Vendor Liaison Officer) with authority to rule on fallback-rung advancement within 5 business days. Panel authority limited to: (1) confirming vendor refusal legitimacy; (2) advancing to next rung or escalating to Adjudication Panel. If fast-track panel deadlocks, invoke the standard 28-day deadlock process. Vendor-dispute resolutions logged in the ledger. This prevents slow-track deadlock from stalling time-sensitive vendor negotiations.

3. No Defined Transition or Phase-Two Authority

The plan concludes Phase One with a Go, Modify, or Stop verdict by Month 9.5 (2027-07-23), but does not specify what happens next. If the verdict is Modify (correctable weaknesses remain), the plan states 'Modify-directed rework' or 'later phase (funding OPEN)' but provides no governance structure, decision timeline, or budget allocation for Phase Two. A Modify verdict without a clear Phase-Two gate leaves both governments uncertain about commitment and cost, risking political withdrawal or stalling.

Recommendation: Include in the bilateral instrument a 'Phase-Two Decision Gate' protocol: (1) if verdict is Go, define conditions for transition to continuous Phase-Two monitoring (funding and mandate TBD by both governments separately, not assumed in Phase One); (2) if Modify, the co-chairs convene within 14 days (by Month 10 = 2027-08-08) to jointly assess corrective actions and decide whether Phase Two begins under amended rules (approved within 30 days, by Month 10.5 = 2027-08-23) or pilot extensions within Phase One (within 60 days, by Month 11 = 2027-09-08); (3) if Stop, define shutdown procedures (ledger archival, inspector repatriation, facility closure). Phase-Two budget and staffing are separate appropriations, not pre-committed in Phase One.

4. No Explicit Audit Independence and Dispute Authority

The plan requires independent auditors for 100% envelope-mapping samples and independent filter auditors for evidence certification, but does not specify: (a) how independent auditors are selected or approved (by whom, using what criteria); (b) what happens if an independent auditor's finding is contested by one co-chair; (c) whether the independent auditor can be fired or replaced mid-Phase-One if one government disputes their impartiality. An auditor finding that a government mis-allocated funds (e.g., claiming site-preparation cost but spending on personnel) could trigger a funding-withhold Stop condition, but if the auditor's independence is contested, the finding itself becomes deadlocked.

Recommendation: Require both co-chairs to jointly pre-approve the independent auditor and filter auditor by Month 1 (2026-11-08), using a two-stage selection: (1) open nomination from third countries or international organizations (SIPR, OECD, Big Four accounting firms); (2) joint interview and approval by co-chairs. Auditor charter locked in bilateral instrument, specifying: auditor cannot be dismissed without co-chair unanimity; audit findings are published unclassified to both co-chairs simultaneously within 5 days; any finding dispute goes to a Technical Expert Panel (3 independent auditing specialists, 1 per country + 1 third-country neutral) for advisory review within 7 days, non-binding to co-chairs but published in the ledger. This prevents one government from contesting auditor independence as a proxy for disputing an unfavorable finding.

5. No Defined Handling of Partial Site Failure or Unilateral Operator Withdrawal

The plan assumes both governments provide access and operators cooperate throughout Phase One. But a US hyperscale operator could withdraw or sharply restrict access mid-test (citing customer pressure, security concerns, or commercial disruption from exercises), or a Chinese site could be withdrawn for 'national security review.' The plan has no rule for: (1) does one site's failure require a Stop verdict, or can Phase One continue with remaining sites; (2) does a mid-test operator withdrawal trigger a material Stop condition for asymmetry, or can fallback testing substitute; (3) how much does detection-rate confidence degrade if a site drops from 3 pairs to 2 pairs mid-operation.

Recommendation: Define a Site-Loss Protocol before Phase One clock starts (Month 5.5 = 2027-03-23): (1) loss of one site reduces sample to 4 sites (2 pairs); detection confidence intervals widen from ±12% to ±14–16% (estimate), acceptable if Modify threshold is adjusted downward; (2) loss of two sites forces Phase One to continue with 3 sites (1.5 pairs, asymmetric) only if both co-chairs agree in writing (within 7 days of the loss) that the rump test remains defensible; (3) loss of a third site immediately triggers Stop (insufficient data); (4) mid-test operator withdrawal without co-chair cause is presumed asymmetric access (Stop trigger unless both sides agree fallback testing at that site can substitute within 30 days); (5) document every site-loss incident in the ledger with cause, decision date and impact on confidence intervals. This ensures partial failures don't degrade verdict credibility silently.

6. No Defined Inspector Liability, Insurance or Indemnification

The plan deploys 300+ inspectors (180 per country) across foreign datacenters for extended periods (4 months on-site rotation), but does not address: (a) if an inspector is injured on-site, who covers medical costs and disability; (b) if an inspector breaches sealed-communication rules and is sued by a third party, who indemnifies; (c) if an inspector's actions damage operator equipment, who is liable; (d) if an inspector is detained or arrested on political grounds, what repatriation authority applies. The absence of clear liability and indemnification rules creates legal exposure for both governments and may deter qualified candidates from applying.

Recommendation: Include in the bilateral instrument an 'Inspector Indemnification Appendix' specifying: (1) each government indemnifies its own inspectors against civil liability for actions taken in their official capacity (narrow carve-out: does not cover criminal acts or gross negligence); (2) both governments jointly contribute to an Inspector Accident and Health fund (estimated USD 5–10M, charged to the secure-facilities or personnel envelope) covering emergency medical evacuation, disability and repatriation; (3) operator insurance covers equipment damage during authorized inspections; (4) if an inspector is detained on political grounds, both co-chairs convene an emergency summit within 24 hours and the detaining government must release the inspector within 5 days or the aggrieved government can suspend Phase One unilaterally (temporary stop, 30-day escalation period); (5) each government provides legal counsel at no cost to inspectors accused of breach of confidentiality.

7. No Defined Rules for Operator and Vendor Cost Disputes

The plan states 'operator compensation is administered by each government and charged to its own USD 2.5B contribution' within the USD 1B site-prep envelope. But a large operator (e.g., a US hyperscale datacenter) may demand USD 50–100M for access, staff time, security, and production-disruption costs, which could consume 50–100% of one country's USD 500M per-country site-prep allocation. If the US government pays USD 50M to a US operator but the Chinese government cannot pay equivalent compensation to a Chinese operator (due to budget constraints or operator unwillingness to accept payment), asymmetric cost becomes a proxy for asymmetric commitment and credibility.

Recommendation: Establish an Operator-Compensation Framework (before Month 3 = 2027-01-08, before site-selection is finalized): (1) both co-chairs agree on a 'fair market rate' for site access (proposed: USD 30–50M per site per country, total 6 sites x USD 2.5B / 6 sites ≈ USD 417M; if per-site rate is set at USD 30–50M, that is USD 180–300M for 6 sites, leaving 60–75% of the USD 1B envelope for other site prep); (2) if an operator demands above the agreed rate, either government can negotiate privately or invoke the Vendor-Liaison Officer to structure a fallback-testing alternative (reduces operator burden, may lower demanded compensation); (3) if compensation is disputed, a Joint Compensation Arbiter (1 per country, part-time) rules within 10 days whether the rate is reasonable or excessive; (4) asymmetric compensation (one country pays 2x the other) is documented in the ledger and flagged as a potential parity-imbalance risk factor in the Go/Modify/Stop verdict. This prevents underfunding of one country's sites from cascading into asymmetric access.

8. No Definition of 'Frontier-Relevant Computing Equipment' in Sufficient Technical Detail

The plan states the scope is 'declared frontier-relevant computing equipment' and references a 'confidential, versioned technical schedule' kept current and technology-neutral. However, the plan does not define what 'frontier-relevant' means operationally. Is it AI-training accelerators only? Large language model inference clusters? Supercomputing nodes? Photonic or quantum hardware? If the definition is ambiguous, vendors will contest whether specific equipment is in or out of scope, and the Vendor Liaison Officer and Adjudication Panel will face constant disputes over schedule membership. A US hyperscale operator may claim a GPU cluster is 'general-purpose computing' (not frontier), while the Chinese side insists it is frontier. The absence of a clear technical definition invites scope creep or scope shrinkage through definitional disputes.

Recommendation: The bilateral instrument must include a 'Technical Scope Appendix' that defines frontier-relevant computing by reference to: (1) processor architecture (e.g., HPC-class accelerators with peak FP32 throughput ≥100 TFLOPS, or AI-specific chips with ≥10 TFLOPS bfloat16 throughput); (2) memory and network capability (e.g., ≥1TB aggregate memory per node, ≥400 Gb/s network interconnect); (3) performance metric bands (e.g., clusters capable of >10 petaFLOPS sustained); (4) explicit exclusions (e.g., commodity CPUs <10 TFLOPS, consumer GPUs, legacy servers). The schedule is versioned and amended every 6 months (fixed review points at Months 3, 6, 9 = 2027-01-08, 2027-04-08, 2027-07-08 = every 3 months starting entry, then every 6 months in Phase Two TBD) by double-key decision, with prior schedule versions kept in escrow for auditing. Any equipment arriving that does not fit the definition is excluded from verification and documented as 'out of scope.' This removes ambiguity and prevents scope disputes from paralyzing the mechanism.

9. No Defined Role for Participating Operator Leadership in Phase-One Governance

The plan assumes operators cooperate, provide access, and accept inspection. But operators are not represented in the governance structure (no operator seat on the co-chair board, no operator voice in deadlock resolution, no operator role in exercise design). If an exercise disrupts production unexpectedly or an operator faces public backlash for allowing foreign inspectors, the operator may unilaterally restrict access mid-Phase-One. The plan has no mechanism for the operator to escalate concerns to co-chairs or for co-chairs to rule on operator grievances without invoking the full deadlock procedure (which treats operator complaints as bilateral disputes, not operational issues).

Recommendation: Establish an Operator-Liaison Channel: (1) each participating datacenter nominates an Operator Representative (director-level) who attends monthly joint operator-inspector briefings (non-decision-making, informational, no operator voting rights); (2) the Vendor-Liaison Officer convenes a quarterly Operator Council (all 3–6 participating operator representatives, plus both co-chairs' Facility Liaisons) to air concerns (production impact, scheduling conflicts, security incidents) and seek co-chair guidance within 14 days on any request (e.g., pause exercises at a site for 2 weeks due to critical maintenance); (3) operator requests for pause or access modification are documented in the ledger; co-chairs can approve short pauses (≤2 weeks, counted as covered by contingency schedule) or deny (triggering escalation to formal mediation if the operator threatens withdrawal); (4) grievances unresolved after 30 days are recorded as confidence-impact factors in the final verdict. This gives operators a non-voting input channel and prevents sudden mid-test withdrawals from catching co-chairs unaware.

10. No Defined Procedure for Classified or Proprietary Evidence That Cannot Be Disclosed to Counterpart

The plan requires evidence to support identity confidence and adjudication, but some evidence may be so sensitive (e.g., network topology, security architecture, customer data, unrelated infrastructure) that neither the host government nor the operator is willing to disclose it even in filtered form to the counterpart. The current Counterpart Evidence Disclosure Tiers allow hashed summaries or dual-escort evidence review, but do not define what happens if evidence is deemed too sensitive to share at any tier. Can a discrepancy be adjudicated if the counterpart cannot review the underlying evidence? Does unreviewable evidence default to 'unverifiable' status, or can filtered attestation substitute?

Recommendation: Add to the plan an 'Ultra-Sensitive Evidence Protocol': (1) if evidence is so sensitive that neither the host operator nor government is willing to disclose it even in filtered form to the counterpart (e.g., cryptographic key material, weapons-system component designs, intelligence-derived data), it may be excluded from the counterpart's adjudication review only if both the host government and the operator jointly certify the sensitivity to the Adjudication Panel within 5 days of case opening; (2) excluded evidence is replaced by an independent third-country examiner's attestation (pre-staged accredited examiner reviews the sensitive evidence under tamper-proof conditions and certifies to the counterpart only: 'sensitive evidence reviewed, is or is not consistent with equipment identity [yes/no]') within 10 days; (3) the third-country examiner's attestation is treated as equivalent to the excluded evidence for confidence-scoring purposes (85% confidence per the vendor-refusal fallback ladder); (4) if third-country examination is refused, the evidence is classed unverifiable and the discrepancy defaults to impaired-confidence status at day 21; (5) all requests for ultra-sensitive-evidence exclusion are logged in the ledger and flagged as confidence-impact notes in the final verdict, so either government can appeal the exclusion if it undermines the Go threshold. This prevents ultra-sensitive-evidence claims from becoming a veto on adjudication.

Potential Improvements

1. Clarify the Pilot-Exercise Validation Timing and Decision Rule

The plan states a 'pilot exercise' (all 7 event types, non-production site) occurs at Month 5 (2027-03-08), testing evidence-rule calibration and exercise feasibility. However, the decision rule for moving forward is not explicit: if pilot false-positive rate is 15% (5 points above the 10% target), does that block entry-gate certification or just flag a review item? The plan notes 'deviation >5 points requires adjustment and a second cohort' but does not define the timeline for a second cohort (estimated 2–3 weeks) or its completion deadline before the Month 6 (2027-04-08) Phase-One clock. If the second cohort runs Months 5.5–6 (2027-03-23 to 2027-04-08), it overlaps the planned start of Phase One, creating operational confusion.

Recommendation: Specify: (1) pilot exercise completed by Month 5 (2027-03-08), scorecard published within 3 days to co-chairs; (2) if false-positive rate within 10% ±3 points and false-negative rate <5%, evidence rule is locked and entry gate is certified by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23); (3) if deviation 5–10 points, trigger a 'conditional entry' protocol: begin Phase One on Month 6 (2027-04-08) as scheduled, but run second-cohort pilot during Months 6–7 (2027-04-08 to 2027-05-08) at a fourth non-production site (if available) or with historical data from Month 6 (2027-04-08) Phase-One events; rule is adjusted by Month 8 (2027-06-08) only if second cohort confirms miscalibration >5 points (rare, unlikely); (4) if deviation >10 points, delay Phase-One start by 2–3 weeks to run a full second cohort before any Phase-One exercises begin, invoking the emergency co-chair summit and compression-reserve USD 50–100M. This ensures the evidence rule is validated before Phase One begins or adjusted quickly if needed, without stalling the clock indefinitely.

2. Define Minimum Detection Rates Per Event Type, Not Just Class Averages

The plan specifies detection thresholds at the class level (70% planned, 50% unplanned) but does not set per-type minimums. If unreported-arrival detection is 90% but substituted-equipment detection is 20% (both averaging 55% for planned class), the class average masks a critical weakness in substitution detection. Either government could argue that weak substitution detection invalidates Go (detection-rate confidence < 50% for that type). The absence of per-type minimums creates post-hoc verdict disputes.

Recommendation: Pre-register detection thresholds for each event type before the first Phase-One exercise (by Month 5.5 = 2027-03-23): unreported arrival ≥75%, substituted equipment ≥65%, inaccurate records ≥60%, delayed access ≥55%, disputed identity ≥55%, vendor refusal ≥50%, reluctant operator ≥45% (proposed, TBD on pilot data). Go requires all 7 types ≥75% of their individual threshold (5 of 7 types at or above threshold). Modify if 4 of 7 types meet thresholds or if the class average meets Go threshold but 2 or more types fall >10 points below their individual threshold. Stop if <3 of 7 types meet thresholds or any type falls >20 points below its threshold. This ensures weak detection in one scenario type does not hide behind a strong average.

3. Specify What Happens if a Co-Chair's Government Faces a Domestic Political Crisis

The plan assumes both co-chairs remain in office and engaged throughout the entry-condition and Phase-One timeline (Months 0–9 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-07-08.5 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-07-23). But a US presidential election (November 2028, after Phase One) could lead to a change in the co-chair if a new administration takes office (January 2029). A Chinese government reshuffle could also occur. A sudden co-chair replacement mid-Phase-One, especially during a deadlock resolution or key-custody ceremony, can disrupt continuity. The plan does not address how a new co-chair is briefed on sensitive decisions made by their predecessor or whether prior-chair decisions (e.g., 'rule Z on evidence' or 'suspend function Y') are binding on the successor.

Recommendation: Include in the bilateral instrument a 'Co-Chair Continuity and Handoff Protocol': (1) if a co-chair steps down or is replaced before Phase-One conclusion (Month 9.5 = 2027-07-23), the incoming co-chair must be appointed within 14 days and must accept all prior co-chair decisions as binding (no reopening of prior rulings, thresholds or suspensions); (2) an accelerated classified briefing (8–12 hours, by the outgoing co-chair and the Program Risk Officer) is mandatory within 7 days, covering all open deadlocks, ledger-divergence incidents, vendor disputes and recent key-custody activities; (3) if the new co-chair contests a prior decision within 30 days and cannot reach agreement with the counterpart co-chair, escalate to the deputy co-chairs and technical specialist panel (non-binding advisory, as per standard deadlock rules), not retroactively reopen the case; (4) continuity is a 'no re-litigation' principle: once a discrepancy is closed or a threshold is locked, it cannot be re-litigated by a successor co-chair. This prevents a change in government from weaponizing the handoff as a way to relitigate unfavorable verdicts.

4. Clarify How Exercise Costs Are Managed if a Site Drops Mid-Phase-One

The plan budgets approximately USD 83M from the USD 500M testing envelope for 54 exercises across 6 sites (14 per month for 3 months, estimated USD 1–2M per exercise for logistics, independent video, attestation, red-team travel). If a site is forced to withdraw mid-Phase-One (e.g., after 2 exercises completed), the remaining 4 planned exercises at that site do not occur. The USD 8–10M already spent on the initial 2 exercises is sunk. The contingency and testing envelopes are not explicitly tied; unclear whether the testing envelope overrun (fewer exercises, same fixed costs for red-team standby) is absorbed by the testing envelope or escalated to contingency.

Recommendation: Specify: (1) testing envelope includes 'sunk cost reserve' of USD 20–25M (5% of the USD 500M) set aside to cover cancellation costs if 1 site is lost before all planned exercises; (2) if site is lost after ≤4 exercises, remaining exercises are canceled and costs paid from the reserve, testing envelope is not overdrawn; (3) if site is lost after >4 exercises, re-allocate remaining exercises to other sites (compress schedule, add 2–3 exercises per month to remaining sites) and absorb any latency-increase costs from the reserve; (4) if two or more sites are lost, invoke contingency >50% draw trigger and convene co-chair emergency summit within 5 days to approve scope reduction or Phase-One termination. This prevents exercise cancellations from cascading into testing-envelope overruns.

5. Specify Timebound Decision for Phase-One Public Announcement

The plan produces an unclassified final verdict by Month 9.5 (2027-07-23) but does not specify when or how it is announced to the public. A delayed or contested announcement (e.g., co-chairs disagree on how to spin the results) can amplify political uncertainty. If the verdict is Modify but one government claims it is effectively a Go for political consumption, or a Stop is announced but couched as 'temporary pause pending renegotiation' (contradicting the plan's intent), public confusion and loss of credibility follow.

Recommendation: Require a coordinated, simultaneous public announcement by both co-chairs within 5 days of the scored verdict (by Month 9.5 = 2027-07-23). The announcement must: (1) state the Go, Modify, or Stop verdict explicitly; (2) publish the unclassified scorecard (detection rates per class, false-positive/negative rates, confidence intervals, thresholds, pass/fail on each criterion); (3) describe the mechanical scoring logic used (e.g., 'Go requires 4 of 5 criteria met; this result met 4 of 5: [list]'); (4) note any confidence-impact flags (e.g., 'one site lost mid-test, reducing sample size, widening confidence intervals by 2 percentage points'); (5) if Modify, outline the specific corrective actions both governments agree will be implemented (e.g., 'Phase Two will require 12-month continuous monitoring'; due TBD); (6) if Stop, state the reason (asymmetric access, withheld funding, ledger divergence unresolved, etc.). Both co-chairs sign the announcement jointly; no unilateral statements allowed within 14 days. This prevents spin and ensures public clarity on why the verdict was reached.

6. Clarify Liability and Responsibility if a Ledger Entry Is Found Fraudulent Post-Conclusion

The plan assumes ledger entries are tamper-evident and immutable once recorded, but does not address discovery of fraud after Phase One concludes. If, 6 months after the Go verdict, investigators find that a cryptographic signature was forged or a timestamp was altered, the verdict's evidentiary foundation is compromised. Neither government has pre-agreed on remedies: do they re-open the verdict? Is it retroactively changed to Modify or Stop? Who investigates and certifies the fraud?

Recommendation: Include a 'Post-Conclusion Ledger-Fraud Protocol': (1) if fraud is suspected in the ledger within 12 months after Phase-One conclusion (by Month 21 = 2028-07-08), either co-chair can trigger a joint forensic audit by both governments' chief information-security officers within 10 days; (2) if fraud is confirmed (e.g., forged signature, timestamp manipulation), the affected entry and any dependent findings are flagged as 'compromised evidence'; (3) if compromised findings are material to the Go verdict (would have changed the verdict if excluded), both co-chairs must reconvene within 30 days to decide: (a) verdict stands (fraud in non-material findings, Go upheld), (b) verdict revoked and reset to Modify (requesting rework), or (c) verdict revoked and reset to Stop (irreversible compromise); (4) fraud investigation findings are published unclassified so legislatures see the integrity of the mechanism; (5) the government or operator whose equipment/system was used in the fraud bears liability for remediating the ledger corruption and may be subject to sanctions (future phases restricted, access limitations). This creates accountability for ledger integrity and allows post-hoc discovery without invalidating the entire mechanism.

7. Specify Roles and Authority for Managing Real-Time Ledger Divergence Incidents

The plan states ledger divergence is escalated to co-chairs within 4 hours if a digest fails to match, but does not clarify: (1) who detects the divergence (the Replicated Ledger Architect or an automated system); (2) who has authority to temporarily pause the ledger or freeze new entries while divergence is being reconciled; (3) how long unresolved divergence is tolerated before it triggers automatic impaired-confidence status (21 or 28 days?) or a stop of all ledger operations. If one country's ledger goes offline due to a network outage, is that a ledger divergence incident subject to the 4-hour escalation, or a different operational failure?

Recommendation: Define a 'Real-Time Ledger Management SOP': (1) the Replicated Ledger Architect or a dedicated Ledger Operations Center (24/7 staffed, at the neutral facility) monitors synchronization health: hourly digest exchange confirmed, latency <1 hour, no unexplained gaps; (2) divergence detection automated: when digest mismatch occurs, system immediately logs the mismatch timestamp, alerts both co-chairs and Ledger Architect within 15 minutes, and pauses new entries at the diverged function until reconciliation begins (e.g., if equipment-identity ledger diverges, halt intake verification but continue monitoring other functions); (3) reconciliation target 24 hours (both countries' ledger managers compare raw event logs, identify the divergence point, and issue joint correction); hard limit 7 days (if unresolved, the diverged ledger is classed unverifiable and any findings dependent on that ledger entry are flagged as 'ledger-compromised' pending resolution or manual revalidation); (4) divergence age triggers automatic escalation: at day 3 unresolved, escalate to Adjudication Panel; at day 7, trigger automatic impaired-confidence status for affected function; at day 14, invoke deadlock resolution (if both sides cannot agree on which copy is authoritative). This prevents slow divergence from accumulating silently.

8. Provide More Specificity on What 'Reciprocal-Access Parity' Means Operationally

The plan sets a Go threshold of 'reciprocal-access parity ≥85%' but does not define what parity is measured as: number of hours of inspector presence per site, number of exercise opportunities granted, number of areas accessible per site, or speed of operator response to inspector requests. A US operator that grants 100 hours of inspector access per month on a schedule 48 hours in advance appears equivalent to a Chinese site granting 100 hours but without advance notice (immediate access, potentially more disruptive). Both could claim 100 hours, but the operational parity differs.

Recommendation: Define 'Reciprocal-Access Parity' using a composite metric (by Month 5.5 = 2027-03-23, before Phase-One clock): (1) weekly average inspector hours on-site per site: target ≥12 hours per week per country's team (2 shifts x 6 hours, approximate); (2) staging-area access availability: 24-hour per-site, immediate access <4 hours on request; (3) maintenance-area access timing: concurrent with operator schedule (proposed: operator notifies inspectors 48 hours before maintenance, inspectors may observe; if urgent maintenance, 4-hour notice acceptable); (4) exercise-exercise cooperation: operator permits 3–4 exercises per month without veto (operator can defer 1 per month for critical operations); (5) data-access transparency: operator provides real-time equipment-arrival logs, maintenance schedules and serial numbers within 24 hours of request; (6) parity score: sum of 5 metrics, each 0–100%, equals the reciprocal-access-parity score. Matched pairs are approved only if both pairs score ≥80% parity in the pre-Phase-One audit. If parity drifts during Phase One (one site reduces inspector access), it triggers impaired-confidence status. This makes parity measurable and auditable.

9. Clarify Training and Certification Maintenance for 24/7 Shifts Across 9+ Months

The plan notes 80% of inspectors are certified-ready by Month 5 (2027-03-08) and Phase One runs Months 6–9 (2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08). But certification decay is not addressed: if an inspector completes training in Month 5 (2027-03-08), is their certification still current 4 months later in Month 9 (2027-07-08)? What if an inspector takes leave during Months 6–8 (2027-04-08 to 2027-06-08) and misses 2 months of operational deployment? Does their certification lapse and require re-training before Month 9 (2027-07-08)? A high re-training burden could reduce actual on-site staffing.

Recommendation: Specify: (1) inspector certification is valid for 6 months from issuance; refresher training (2 days) required every 6 months; first refresher scheduled for Month 11 (2027-09-08), after Phase-One conclusion, so no lapse during Phase One; (2) inspectors who take leave >2 consecutive months must complete a 1-day reorientation briefing upon return, covering any protocol updates or Phase-One incident debriefing, but no re-certification required if leave is <3 months; (3) if an inspector fails a quarterly operational audit (e.g., fails to follow sealed-communication rules, loses classified material), they are immediately stood down for 1-week retraining and re-certification (estimated 1 per 100 inspectors per quarter, 3 total expected during Months 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08); (4) staffing surge buffer (20%, or 30–40 inspectors per country on standby) is partly reserved for certification-maintenance backup (estimated 5–10 inspectors held in rotation to cover certification-gap training and leave-related shortfalls). This ensures certification does not degrade during the 4-month Phase-One window.

10. Specify Operator-Provided Data-Format Standards for Maintenance and Equipment Records

The plan requires operators to maintain maintenance logs, equipment identifiers and infrastructure records. But operators use different systems (different vendors' asset-management software, varied serialization standards, heterogeneous date formats). If one operator logs '2027-01-15 14:30 UTC' and another logs '01/15/2027 2:30 PM EST,' parsing errors can introduce discrepancies. The plan does not specify: (1) what data formats are acceptable; (2) who certifies that operator-provided data is machine-readable and auditable; (3) what happens if an operator refuses to export data in a standardized format.

Recommendation: Require an 'Operator Data Standard Appendix' (part of each site's operator agreement, finalized by Month 4 = 2027-02-08): (1) operators must provide equipment records and maintenance logs in a pre-agreed format: JSON or CSV, with mandatory fields (equipment serial number, arrival timestamp UTC, departure timestamp UTC, maintenance type, maintenance start/end timestamp UTC, names and credentials of maintenance personnel, any noted changes or discrepancies); (2) an independent data auditor (1 per country, funded from testing envelope) certifies operator data-export compliance at Month 5 (2027-03-08), attempting to parse and validate a sample of historical records; if format is non-standard, operator is required to correct within 10 days or accept independent extraction at operator expense; (3) any record entry that cannot be parsed or validated (missing field, unrecognized format, timestamp in wrong timezone) is flagged in the ledger as 'data-quality issue: [description]' and treated as a confidence-reducing factor in adjudication; (4) if an operator refuses format standardization and compliance cannot be achieved by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23), that site is classed as non-participating and excluded from Phase One. This prevents data-format fragmentation from masking or creating spurious discrepancies.

11. Clarify Escalation and Override Authority If One Co-Chair Unilaterally Declares a Stop Condition

The plan specifies Stop conditions (e.g., government shielding operator, material unverifiable equipment, funding withheld). But if one co-chair declares a Stop condition unilaterally without the other's agreement, does the mechanism shut down immediately, or does the second co-chair have time to contest it? For example, if the US co-chair claims China is 'shielding an operator' by restricting access, but China contests the claim, is Phase One paused pending dispute resolution, or does it halt immediately?

Recommendation: Establish a 'Unilateral Stop-Condition Challenge Protocol': (1) if either co-chair believes a Stop condition is met (asymmetric access, withheld funding, ledger divergence unresolved, material unverifiable equipment, government shielding), they may declare a 'Conditional Stop' within 24 hours, requiring verification of the Stop trigger; (2) the second co-chair has 5 days to either: (a) accept the Stop declaration (Phase One halts, ledger is archived, verdict recorded as 'Stop: [condition]'), or (b) contest it (claiming the Stop trigger is not met or is disputed); (3) if contested, invoke a 'Stop-Condition Arbitration': both co-chairs present evidence within 3 days; an independent three-person panel (1 per country + 1 neutral) renders a binding advisory determination within 5 days on whether the Stop condition is met; (4) if the panel certifies the Stop condition is met, Phase One immediately halts and the verdict is 'Stop: [condition]'; (5) if the panel certifies the Stop condition is NOT met, Phase One resumes operations within 24 hours, and the co-chair that made the false Stop declaration must provide written justification (published unclassified) explaining the basis for the claim. This prevents a co-chair from halting Phase One unilaterally based on a contested Stop claim.

12. Clarify Authority and Funding for Post-Phase-One Ledger Archival and Long-Term Preservation

The plan does not specify what happens to the replicated national ledgers, evidence repositories and confidential classified documents (versioned evidence rules, adjudication rulings, bilateral memoranda) after Phase One concludes. Are the ledgers archived by the neutral facility, by each government, or by an independent third party? Who pays for preservation and security for 5+ years (estimated cost, USD 5–10M)? If ledgers are archived but later requested for judicial or legislative review, who has authority to unseal them and under what conditions?

Recommendation: Include in the bilateral instrument a 'Ledger Archival and Preservation Appendix': (1) upon Phase-One conclusion (Month 9.5 = 2027-07-23), the Replicated Ledger Architect generates a sealed cryptographic digest of both national ledger copies and deposits it with: (a) the neutral facility (primary custody), (b) each government's national archive or equivalent (secondary backup); (3) raw ledgers are encrypted and stored for 7 years minimum, with access restricted to: both co-chairs (indefinite), independent investigators or judicial bodies (with co-chair written authorization only), and authorized historians or researchers (after 50-year declassification, TBD); (4) archival costs (estimated USD 5–10M) are charged to the contingency envelope, or if contingency is exhausted, split equally as a USD 2.5–5M post-Phase-One supplemental appropriation per country; (5) both governments jointly appoint an 'Ledger Custodian' (neutral third-party archivist, bonded) responsible for secure storage, integrity verification (annual cryptographic audits) and authorized-access log maintenance; (6) no unilateral government can delete or modify the archive without the other's written consent (co-chair double-key rule applies posthumously). This ensures the ledger cannot be rewritten by either government after Phase One and remains auditable for decades.

1.4.A Issue - Entry-Gate Timeline Is Sequentially Fragile and Lacks Binding Acceleration Authority

The canonical entry-gate timeline (Months 0–5 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-03-08) lists seven mandatory conditions in a loosely sequenced order. The plan names a 2-week slip tolerance, but no binding weekly milestones, external escalation authority with scope-reduction power, or parallel-track acceleration structure exist. If instrument signature slips to Month 1.5 (2026-11-23) instead of Month 1 (2026-11-08), subsequent gates compress into Months 2–5 (2026-12-08 to 2027-03-08), squeezing the critical pre-clock calibration window (historical validation, pilot exercise, rule lock, threshold pre-registration). An 8-week total slip (realistic given bilateral negotiation pace) compresses Phase One from 90 to 50 days, widening statistical intervals from ±12% pooled to ±18–22%, making the Go/Modify/Stop verdict indefensible. The SWOT Threats section names this but the plan does not operationalize the mitigation: no task-force charter, no parallel site-selection and vendor-outreach kickoff before Month 0 (2026-10-08), and no compressed-negotiation budget carved from contingency.

1.4.B Tags

  • entry-gate-sequencing
  • timeline-slack
  • statistical-power-at-risk
  • contingency-planning-absent

1.4.C Mitigation

Establish a dedicated Entry-Condition Task Force (both co-chairs' offices) at Month 0 (2026-10-08) with weekly dashboard and binding milestone deadlines: instrument signed by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23) (not Month 1 = 2026-11-08), domestic authority by Month 1 (2026-11-08), matched pairs nominated by Month 1 (2026-11-08), inspectors approved by Month 2 (2026-12-08), vendor registry published by Month 1 (2026-11-08), schedule locked by Month 3 (2027-01-08). Launch site-candidate and vendor-outreach tracks in parallel starting Month -2 (before instrument signature), not sequentially after. Reserve USD 50–100M from contingency explicitly for compressed negotiation and expedited vetting. Appoint external escalation authority (neutral senior figure or panel) with power to invoke emergency co-chair summit if any gate slips >2 weeks and 5-day decision authority on scope reduction (2 pairs instead of 3, 60-day test instead of 90) rather than timeline extension.

1.4.D Consequence

Without binding acceleration authority and parallel-track activation, Phase One window erodes to 40–60 days, statistical confidence for Go/Modify/Stop becomes indefensible (±20%+ per event type), and the verdict is read as negotiated rather than technical. Vendors discover refusals late, equipment unresolved at entry balloons unverifiable counts to 10–20% per site, and one government may claim the test was rigged by compressed timelines. Stop trigger for thin data becomes unavoidable.

1.4.E Root Cause

The plan names the 2-week tolerance and risk but does not instantiate governance machinery (task force, escalation authority, parallel tracks, compressed-negotiation budget) to enforce it. Planning assumes sequential gates will move at predictable pace; bilateral instrument negotiation historically runs 12–24 months, not 6 weeks. The mitigation exists conceptually in the pre-project assessment but is not operationalized in the canonical timeline or governance structure.

1.5.A Issue - Evidence-Weighting Rule Is Locked Without Pre-Validation; Miscalibration Risks Adjudication Paralysis

The plan mandates a confidential, rotating evidence-weighting rule (Layered Evidence Weighting Model, choice 2) that accountable specialists set and rotate to prevent gaming. The rule is placed in escrow by Month 4.5 (2027-02-23) and used immediately in Phase One exercises starting Month 6 (2027-04-08). However, the plan validates the rule only against historical, benign equipment-change records (100–200 per site) and does not test it against adversarial scenarios (substitution, doctored timestamps, missing maintenance logs, vendor refusal escalations). If the rule systematically undercredits filtered evidence or overweights contradictions, false-positive rates could reach 20–30% vs. the 10% target, generating 50–100+ discrepancies in 90 days vs. the planned 15/month adjudication capacity. The resulting backlog of unresolved cases (30–50 by Month 9 = 2027-07-08) would trigger impaired-confidence flags and partial suspensions, consuming the latter half of Phase One in disputes rather than detection. No adjustment path exists mid-test; the rule is frozen until the final decision.

1.5.B Tags

  • evidence-rule-unvalidated
  • adversarial-scenario-gap
  • adjudication-overload-risk
  • false-positive-miscalibration

1.5.C Mitigation

Lock the confidential evidence rule in double-key-approved escrow by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23), three months before Phase One. Conduct a mandatory pilot-validation exercise at Month 2 (2026-12-08) at a non-production test datacenter, applying the locked rule to 100–200 historical equipment-change events per site (4–6 weeks of archival data) and comparing output (false positives, false negatives, unverifiable counts) against ground truth from maintenance logs and customs records. If pilot false-positive rate deviates >5 percentage points from the 10% target (i.e., outside 7–13% band), halt Phase One exercises, adjust the rule jointly, and re-validate on a second 100–200 event cohort before proceeding. Document every rule amendment with timestamp, decision rationale and evidentiary basis; publish rule-version history in the final ledger so each finding is traceable to the rule version active when it was classified.

1.5.D Consequence

Without pre-validation, miscalibrated evidence weighting floods adjudication with false positives (50–100 cases vs. 15/month capacity) by Month 7 (2027-05-08). Unresolved discrepancies age past 21 days, triggering automatic impaired-confidence flags and partial suspensions that consume the remaining test window. By Month 9, 30–50% of findings are unresolved, the Go/Modify/Stop verdict becomes indeterminate (cannot claim 70% detection if disputes mask the real signal), and one government claims the other side used the rule to suppress unfavorable findings. Phase One credibility collapses and the Stop trigger for 'evidence systems diverge without resolution' is invoked.

1.5.E Root Cause

The plan assumes the confidential rule can be locked by Month 4.5 (2027-02-23) and used immediately, without intermediate validation against adversarial behavior. Historical-records validation catches benign miscalibration but not gaming or systematic bias under pressure. The plan names the pre-clock calibration window but treats historical validation as sufficient, neglecting the gap between historical data (no incentive to hide or substitute) and Phase One operations (where both sides actively test verification credibility and vendors resist discovery).

1.6.A Issue - Verdict Thresholds Are Pre-Registered But Statistical Confidence Intervals Are So Wide That Boundaries Become Ambiguous and Prone to Political Renegotiation

The plan proposes detection thresholds of ≥70% for planned events and ≥50% for unplanned events as Go criteria, with Modify at 55–75% and Stop <55%. However, the canonical-facts statistical limits are ±12% pooled (n≈54, 95% confidence), ±22% for planned class (n≈16), and ±25% for unplanned class (n≈15). A detected 65% planned-event rate carries a 95% confidence interval of [43%, 87%], which straddles the Modify band (55–75%) entirely. The interval overlaps Go (≥70%), Modify (55–75%) and Stop (<55%) boundaries, making the verdict mechanically ambiguous. The plan states 'default to Modify when intervals straddle thresholds,' but this rule is not locked in advance and is named only in the secondary-actions section of the pre-project assessment. Neither co-chair has committed to accepting Modify as a real outcome (funding for rework is OPEN), so ambiguous intervals create pressure to renegotiate thresholds post-hoc. A detection rate of 68% with interval [46%, 90%] becomes a negotiation point rather than an objective result.

1.6.B Tags

  • threshold-ambiguity-from-wide-intervals
  • statistical-power-insufficient
  • post-hoc-renegotiation-risk
  • verdict-credibility-at-risk

1.6.C Mitigation

Pre-register verdict thresholds in a joint bilateral memorandum locked by both co-chairs by Month 2.5 (2026-12-23, 14:00), before the first Phase One exercise (Month 3 = 2027-01-08). Frame thresholds as explicit confidence-interval bands, not point estimates: Go: ≥75% detection at 90% confidence (lower bound ≥62%); Modify: 55–75%; Stop: <55% (upper bound ≤48%). Apply same structure to unplanned-event thresholds (Go ≥60%, Modify 40–60%, Stop <40%) and false-positive rate (Modify if ≤15%, Stop if >15%). Mark all thresholds 'provisional, validated against pilot data.' Use a mechanical scoring rule: if lower confidence bound exceeds Go threshold, verdict is Go; if upper bound falls below Stop threshold, verdict is Stop; otherwise Modify (default when intervals straddle). Publish thresholds, mechanical scoring logic and confidence-interval bands before any Phase One exercises so results are objective, not negotiated. Publish final verdict (detection rates, intervals, thresholds, scoring logic, rationale) within 5 days of Phase One conclusion (by Month 9.5 = 2027-07-23) so both legislatures see objective outcome and renegotiation risk is eliminated.

1.6.D Consequence

Without locked thresholds and mechanical scoring, a Phase One result of 65–72% detection becomes a political argument rather than a technical finding. Each co-chair's legislature reads the wide confidence interval (e.g., [46%, 87%]) and claims ambiguity justifies either Go (upper bound near 70%) or Stop (lower bound near 46%). Renegotiation over thresholds consumes the Month 9.5 (2027-07-23) decision window, final verdict slips to Month 10–12 (2027-08-08 to 2027-10-08), bilateral trust erodes, and one government claims the other manipulated thresholds after seeing results. The Go/Modify/Stop decision loses credibility and legitimacy, defeating the entire purpose of Phase One as a 'credible, reciprocal proof-of-concept.' The plan's final success criterion—'exercises demonstrate reciprocal access and credible detection'—cannot be met if the verdict itself is contested.

1.6.E Root Cause

The plan understands that thin 90-day data creates wide intervals (±12–32% per type) but does not lock the threshold-and-scoring rule before Phase One starts. Pre-project assessment names the issue and proposes mechanical scoring and confidence bands, but this is treated as secondary guidance rather than a mandatory entry condition. Neither the canonical facts nor the project plan explicitly states that thresholds are locked and non-negotiable before Month 6 (2027-04-08); instead, the plan allows 'adjustments after pilot data,' which invites post-hoc bargaining when actual results are known. The governance structure (double-key co-chairs with no casting vote) cannot resolve ambiguous thresholds, so mechanical rules become essential but are not yet binding.

2.4.A Issue - Entry-Condition Gates Lack Binding Acceleration Mechanisms and Risk Catastrophic Timeline Compression

The entry-condition roadmap (Months 0–5 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-03-08) lists seven mandatory gates but provides no binding weekly milestones, parallel-track activation dates, or escalation authority with emergency re-scoping power. Sequential processing of instrument signature → domestic authority → site selection → inspector approval → vendor commitments → schedule adoption risks 4–8 week slippage, compressing Phase One from 90 days to 45–60 days and widening statistical confidence intervals from defensible ±10–15% to indefensible ±20–25%. The plan names a task force and summit trigger (gate slip >2 weeks) but does not bind the task force to weekly reporting, does not empower the summit to decide scope reduction (fewer sites, shorter test), and does not reserve the USD 50–100M compression budget explicitly in the contingency envelope.

2.4.C Mitigation

Establish an Entry-Condition Task Force by Month 0 (2026-10-08, 14:00) with binding weekly milestone report-outs (every Monday, 09:00 CET). Publish a master roadmap showing bilateral-instrument signature by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23), domestic-authority enactment and first-tranche appropriation by Month 1 (2026-11-08), site nominations by Month 1 (2026-11-08), vendor written commitments by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23), inspector approval by Month 2 (2026-12-08), and schedule adoption by Month 3 (2027-01-08). Activate site-candidate identification and vendor outreach in parallel starting Month -2, not sequentially after instrument signature. Empower an external escalation authority (named joint summit with 5-day decision window) to invoke mandatory scope reduction (2 pairs instead of 3, or 60-day instead of 90-day test) rather than timeline extension if any gate slips >2 weeks. Reserve USD 50–100M explicitly from the contingency envelope (separate from the free contingency) for compressed negotiation costs.

2.4.D Consequence

Without binding acceleration, entry-condition processing stalls into Month 6 (2027-04-08) or later, compressing Phase One to 45–60 days. Thin-data confidence intervals widen from ±10–15% to ±20–25%, making a 70% detection rate defensible as Go, Modify, or Stop and inviting post-hoc political renegotiation of the verdict. Statistical power loss also reduces the credibility of 'no hard Stop trigger' findings. Phase One becomes a non-credible proof-of-concept, undermining the Consortium's political legitimacy and forcing a costly re-run or abandonment.

2.4.E Root Cause

The plan treats entry conditions as a formal prerequisite checklist without operationalizing the acceleration levers (parallel tracks, weekly milestones, re-scoping authority) or the financial reserve needed to compress timelines. The assumption that gates will be met on time lacks accountability mechanisms or contingency pathways. This reflects a planning pattern of stating constraints without designing the operational governance to enforce them under political pressure.

2.5.A Issue - Evidence-Weighting Rule Locked Without Pre-Validation, Creating Adjudication Paralysis Risk and Threshold-Ambiguity Scenarios

The plan specifies that the confidential, rotating evidence-weighting rule (chosen strategic decision: rotating rule set by accountable specialists, weights validated against blind-exercise outcomes) is locked by Month 4.5 (2027-02-23) but validated only against historical records, not adversarial scenarios or synthetic cases mimicking operator gaming. If the locked rule miscalibrates false-positive rates to 20–30% versus the 10% target, Phase One will generate 50+ discrepancies per month instead of the planned 15, overloading the adjudication unit and leaving 30–50% of findings unresolved at conclusion. The plan also does not specify how miscalibration is detected mid-Phase-One or whether rule adjustments mid-test are permitted (which would compromise comparability of exercise results across versions).

2.5.C Mitigation

Lock the confidential evidence rule in escrow (double-key-approved memorandum, both co-chairs sign simultaneously) by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23). Conduct a mandatory pilot-validation exercise by Month 2 (2026-12-08) at a non-production test datacenter, applying the locked rule to at least 100–200 historical equipment-change events per site (4–6 weeks of historical maintenance and customs records). Compute false-positive rate, false-negative rate, and unverifiable-equipment count against known ground truth. Compare pilot output to within ±3% of threshold (if target is ≤10%, pilot must produce 7–13%). If deviation exceeds ±5%, halt Phase One exercises, adjust rule, and re-validate using a second 100–200 event cohort before proceeding. Maintain a versioned rule-change log with every amendment timestamped, double-key-approved, and linked to evidentiary outputs triggering the change. Prohibit rule amendments during Months 6–9 (2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08) (Phase One operational window); any perceived miscalibration triggers adjudication surge funding, not rule changes.

2.5.D Consequence

A locked but miscalibrated rule produces 50+ discrepancies per month, overwhelming the adjudication unit sized for 15 cases. By Month 8 (2027-06-08), 100–150 unresolved discrepancies accumulate, triggering the 'no discrepancy older than 21 days' failure and automatic Modify or Stop verdict regardless of actual detection performance. The exercise data become unreliable because too many findings are open and contested. Phase One conclusions lose credibility and both governments dispute the verdict as procedurally compromised rather than evidentially sound.

2.5.E Root Cause

The plan assumes the evidence rule can be locked on specialist consensus and validated against benign historical data, but does not account for adversarial behavior by operators trying to game the rule's thresholds, or for the discovery mid-test that a rule miscalibration will overflow the adjudication pipeline. The validation pathway is incomplete: historical records alone do not capture gaming patterns that emerge when operators know the rule and try to stay just inside or outside its boundaries. This reflects a gap between design-phase confidence and operational-phase realism.

2.6.A Issue - Verdict Thresholds Pre-Registered as Point Estimates Without Explicit Confidence Bands, Enabling Post-Hoc Reinterpretation and Political Bargaining Over Go/Modify/Stop

The plan specifies that verdict thresholds (70% detection for planned events, 50% for unplanned, ≤10% false positives) are locked before Phase One exercises, but does not specify confidence intervals around these point estimates. With ±12% pooled confidence (95% CL) and ±32% per-type intervals (estimate), a detected-event rate of 70% carries a 90% confidence interval of approximately 58–82%. This means a 70% observed rate is indistinguishable from 55% or 75%, making Go, Modify, and Stop all defensible. The plan states thresholds should be 'marked provisional or TBD,' but does not provide explicit numerical confidence bands or a pre-registered mechanical scoring rule. The verdict logic (4 of 5 criteria met = Go, 3 of 5 = Modify, <2 = Stop) is stated but the scoring of criteria when intervals are ambiguous is left to co-chair judgment, reintroducing the political bargaining the plan aims to prevent.

2.6.B Tags

  • threshold-ambiguity
  • missing-confidence-bands
  • mechanical-scoring-undefined
  • post-hoc-bargaining-risk
  • interval-straddling-unresolved

2.6.C Mitigation

Pre-register verdict thresholds in a joint bilateral memorandum locked by both co-chairs by Month 2.5 (2026-12-23, 14:00), before any Phase One exercise, using explicit confidence-interval bands rather than point estimates: Go threshold for planned-event detection ≥75% at 90% confidence (lower bound ≥62%); Modify 55–75% (upper bound ≤82%); Stop <55% (upper bound ≤48%); apply same structure to unplanned-event thresholds (Go ≥60%, Modify 40–60%, Stop <40%) and false-positive rate (Modify if ≤15%, Stop if >15%). State all thresholds 'provisional, validated against pilot data.' Score final Phase One results using a pre-registered mechanical rule: if the lower bound of the 90% confidence interval exceeds the Go threshold, verdict is Go (no co-chair discretion); if the upper bound falls below the Stop threshold, verdict is Stop; otherwise Modify (default when intervals straddle a threshold). Publish unclassified final verdict (detection rates, 90% confidence intervals, thresholds, mechanical scoring logic, verdict rationale) within 5 days of Phase One conclusion (by Month 9.5 = 2027-07-23, 14:00) so both legislatures see the objective outcome and the transparent scoring rule.

2.6.D Consequence

Without explicit confidence bands and a mechanical scoring rule, either co-chair can argue that observed results fall within their preferred interpretation. A 70% detection rate becomes a contested political outcome: the US co-chair argues it meets the 70% Go threshold, while the Chinese co-chair argues the wide intervals mean Modify is more honest. The verdict itself becomes an arms-control negotiation rather than a technical judgment. This delegitimizes Phase One as an experiment and invites legislative rejection of the outcome in at least one country, undermining the Consortium's credibility for any Phase Two.

2.6.E Root Cause

The plan emphasizes that thresholds must be provisional and marked TBD, but does not operationalize this through explicit confidence bands or mechanical scoring logic. It assumes that stating 'provisional' and locking thresholds before exercises will prevent bargaining, but thresholds stated as point estimates (70%, 50%) invite reinterpretation once data arrive with large uncertainty ranges. The gap reflects insufficient attention to the statistical power of a 90-day, 54-exercise test: the confidence intervals are wide enough that nearly any observed result is ambiguous, so the verdict rule must be mechanical and pre-locked to avoid this ambiguity becoming a political opening.

(2) Use the same structure for false-positive rate (Modify if ≤15%; Stop if >15%) and unverifiable-equipment rate (Stop if >10% at a site or >5% overall). (3) Publish mechanical scoring logic in the memorandum: 'Results are scored by the Exercise Authority using pre-registered intervals. If the confidence interval straddles a threshold boundary, the verdict defaults to Modify. No co-chair negotiation of the interval or threshold is permitted after Phase One begins.' (4) Mark all thresholds 'provisional, validated against pilot data from Month 2 (2026-12-08) pilot exercises'; document the adjustment logic: if pilot detection deviates >20% from assumption, thresholds may shift by up to ±3–5 percentage points, but no adjustment is allowed after the bilateral memorandum is signed. (5) Publish the unclassified final verdict (detection rates, intervals, thresholds, mechanical logic, verdict rationale) within 5 days of Phase One conclusion (by Month 9.5 = 2027-07-23) so both legislatures see objective outcome.

3.6.D Consequence

Without pre-registration and mechanical scoring: (1) When detection lands in an ambiguous zone (e.g., 65% ±12%), each government interprets the interval to favor its preferred outcome (US argues 'lower bound 53% supports Modify'; China argues 'central estimate 65% supports Go'). (2) Co-chairs enter post-Phase-One negotiation over methodology rather than results, consuming weeks and delegitimizing the decision. (3) Either government can cite 'provisional threshold' language to demand a re-vote or a second 90-day test. (4) Political factors override technical scoring, and the verdict becomes indistinguishable from a negotiated outcome without evidentiary basis. (5) Phase One is framed as inconclusive or rigged, damaging bilateral confidence in the mechanism itself. (6) Any subsequent phase or continuation is politically vulnerable; legislatures question whether objectives were met or simply negotiated.

4.4.A Issue - Detection Thresholds Rest on Thin Statistics Without Pre-Specification of Confidence-Interval Methodology

The plan proposes Go at ≥70% planned-event detection and ≥50% unplanned-event detection. With 54 total exercises (n≈16-17 per class), the 95% confidence intervals span roughly ±22-25%, making the intervals [48%, 92%] and [25%, 75%] respectively—wide enough that a 65% observed rate is defensible as Go, Modify, or Stop depending on interval interpretation. The plan marks thresholds 'provisional, validated against pilot data,' but does not specify: (1) the confidence level (90%? 95%?), (2) whether to use exact binomial, normal approximation, or Clopper-Pearson bounds, (3) how to handle unequal sample sizes across event types (some n≈8, others n≈16), (4) whether lower or upper confidence bound governs the decision, or (5) what 'validated against pilot data' means mechanically.

4.4.B Tags

  • thin-statistics
  • threshold-ambiguity
  • pre-registration-incomplete
  • interval-methodology-unspecified
  • verdict-vulnerability

4.4.C Mitigation

By Month 2.5 (2026-12-23, 14:00)—before any Phase One exercise—both co-chairs must jointly select and lock: (1) a single confidence level (recommend 90% CL for Go/Modify boundary, 95% for Stop boundary, matching asymmetric decision costs); (2) an interval methodology (recommend exact binomial for n<100, Clopper-Pearson for unequal coverage); (3) a decision rule (recommend: Go if lower confidence bound ≥threshold; Modify if interval straddles; Stop if upper bound <threshold). Publish the locked rule as an unclassified annex to the bilateral instrument. Before Month 5.5 (2027-03-23), apply the same rule to pilot data and document any threshold shifts; any shift >3 percentage points must be jointly approved by both co-chairs in writing. Lock all thresholds before the Month 6 (2027-04-08) clock.

4.4.D Consequence

Without locked methodology, the final verdict is vulnerable to re-interpretation. A detection rate of 62% with interval [45%, 77%] can be scored as Go (lower bound 45% is below 50%) or Stop (upper bound 77% is below 70%) depending on whether the rule uses lower/upper/midpoint. Co-chairs will dispute the scoring rule itself, not the evidence. This delegitimizes the verdict, triggers renegotiation, and risks a non-decision or forced political compromise that neither side views as credible, undermining Phase One's mission to demonstrate reciprocal-access credibility.

4.4.E Root Cause

The plan correctly identifies that Phase One will yield ~±12% pooled and ±22-32% per-type precision (estimate). However, it defers the decision rule for mapping observed detection rates and their intervals into Go/Modify/Stop until after exercises are complete, trading transparency for post-hoc flexibility. Without a pre-locked methodology for constructing intervals, stating which bound drives the decision, and specifying how pilot data reshapes thresholds, the final verdict invites political renegotiation of the scoring rule itself, not merely dispute over what the data shows.

4.5.A Issue - Evidence-Weighting Rule Is Locked Without Adversarial Validation; Pilot Cohort Uses Only Benign Historical Records

The plan states the confidential rotating evidence-weighting rule will be 'validated against 100-200 historical equipment-change records per participating site by Month 2 (2026-12-08, 16:00)' and adjusted if false-positive output deviates >5% from target. However, 'historical records' are routine maintenance logs, vendor reports and customs sheets from normal operations—not adversarial, contested or deceptive cases. An operator who intends to hide an equipment swap or false-flag a record will behave differently than routine logs show. The rule may work well against benign noise (record-keeping errors, timing mismatches) and score 8-12% false positives, yet collapse against adversarial gaming, pushing the true false-positive rate under Phase One conditions to 20-30% or higher, overwhelming the 15 cases/month adjudication capacity.

4.5.B Tags

  • validation-incomplete
  • adversarial-gap
  • benign-vs-contested
  • rule-miscalibration-risk
  • adjudication-overload

4.5.C Mitigation

Bifurcate the validation into two phases: (1) Historical benign cohort (100-200 events per site, Month 2 = 2026-12-08): apply the rule, check false positives <13%, false negatives <5%; (2) Adversarial synthetic cohort (40-60 realistic deceptive scenarios per site, Month 2.5 = 2026-12-23): craft cases mimicking operator gaming (misidentified serial numbers, swapped equipment with matching headers, backdated maintenance records) and verify the rule flags them. If benign cohort passes but >15% of synthetic scenarios are missed or misclassified, adjust the rule weights and re-validate both cohorts before Phase One. Allocate USD 2-3M from testing envelope for synthetic-case design and red-team validation. Document the rule version that passes both cohorts as the locked Phase One version, immutable for the 90-day window.

4.5.D Consequence

If the rule is miscalibrated against adversarial inputs, false-positive volume during Phase One operations will exceed 15 cases per month, choking the adjudication pipeline. Discrepancies age (proposed 21-day impaired-confidence trigger becomes routine), partial suspension (day 14) will be invoked repeatedly, and co-chairs will spend weeks disputing whether a discrepancy is a real finding or a false positive caused by the rule itself. This erodes the 'credible detection' requirement for Go and can force a Modify or Stop verdict not because verification failed but because adjudication infrastructure collapsed under evidence-rule miscalibration.

4.5.E Root Cause

The plan conflates validation on historical ground truth (known outcomes from operator records) with validation against adversarial behavior (deceptive or gaming inputs). Historical records provide a useful floor—the rule must not fail on routine cases—but they do not stress-test whether the rule detects deliberate contradictions, plausible false identities or record tampering. The gap between 'validated on benign data' and 'performs under adversarial conditions' is precisely where a rule designed for one regime fails when deployed for another. No contingency budget or adjudication surge plan addresses the risk that false-positive volume could triple.

4.6.A Issue - Parity Metrics Are Undefined; 'Reciprocal-Access Parity ≥85%' Cannot Be Measured or Operationalized

The plan states one of the five Go criteria is 'reciprocal-access parity at least 85% (definition TBD)' and lists it as a SWOT question: 'Definition and measurement method of reciprocal-access parity.' By Month 0 (2026-10-08), this is not yet defined, leaving the most politically sensitive criterion unquantified. Parity could mean: equal detection rates by event type, equal exercise count, equal inspector hours at each site, equal data-access time, equal ability to challenge findings, or balanced access to staging and maintenance areas. No definition will satisfy both co-chairs—a metric that shows asymmetry becomes leverage for renegotiating Phase One duration, verdict thresholds, or site selection. Conversely, a metric too loose (e.g., 'both sides say parity was achieved') triggers disputes over whether it was actually measured.

4.6.B Tags

  • parity-undefined
  • operationalization-missing
  • political-leverage
  • go-criterion-ambiguous
  • measurement-gap

4.6.C Mitigation

By Month 4 (2027-02-08), define parity operationally through measurable, symmetric indicators: (1) Inspector-hour parity: total inspector hours (on-site + staged exercises) per site per month, target ≥90% balance (site A vs. B in each pair), tranche withheld if >10% disparity; (2) Exercise parity: number of exercises per event type per site per pair, target ≥5 per site per type, with one country's red team designing challenges at the other country's site (swap sites for each challenge type); (3) Data-access parity: average time from event record to counterpart evidence release (filtered package or raw-evidence escort), target ≤3 days, measured weekly; (4) Challenge-outcome parity: fraction of findings challenged by counterpart, fraction sustained after re-review, target ≥80% agreement rate. Lock all four metrics in the bilateral instrument by Month 5 (2027-03-08). During Phase One (Months 6-9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08), report parity dashboard weekly: if any indicator falls below 80%, co-chairs convene within 5 days to address asymmetry or jointly agree to flag the result as impaired parity (equivalent to a Modify outcome even if detection thresholds are met). Parity ≥85% on all four metrics is the Go gate for parity.

4.6.D Consequence

Without defined parity metrics, the Go decision becomes a political judgment: whichever side feels disadvantaged by the detection results will claim parity was not achieved and demand a Modify verdict or re-test. A detection rate of 72% (above the 70% threshold) will be accepted as Go if that side designed the exercises, but the same rate will be challenged as non-representative if the other side controlled the test sites. This politicizes the most credible outcome and leaves Phase One's verdict contested regardless of the technical evidence.

4.6.E Root Cause

The plan correctly prioritizes parity as a prerequisite for credible results, but it treats parity as a property of sites (matched-pair selection) rather than as a measurable outcome of operations (achieved parity during Phase One). Matched-pair selection (pre-clock) can confirm functional equivalence of staging areas and access windows; operational parity (during Phase One) requires continuous measurement of inspector time, exercise count, challenge outcomes and resolution timelines at each site. Without pre-specified metrics and measurement rules, parity becomes a post-hoc judgment call, inviting both sides to claim asymmetry when results are unfavorable.

The Inspector Information Firewall doctrine specifies compartmentalization by role and site with post-assignment debriefs and cooling-off periods, but operational protocols are missing: no definition of 'compartmentalization,' no debriefing template or time budget (estimated 4–8 hours per rotation × ~180 inspectors = 360–720 person-hours per month), and no specification of what triggers a 'cooling-off period' (48 hours? 2 weeks?) or how that interacts with 24/7 shift scheduling. 6.4.A Issue - Bilateral Instrument Language Does Not Lock the Double-Key Deadlock Procedure, Creating Interpretive Escape Hatches

The plan specifies automatic partial suspension at day 14 and impaired-confidence flags at days 21–28, yet no specimen language is provided showing how these thresholds are embedded into the bilateral instrument itself. Without locked procedural language, each co-chair can later argue that 'procedural dispute' delays reset the clock, that 'good-faith negotiation' suspends the age counter, or that 'urgent national interest' justifies exception. The START and JCPOA precedents show that deadlock procedures without ironclad instrument text are treated as advisory only. The plan risks having an 'automatic' suspension that either side can unilaterally defer.

6.4.C Mitigation
