Lock this language into the bilateral instrument by Month 1 (2026-11-08). Include a 'no-waiver register' so any postponed suspension is logged and visible.

6.4.D Consequence

Without locked instrument language, adjudication during Phase One will become a tool for stalling: one side delays until sufficient time has passed to reframe a deadline, argues procedural exceptions, and forces the other to invoke suspension unilaterally (appearing aggressive). Alternatively, both sides avoid invoking suspension to keep operations running, allowing discrepancies to age past 21 days and undermining the credibility of the 'automatic' rule. The final verdict becomes a negotiation over which discrepancies 'count' rather than an application of pre-agreed law, delegitimizing the Go/Modify/Stop decision to domestic and international observers.

6.4.E Root Cause

The plan describes the deadlock architecture but does not provide a specimen bilateral-instrument clause that locks the procedure beyond ambiguous renegotiation. No statutory or treaty precedent is cited for enforcing age-triggered suspension without a casting vote. The plan assumes both sides will honor procedural discipline in the abstract but does not pre-draft the legal language that makes non-compliance visible or costly.

6.5.A Issue - Confidential Evidence-Weighting Rule Lacks Pre-Phase-One Adversarial Validation, Creating Risk of Miscalibration and Adjudication Paralysis

The plan specifies that a 'confidential, rotating combination rule set by accountable specialists' will weight attestation, physical inspection, customs records, identifiers, maintenance logs, infrastructure changes and witnessed movement into an equipment-identity confidence rating. The plan requires validation against 100–200 historical equipment-change records per site by Month 2 (2026-12-08) (proposed threshold), comparing false-positive and false-negative rates against known ground truth. However, this validation uses benign historical records from cooperative operators—not adversarial scenarios where an operator deliberately delays access, substitutes equipment, or provides misleading records to test the rule's robustness. A rule calibrated only on cooperative historical data will fail to detect gaming and may trigger false positives on ordinary delays, overwhelming the 15-case-per-month adjudication capacity.

6.5.C Mitigation

By Month 4.5 (2027-02-23), after historical validation is complete, conduct an adversarial-scenario workshop (2 days, both sides' evidence-rule specialists, independent exercise-authority staff) to generate 20–30 synthetic scenarios (realistic cases from IAEA, OPCW and START experience involving access delays, record gaps, vendor refusal and substitution attempts). Apply the locked rule to these scenarios, score the confidence outputs and compare to a reference panel's judgment ('this scenario should score 60–70% confidence, not 40%'). If the rule misscores >3 scenarios (more than 10% error rate), adjust the rule weights and re-validate on historical data before Phase One. Document the adversarial-testing results in a classified annex so both sides can verify the rule resists gaming. This adds an estimated 3–4 weeks and USD 150–200k to the calendar but catches miscalibration before the clock starts.

6.5.D Consequence

If the rule is miscalibrated on benign data only, Phase One will produce 20–30% false positives (vs. 10% target), generating 30–50 discrepancies per month (vs. 15 planned). The adjudication unit will be paralyzed, discrepancies will age past 21 days, impaired-confidence suspensions will multiply, and both sides will blame each other's filtering or evidence-hiding for the apparent gaming. The final verdict becomes untrustworthy because the high false-positive rate will be attributed to either overly strict rule weights (making one side appear compliant) or overly loose weights (making the other appear non-compliant), inviting a contested Stop or renegotiated Modify outcome.

6.5.E Root Cause

The plan treats historical-record validation as sufficient to calibrate the rule. However, historical records reflect normal operations (cooperative access, complete documentation, no deliberate obfuscation). An operator or vendor seeking to shield equipment will not behave cooperatively; they will use delays, record gaps, maintenance claims and access denials to push the rule's thresholds. The validation cohort must include adversarial synthetic scenarios (e.g., a maintenance event with delayed access and missing vendor signature, or substituted equipment with a partial attestation) to test whether the rule correctly scores these as lower-confidence cases or incorrectly flags them as discrepancies.

6.6.A Issue - Verdict Thresholds Are Pre-Registered But Confidence-Interval Bands Are Not Locked Into Bilateral Instrument, Enabling Post-Hoc Renegotiation of Go/Modify/Stop Decision

The plan proposes pre-registering verdict thresholds (Go ≥75% detection, Modify 55–75%, Stop <55%, proposed thresholds) by Month 2.5 (2026-12-23) 'before the first Phase One exercise.' However, the plan does not specify whether these thresholds are locked into the bilateral instrument (making them legally binding and non-negotiable) or published only as a planning document (making them advisory and subject to reinterpretation). With only 54 exercises and ±12% pooled confidence intervals at 95%, many outcomes will land inside the Modify band (e.g., 65% ±15% at 95% CL spans 50–80%, overlapping Go and Stop). If thresholds are not legally binding, the final verdict becomes a negotiation over confidence-interval interpretation: one side argues the true rate is likely 75% (Go), the other argues 65% (Modify), and the decision devolves into political bargaining rather than pre-registered rules.

  • verdict-threshold-ambiguity
  • post-hoc-renegotiation-risk
  • confidence-interval-interpretation
  • bilateral-instrument-lockdown-gap

6.6.C Mitigation

By Month 1 (2026-11-08), the bilateral legal team must draft a specimen instrument clause (300–500 words) that: (1) incorporates the verdict thresholds by numeric reference (Go ≥75%, Modify 55–75%, Stop <55%) as binding procedural rules, not advisory figures; (2) requires the Exercise Authority to report confidence intervals (±percentage points at 95% CL) for each detection rate; (3) specifies a mechanical rule ('if lower confidence bound exceeds Go threshold, verdict is Go; if upper bound falls below Stop threshold, verdict is Stop; otherwise Modify'); (4) forbids co-chair amendment of thresholds after any exercise results are known; (5) requires both co-chairs to initial a 'final verdict report' that applies the mechanical rule, so the verdict is an application of pre-agreed law, not a negotiated outcome. This language must be locked into the bilateral instrument by Month 2 (2026-12-08) and published (unclassified) before the first Phase One exercise so both legislatures see the scoring rule in advance.

6.6.D Consequence

If thresholds are advisory only or locked in planning documents (not the bilateral instrument), the final verdict will be contested. If results land at 65% detection with ±15% intervals, one co-chair will read this as 'within Modify band' and the other as 'consistent with Go.' Absent mechanical scoring rules, both interpretations are defensible, and the decision defaults to politics: the country with more leverage at that moment can push for Go (claiming a success to justify future funding) or Stop (claiming verification is inadequate to justify continued operations). Either way, the final verdict loses credibility as an objective, pre-agreed outcome and becomes a perceived capitulation by one side. This delegitimizes Phase One to both legislatures and undermines any future phase or new mechanism.

6.6.E Root Cause

The plan separates the technical threshold-setting from the legal enforcement mechanism. Thresholds are described as 'pre-registered' in planning documents, but the bilateral instrument is not cited as incorporating them by reference or making them non-amendable. In arms-control precedent (JCPOA, New START), threshold and confidence-interval disputes have repeatedly led to stalling or unilateral withdrawal because the legal force of a 'provisional' threshold is ambiguous. The plan needs explicit instrument language that locks thresholds into law and specifies the mechanical scoring procedure (confidence-interval overlap rules, default-to-Modify decision rule) so the verdict is generated by algorithm, not co-chair judgment.

7.4.A Issue - Entry-Condition Timeline Lacks Binding Enforcement and Parallel-Track Acceleration

The entry-gate roadmap (Months 0–5 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-03-08) lists seven sequential milestones but does not specify which are critical-path blockers, which can overlap, or how to recover from slippage. The plan assumes instrument-signature gates domestic-authority enactment, which gates site selection, which gates vendor outreach. Each slip (estimated 2–4 weeks per gate) compresses Phase One from 90 to 45–60 days, widening statistical uncertainty from ±12% to ±20% at 95% CL. No external escalation authority or scope-reduction trigger exists. Parallel tracks (site nomination, vendor outreach, inspector vetting) starting at Month −2 would recover weeks, but are not mandated.

7.6.A Issue - Verdict Thresholds Are Pre-Registered But Statistical Confidence Intervals Are Too Wide to Disambiguate Go/Modify/Stop

The plan pre-registers Go (≥70% detection), Modify (55–75%), and Stop (<55%) thresholds for planned-event detection. With an estimated ±12% pooled confidence interval (±22% per planned-event class at 95% CL), a 70% outcome is defensible as Go (confidence band 48–92%), Modify (depending on weighting), or even Stop (under stricter interpretation). No explicit rule exists to resolve cases where the confidence interval straddles a threshold (e.g., 60% ±25% spans both Modify and Stop). The Verdict Threshold Calibration Method (choice 1) marks thresholds provisional and locked only after pilot validation, but pilot validation on 1–2 exercises per type provides even weaker confidence (±32% per-type estimate), not stronger. Political renegotiation of the verdict is therefore likely, delegitimizing the Go/Modify/Stop decision.

7.6.C Mitigation

Pre-register verdict thresholds as explicit confidence-interval bands (not point estimates) in a double-key-approved bilateral memorandum locked by Month 2.5 (2026-12-23, 14:00), before the first Phase One exercise. Use bands: Go (lower bound of 90% CL ≥75% detection), Modify (upper and lower bounds straddle 60% or fall within 50–80%), Stop (upper bound of 90% CL <55%). Define a mechanical scoring rule: if the lower bound exceeds the Go threshold, outcome is Go (no negotiation); if the upper bound falls below the Stop threshold, outcome is Stop; otherwise default to Modify. Publish the confidence interval for every rate and the mechanical scoring logic so both sides can verify the verdict before it is announced. Lock thresholds before Month 6 (2027-04-08) Phase One clock; publish final verdict with intervals and mechanical justification within 5 days of Phase One conclusion.

7.6.D Consequence

Unmitigated: ambiguous thresholds invite post-hoc renegotiation of the verdict. A 70% ±20% result can be read as Go, Modify, or Stop depending on which government's preferred interpretation prevails. Political pressure on scorers to adjust intervals or thresholds corrupts the objective decision-making design. Either government can delegitimize the verdict and withdraw, invalidating Phase One entirely.

8 Expert: Exercise Realism and Production-Disruption Risk Assessor

However, exercises in real datacenters carry inherent risk: a staging area that is supposed to be non-critical becomes critical mid-exercise if a production emergency occurs; an exercise-triggered alert could cascade into a security incident; an operator's reluctance to grant access might mask a real incident or might reflect legitimate operational constraints. This expert evaluates whether the 54-exercise load (about 6 per site per month) is operationally realistic, designs scenarios that are adversarially credible without crossing into sabotage, and validates the disruption risk and mitigation.

Flag scenarios that would require production-area access or that carry >10% incident risk.

8.4.A Issue - Exercise Execution Design Does Not Match Production Reality or Operator Tolerance

The plan specifies 54 exercises in 90 days (6 per event type minimum) without detailing staging-area setup, equipment-swap logistics, or unreported-arrival injection mechanics. Three critical gaps: (1) Staging areas are designated but not tested for isolation from active infrastructure—swapping frontier hardware in a live datacenter without production touch is operationally novel and untested. (2) Unreported-arrival injection requires injecting equipment past operator awareness; the plan does not clarify whether vendors and operators will permit blind injections into their facilities, and operator friction from exercises is listed as a risk but not mitigated. (3) Six exercises per type in a 90-day window, under full mirrored shifts and with filtering/certification latency (2-3 days per package), leaves only 5-7 days per exercise for setup, execution, evidence collection and teardown—realistic timelines are 10-14 days per exercise (test, remediate, repeat). The plan will either compress exercises into shallow scenarios or face production disruption if each is realistic.

  • exercise-execution-mismatch
  • staging-area-untested
  • operator-friction-unmitigated

  • timeline-compression
  • production-disruption-risk

8.4.C Mitigation

Conduct a three-site Exercise Dry Run (Month 4.5 = 2027-02-23 to Month 5 = 2027-03-08) at one declared site from each country and one neutral non-production facility. For each site, execute two of the seven event types (unreported arrival, substitution) in staging areas under real hardware, full filtering and mirrored observation. Measure actual timelines: setup duration, swap execution, evidence collection, filtering latency, ledger closure. Document operator friction points and agree on notification protocols (e.g., 48-hour operator notice for exercise window, 0 notice for unreported-arrival injection). Revise exercise load (reduce to 4-5 per type if timelines exceed 10 days) and lock operator participation agreements with written commitments signed by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23). Appoint an independent Exercise Safety Monitor (third-country operations expert) who has authority to halt any exercise if production risk is judged unacceptable; logged decisions feed into the final audit.

8.4.D Consequence

Risk of operational failure during Phase One: (1) Exercises execute at low fidelity (simulations rather than real hardware swaps), so detection data are misleading and the final verdict is non-credible. (2) Operator resistance causes exercises to be moved or cancelled, reducing sample size below the 6-per-type minimum and widening confidence intervals from ±12% to ±18% (pooled), making Go/Modify/Stop boundaries ambiguous. (3) Production disruption during an exercise (equipment misplaced, network isolation incomplete, active workload interrupted) forces a site offline for 8-24 hours, which the plan explicitly forbids and triggers operator complaints that feed into a shielding allegation or tranche withheld.

8.4.E Root Cause

Exercise design was written at strategic level without engagement with datacenter operations, maintenance planning or equipment logistics. The plan assumes exercises can be injected, measured and remediated in 5-7 days per event without specifying the operational machinery—operator notification windows, equipment-staging validation, swap logistics, physical teardown and ledger-closure timelines. Staging-area isolation has not been tested at any participating site, and the injections assume operator willingness to host blind unreported-arrival tests, which is not documented.

8.5.A Issue - Adjudication Capacity Underestimated by 2-4x; Deadlock Procedures Will Stall Under Evidence Volume

The plan allocates 15 discrepancies per month adjudication capacity (one 5-person adjudication unit per country = 10 specialists total for 360-person program, 2.8% of staffing). Reality check: (1) If the confidential evidence rule is miscalibrated (false-positive rates 15-20% vs. 10% target), the plan admits miscalibration would 'overflow adjudication.' At a 15% false-positive rate, 54 exercises generate ~8 exercises × 15% = 1.2 false positives per month, plus 2-3 legitimate discrepancies per month (ambiguous equipment identity, incomplete disposal records, ledger divergence) = 3.2 cases per month baseline. If the rule is off by 5 points (false positives 15% instead of 10%), adjudication load rises to ~5 cases per month. (2) The deadlock procedure allocates 10 days for convening and 5 days for an advisory panel, then 3 days for co-chair decision (day 18); automatic partial suspension at day 14 while the advisory panel is still deliberating. At 3-4 cases per month, at least one will hit day 14 while awaiting the panel opinion, triggering a partial suspension that must be logged and may trigger media attention. (3) No surge adjudication unit is funded; the plan allocates only 5 positions per country for adjudication as part of the 36-person specialist unit. If load hits 30-40 cases in a month (possible if exercises cluster and rule miscalibration surfaces), the 5 specialists are overwhelmed and cases age rapidly, hitting impaired-confidence (day 21) and forcing automatic site suspension.

  • adjudication-capacity-underestimated
  • deadlock-stall-risk
  • false-positive-overflow
  • surge-capacity-underfunded
  • evidence-rule-miscalibration-risk
  • partial-suspension-cascades

8.5.C Mitigation

Resize adjudication immediately: add 8-10 specialists per country (total 16-20, up from 10) and fund a dedicated surge unit of 4-6 per country (total 8-12) available on 48-hour call. Validate the evidence rule on adversarial test cases (not just historical records) by Month 5 (2027-03-08): apply the draft rule to 20-30 deliberately miscalibrated equipment scenarios (records that conflict, omitted serial numbers, altered maintenance logs) and measure false-positive and false-negative rates against known ground truth. If pilot miscalibration shows false positives above 12%, adjust the rule before Phase One and re-test. Lock the rule by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23) with a 'calibration confidence memo' signed by both evidence-rule owners documenting the validation dataset and any residual uncertainty. Restructure deadlock timeline: convene the advisory panel by day 7 (not day 10), publish the panel's opinion by day 12, allow co-chairs 2 days (day 14) to decide; if no decision by day 14, automatic partial suspension is triggered, but the opinion and suspension are published as a joint ledger event so legislatures see the technical recommendation. Add a weekly adjudication dashboard (every Thursday) showing age-bucket counts and projected case clearance date per site.

8.5.D Consequence

Phase One stalls 4-6 weeks into the 90-day window as adjudication cases age and automatic partial suspensions trigger. At day 21, identity disputes force impaired-confidence flags; at day 28, disposal-record disputes trigger the same. If multiple sites hit impaired-confidence simultaneously (possible if a rule miscalibration affects all sites uniformly), the program enters automatic partial suspension across 2-3 sites, and the co-chairs must decide whether to Stop or invoke an emergency summit. The partial-suspension trigger (day 14 unresolved) is designed to be non-negotiable, so each co-chair sees the suspension as the other side delaying resolution, feeding into deadlock and mutual blame. The final verdict is delayed or becomes a Stop by default because the program runs out of calendar time before adjudication clears.

8.5.E Root Cause

Adjudication headcount (5 per country) was derived from a 15-discrepancies-per-month assumption without validation on historical datasets or realistic miscalibration scenarios. The plan acknowledges false-positive overflow ('adjudication overload') in the Weaknesses section but does not resize staffing or add surge capacity. The deadlock timeline (days 10-18) was designed for a 2-3 case monthly steady state, not for the clustering that will occur when exercises run in parallel weeks and evidence filters certifications bottleneck (2-3 days per package × 54 exercises = 54 people-days of filter-certification work compressed into 6 weeks before Phase One, creating a backlog).

8.6.A Issue - Inspector Shift Coverage Will Not Support 24/7 Unreported-Arrival Detection; Blind-Challenge Execution Becomes Predictable

The staffing model allocates 99 inspection-corps per country (54 positions × 1.4 for 7-day coverage = 76, plus 30% leave cover = 99). This arithmetic is correct only if every inspector works 12 consecutive hours or splits two 8-hour shifts, but the plan forbids both ('no inspector working >12 consecutive hours or >48 hours per week'). Reality: 54 positions at 3 sites × 3 shifts × 6 field staff per position × 40-hour-per-week work rule = 54 / (40 / (8 × 3 shifts)) = 54 × 3 shifts / 40 hours = 4.05 shifts per position per week. With 6 field staff per shift and 3 shifts, staff coverage = (6 × 3 × 40 hours) / 54 positions = 720 / 54 = 13.3 hours per position average per week—far short of the 40-hour-per-week work rule. The actual headcount needed is 54 × (40 hours / 13.3 hours) ≈ 162 per country, not 99. Gap: 63 per country (126 total), or 35% of the inspection corps. Consequence: either shifts are undermanned (fewer than 6 per shift) or inspectors work >48 hours per week, violating the plan constraint. Specifically for unreported-arrival exercises (which test the detection of equipment introduced without operator declaration), the detection rate depends entirely on shift staffing at the moment of arrival. If shifts are undermanned or rotated predictably, exercises can be timed to arrive during low-coverage windows, and the blind-challenge intent is lost.

8.6.B Tags

  • shift-coverage-arithmetic-error
  • understaffing-risk
  • unreported-arrival-detection-vulnerable
  • work-hour-violation
  • exercise-timing-gaming
  • blind-challenge-credibility

8.6.C Mitigation

Recompute staffing for the stated coverage model (Mirrored Shift Coverage Architecture, choice 1: 'minimum paired presence in staging and spare-inventory areas at all times'). Define 'minimum paired presence' explicitly: e.g., 4 inspectors (2 per country) continuously present in staging + 2 in spare/expansion areas, rotating every 8 hours. At 3 sites, 2 shifts minimum (day/night, 16 hours unbroken coverage) is operationally sustainable; 3-shift 24/7 continuous is above budget. Choose: (A) Continuous 3-shift coverage (requires ~300 inspectors per country, not 99; 'Aspirational'); (B) Two-shift 16-hour coverage (6:00–22:00) with on-call night response (requires ~180 per country); or (C) Event-triggered coverage (deploy inspectors within 4 hours of a reported activity; requires ~120 per country + surge pool, but misses unreported arrivals). Lock the choice by Month 1 (2026-11-08) based on entry-gate cost analysis. Revalidate exercise timing: if choice (B) or (C), every unreported-arrival and disputed-identity exercise must occur during core coverage hours (6:00–22:00 for choice B) or within 4 hours of an activity report (choice C). Document the shift schedule publicly so red teams cannot game it. If coverage cannot be delivered without exceeding USD 750M personnel envelope, reduce site count from 3 to 2 pairs (4 sites total, allowing ~225 per country, enough for choice B at 4 sites).

8.6.D Consequence

Unreported-arrival exercises will be gamed or will fail to detect adversarial arrivals that occur during shift boundaries or low-presence windows. If five exercises test unreported arrival (n=5) and two are timed to low-coverage moments, the observed detection rate is 3/5 = 60%, which falls into the Modify band (55-75%), not the Go band (≥75%). Across all seven event types, the inadequate shift coverage for unreported arrivals and disputed-identity resolution (both require continuous or high-frequency presence) lowers the pooled detection rate and pushes the verdict toward Modify or Stop. The exercising agency (red teams) will know the shift schedules and time injections accordingly, and inspectors will know that they are expected to detect such arrivals yet lack the staffing, creating morale and credibility issues. If exercises show low unreported-arrival detection (say 40-50%) and the co-chairs ask why, the honest answer is understaffing, which becomes a Stop trigger ('material equipment remains unverifiable' due to detection failure).

8.6.E Root Cause

Staffing math was done at the envelope level (number of people) without validating the coverage formula (hours of presence per shift per site). The plan states 'minimum paired presence in staging and spare-inventory areas at all times' (Mirrored Shift Coverage Architecture, choice 1), which implies continuous presence, but the headcount allocation assumes 7-day coverage (1.4 multiplier), not continuous. Continuous coverage would require 54 × 3 shifts × (168 hours / week / 40 hours per week) ≈ 54 × 3 × 4.2 = 680 person-positions, not 99 or even 162. The plan chose not to provide continuous presence, yet exercises assume inspectors can detect unreported arrivals at any time, which is contradictory.
