Review 1: Critical Issues

  1. Entry-Condition Timeline Compression Exhausts Contingency and Narrows Statistical Confidence. An 8-week slip in any entry gate (instrument signature, domestic authority, site selection) consumes USD 100–200M of the USD 500M contingency (20–40% of contingency; 22–50% of free contingency), compressing Phase One from 90 to 50–60 days. Statistical confidence intervals widen from ±12% (pooled) to ±18–22%, making Go/Modify/Stop boundaries ambiguous (e.g., 70% detection no longer defensible as Go). No binding acceleration authority or external escalation with scope-reduction power exists to enforce parallel-track entry processing, creating cascading delays.

  2. Adjudication Capacity Miscalibrates if Evidence Rule Deviates Beyond ±3 Points; Partial Suspensions Cascade. If the confidential evidence-weighting rule achieves false-positive rates of 15–20% instead of 10% target (deviation of 5–10 points), adjudication caseload rises from 15 to 30–50 cases per month, overwhelming the 5-person per-country adjudication unit. Discrepancies age past 21 days, triggering automatic impaired-confidence flags and partial suspensions across multiple sites simultaneously, paralyzing unrelated functions and violating the plan's continuity guarantee.

  3. Shift Coverage Model Under-Resources 24/7 Detection Requirement; Unreported-Arrival Exercises Become Predictable and Gamed. Staffing math allocates 99 inspectors per country assuming 1.4 multiplier for 7-day coverage, but continuous 24/7 presence (implied by unreported-arrival detection and blind-exercise scheduling) is not fully covered by the 3-shift, 99-corps model unless exercise timing is distributed across all hours. Exercise timing becomes predictable to red teams, who can inject arrivals during low-coverage windows; detection rates for unreported arrival fall below the 70% threshold, pushing the verdict toward Modify or Stop regardless of other evidence.

Review 2: Implementation Consequences

  1. Successful Entry-Gate Completion and Parallel-Track Acceleration Unblock Phase One but Consume Contingency; Remaining Free Contingency USD 400–450M Supports Only Modest Overruns. If entry gates complete on schedule (bilateral instrument Month 1 = 2026-11-08, domestic authority Month 2 = 2026-12-08, sites Month 3 = 2027-01-08, vendors/schedule by Month 4 = 2027-02-08) without the 8-week compression risk, the program avoids USD 100–200M delay costs and preserves most of the USD 500M contingency (50–100% retained as free contingency USD 400–450M). However, this success depends on activating parallel-track acceleration (USD 50–100M compression reserve) and external escalation authority by Month 0 (2026-10-08). Consequence: Phase One gains a sustainable contingency buffer, but any mid-test overrun (adjudication surge, ledger failure recovery, site loss) above 8–9% of total budget (USD 400–450M) exhausts the free contingency and forces a new funding decision or Stop trigger.

  2. Evidence-Rule Validation Before Phase One (Months 4.5–5.5) Prevents Adjudication Paralysis and Unlocks Credible Detection Claims, But Validation Gap Risks Cascade. If the confidential evidence-weighting rule is validated on both historical records (100–200 per site) and adversarial synthetic cases (40–50 per site, proposed threshold) by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23), and pilot false-positive rate confirms 7–13% (within ±3 points of 10% target), adjudication capacity matches the 15–20 cases per month demand. This enables Go/Modify/Stop verdicts to rest on defensible detection rates (70%+ for planned, 50%+ for unplanned). Conversely, if validation is skipped or deviates ±5–10 points (false positives 15–20%), adjudication load surges to 30–50 cases per month, discrepancies age past 21 days by Month 7 (2027-05-08), automatic partial suspensions cascade across sites, and the final verdict becomes a Stop by default due to unresolved caseload, not evidence quality.

  3. Shift Coverage Integrity and Exercise Timing Predictability Determine Unreported-Arrival Detection Credibility; If Resources Are Insufficient, Exercises Become Gamed and Detection Thresholds Fall. The plan assumes 3-shift coverage with 99 inspection corps per country. If exercises are executed during announced windows, red teams can time unreported-arrival injections to low-coverage moments (night shift, shift boundaries), driving observed detection rates below 70% and forcing the verdict toward Modify. Conversely, if shift schedules are published and kept consistent, and exercises are distributed across all hours, detection rates reach 70%+ and support Go threshold. Interaction: if entry-gate delays compress Phase One from 90 to 50–60 days, only 32–36 exercises run (vs. 54 planned), reducing sample size per type from 6–8 to 4–5, widening confidence intervals from ±12% to ±18%, making the final verdict ambiguous regardless of detection rates. Recommendation: confirm the 3-shift coverage model by Month 1 (2026-11-08), publish shift schedules by Month 4 (2027-02-08), and confirm exercise timing distribution across all 24 hours before Phase One clock starts (Month 6 = 2027-04-08) to prevent gaming.

Review 3: Recommended Actions

  1. Establish External Escalation Authority with Binding Scope-Reduction Power by Month 0 (2026-10-08); Expected Impact: USD 100–200M Contingency Preservation and 90-Day Phase One Window Protection. Appoint a neutral third-country official or pre-authorized co-chair deputies with power to invoke emergency co-chair summit within 48 hours if any entry gate slips >2 weeks, with 5-day authority to decide scope reduction (2 pairs over the full 90 days, 4 exercises per site per month = 48 total) rather than timeline extension. This mechanism prevents sequential processing delays from compressing Phase One below statistical credibility. Impact: preserves a viable exercise load (48 at 2 pairs, vs. below the minimum if the clock is compressed to 50–60 days, which cannot support Go), maintains ±12% confidence intervals, and avoids USD 100–200M sunk delay costs from the free contingency USD 400–450M.

  2. Commission Independent Bilateral Statistical Advisory Panel and Confidence-Interval Auditor by Month 2 (2026-12-08); Expected Impact: USD 5–10M Audit Cost; Risk Reduction of Verdict Contestation by 40–60% and False-Positive Miscalibration Detection by 80%. Retain a third-country statistician to audit confidence-interval construction, mechanical scoring rule methodology, and evidence-rule calibration against pilot data (Months 4.5–5 = 2027-02-23 to 2027-03-08). Independent sign-off on threshold fitness and rule validation prevents co-chair disputes over statistical methodology and catches evidence-rule miscalibration (false positives above 13%) before Phase One. Impact: reduces post-verdict renegotiation risk and enables Go verdict to survive bilateral scrutiny.

  3. Fund and Pre-Stage Bilateral Adjudication Surge Unit (8–12 specialists per country, Total USD 2–3M) by Month 4 (2027-02-08); Expected Impact: Risk Reduction of Deadlock Cascade by 50–70% and Unresolved-Discrepancy Backlog by 60–80%. Allocate dedicated surge adjudication staff (above the 5-person baseline per country) from the 750M personnel envelope, on 48-hour call for caseload spikes above 15 per month. Validate evidence-rule miscalibration scenarios (false positives 15–20%) during pilot testing (Month 5 = 2027-03-08) and pre-fund surge staffing ($2–3M) to absorb 25–40 cases per month if the rule deviates. Impact: prevents discrepancies from aging past 21–28 day impaired-confidence thresholds and the cascade of automatic partial suspensions that paralyze Phase One.

Review 4: Showstopper Risks

  1. Neutral Facility Site Selection and Key-Custody Ceremony Readiness Remain Unresolved; Delayed Operationalization Blocks Ledger Validation and Entry Certification. Impact: If Geneva or Singapore site decision (Month 1 = 2026-11-08) slips 4–6 weeks, facility hardening (ISO 27001, Tempest equivalent) cannot complete by Month 3 (2027-01-08); key-recovery rehearsal (Month 5 = 2027-03-08) is compressed or cancelled; entry certification (Month 5.5 = 2027-03-23) is jeopardized. A 4-week facility slip costs USD 30–50M, funded from free contingency rather than the compression reserve, and consumes 3–4 weeks of pre-clock calibration buffer. Likelihood: Medium (site selection is OPEN; host-country negotiation precedent: 8–12 weeks). Interaction: facility delay cascades into delayed ledger synchronization validation and key-custody ceremony rehearsal, leaving Phase One operations at risk of ledger divergence or key loss (8–24 hour recovery window unvalidated). Contingency: Designate a backup neutral facility (secondary host country) by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23) and pre-stage procurement for both sites so selection at Month 1 (2026-11-08) triggers immediate construction at the primary, with fallback activation within 2 weeks if primary slips.

  2. Operator and Vendor Participation Confidence Commitments Lack Legal Enforcement; Mid-Phase-One Withdrawal or Access Restrictions Trigger Asymmetric-Access Stop Condition. Impact: Operator Statements of Cooperation (locked before Month 3 = 2027-01-08 matched-pair approval; binding status stated in the instrument) are at risk of weak enforcement; if a US hyperscale operator cites customer-confidentiality or production-disruption risk mid-Phase-One (Month 7–8 = 2027-05-08 to 2027-06-08) and restricts access, one site's detection rates fall >10% below the other country's, breaching reciprocal-access parity (proposed ≥85%) and triggering a hard Stop. Estimated impact: loss of 1 site reduces exercise load to 48 (4 sites, 2 pairs) or below viable thresholds; estimated cost USD 30–50M in sunk exercise and personnel costs. Likelihood: Medium (commercial operators are independent entities; precedent: START inspections saw access restrictions in 2019–2020 before suspension). Interaction: operator withdrawal coinciding with evidence-rule miscalibration (false positives 15–20%) or late vendor-refusal escalations (Month 6–7 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-05-08) overwhelms adjudication and forces Stop by default. Contingency: Embed binding operator participation agreements in the bilateral instrument (Month 1 = 2026-11-08) with domestic home-government enforceability; include operator compensation USD 30–50M per site (ceiling) as an incentive; schedule a pre-Phase-One operational dry run (Month 4.5 = 2027-02-23) at each site to validate operator cooperation and access-denial risk before the clock starts.

  3. Ledger Divergence Recovery Procedure Unvalidated; Lost or Contested Signing Key Can Block Evidence Custody for 8–24 Hours Without Precedent for Resolution. Impact: Dual-share key-custody ceremony (Month 4 = 2027-02-08) is planned but not rehearsed before Phase One; if a key is lost or contested mid-Phase-One (Month 7 = 2027-05-08), both co-chairs must invoke key recovery (estimated 8–24 hours). During recovery, new ledger entries are not signed and cannot be replicated to the counterpart copy, creating a ledger-divergence gap. The plan specifies 72-hour reconciliation target but no agreed recovery procedure if both shares are inaccessible or one co-chair contests the recovery legitimacy. Estimated impact: 8–24 hour observation blackout per incident; 2–3 incidents in 90 days would lose ~50 person-hours of equipment-monitoring data and age discrepancies toward automatic impaired-confidence (day 21). Likelihood: Medium (cryptographic key operations are error-prone; precedent: CTBTO and IAEA key recovery required 1–3 days in 2015–2018 incidents). Interaction: ledger-custody failure occurring during an exercise (loss of evidence integrity for that event) combines with adjudication backlog (30–50 cases per month if rule miscalibrates) to render the event non-credible and force re-execution or exclusion, reducing sample size below statistical minimum (6 per type). Contingency: Conduct full key-recovery dress rehearsal at Month 5 (2027-03-08) with both countries' key-custody officers, independent timekeeper, and neutral-facility staff; produce a Ledger-Recovery SOP with explicit steps, decision trees, and co-chair escalation protocol; pre-authorize a recovery-contingency team (2 cryptographic engineers per country) on standby for Phase One with documented appointment by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23).

Review 5: Critical Assumptions

  1. Assumption: Inspector Compartmentalization and Sealed-Communication Protocols Will Prevent Counterintelligence Breaches. Impact if false: If inspectors retain classified data or coordinate with foreign intelligence services despite compartmentalization (14-day cooling-off, sealed phones, 7-day breach adjudication), either government withdraws within 30–40 days, costing USD 200–400M sunk setup cost and invalidating Phase One as proof-of-concept. Interaction: A confirmed breach compounds entry-gate delays (emergency bilateral summit, vetting review) and pauses Phase One operations (day 1–14 pause while adjudication runs), consuming critical calendar days. Recommendation: Pre-deploy CI Oversight Board by Month 0 (2026-10-08) and complete baseline polygraph vetting by Month 2 (2026-12-08); conduct a compartmentalization stress-test during pilot exercise (Month 5 = 2027-03-08) to validate debriefing procedures and sealed-communication discipline before Phase One clock.

  2. Assumption: Entry Gates Will Meet Binding Deadlines (Instrument Month 1 = 2026-11-08, Authority Month 2 = 2026-12-08, Sites Month 3 = 2027-01-08, Entry Certified Month 5.5 = 2027-03-23) Without Exceeding Compression Reserve USD 50–100M. Impact if false: An 8-week cumulative slip costs USD 100–200M (20–40% of total contingency; 22–50% of free contingency), compressing Phase One from 90 to 45–60 days. Statistical confidence widens from ±12% to ±18–20%, making detection thresholds (≥70%) ambiguous and the final Go/Modify/Stop verdict non-defensible to legislatures. Phase One loses credibility as a rigorous proof-of-concept. Interaction: Delayed entry gates prevent rule and threshold lock-down before Phase One, forcing calibration adjustments mid-test and invalidating cross-exercise comparability. Recommendation: Establish Entry-Condition Task Force by Month 0 (2026-10-08) with binding weekly milestones, parallel-track activation (site, vendor, vetting), and external escalation authority empowered to invoke 5-day scope-reduction decision (2 pairs, full 90 days, 48 exercises) by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23).

  3. Assumption: Both Countries Will Ratify the Mechanical Scoring Method in the Bilateral Instrument by Month 1 (2026-11-08), with Numeric Thresholds Locked at Month 5.5 (2027-03-23) and Will Accept Modify as a Real, Binding Outcome When Confidence Intervals Straddle Thresholds. Impact if false: If thresholds remain 'provisional' or unembedded in binding law, and a Phase One result lands in an ambiguous zone (e.g., 70% ±15% at 95% CL spanning 55–85%), both co-chairs will contest the verdict and renegotiate the scoring rule post-hoc for 4–8 weeks, delaying the final Go/Modify/Stop decision past Month 10 (2027-08-08). Phase One is delegitimized; one country or legislature rejects the verdict as manipulated or inconclusive, triggering withdrawal threat. Interaction: Unresolved verdict timing compounds with unspent tranche 4 (USD 500M, due Month 9.2–9.5 on Go/Modify outcome), creating financial leverage for renegotiation and mutual blame. Recommendation: Lock the mechanical scoring method (rule, interval handling, no-amendment clause) in a double-key-signed bilateral memorandum by Month 1 (2026-11-08), lock numeric thresholds at Month 5.5 (2027-03-23), mark as binding non-amendable procedural law, and publish unclassified thresholds and decision logic before the first Phase One exercise (by Month 6 = 2027-04-08) so both legislatures see the objective verdict machinery in advance.

Review 6: Key Performance Indicators

  1. KPI 1: Detection Rate by Event Type with Confidence Interval Tracking (Target: ≥70% planned-event class, ≥50% unplanned-event class; Acceptable Range ±12% pooled, ±32% per-type at 95% CL). Measure observed detection per event type (unreported arrival, substitution, inaccurate records, delayed access, disputed identity, vendor refusal, reluctant operator) monthly during Phase One (Months 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08). Calculate 95% confidence intervals; compare lower bound to Go threshold (≥70% planned, ≥50% unplanned). Interaction: narrow intervals (±12%) enable a defensible Go verdict; wide intervals (±18–22%) due to entry-gate delays or compressed exercise load (48 vs. 54) force Modify. Recommendation: publish monthly detection-rate dashboard visible to both co-chairs and legislatures; if any event type falls >10 percentage points below target by Month 7 (2027-05-08), convene co-chairs within 5 days to assess whether exercises require redesign or detection threshold recalibration.

  2. KPI 2: Discrepancy Age and Unresolved-Case Backlog (Target: No discrepancy older than 21 days at Phase One conclusion; Acceptable Backlog <5 material cases open at Month 9 = 2027-07-08). Track elapsed days from discrepancy opening to closure; flag cases at day 14 (automatic partial suspension trigger) and day 21 (impaired-confidence status). Monthly target: <3 cases in backlog; if >5 cases remain open at Month 9 (2027-07-08), the Go criterion fails. Interaction: evidence-rule miscalibration (false positives 15–20% instead of 10%) produces 30–50 cases per month, overwhelming 15-case adjudication capacity and pushing cases past day 21 by Month 7–8 (2027-05-08 to 2027-06-08), cascading into automatic site suspensions. Recommendation: establish independent timekeeper (one per country) reporting weekly dashboard every Monday, 09:00 CET; if any case approaches day 14, activate adjudication surge unit (8–12 specialists, pre-positioned by Month 4 = 2027-02-08) within 48 hours.

  3. KPI 3: Envelope Reconciliation and Contingency Burn Rate (Target: Contingency draw <30% by Month 6 = 2027-04-08; Acceptable Range 30–50% by Month 9 = 2027-07-08; over 75% drawn = joint review with external audit; envelope over 120% = supplemental appropriation (veto point)). Track monthly actual spending against the seven USD 500M–USD 1.25B allocations; report cumulative contingency draw weekly to co-chairs. Triggers: contingency >30% (co-chair briefing), >50% (scope-reduction planning), >75% (joint external audit review). Interaction: entry-gate delays consume USD 100–200M of the free contingency USD 400–450M (22–50% depletion); if also adjudication surge (USD 2–3M additional) or ledger-recovery incidents (USD 5–10M re-certification costs) occur, cumulative draw reaches 50–75% by Month 8 (2027-06-08), leaving <USD 125–250M for final Phase One operations or Phase Two. Recommendation: appoint bilateral Finance Authority (one officer per country) with draw limits set by both co-chairs in the instrument; draws above the compression reserve require double-key (both co-chairs) approval and are executed jointly by both countries' budget officers; the compression reserve is for entry negotiation and vetting only, and the adjudication surge is funded from free contingency; conduct monthly envelope reconciliation by independent auditor (sampled 100% high-risk, 10% routine) and publish unclassified monthly summary so legislatures see spending discipline.

Review 7: Report Objectives

  1. Primary Objective: Inform Bilateral Go/Modify/Stop Decision on Declared-Equipment Change Verification Feasibility. This report evaluates whether a 90-day Phase One operational test (Months 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08) at 3 matched datacenter pairs can deliver credible detection of frontier-computing equipment changes between the US and China, with USD 5.0 billion total funding and mirrored inspectorates. Intended audience: both national co-chairs, bilateral oversight bodies, and legislative appropriations committees. Key decisions: whether entry gates (instrument signature Month 1 = 2026-11-08, domestic authority Month 2 = 2026-12-08, site approval Month 3 = 2027-01-08, entry certification Month 5.5 = 2027-03-23) proceed on schedule; whether evidence-weighting rule and verdict thresholds are locked (method by Month 1 = 2026-11-08, numeric thresholds by Month 5.5 = 2027-03-23) to prevent post-hoc renegotiation; whether staffing, ledger, and adjudication infrastructure are operationally ready by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23).

  2. Deliverables: Risk Assessment, Critical-Path Validation, and Quantified Mitigation Framework. The report identifies 19 specific risks (entry-gate compression, evidence-rule miscalibration, adjudication overload, facility delays, operator withdrawal, ledger divergence, staffing gaps, inspector breaches, vendor refusals) with quantified impacts (USD 100–500M contingency consumption, statistical confidence degradation from ±12% to ±20%, detection-rate ambiguity, partial-suspension cascades). It provides 12 expert reviews (bilateral verification, hardware attestation, counterintelligence, facility operations, legal instruments, statistics, exercise realism) grounding recommendations in precedent (IAEA, OPCW, START mechanisms). Accompanying work-breakdown structure maps 70+ tasks across governance, staffing, evidence validation, neutral-facility setup and Phase One operations to the USD 5.0 billion envelope and the 9.5-month timeline.

  3. Version 2 Divergence from Version 1: Operationalize Unresolved Items and Lock Pre-Clock Calibration. Version 1 marked as OPEN: neutral-facility site (Geneva or Singapore decision Month 1 = 2026-11-08), post-Phase-One funding route (Modify rework vs. Phase Two), reciprocal-access parity definition, language-of-record translation turnaround, and adjudication surge staffing. Version 2 must embed binding decisions in the bilateral instrument by Month 1 (2026-11-08)—site selection with host-country MOU, facility hardening by Month 3 (2027-01-08), evidence-rule validation with double-key sign-off by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23), and verdict-threshold mechanical-scoring rule locked before any exercise (by Month 6 = 2027-04-08). Version 2 also quantifies entry-gate slippage cost (USD 100–200M per 8 weeks) and specifies scope-reduction backstop (2 pairs, full 90 days, 4 exercises per site per month = 48 total) with external escalation authority by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23).

Review 8: Data Quality Concerns

  1. Inspector Recruitment and Vetting Timeline Lacks Validated Attrition and Throughput Data; Recruitment Baseline 300+ Candidates May Undershoot or Overshoot Actual Certified Personnel. The plan assumes recruitment of 300+ candidates per country (Months 0–4 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-02-08) will yield 180 certified personnel (99 inspection corps + 36 surge + 45 specialists) by Month 5 (2027-03-08), with security-clearance vetting running Months 1–4 (2026-11-08 to 2027-02-08; 50% cleared as a Month 2 = 2026-12-08 milestone). However, no historical attrition rate is cited from bilateral or comparable programs (IAEA, OSCE precedent). If attrition exceeds 20% (typical for military/security selection), actual certified personnel drop to 144 (20% shortfall); if below 10%, surplus personnel (36) consume additional personnel-budget dollars. Impact: a 20% attrition gap means shift coverage at Month 5.5 (2027-03-23) falls 18 inspectors short per country, reducing on-site presence from 99 to 81 and violating minimum 6-per-shift staffing for 3 sites. Recommendation: validate attrition against START treaty precedent (estimated 8–15% per US and Russian records) and commission a bilateral pre-vetting feasibility audit (Month 0 = 2026-10-08) of both countries' security-clearance systems to confirm the Month 2 (2026-12-08) 50% milestone is achievable without cascading delays.

  2. Evidence-Rule Validation on Historical Records Alone Cannot Confirm False-Negative Rate on Adversarial Substitution and Gaming Scenarios; Pilot Pilot False-Positive Rate May Not Predict Phase-One Miscalibration. The plan specifies validation on 100–200 historical equipment-change events per site (Months 4.5–5 = 2027-02-23 to 2027-03-08) and proposes adversarial synthetic test cases (40–50 per site, proposed threshold) but does not quantify how many synthetic cases are required to claim statistical confidence in the rule's anti-gaming properties. Historical records reflect cooperative operator behavior; adversarial cases test deliberate obfuscation (forged attestations, delayed access, omitted vendor signatures). If synthetic validation shows <5% false-negative rate (rule detects 95% of seeded gaming), but Phase One operators employ novel gaming tactics (e.g., colluding vendors, multi-step equipment swaps), actual Phase-One false-negative rate could reach 10–15%, pushing false-positive rate to 15–20% via compensation effects. Impact: adjudication load surges from 15 to 30–50 cases per month by Month 7 (2027-05-08), exceeding the 5-person adjudication unit capacity and aging discrepancies past day 21 automatic impaired-confidence threshold. Recommendation: design adversarial synthetic cases with red-team input (Month 4 = 2027-02-08) using at least 40–50 scenarios per site (proposed threshold; a second cohort is run within the Month 4.5–5.5 window or the clock slips and the 2-week gate-slip procedure applies) spanning multiple gaming modes (vendor collusion, record backdating, maintenance delays, substitution with partial matching headers); validate false-negative rate <10% and false-positive rate within 7–13% before Phase One clock or trigger adjudication surge staffing pre-positioning.

  3. Reciprocal-Access Parity Definition Remains Unspecified; 'Parity ≥85%' Has No Operationalized Measurement Method, Creating Risk of Post-Hoc Dispute Over Whether the Criterion Was Met. The plan lists 'reciprocal-access parity at least 85%' (proposed threshold) as one of the five scored Go criteria but marks the definition as TBD (to be determined). Without a pre-agreed quantitative parity metric (e.g., inspector-hour balance within 10%, exercise-opportunity symmetry, data-access turnaround parity, challenge-outcome agreement rate), either co-chair can claim the other violated parity if Phase-One results are unfavorable, disputed as justification to demand Modify over Go. Impact: if detection rates are 72% (marginally Go-defensible at lower confidence bound), but one country claims asymmetric access gave the other side an advantage, renegotiation of the parity metric could retroactively downgrade the Go verdict to Modify. This consumes 2–4 weeks of the final decision window (Month 9–9.5 = 2027-07-08 to 2027-07-23) with dispute adjudication instead of final verdict publication. Recommendation: define parity operationally before Month 3 (2027-01-08) matched-pair approval using four measurable indicators—inspector-hour balance ≥90% (on-site hours per country per month), exercise-distribution parity (unreported arrival and substitution tests evenly split across day/night shifts), data-access turnaround ≤3 days average, and challenge-outcome agreement ≥80%—and lock the definition, aggregation method and operator commitments in the bilateral instrument before Month 3 (2027-01-08), keeping Month 5.5 (2027-03-23) only for dry-run confirmation; report weekly parity dashboard during Phase One so asymmetry is visible in real time and does not become a post-hoc renegotiation weapon.

Review 9: Stakeholder Feedback

  1. Bilateral Co-Chair Commitment to Binding Verdict Thresholds and No-Amendment Clause; Without Executive Sign-Off, Post-Hoc Renegotiation Risk Is 40–60%. Critical because: if thresholds (Go: at least 4 of 5 criteria including detection and parity; Modify: 3 of 5; Stop: 2 or fewer) and mechanical scoring rule remain advisory planning documents rather than locked bilateral-instrument law (method by Month 1 = 2026-11-08, numeric thresholds by Month 5.5 = 2027-03-23), either co-chair can contest the verdict if Phase-One results land in an ambiguous confidence-interval band (e.g., 70% ±15% spanning 55–85%). Quantified impact: 4–8 week verdict-renegotiation delay consumes the final decision window (Month 9–9.5 = 2027-07-08 to 2027-07-23), displacing the scheduled Go/Modify/Stop publication and inviting legislative rejection in at least one country as a perceived capitulation. Recommendation: obtain written co-chair attestation by Month 1 (2026-11-08) that verdict thresholds will be embedded in the bilateral instrument as non-negotiable procedural law and that both governments accept Modify as a binding real outcome when confidence intervals straddle thresholds; publish unclassified thresholds and mechanical-scoring logic by Month 6 (2027-04-08) so legislatures see the objective verdict machinery before exercises begin.

  2. Operator Participation Confidence and Mid-Phase-One Access-Denial Risk Mitigation; Statements of Cooperation Lack Enforceability and Operator Compensation Ceiling Clarity. Critical because: Operator Statements of Cooperation (locked before Month 3 = 2027-01-08 matched-pair approval; binding status stated in the instrument) may lack enforceability; a US hyperscale operator citing customer-confidentiality constraints could restrict staging-area access mid-Phase-One (Month 7–8 = 2027-05-08 to 2027-06-08), reducing detection opportunities by 15–25% at that site. Quantified impact: asymmetric detection across paired sites (e.g., 75% at unrestricted site vs. 55% at restricted site) breaches reciprocal-access parity (proposed ≥85%) and triggers a hard Stop condition; estimated sunk cost USD 30–50M in unused exercise and personnel budgets; timeline loss 2–4 weeks investigating and adjudicating the parity breach. Recommendation: obtain binding operator participation agreements embedded in the bilateral instrument by Month 1 (2026-11-08) with domestic home-government enforceability; confirm operator compensation ceiling (USD 30–50M per site, mapped to the 1,000M site-prep envelope) and document operator buy-in via signed Statements of Cooperation locked before Month 3 (2027-01-08), with Month 4.5–5.5 for dry-run confirmation; conduct a pre-Phase-One dry-run exercise (Month 4.5 = 2027-02-23) at each site to validate operator cooperation and access-denial risk before the clock starts.

  3. Neutral Facility Site Finalization and Key-Custody Ceremony Validation; OPEN Decision (Geneva or Singapore) and Unrehear­sed Recovery Procedure Block Ledger Operationalization. Critical because: facility site selection (Month 1 = 2026-11-08) and hardening (ISO 27001, Tempest equivalent by Month 3 = 2027-01-08) remain unresolved; key-custody ceremony is planned for Month 4 (2027-02-08) but no recovery rehearsal is scheduled until Month 5 (2027-03-08). Quantified impact: a 4–6 week facility slip costs USD 30–50M, funded from free contingency (not the 50–100M compression reserve), and jeopardizes entry certification (Month 5.5 = 2027-03-23) and key-recovery validation before Phase One. If key recovery is untested and a key is lost mid-Phase-One (Month 7 = 2027-05-08), both co-chairs must invoke 8–24 hour recovery procedures unvalidated, creating evidence-custody gaps and ledger divergences unresolved within 72-hour reconciliation target (proposed threshold). Recommendation: designate both Geneva and Singapore host-country nominees and pre-stage procurement at both sites by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23); lock site selection by Month 1 (2026-11-08) and escalate facility construction to achieve hardening certification by Month 3 (2027-01-08); schedule and conduct full key-recovery dress rehearsal (Month 5 = 2027-03-08) with both countries' key-custody officers and produce a bilateral Ledger-Recovery Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) locked by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23).

Review 10: Changed Assumptions

  1. Assumption: Both Countries' Domestic Legislatures Will Ratify Appropriations and Access Authority by Month 2 (2026-12-08) Without Amendment Pressure or Veto. Original planning assumed synchronized legislative approvals in both countries on a 2-month timeline (Months 0–2 = 2026-10-08 to 2026-12-08). Risk revision: US Senate arms-control treaty oversight and Chinese Standing Committee legislative review may introduce amendment demands (e.g., stricter IP-protection language, inspector-immunity carve-outs, or cost-sharing revisions), potentially delaying appropriations past Month 2 (2026-12-08). Impact: 4–6 week legislative delay consumes USD 50–100M of the compression reserve and pushes the first tranche release to Month 3–3.5 (2027-01-08 to 2027-02-08), compressing the vetting and training window (Months 2–5 = 2026-12-08 to 2027-03-08) by 25%. Personnel certification (80% target by Month 5 = 2027-03-08) risks falling to 60–65%, undermining deployment readiness by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23). Interaction: legislative slippage cascades into adjudication staffing shortfall (fewer trained specialists ready by Phase One) and weakens shift coverage (fewer certified inspectors per shift). Recommendation: obtain bilateral preliminary legislative-language concurrence from both countries' foreign/defense ministry and finance committees by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23); identify likely amendment triggers (IP language, liability) and pre-negotiate compromise text before formal submission to legislatures by Month 1 (2026-11-08).

  2. Assumption: Frontier-Computing Hardware Refresh Cycles Will Remain Stable Over Entry Conditions and Phase One (9.5 Months Total); No Major New Generational Release Will Render the Covered-Equipment Schedule Obsolete. Original planning froze the covered-equipment schedule (confidential, technology-neutral, versioned) by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23) and locked it for Phase One (Months 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08). Hardware realities: GPU and AI-accelerator refresh cycles are 12–18 months (NVIDIA, AMD, Cerebras); a major new generation (e.g., post-H200 architecture) released during Months 5–9 (2027-03-08 to 2027-07-08) could render performance-band classifications in the locked schedule non-comparable or obsolete. Impact: if a major hardware release occurs in Month 7–8 (2027-05-08 to 2027-06-08) mid-Phase-One, one country may claim new equipment is 'frontier-relevant' and outside the locked schedule, or claim the schedule is now stale and non-representative. This triggers a formal discrepancy dispute (equipment classification ambiguity) aged against the 21–28 day impaired-confidence thresholds, consuming 3–4 weeks of adjudication and delaying final verdict by 2–4 weeks. Interaction: schedule-classification disputes during Phase One compound with evidence-rule miscalibration (false positives 15–20%) to overflow adjudication capacity (30–50 cases per month instead of 15 planned), creating a cascade of automatic partial suspensions. Recommendation: survey Tier-1 vendors (NVIDIA, AMD, Cerebras, Graphcore, Cerebras) by Month 1 (2026-11-08) to confirm hardware-release roadmaps through Month 9.5 (2027-07-23); if a major release is scheduled for Months 5–9 (2027-03-08 to 2027-07-08), negotiate a 'schedule amendment exception' clause in the bilateral instrument (Month 1 = 2026-11-08) allowing single-case re-classification of new equipment within 10 days without double-key deadlock.

  3. Assumption: Operator Site Availability Will Not Require Maintenance Shutdowns or Unplanned Access Restrictions During Entry Conditions (Months 0–5 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-03-08) or Phase One (Months 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08). Original planning allocated staging-area access windows (48-hour operator notice for exercises, immediate for unreported-arrival injections) and assumed operators will cooperate with site-selection audits (Month 3 = 2027-01-08), statement-of-cooperation sign-off (before Month 3 = 2027-01-08 matched-pair approval), and full-strength inspector deployment (Months 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08) without critical-system maintenance or emergency shutdowns. Risk revision: hyperscale datacenters experience unplanned maintenance (hardware failures, security updates, BIOS patches, power-infrastructure work); state-operated Chinese sites face routine infrastructure maintenance that is not negotiable. If a major maintenance window (estimated 2–4 days per site per quarter) conflicts with exercise windows (scheduled for Months 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08 at 3 per month = 9 windows per site), operator may request 1–2 exercise deferrals per site. Impact: exercise deferrals compress the 54-exercise load into fewer available windows (e.g., 48 exercises if 6 are deferred), reducing replicates per event type from 6–8 to 5–6, widening confidence intervals from ±12% (pooled) to ±15%, and pushing borderline detection rates into the Modify band (e.g., 70% ±15% straddles the Go threshold). Interaction: unplanned site downtime coinciding with entry-gate delays (8-week slip, Phase One compressed to 50–60 days) forces further exercise compression and statistical ambiguity. Recommendation: secure written operator maintenance calendars (12-month outlook) from all 3 sites by Month 2 (2026-12-08); designate exercise-blackout dates in the schedule by Month 4 (2027-02-08) and publish the locked exercise schedule by Month 5 (2027-03-08) to give operators maximum notice and to allow rescheduling conflicts to surface before Phase One clock (Month 6 = 2027-04-08).

Review 11: Budget Clarifications

  1. Operator Compensation Ceiling and Payment Schedule Ambiguity; USD 1,000M Site-Prep Envelope Must Cover Both Site Hardening and Operator/Vendor Payments. The plan allocates USD 500M per country for site preparation and operator compensation within the 1,000M envelope, averaging USD 167M per site (1,000M / 6 sites). However, no documented operator-compensation baseline exists from bilateral precedent, and the plan does not specify whether USD 167M/site covers both access costs (staff time, facility support) and production-disruption risk. If a US hyperscale operator demands USD 50–75M (citing customer-confidentiality compliance and maintenance scheduling), and a Chinese site demands equivalent USD 50–75M, such demands fit within the USD 167M per site ceiling; operator cost is unquantified (estimate) until operator cost proposals exist, and could leave little for the remaining sites or for site-hardening/infrastructure costs. Impact: if costs exceed the ceiling, site preparation forces either site exclusion (reducing from 3 to 2 pairs, compressing exercise load and widening confidence intervals from ±12% to ±15%) or contingency draw of USD 50–100M (11–25% of free contingency USD 400–450M), leaving <USD 300M for Phase One operations, adjudication surge, or ledger recovery. Recommendation: obtain binding operator cost proposals from all 6 candidate sites by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23); lock operator-compensation ceiling (USD 30–50M per site, proposed) in the bilateral instrument by Month 2 (2026-12-08); allocate separate line-item budgets for operator compensation (USD 30–50M per site ceiling, 90–150M per country) vs. site hardening (the remainder) within the 500M per-country site-prep envelope by Month 2 (2026-12-08).

  2. Entry-Condition and Phase-One Ramp-Up Personnel Costs Unbudgeted; Full-Strength Staffing USD 86–115M Over Months 5.5–9.5 (2027-03-23 to 2027-07-23) But Early Recruitment and Training Costs (Months 0–5 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-03-08) Are Not Itemized Against the 750M Personnel Envelope. Personnel cost estimate: approximately USD 29M per month at full strength (360 staff × USD 80k loaded per person-month); the 3-month Phase One window at full strength ≈ USD 86M, and Month 5.5 (2027-03-23) to Month 9.5 (2027-07-23) (4 months) ≈ USD 115M. However, ramp-up cost—recruitment (Months 0–4 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-02-08), vetting (Months 1–4 = 2026-11-08 to 2027-02-08), and training (Months 3–5 = 2027-01-08 to 2027-03-08)—is marked TBD. Estimated ramp-up cost: ~USD 60–80M (partial staffing, consultant trainers, dual-cohort courses) is not accounted for separately. Impact: if ramp-up costs total USD 70M and Phase One costs USD 115M, total personnel spend ≈ USD 185M against the 750M envelope leaves USD 565M for all other personnel roles (specialist units, adjudication, CI, legal, translation), retention bonuses USD 15–22.5M, and translation/audit surge. A 10% personnel cost overrun (USD 18.5M) consumes USD 18.5M of the 400M free contingency. Recommendation: itemize personnel costs by phase (Months 0–5 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-03-08 ramp-up vs. Months 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08 Phase One vs. Month 9.5+ conclusion) and lock the per-phase budget by Month 2 (2026-12-08); confirm that retention-bonus allocation (USD 15–22.5M for 12-month tenure) is mapped within the 750M personnel envelope, not as a contingency draw; track actual personnel costs weekly starting Month 0 (2026-10-08) and flag any envelope overrun >10% by Month 4 (2027-02-08) for rebalancing before Phase One begins.

  3. Post-Phase-One Funding Route and Modify-Rework Scope Are OPEN; Phase-One Verdict May Default to Modify Due to Ambiguous Intervals, Committing Both Countries to Undefined Phase-Two Budget and Timeline Without Pre-Authorization. The plan specifies four tranches (25/25/30/20% = USD 625M/625M/750M/500M per country), with the final 500M tranche (Month 9.2–9.5 = 2027-07-14 to 2027-07-23) released on Go/Modify verdict. However, 'Modify-directed rework' and any Phase Two are marked OPEN funding decisions. If Phase One yields Modify (e.g., 70% detection ±15% confidence interval straddling the 70% Go threshold), the plan does not specify whether: (a) the fourth tranche (USD 500M per country) is withheld pending rework authorization, (b) rework is pre-budgeted within the existing USD 5B or requires new appropriations, or (c) Phase Two is a separate funding cycle entirely. Impact: ambiguity creates political leverage for renegotiation mid-verdict (either co-chair can demand post-hoc threshold adjustment or rework specification in exchange for approving the final tranche release). If Modify outcome triggers a 4–8 week rework-definition negotiation, final verdict publication slips from Month 9.2–9.5 (2027-07-14 to 2027-07-23) to Month 10–11 (2027-08-08 to 2027-09-08), delaying legislatures' approval and risking political withdrawal in the interim. Recommendation: pre-authorize and define the post-Phase-One decision path by Month 8 (2027-06-08): specify whether Modify triggers rework within the existing USD 5B (estimated USD 250–400M for extended Phase One or Phase Two pilot) or requires new appropriations; lock the final tranche release logic in the bilateral instrument by Month 2 (2026-12-08) so tranche 4 is released on verdict publication (not pending rework scope agreement), separating the verdict from funding leverage; publish unclassified post-Phase-One funding decision framework by Month 8 (2027-06-08) so legislatures see whether a Modify outcome commits them to rework before the final verdict is announced.

Review 12: Role Definitions

  1. Independent Timekeeper: Report Deadlock Clock Status Weekly and Escalate Automatic Suspension Triggers. The plan specifies an independent timekeeper (one per country, reporting to both co-chairs) tracking discrepancy age and triggering automatic partial suspension at day 14 and impaired-confidence flags at days 21–28 (proposed threshold). Lack of clarity: no explicit authority defined for who certifies the clock timestamp, whether either co-chair can contest the timekeeper's age calculation, or whether the timekeeper has power to enforce suspension logging in the ledger. Impact if unresolved: a contested timestamp (e.g., one co-chair claims clock should reset on a procedural waiver) delays suspension by 2–4 weeks, aging discrepancies past the impaired-confidence threshold without automatic escalation, violating the plan's 'non-negotiable' suspension design. Recommendation: embed explicit timekeeper authority in the bilateral instrument (Month 1 = 2026-11-08) specifying: timekeeper certifies age monthly, publishes unclassified dashboard every Monday, 09:00 CET; suspension triggers automatically with ledger annotation at day 14 and 21–28 without co-chair discretion; any co-chair contesting the age must invoke a formal double-key variance request within 24 hours, logged and published.

  2. Adjudication Panel Chair: Convene Advisory Panel Within 10 Days; Deliver Non-Binding Recommendation; Escalate to Co-Chairs Within 7-Day Total Deadlock Window. The deadlock procedure specifies an adjudication panel (3 specialists per country) convened by day 10, delivering an advisory by day 15, and co-chair decision by day 18 (proposed threshold). Lack of clarity: no named or pre-appointed panel chair is specified; no procedure defined for breaking deadlock within the panel itself if members disagree on evidence classification; no escalation path if the panel's recommendation is rejected by a co-chair. Impact if unresolved: panel convening is delayed 3–5 days waiting for a chair decision; internal panel disputes consume 2–4 days of the 5-day advisory window; a co-chair rejection without a binding alternative leaves the discrepancy unresolved past day 21 impaired-confidence, triggering automatic suspension without a clear rationale. Recommendation: pre-appoint a neutral panel chair (third-country senior technical specialist, pre-approved by both co-chairs by Month 0.5 = 2026-10-23); embed binding panel-decision protocol in the bilateral instrument (Month 1 = 2026-11-08) specifying chair convenes and votes within the 5-day advisory window; publish all panel recommendations (even rejected ones) in the ledger so either co-chair's override is documented and visible to legislatures.

  3. External Escalation Authority: Invoke Emergency Co-Chair Summit Within 48 Hours if Any Entry Gate Slips Over 2 Weeks; Authorize Scope Reduction (2 Pairs, Full 90 Days) Within 5-Day Decision Window. The plan invokes an 'external escalation authority' with power to convene an emergency summit and decide scope reduction (proposed threshold) if entry gates slip >2 weeks. Lack of clarity: no specific third-country official, deputy co-chair, or decision-making panel is named; no pre-authorized funding (compression reserve USD 50–100M) is explicitly allocated to the authority's operations; no procedure defined for how the authority validates that a gate has slipped >2 weeks vs. encountering recoverable delays. Impact if unresolved: entry-gate slippage is reported informally, disputed between co-chairs, and consumed by negotiation; no external body convenes to force the scope-reduction decision; Phase One is compressed from 90 to 45–60 days by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23), statistical confidence widens from ±12% to ±18–20%, and verdict credibility collapses. Recommendation: appoint a named neutral third-country official (or explicitly authorized co-chair deputies) as External Escalation Authority by Month 0 (2026-10-08); embed binding authority in the bilateral instrument (Month 1 = 2026-11-08) to convene summit within 48 hours of gate slip >2 weeks and to decide scope reduction (funded from compression reserve) within 5 days; require weekly entry-milestone reporting to the authority so gate delays are transparent and trigger escalation automatically, not via co-chair negotiation.

Review 13: Timeline Dependencies

  1. Evidence-Rule Lock-Down (Month 4.5 = 2027-02-23) Must Precede Pilot Exercise (Month 5 = 2027-03-08) to Enable Baseline Calibration. If the confidential evidence-weighting rule is placed in escrow after the pilot exercise, pilot results cannot be scored against the locked rule, invalidating calibration validation. Impact: adjudication capacity remains unvalidated; false-positive rates may reach 15–20% instead of 7–13% target, overloading the 15-case/month capacity by Month 7 (2027-05-08). Interaction: miscalibrated rule compounds with adjudication backlog, aging discrepancies past day 21 automatic impaired-confidence and cascading partial suspensions. Recommendation: lock rule in versioned escrow by Month 4.5 (2027-02-23), execute pilot by Month 5 (2027-03-08), and deliver Calibration Confidence Memo by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23) before entry certification.

  2. Neutral Facility Hardening (Target Month 3 = 2027-01-08) Gates Key-Custody Ceremony (Month 4 = 2027-02-08) and Recovery Rehearsal (Month 5 = 2027-03-08); 4-Week Facility Slip Compresses Pre-Clock Calibration by 25%. If facility site selection slips to Month 1.5 (2026-11-23) instead of Month 1 (2026-11-08), hardening certification is delayed to Month 3.5–4 (2027-02-08 to 2027-03-08), pushing key-recovery rehearsal into the pilot exercise window (Month 5 = 2027-03-08) or eliminating it. Impact: unvalidated key recovery creates 8–24 hour ledger-custody gap mid-Phase-One with no tested recovery procedure; estimated cost USD 5–10M for emergency re-certification. Interaction: facility delay cascades into compressed pre-clock calibration (rule, threshold lock-down, entry certification) and reduces time for bilateral adjustment if validation reveals miscalibration. Recommendation: designate backup neutral-facility site by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23) and pre-stage procurement at both locations; lock site decision by Month 1 (2026-11-08); complete hardening by Month 3 (2027-01-08).

  3. Inspector Recruitment (Months 0–4 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-02-08) and Security-Clearance Vetting (Months 1–4 = 2026-11-08 to 2027-02-08) Must Complete Before Training Ramp-Up (Months 3–5 = 2027-01-08 to 2027-03-08); 4-Week Recruitment Slip Reduces Certified Personnel by 20–30% by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23). If recruitment starts late (Month 2 = 2026-12-08 instead of Month 0 = 2026-10-08), vetting pipeline misses the Month 2 (2026-12-08) 50% clearance milestone; only 60–70% of inspectors are certified by Month 5 (2027-03-08) instead of 80% target, leaving ~30–40 inspector shortfall at Phase One start (Month 6 = 2027-04-08). Impact: shift coverage falls below 6-per-shift minimum; unreported-arrival detection rate drops from 70%+ to 50–60% due to predictable low-coverage windows. Interaction: staffing gap cascades with entry-gate delays to compress Phase One from 90 to 50–60 days, reducing exercise sample size from 54 to 36–48, widening confidence intervals from ±12% to ±18%, making Go verdict indefensible. Recommendation: launch recruitment pipeline at Month 0 (2026-10-08) in parallel with site nomination and vendor outreach; complete 80% certification by Month 5 (2027-03-08); activate surge cohort training (Months 2–4 = 2026-12-08 to 2027-02-08) to protect against attrition.

Review 14: Financial Strategy

  1. Phase-Two Funding Path and Rework Authorization Remain Open; Modify Verdict Triggers Undefined Appropriations Decision, Risking 4–8 Week Delay in Final Decision or Political Withdrawal. The plan allocates USD 5.0 billion across entry conditions and Phase One (Months 0–9 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-07-08) with fourth tranche (USD 500M per country) released on Go/Modify verdict (Month 9.2–9.5 = 2027-07-14 to 2027-07-23). However, post-Phase-One funding is marked OPEN: Modify outcome may require rework (extended Phase One, additional exercises, threshold recalibration) estimated at USD 250–400M, but whether this is pre-authorized within the existing USD 5B or requires new appropriations is unspecified. Impact: if Modify outcome triggers a rework-definition negotiation, final decision slips 4–8 weeks past Month 9.5 (2027-07-23), delaying tranche-4 release and inviting legislative withdrawal pressure in both countries. Interaction: Modify probability is high (estimated 40–60% if intervals straddle a threshold or only 3 of 5 criteria are met due to entry-gate delays or evidence-rule miscalibration). Recommendation: pre-authorize and lock post-Phase-One decision path by Month 8 (2027-06-08) specifying whether Modify rework is funded from existing USD 5B (estimated USD 250–400M reallocation within envelopes) or needs supplemental appropriations; publish framework by Month 8 (2027-06-08) so legislatures know funding commitment before verdict.

  2. Operator Compensation Ceiling (USD 30–50M Per Site Proposed) Has No Binding Legal Enforcement or Contract Template; Mid-Phase-One Operator Cost Escalation Could Strain the 1,000M Site-Prep Envelope (Overrun Unquantified, Estimate). The plan allocates USD 500M per country (1,000M total) for site preparation and operator compensation across 3 paired sites (6 total). Cost baseline: USD 167M per site (1,000M / 6), but no operator cost proposals have been obtained from candidate sites, and no ceiling or payment-schedule language is embedded in operator Statements of Cooperation. Impact: if a US hyperscale operator demands USD 75M (citing customer-confidentiality and production-disruption compliance) and a Chinese site demands equivalent USD 75M, the amounts remain within the USD 167M per site ceiling, but the sub-line split must be set accordingly. Operator cost is unquantified (estimate) until operator cost proposals exist. Interaction: operator budget overrun consumes 12–25% of the 400–450M free contingency, limiting surge capacity for adjudication, ledger recovery or entry-gate acceleration. Recommendation: obtain binding operator cost proposals from all 6 candidate sites by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23) and lock operator-compensation ceiling (USD 30–50M per site) in the bilateral instrument by Month 2 (2026-12-08); allocate separate line items: operator compensation at the ceiling (USD 90–150M per country), site hardening as the remainder, as a sub-envelope within the 500M per-country site-prep envelope; overrun unquantified (estimate) until operator cost proposals exist.

  3. Contingency Reserve Structure (USD 50–100M Compression Reserve vs. USD 400–450M Free Contingency) Creates Ambiguity on What Triggers Draw-Down Authorization; Mid-Phase-One Surge Costs May Consume Both Reserves Without Clear Escalation Sequence. The plan allocates USD 500M total contingency (10% of USD 5B budget) with USD 50–100M earmarked as 'compression reserve' (for accelerated entry-condition negotiation) and USD 400–450M remaining as 'free contingency' for phase-specific overruns. However, no integrated draw-down authorization procedure is specified: unclear whether adjudication surge (USD 2–3M for 8–12 additional specialists), ledger-recovery incident (USD 5–10M for emergency cryptographic re-certification) or personnel-training overrun (estimated USD 60–80M ramp-up cost, TBD) draws from compression reserve, free contingency, or triggers supplemental appropriations. Impact: ambiguity creates mid-phase delays while co-chairs negotiate draw authority; if adjudication surge (USD 2–3M) plus training overrun (USD 10–20M) plus evidence-rule re-validation (USD 3–5M) total USD 20–30M by Month 7 (2027-05-08), and these draws are unauthorized, co-chairs may block them and accept unmitigated adjudication backlog (30–50 cases per month vs. 15 planned). Interaction: unautho rized contingency draws cascade with evidence-rule miscalibration (false positives 15–20%) to overflow adjudication, age discrepancies past day 21, and trigger automatic impaired-confidence suspensions. Recommendation: establish Joint Budget Authority (one officer per country) by Month 0 (2026-10-08) with pre-authorized draw limits: compression reserve (USD 50–100M) for entry-condition acceleration (signed bilateral authorization by Month 0.5 = 2026-10-23); free contingency draws (adjudication surge, ledger recovery, training) within limits set by both co-chairs in the instrument and executed jointly by both countries' budget officers; draws beyond those limits trigger scope-reduction planning or supplemental-appropriations decision.

Review 15: Motivation Factors

  1. Transparent Progress Metrics and Weekly Public KPI Dashboard Build Bilateral Trust and Sustain Executive Engagement. Motivation falters when progress is opaque or contested; weekly published KPI dashboard (every Monday, 09:00 CET) reporting discrepancy-age distribution, contingency burn (% drawn), personnel certification status, and exercise completion rate makes progress measurable to both co-chairs and legislatures. Without visible metrics, entry-gate slippage or adjudication backlog (30–50 cases per month vs. 15 planned) go unnoticed until Month 7 (2027-05-08), at which point USD 100–200M contingency is already consumed and credibility is damaged. Recommendation: establish Joint Finance Authority and Program Risk Officer by Month 0 (2026-10-08); publish unclassified dashboard weekly; escalate any metric >2 standard deviations from baseline within 5 days.

  2. Pre-Authorization of Scope-Reduction Backstop (2 Pairs, Full 90 Days) Removes Political Stalling and Protects Psychological Commitment to the 90-Day Phase One Window. Motivation collapses when entry-gate delays consume weeks in political negotiation over whether to extend or compress timelines. Without pre-authorized scope reduction, bilateral teams waste energy arguing ('extend to preserve rigor' vs. 'compress to meet the 90-day clock') rather than executing. Impact if unstated: entry-condition delays are negotiated case-by-case, consuming 3–5 weeks per slip; cumulative 8-week slippage exhausts USD 100–200M contingency (20–40% of contingency; 22–50% of free contingency USD 400–450M) and compresses Phase One to 50–60 days, degrading statistical confidence (±12% to ±18–20%), undermining Go verdict credibility. Recommendation: pre-authorize scope-reduction authority by Month 0 (2026-10-08) with explicit co-chair approval; publish scope-reduction decision framework by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23) so entry slippage triggers mechanical 5-day decision (reduce to 2 pairs) rather than renegotiation.

  3. Bilateral Operator Compensation Agreements and Binding Site Access Commitments (Locked by Month 3 = 2027-01-08) Prevent Mid-Phase-One Withdrawal and Preserve Inspector Morale and Deployment Continuity. Motivation of 360 deployed inspectors erodes if operator access restrictions occur mid-Phase-One (Month 7–8 = 2027-05-08 to 2027-06-08), reducing shift coverage from 6 to 3–4 per shift and rendering half the detection work unexecutable. Operator withdrawal at a single site reduces exercise load from 54 to 48 or 36 (depending on fallback), widening confidence intervals from ±12% to ±15–18%, pushing Go verdict to Modify and wasting 4 months of personnel deployment. Impact: 360 inspectors morale-degrade if their work is made non-credible by asymmetric site access. Recommendation: embed binding operator Statements of Cooperation in the bilateral instrument by Month 1 (2026-11-08) with home-government enforcement, lock operator compensation ceiling (USD 30–50M per site) by Month 2 (2026-12-08), and conduct pre-Phase-One dry-run at all 3 sites by Month 4.5 (2027-02-23) to validate cooperation before the clock starts.

Review 16: Automation Opportunities

  1. Automate Weekly KPI Dashboard and Contingency-Burn Tracking Using Bilateral Ledger Data Feed. The plan requires manual weekly reporting (contingency %, discrepancy-age distribution, personnel certification, envelope reconciliation) by the Joint Finance Authority and Program Risk Officer. Automated extraction from the tamper-evident ledger (hourly digest sync, event logging) and personnel/vetting database could generate unclassified dashboard outputs within 2 hours of reporting deadline (every Monday, 09:00 CET). Estimated savings: 40–60 person-hours per month (2–3 FTE) from manual data aggregation and reconciliation; reduces reporting latency from 3 days to 2 hours, enabling real-time escalation if contingency draw exceeds 30% threshold. Implementation: establish secure API integration between ledger infrastructure and dashboard platform by Month 3 (2027-01-08); validate data feeds during facility operational dry-run (Month 5 = 2027-03-08).

  2. Standardize and Automate Evidence-Filter Certification and Dispute Resolution Workflow Using Coded Schema and AI-Assisted Redaction Verification. Current filter process: independent auditor reviews 100% of packages manually (2–3 days per package × 54 exercises = 108–162 person-days). Coded language-neutral evidence schema (timestamps, serial numbers, arrival/departure, maintenance) enables automated redaction verification: system checks that filtered package preserves all event-relevant fields while redacting network topology, architecture, weights, source code. Estimated savings: reduce manual certification to 5–10% sampling (quality assurance only) instead of 100%, freeing ~150 person-days for Phase One; accelerate turnaround from 2–3 days to 24 hours routine, 4 hours for disputes. Implementation: design schema by Month 3 (2027-01-08); prototype automation during pilot exercise (Month 5 = 2027-03-08); deploy at Phase One start (Month 6 = 2027-04-08).

  3. Automate Discrepancy-Age Tracking and Automatic Suspension Ledger Annotation Using Pre-Registered Clock Logic. The independent timekeeper manually calculates elapsed days per discrepancy, flags cases approaching day 14 (partial suspension) and day 21–28 (impaired-confidence), and publishes the dashboard weekly. Automated clock engine embedded in the ledger infrastructure can timestamp case opening, calculate age, compare to thresholds (day 14, 21, 28), and auto-annotate ledger entries with suspension events and impaired-confidence flags when thresholds trigger. Estimated savings: eliminate ~20–30 person-hours per month of timekeeper calculation and reporting; reduce decision latency from 5–7 days to real-time flagging; prevent disputes over clock validity by making timestamps cryptographically signed. Implementation: specify clock-automation logic in bilateral instrument (Month 1 = 2026-11-08); code into ledger infrastructure by Month 3 (2027-01-08); rehearse during key-recovery drill (Month 5 = 2027-03-08).

Q1: What does the 'Pragmatic Foundation: Reciprocal Proof with Controlled Risk' strategic pathway choose for the five critical decision levers, and why are these choices considered optimal for the Consortium?

A1: The pathway selects: (1) Confidential rotating evidence-weighting rule validated against blind outcomes (resists gaming without false-positive overload); (2) Automatic partial suspension at day 14, leaving unrelated verification running (keeps the mission alive under deadlock); (3) Cross-designed red-team challenges under independent referee (reciprocal trust, parity-building); (4) Provisional thresholds locked before Phase One, validated against pilot data (matches thin-data reality); (5) Compartmentalized inspectors with post-rotation debriefs (protects IP while enabling evidence collection). These choices balance rigor, reciprocity and workability—the core tension in a bilateral US–China mechanism.

Q2: Why does the plan mark 'reciprocal-access parity at least 85%' and 'post-Phase-One funding route' as OPEN items, and what is the consequence if these remain unresolved before entry certification (Month 5.5 = 2027-03-23)?

A2: Reciprocal-access parity lacks an operationalized measurement method (inspector-hour balance, exercise-opportunity symmetry, data-access turnaround, challenge-outcome agreement all proposed but not locked), so either co-chair can later claim asymmetry and contest the verdict. Post-Phase-One funding is undefined because Modify outcome may trigger rework (estimated USD 250–400M) but whether this is pre-authorized within the USD 5B or needs new appropriations is unspecified. Consequence: if unresolved, a Modify verdict (estimated 40–60% probability) triggers 4–8 week renegotiation over rework scope, delaying the final decision past Month 9.5 (2027-07-23) and inviting legislative withdrawal.

Q3: What is the difference between the 'compression reserve' (USD 50–100M) and the 'free contingency' (USD 400–450M) within the USD 500M total contingency, and how does an 8-week entry-condition delay consume both?

A3: The compression reserve (10–20% of USD 500M) is earmarked specifically for accelerated entry-gate negotiation, expedited vetting, and 24/7 task-force surge to prevent timeline slippage. The free contingency (80–90% of USD 500M, i.e., USD 400–450M) is for Phase-One operational overruns (adjudication surge, ledger recovery, training gaps). An 8-week entry-condition slip costs USD 100–200M (compressed timelines, parallel-track acceleration, extended negotiations), consuming 20–50% of the free contingency. If combined with mid-Phase-One adjudication miscalibration (USD 2–3M), ledger incident (USD 5–10M) and personnel overrun (estimated USD 10–20M), total contingency draw reaches 50–75%, leaving <USD 125–200M for final operations or Phase Two.

Q4: What is the relationship between the confidential evidence-weighting rule's false-positive rate (target ≤10%) and the planned adjudication capacity (15 cases per month), and what happens if the rule miscalibrates to 15–20% false positives?

A4: The rule's false-positive rate directly determines discrepancy volume. At 10% false positives across ~54 exercises and continuous monitoring, baseline caseload is ~15 discrepancies per month (manageable). If the rule deviates to 15–20% false positives (±5–10 points from target), caseload surges to 30–50 cases per month, overwhelming the 5-person adjudication unit per country (total 10). Discrepancies age past the 21-day automatic impaired-confidence threshold by Month 7 (2027-05-08), triggering partial suspensions of disputed functions. Cascading suspensions across multiple sites paralyze unrelated verification and force a Stop verdict by default (unresolved-caseload failure), not evidence quality.

Q5: The plan allocates approximately 180 full-time inspectors per country but assumes they can achieve 'minimum paired presence in staging and spare-inventory areas at all times.' Is this consistent with the stated work-hour rules (no inspector >48 hours per week), and what is the shortfall if 24/7 continuous presence is actually required?

A5: The 99-person inspection corps per country (baseline for 3 sites × 3 shifts × 6 positions per shift × 1.4 for 7-day coverage) assumes only 7-day coverage (one inspector working any given shift), not continuous 24/7 presence. Continuous presence at 40 hours per week per inspector would require ~300+ inspectors per country (a 3× multiplier), not 99. Consequence: unreported-arrival exercises (which depend on round-the-clock detection) become predictable to red teams—they can time injections to night shifts or shift boundaries when staffing is lowest. Detection rates for unreported arrival fall below the 70% Go threshold, pushing the verdict toward Modify or Stop regardless of other evidence.

Q6: The plan explicitly states that Phase One does 'not include estimates of total computing capacity, workload or model-weight verification, or hidden-facility detection.' Why are these boundaries set, and what are the strategic implications if either government later claims the Consortium failed to address these larger verification questions?

A6: The scope boundary (user constraint) restricts verification to declared-equipment changes at participating sites only, excluding capacity estimation, workload monitoring, and covert-facility detection. This is set because: (1) hidden-facility detection requires intelligence methods outside the inspectorate's mandate; (2) workload verification requires access to classified algorithms and operational parameters neither government will disclose; (3) capacity estimation rests on performance metrics vendors protect. Strategic implication: if Phase One succeeds (Go verdict) but one government later claims 'the Consortium does not verify total strategic capacity,' the mechanism loses perceived relevance to national-security policy, inviting political withdrawal or demands for Phase Two scope expansion that may be unfeasible.

Q7: The plan requires inspectors to be 'compartmentalized by role and site, with post-assignment debriefs and monitored cooling-off periods before any reassignment to other duties.' How does this constraint protect IP while maintaining verification credibility, and what is the ethical tension between compartmentalization and inspectors' right to privacy or free movement?

A7: Compartmentalization limits each inspector's knowledge to a single site and role (e.g., 'equipment-identity verifier at Site A'), preventing any individual from retaining a map of topology, workloads or infrastructure across sites. Post-rotation debriefs (4–6 hours, CI-led, mandatory) extract information on unusual access requests or data retention; 14-day cooling-off before reassignment prevents informal intelligence collection. Ethical tension: inspectors lose freedom of movement (cannot visit family or conduct personal business abroad during rotation), their communications are monitored (sealed phones only), and debriefing is intrusive (questions about what they observed). The plan accepts this as necessary counterintelligence discipline, but neither government has pre-committed to how compartmentalization rules survive legal challenge (labor law, privacy rights, due process) if an inspector later claims coercion or unjustified surveillance.

Q8: Why does the plan classify the evidence-weighting rule as 'confidential' and prohibit amendment during Phase One (Months 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08), and what is the risk if the rule is discovered to be systematically miscalibrated mid-test?

A8: The rule is confidential to prevent operators from learning which evidence combinations carry the most weight and gaming the system accordingly (e.g., if 'customs records' are weighted heavily, an operator might forge customs documents knowing other evidence will be downweighted). No-amendment clause during Phase One ensures all findings are scored against the same rule, preserving cross-site comparability. Risk if miscalibration surfaces mid-test: if false-positive rate reaches 15–20% instead of the 7–13% target, adjudication load surges from 15 to 30–50 cases per month by Month 7 (2027-05-08). The plan cannot adjust the rule (frozen by bilateral commitment), so adjudication capacity is exceeded, discrepancies age past 21 days, automatic impaired-confidence status cascades, and Phase One partially suspends itself. One government may then claim the other side's rule was deliberately miscalibrated to hide equipment changes, escalating into a bilateral accusation rather than a technical fix.

Q9: The plan designates hard Stop triggers for 'government shields an operator' and 'asymmetric inspector access,' but neither trigger is operationally defined. How would a co-chair prove shielding occurred, and what happens if both sides dispute whether asymmetry is deliberate or circumstantial?

A9: Shielding is proposed to mean: 'a government-directed refusal to grant inspector access inconsistent with the Operator Statement of Cooperation, or unexplained restrictions on staging-area entry or maintenance scheduling.' But no proof standard is specified: Is two delays sufficient, or must a pattern of >50% access-denial emerge? Asymmetric access similarly lacks threshold definition (proposed ≥85% parity, but measurement method is TBD). If one country claims shielding but the other claims 'legitimate operational emergency' or 'security upgrade,' adjudication of the Stop trigger itself requires deadlock resolution (co-chairs must agree). If they deadlock, automatic impaired-confidence (day 21) and partial suspension (day 14) apply to the shielding dispute, paralyzing Phase One before any Stop decision occurs.

Q10: The plan allocates USD 5.0 billion split 50/50 by country, but operator compensation is 'administered by each government and charged to its own USD 2.5B contribution.' If a US operator demands USD 50M but a Chinese site demands only USD 30M, does the US government absorb the USD 20M imbalance from its own tranche, creating domestic budget pressure and asymmetric commitment to Phase One?

A10: Yes. Operator compensation is domestic responsibility: each country pays its own operators from its USD 500M site-preparation envelope (projected USD 167M per site average across 3 sites, but highly variable). If US operator cost is USD 50M and Chinese is USD 30M, the US government absorbs the USD 20M gap within its USD 500M allocation. Asymmetric cost translates to asymmetric domestic political pressure: the US government may face legislative scrutiny ('why did we pay more?') and the Chinese government may face pressure ('why did the US pay more, suggesting our sites are less strategic?'). This domestic-political asymmetry can undermine the bilateral message of equal commitment, potentially affecting Go/Modify/Stop verdict perception if one side later claims the other underfunded or overvalued its participation.

A premortem assumes the project has failed and works backward to identify the most likely causes.

Assumptions to Kill

These foundational assumptions represent the project's key uncertainties. If proven false, they could lead to failure. Validate them immediately using the specified methods.

ID Assumption Validation Method Failure Trigger

Walk the contingency draw hierarchy with the Joint Budget Authority. Either government declines to pre-commit tranche release or draw authority in writing, or projects appropriation beyond Month 2 (2026-12-08) by more than 2 weeks.
A2 The confidential rotating evidence rule, validated on benign historical records plus synthetic cases, will hold false positives near 10% and keep discrepancies near 15 per month under adversarial operator behavior. Run the draft rule on 100-200 historical events per site and 20-30 adversarial synthetic cases per site. Model the caseload at 10%, 15% and 20% false positives. False positives fall outside 7-13%, false negatives on synthetic cases are 5% or higher, or modeled caseload exceeds 15 per month with no funded surge.
A3 Operators, host governments and vendors will give matched, symmetric access (including unreported-arrival injections) for all of Phase One without shielding, withdrawal or throttling. Hold dry-run exercises at each candidate site. Obtain operator Statements of Cooperation and 12-month maintenance calendars. Measure staging access time against the 4-hour baseline. A4 The neutral facility (Geneva or Singapore) can be sited, hardened and staffed by Month 3 (2027-01-08), and dual-share key ceremonies and ledger hosting there will run without a host-country or custody chokepoint. Open parallel host-country talks with both candidates. Request written timelines for permits and hardening. Schedule a key-ceremony rehearsal slot at each candidate. Neither host confirms a signed MOU by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23), or certified hardening is projected after Month 3 (2027-01-08) by more than 4 weeks (estimate).
A5 About 180 full-time staff per country (estimate) can be recruited, vetted and certified (80% by Month 5 = 2027-03-08) and held through 4-month rotations without breaching counterintelligence rules or coverage minimums. Audit both clearance systems for throughput. Run a pilot training cohort. Simulate the rotation roster against the 6-position shift minimum and the 48-hour weekly limit. Projected certification by Month 5 (2027-03-08) is below 80%, vetting attrition exceeds 20% (proposed threshold), or the roster cannot fill 6 positions per shift.
A6 A Modify or ambiguous verdict will be accepted by both governments and legislatures as a real, binding outcome, with the 20% final tranche released on publication and not used as leverage. Obtain written positions on tranche 4 and on the post-Phase funding route (OPEN). Collect written vendor positions by Month 3 (2027-01-08). Map each refusal to the rung that can finish before Month 6 (2027-04-08), given 8-12 weeks per rung. Compute the share of scheduled equipment left unverifiable or excluded. Projected unverifiable or excluded equipment exceeds 5% overall or 10% at any site (proposed threshold), or two or more Tier-1 vendors refuse all rungs.

Run a 48-hour tabletop breach case with both CI officers. Time the 48-hour investigation, 72-hour recommendation and 7-day decision. Obtain written confirmation from both CI agencies and legal offices that the fast-track is lawful domestically. Either government cannot legally accept the 7-day adjudication timeline, the tabletop exceeds 7 days, or baseline vetting flags a sustained breach among more than 1% of candidates (proposed threshold).
A9 Domestic legislatures, media and public opinion in both countries will tolerate reciprocal foreign inspection of frontier-computing sites for the full entry and Phase One period without forcing withdrawal over sovereignty or competitiveness concerns. Brief the oversight committees of both countries with the unclassified summary by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23). Record written positions and monitor public and press framing for sovereignty concessions. A committee in either country conditions funding or access authority on changes to inspector immunity, IP language or scope, or hostile framing prompts a formal withdrawal motion before Month 6 (2027-04-08).

Failure Scenarios and Mitigation Plans

Each scenario below links to a root-cause assumption and includes a detailed failure story, early warning signs, measurable tripwires, a response playbook, and a stop rule to guide decision-making.

FM2 The Flood of False Alarms Technical/Logistical A2 Bilateral Arms-Control Verification Lead CRITICAL (16/25)
