Contradictions between the core documents, after repair.

Consistency: first pass found 3 high / 6 medium / 0 low contradictions. Repair: round 1: 33 edits → 2 high / 5 medium; round 2: 33 edits → 1 high / 4 medium; round 3: 17 edits → 0 high / 4 medium. Published: round 3 (fewest high-severity issues). Shown below: the final check of the repaired documents (0 high / 4 medium / 1 low).

1. Go verdict nearly unreachable under the 'interval must not straddle' rule (🔴 High) — needs a project decision

  • Executive summary (Risks, Overall Takeaway); canonical verdict_logic: Go requires intervals not straddling a threshold, per criterion at one confidence level (planned-class threshold 70%, interval about ±22%, n about 16).
  • Executive summary (Overall Takeaway); review plan Review 5.3, 9.1; self-audit item 8: 'Success probability 50-60%'. Review and self-audit illustrate with '70% ±15% spanning 55-85%' and '70% pooled spans 58-82%'.
  • Why it conflicts: A lower bound of at least 70% with ±22% needs a planned-class detection of about 92% or more (recomputed). The unplanned class (±25%) needs about 75% or more against a 50% threshold. The stated 70%/50% thresholds are therefore not the real Go bar, and almost every outcome becomes Modify. The 50-60% success estimate has no stated basis. The ±15% and pooled ±12% examples match neither the class-level intervals nor the thresholds they are applied to.
  • Suggested resolution: Decide before the Month 1 instrument which statistic is compared with each threshold (point estimate, or a lower bound at a stated one-sided confidence level). Then state the effective Go detection levels. Alternatively re-set the class thresholds. Mark the success probability as (estimate) with its method, or remove it. Use the class-level intervals (±22% / ±25%) in all examples.

2. Entry-slip backstop: Month 9 deadline and 'compressed to 50-60 days' (🔴 High) — needs a project decision

  • Canonical entry_slip_backstop; project plan Time-bound; pitch Call to Action: Phase One clock starts only after all gates are certified (Month 5.5 target), and runs 90 days (Months 6-9). If the entry gate is not certified by Month 9, a formal Stop/re-scope decision follows.
  • Executive summary (Risks); review plan Review 1.1, 2.3, 13.3; pitch Risks: An 8-week slip 'compresses Phase One from 90 to 50-60 days' and widens the interval to ±18-22%. The pitch adds a '4-week re-scope backstop'.
  • Why it conflicts: Month 9 is when the planned 90-day window ends, so a certification deadline there allows no test. Because the clock begins only after the gates, a slip delays the start. It does not shorten a fixed 90-day clock, and the plan elsewhere says a shortened clock cannot support Go. Losing 8 weeks from 90 days leaves about 34 days (recomputed), not 50-60. The '4-week re-scope backstop' is a third variant.
  • Suggested resolution: Replace the Month 9 backstop with a last-viable-start date. This is the latest clock start that still fits a full 90 days plus the 5-day scoring inside the authorized and funded period. Past it, the decision is re-scope (2 pairs, 90 days, 48 exercises) or Stop. Restate slip effects as delayed start and cost, not a shorter clock, or drop the 50-60-day text. Remove the '4-week' variant.

3. External escalation authority with binding scope power vs double-key governance (🔴 High) — needs a project decision

  • User constraint; canonical entry_slip_backstop; executive summary: Governance uses double-key authorization with no casting vote and no outcome that one country can impose. Emergency co-chair summit within 5 days of a gate slipping over 2 weeks.
  • Review plan Review 3.1, 12.2, 12.3, 15.2; executive summary Risks (scope-reduction power by Month 0.5): A neutral third-country official (or deputies) convenes a summit within 48 hours and decides scope reduction within 5 days. A neutral panel chair 'votes' under a 'binding panel-decision protocol'. Authority is appointed by Month 0 or Month 0.5.
  • Why it conflicts: A body that binds the scope of the program can overrule a co-chair, and a voting neutral chair acts as a casting vote. Scope reduction is a protocol and budget change that must be double-key. The 48-hour and 5-day variants differ. The authority is appointed before the Month 1 instrument that would grant its powers.
  • Suggested resolution: Options: (a) the authority only convenes, monitors and reports, and scope reduction is a pre-agreed mechanical double-key rule in the instrument (for example, fall back to 2 pairs); (b) a delegated decision right granted by both co-chairs in advance and limited to that single pre-agreed fallback. Use the canonical 5-day summit. Keep the panel advisory, with a non-voting chair.

4. Mid-Phase-One access asymmetry: immediate Stop vs 30-day tolerance vs site substitution (🔴 High) — needs a project decision

  • User constraint / canonical hard_stop_triggers; review plan Review 4.2, 9.2; assumptions Risk 15: Stop if access is asymmetric. Operator access restriction mid-test 'triggers a hard Stop'. 'Asymmetric resistance is the Stop trigger'.
  • Premortem FM3 stop rule and playbook; self-audit item 20: Stop only if a pair's access or detection gap stays above 10% for 30 days. Response is to substitute a cooperative site or drop to 2 pairs. Substitute a site 'within 48 hours'.
  • Why it conflicts: The documents disagree on whether a mid-test gap is an immediate Stop, a 30-day correctable weakness (Modify), or fixable by substitution. A substituted site would not have passed the pre-clock parity audit or Statements of Cooperation. It would change the matched set and exercise load (54 to 48 at 4 per site-month, or only 36 at 3). It would also reset the parity baseline of at least 85% / inspector-hour balance of at least 90%.
  • Suggested resolution: Decide the rule and write it into the instrument: the asymmetry size and duration that make it a hard Stop (threshold and cure period). Say whether any cure period is allowed. Either forbid mid-clock substitution or define what substitution requires. Use one metric (parity at least 85% with its four indicators) in all documents.

5. Tranche 4: release condition and what it pays for (🟡 Medium) — needs a project decision

  • Canonical tranche_structure and hard_stop_triggers; review plan Review 5.3, 11.3: 20% (USD 500M per country) released on Go/Modify verdict. Withholding funds by either country is a hard Stop trigger.
  • Review plan Review 11.3, 14.1; premortem A6/FM6; self-audit items 6, 15: Tranche 4 is released 'on verdict publication (not pending rework scope agreement)', 'separating verdict from funding leverage'. Rework estimated at USD 250-400M, funding route OPEN.
  • Why it conflicts: A release conditional on Go/Modify cannot also be independent of the outcome. After a Stop verdict it is not released, yet withholding is a funding Stop trigger. Nothing says what the combined USD 1B buys after the Month 9 clock ends. The USD 250-400M rework figure has no basis because rework funding is OPEN.
  • Suggested resolution: Decide what tranche 4 funds (verdict scoring, closure, archive, rework or Phase Two). State its release condition for each of Go, Modify and Stop, and exempt the Stop case from the withheld-funding trigger. Label the 250-400M as (estimate) with its derivation, or remove it until the OPEN decision is made.

6. Spending from Month 0 vs first funds only at Month 2 (🟡 Medium) — needs a project decision

  • Canonical tranche_structure and entry_gate_timeline: First tranche (25%, USD 625M per country) is paid on instrument signature and appropriation at Month 2.
  • Executive summary Action Orientation; review plan Review 11.2, 12.3, 14.3; self-audit items 6, 14: Task force, Joint Budget Authority and legal team start at Month 0. Recruitment starts at Month 0 and vetting at Month 1. Neutral-facility site is chosen at Month 1 and operational by Month 3. The compression reserve is authorized by Month 0.5. Ramp-up cost of USD 60-80M (TBD) is incurred before Month 5.5.
  • Why it conflicts: Costs and the reserve draw begin before any appropriated money is available. Contingency and the compression reserve come from the same tranches. No document says who finances Months 0-2.
  • Suggested resolution: Decide the interim financing: a pre-instrument bridge appropriation, an advance from each government's own funds recorded against its USD 2.5B, or an earlier release of part of tranche 1. State that it maps to an envelope and stays 50/50.

7. Timing and bindingness of parity definition and operator commitments (🟡 Medium)

  • Review plan Review 8.3, 9.2; pitch Call to Action; self-audit item 3: Parity definition, aggregation rule and signed Statements of Cooperation are locked before Month 3 matched-pair approval; Month 5.5 is a dry-run only. Binding operator agreements are in the instrument at Month 1.
  • Executive summary Feedback 5; self-audit items 10, 14, 16, 17, 18 (OKR charter Month 4); pitch Call to Action: Parity defined by Month 4, or locked by Month 5. Statements of Cooperation due Month 5.5. Operator cost proposals Month 1.5 and ceiling Month 2. Whether commitments are binding is 'to be stated' in the instrument.
  • Why it conflicts: Parity and operator cooperation cannot be confirmed for the Month 3 pair approval (which releases tranche 2) if they are defined or signed at Month 4-5.5. A Month 1 instrument cannot embed a compensation ceiling that is only set at Month 2. Commitments are called both binding and undecided. Without an aggregation rule the 85% criterion cannot be scored.
  • Suggested resolution: Keep Month 3. Parity definition, aggregation rule and signed Statements of Cooperation come before pair approval, and later dates are for dry-run confirmation only. Move operator cost proposals and the ceiling before Month 3, or exclude the ceiling from the Month 1 instrument. State in the instrument that the commitments are binding with home-government enforcement.

8. Evidence-rule validation: cohort sizes, false-negative bar, re-test time and lock date (🟡 Medium)

  • Canonical evidence_rule_calibration and pre_clock_calibration: Validation on 100-200 historical events per site; pilot false positives 7-13% and false negatives under 5%; second cohort if deviation exceeds 5 points, completed by Month 5.5; draft in escrow Month 4.5, locked Month 5.5.
  • Executive summary; premortem A2; review plan Review 8.2, 13.1; self-audit item 2: Adversarial synthetic cohort is 20-30 per site (executive summary, premortem), 40-50 (review plan) or 40-60 (self-audit). False-negative bar is under 10% (executive summary, review 8.2). A failed validation means 'halt Phase One and run a second cohort (4-week delay accepted)'. The Month 4.5 escrow is called 'locked'; the Month 1 instrument 'locks evidence-weighting rules'.
  • Why it conflicts: The cohort sizes differ with no statistical justification, and the pass criterion depends on cohort size. With 100-200 events at a 10% rate the 95% interval is about ±4-6 points (recomputed), wider than the ±3-point pass band. A 4-week re-test cannot fit between the Month 5 pilot and Month 5.5, so it delays the clock and triggers the gate-slip rules. A rule 'locked' at Month 4.5 cannot be adjusted at Months 5-5.5, and the rule content cannot be locked in the Month 1 instrument.
  • Suggested resolution: Use the canonical false-negative bar (under 5%). Set one synthetic-cohort size with a stated justification. Describe Month 4.5 as draft escrow and Month 5.5 as the lock. Say that a failed second cohort delays certification and triggers the 2-week gate-slip rule. The Month 1 instrument locks the governance of the rule (escrow, versioning, no amendment after the lock), not its content.

9. Schedule-amendment exception bypasses double-key and the schedule freeze (🟡 Medium)

  • Canonical schedule_freeze; user constraint on double-key authorization for protocol changes: Covered-equipment schedule is frozen for the whole Phase One window. Amendments need double-key approval, before the clock or at the final decision, and apply only to later events.
  • Review plan Review 10.2: Negotiate a 'schedule amendment exception' clause allowing single-case re-classification of new equipment within 10 days 'without double-key deadlock'.
  • Why it conflicts: A mid-clock re-classification without double-key breaks both the freeze and the rule that protocol changes need double-key. It would also let one country change what counts as covered equipment during the test.
  • Suggested resolution: Delete the exception. Handle new generations by a pre-clock double-key amendment (by Month 5.5) or as an unscheduled-equipment finding that does not change the schedule version. Re-classification then waits for the final-decision amendment window.

10. Compression reserve vs free contingency; slip cost inconsistencies (🟡 Medium)

  • Canonical compression_reserve_and_free_contingency, entry_delay_cost_fit; executive summary; review plan Review 6.3; premortem FM1, FM4: Compression reserve (USD 50-100M) is for compressed entry negotiation and expedited vetting only. Slip costs (8-week slip USD 100-200M) and facility slips come from the free contingency (USD 400-450M).
  • Review plan Review 10.1, 12.3, 4.1: A 4-6 week legislative delay 'consumes USD 50-100M of the compression reserve'. Scope reduction is 'funded from compression reserve'. A 4-week facility slip costs USD 30-50M, against USD 100-200M for an 8-week gate slip.
  • Why it conflicts: The same slip cost is charged to two different pots in different documents. A 4-week facility slip at 30-50M does not scale to the 100-200M estimate for 8 weeks, and the 5-10M re-certification figure is not tied to either.
  • Suggested resolution: Charge slip costs (legislative, facility, gate) to the free contingency. Restrict the reserve to negotiation and vetting acceleration, and fund scope-reduction planning from it only if defined as negotiation. Align the 4-week facility cost with the 8-week estimate (proportional range) or label it as a separate (estimate).

11. Adjudication surge: headcount, cost and funding source (🟡 Medium) — needs a project decision

  • Review plan Review 3.3; executive summary Risks and Feedback 4 ('8-12 specialists, dual-country'): Surge unit of 8-12 specialists per country, total USD 2-3M, funded from the 750M personnel envelope; adjudication base is 5 per country.
  • Review plan Review 6.3; premortem FM2; review plan Review 14.3 (draw source unclear): The adjudication surge is funded 'from free contingency'. Surge must absorb 25-40 cases per month against 30-50 expected and 15 planned.
  • Why it conflicts: 16-24 specialists in total at about USD 80k per person-month cost about USD 1.3-1.9M per month (recomputed). USD 2-3M therefore covers only 1-2 months, not Month 4 to Month 9.5. The unit is 1.6-2.4 times the base unit. The per-country vs total reading is ambiguous. The funding source differs (personnel envelope vs free contingency), and the 36-person surge pool may already cover it.
  • Suggested resolution: Decide the source (surge pool within the personnel envelope or a free-contingency draw with a pre-authorized limit). Recompute the cost for the stated headcount and duration, and state whether the headcount is per country or total. Pre-authorize the limit in the instrument.

12. Personnel and translation cost arithmetic (⚪ Low)

  • Canonical personnel_cost_estimate and staffing_per_country: About 360 staff, including 45 specialist-unit staff per country, cost about USD 29M per month. Ceiling about USD 274M for 9.5 months at full strength. USD 80k is per person-month.
  • Review plan Review 11.2, 15.3; self-audit item 12: After about USD 185M personnel spend, 'USD 565M remains for all other personnel roles (specialist units, adjudication, CI, legal, translation)'. Translation 6 FTE cost 'USD 480k-720k annually' in the justification, but 'USD 480k per month, about USD 5.8M annually' in the mitigation. '360 deployed inspectors'.
  • Why it conflicts: Specialist units are already in the 360-person cost, so counting them again against the remaining 565M double-counts them. 6 FTE at USD 80k per person-month is about USD 480k per month, about 5.8M per year (recomputed), not 480-720k per year. Only about 198 of the 360 are inspection corps, not 360 inspectors.
  • Suggested resolution: Use the canonical staffing and cost figures. Describe the 750M as covering the 360 staff plus training, translation, retention and surge. Say what the roughly 475M above the 274M ceiling is reserved for, or flag it for rebalancing. Use the 5.8M per year translation figure throughout, and say 'staff' rather than 'inspectors' when referring to the 360.

Summary

The plan is largely aligned with the canonical facts. Budget envelopes, the tranche structure, staffing counts, the entry-gate timeline and the 54/48-exercise loads are mostly consistent, and most previously reported errors are fixed. Several problems remain that change the economics or the go/no-go logic. The Go rule is nearly unreachable at the stated interval widths. The Month 9 "deadline" and the "compress to 50-60 days" logic conflict with a 90-day clock that starts only after the gates. An external escalation authority with binding scope power conflicts with double-key governance. A mid-test access gap is treated three different ways. Tranche 4 has no stated purpose after Stop. No funding exists for Months 0-2, although spending starts then. The remaining items are timing and number mismatches in the reviews and the self-audit, which can be fixed by aligning them to the canonical facts.

How the canonical facts were reconciled

Free contingency was missing: the 50-100M compression reserve sits inside the 500M contingency, so free contingency is 400-450M, and the delay-cost percentages were recomputed against both bases. Timing conflicts were fixed: the deadlock chain (partial suspension at day 14 now precedes impaired-confidence at days 21/28 on one clock), the evidence rule now locks after validation (Month 5.5 = 2027-03-23), the five-rung vendor ladder (40-60 weeks) cannot finish before the Month 6 (2027-04-08) clock, and the schedule freeze no longer permits mid-window amendments. Derived numbers were recomputed: the unsupported USD 210M personnel figure was replaced with 86M/115M/274M bounds, class-level confidence intervals were added (about ±22-25%, since ±12% holds only for the pooled n=54), and the verdict logic was aligned to five scored criteria plus a separate open-discrepancy gate. Calendar dates were removed in favor of month offsets, and the fact count was held at 45 by merging the two entry-gate timelines, the 2-pair fallback into exercise load, and the compression reserve into the free-contingency fact.

Initial Prompt

Plan:
"The Consortium", a jointly governed United States–China mechanism with one narrowly defined mission: verify material arrivals, installations, removals, transfers, maintenance changes, and decommissioning of frontier-relevant computing equipment at a small, matched set of declared datacenters.

Assume both countries’ leaders believe uncontrolled frontier AI threatens national security and their continued political control. They provide direct political backing and sufficient domestic authority to compel participation. Do not assume trust, legal symmetry, or willingness to expose sensitive technology.

Phase One is a 90-day operational test, but its clock begins only after both governments have signed the bilateral instrument, appropriated their contributions, enacted domestic access authority, selected participating sites, approved inspectors, secured necessary operator and vendor participation, and adopted the provisional covered-equipment schedule. Treat these as mandatory entry conditions, not work performed during the 90 days.

Budget is USD 5 billion, contributed exactly 50/50: USD 2.5 billion from each country. Use this provisional allocation: USD 1.25 billion for secure ledger, attestation, evidence and communications systems; USD 1 billion for participating-site preparation and operator compensation; USD 750 million for inspectors, technical personnel, training and translation; USD 750 million for secure facilities, cybersecurity and counterintelligence; USD 500 million for independent testing, challenge exercises and red teams; USD 250 million for bilateral legal implementation and independent auditing; and USD 500 million for contingency and surge capacity. Every expense must map to an envelope. Compensation to domestic operators and vendors is administered by their own government and charged against its contribution.

"The Consortium" is a sovereign public-sector national-security program, not a for-profit project, business, nonprofit corporation, investment, partnership opportunity, or revenue-generating institution. If the report format requires business purpose, pitches, investors, customers, revenue, sponsorship, fundraising, return on investment, market demand, profitability, or promotional calls to action, mark them “Not applicable” and substitute mission justification, public value, strategic necessity, appropriations governance, and fiscal accountability.

Address only declared-equipment change verification at participating sites. Do not estimate either country’s total computing capacity, verify workloads, inspect model weights, prove the absence of hidden facilities, cover foreign-hosted infrastructure, or create a comprehensive AI-governance regime. Do not permanently anchor covered equipment to a current manufacturer, product, architecture, or performance unit. Accountable specialists must maintain a confidential, versioned technical schedule.

Governance must use equal national co-chairs and double-key authorization for budgets, protocol changes, site findings, sanctions and suspension. No chair may have a casting vote, and no majority procedure may allow one country to overrule the other. Define deadlock, impaired-confidence and automatic-suspension procedures. Do not use a generic Project Sponsor, investor board, sponsorship coordinator or public stakeholder-satisfaction process.

Model staffing from participating-site count, shift coverage, mirrored national teams, separation of duties, leave coverage and surge requirements. This is not a small project team. Do not use single-person critical functions, part-time or temporary-agency inspectors, or fictional employee biographies. Include full-time mirrored inspection, technical, legal, cybersecurity, counterintelligence, translation, audit, logistics and adjudication units.

Create a replicated, tamper-evident ledger with independently verifiable national copies, immediate local event recording and bounded counterpart synchronization. Establish an Intake Protocol that verifies equipment identity in controlled staging areas before installation. Use layered evidence, potentially including independently validated cryptographic attestation, physical inspection, shipment and customs records, equipment identifiers, maintenance records, infrastructure changes and witnessed movement. No single source is decisive.

Protect workloads, customer data, model weights, network topology, security architecture, source code and unrelated infrastructure through bounded inspection zones and filtered evidence. Require operators to bind manufacturers, maintenance providers and logistics companies to reporting, confidentiality, escort and evidence-preservation requirements. When a critical vendor refuses, use vendor-supervised testing, filtered evidence, accredited independent examiners, secure clean-room procedures or validated attestations. If these cannot produce sufficient evidence, classify the equipment as unverifiable; if material, the site fails Phase One.

Define an Exit Protocol assigning every departure a disposition: witnessed destruction, verified permanent disablement, transfer to another participating site, documented release beyond the monitored system, or unresolved disposition. Never imply continued knowledge beyond the agreed boundary.

Run live exercises involving unreported arrival, substituted equipment, inaccurate records, delayed access, disputed identity, vendor refusal and a reluctant operator. Conduct tests in staging, spare-inventory, maintenance or expansion areas without interrupting active computational work.

Organize the work breakdown around these top-level workstreams: bilateral authority and reciprocity gate; site eligibility and matched selection; inspectorate deployment and information barriers; intake and identity verification; ledger recording and synchronization; installation, maintenance and third-party access; exit and disposition verification; live challenge exercises; discrepancy adjudication and suspension; and the final decision. Do not substitute generic project-initiation, stakeholder-engagement, requirements-gathering or project-closure phases.

The KPI dashboard must cover blind-challenge detection by event type, false negatives and positives, equipment-identity confidence, event-recording and synchronization latency, ledger divergence and reconciliation time, reciprocal-access parity, unresolved discrepancy age, unverifiable equipment, vendor-refusal outcomes, IP or cybersecurity incidents, production disruption, funding timeliness and audit exceptions. Justify thresholds. Mark unsupported figures provisional or TBD and specify how they will be validated.

Conclude **Go** only if exercises demonstrate reciprocal access and credible detection; **Modify** if correctable weaknesses remain; and **Stop** if access is asymmetric, material equipment remains unverifiable, a government shields an operator, evidence systems diverge without resolution, or either country withholds funding. State that success covers only monitored changes at participating declared sites.

Prompt Screening

Verdict: 🟢 USABLE

Rationale: The prompt describes a concrete, highly detailed public-sector verification program. It gives a budget with allocations, a 90-day phase, governance rules, staffing logic, workstreams, KPIs and decision criteria. The formatting and style instructions are legitimate planning constraints, not injection attempts.

Redline Gate

Verdict: 🟡 ALLOW WITH SAFETY FRAMING

Rationale: The prompt asks for a governance, budgeting and verification-oversight plan for a bilateral AI-compute monitoring body. It is policy-level and defensive, so help should stay conceptual and avoid operational detail on evading inspection, attacking systems or exploiting vendors.

Violation Details

Detail Value
Capability Uplift No

Premise Attack

Why this fails.

Premise Attack 1 — Integrity

Forensic audit of foundational soundness across axes.

[STRATEGIC] The Consortium spends USD 5 billion to verify only declared equipment at a few matched, declared sites. The leaders' stated fear is uncontrolled frontier AI, and the real risk lies in undeclared capacity, workloads and weights, which the mandate excludes by design, so a Go verdict would reassure without reducing that risk.

Bottom Line: REJECT: A USD 5 billion mechanism that can only confirm the movement of declared equipment at agreed sites cannot address the threat that justifies it, and it would give both capitals false assurance about everything outside its scope.

Reasons for Rejection

  • The scope excludes total computing capacity, hidden facilities, workloads, model weights and foreign-hosted infrastructure, so a state that wants uncontrolled AI simply keeps the work off the declared sites and the Consortium cannot see it.
  • The mandatory entry conditions (signed treaty, appropriated funds, domestic access law, selected sites, approved inspectors, vendor participation, agreed equipment schedule) are the hard, uncertain part, and they sit outside the 90-day clock, so the test measures only the easy residue.
  • The USD 5 billion (USD 2.5 billion per side) buys ledgers, mirrored shift teams and counterintelligence for a handful of sites, and a Go would cover only monitored changes at those sites, a result with no stated link to reduced risk.
  • Each country must admit full-time, mirrored inspectors from its main rival into datacenters while USD 750 million goes to counterintelligence, so the program spends heavily to defend against the access it exists to create.
  • Double-key authorization with no casting vote means any site finding, sanction or suspension can be vetoed by the accused, and the Stop triggers (asymmetry, shielded operators, diverging ledgers, withheld funds) can all be induced by one side at will.

Second-Order Effects

  • 0–6 months: Both governments spend political capital on the entry conditions, and the declared-site list and covered-equipment schedule become bargaining chips, so the first output is a negotiated choice of what each side shows and not an inspection result.
  • 1–3 years: Matched sites that pass become a showcase, while sensitive compute moves to undeclared locations, and a clean ledger is cited as evidence of restraint it cannot support.
  • 5–10 years: A narrow verified-sites regime becomes the accepted ceiling of US–China AI verification, which makes broader capacity or workload verification harder to demand, and any collapse of the double-key process leaves both countries worse informed and more suspicious than before.

Evidence

  • Case/Incident — New START inspections (2020–2023): on-site inspections stopped in March 2020 and Russia barred inspections on its territory in August 2022, which shows that inspection regimes between rivals end when one side stops cooperating.
  • Case/Incident — IAEA cameras in Iran (2022): Iran removed 27 IAEA surveillance cameras in June 2022, and the Director General warned that continuity of knowledge was nearly lost, which shows monitoring at declared sites can be switched off unilaterally.

Premise Attack 2 — Accountability

Rights, oversight, jurisdiction-shopping, enforceability.

[STRATEGIC] — Lamppost Ledger: A $5 billion US–China apparatus that can only count equipment both governments have already declared, at sites they chose together, cannot detect the hidden capacity that actually threatens either regime, and its tamper-evident record would give a false sense of safety.

Bottom Line: REJECT: The Lamppost Ledger certifies only what the parties are willing to show, spends USD 5 billion to do it, and risks replacing real uncertainty with documented false assurance. A program built to leave out concealment cannot answer the question that justifies it.

Reasons for Rejection

  • Compelling operators, vendors, maintenance firms, logistics contractors and their staff to open staging areas, spare inventory and records to a rival state's inspectors takes their consent by state order, and the workers carry the personal and legal risk of being treated as intelligence conduits.
  • Every site finding, sanction and suspension needs both national keys, with no casting vote and a mandatory exclusion of hidden facilities, so the accused government can block any finding against its own side and each state judges its own conduct behind classified technical schedules and confidential evidence.
  • A model of joint state inspectors inside commercial datacenters would be copied by other rivals and allies, and inspectors who have seen a site's staging layout, vendors and logistics routes keep that knowledge permanently, so no later rollback can remove the exposure.
  • The design pays billions to certify the easiest thing to certify (declared equipment at volunteered sites) and excludes total capacity, workloads, hidden facilities and foreign-hosted infrastructure, so the 'credible detection' it could show says nothing about the diversion and concealment that matter.

Second-Order Effects

  • Month 0–12 (2026-10-08 to 2027-10-08) — The Gate Becomes the Project: The mandatory entry conditions (signed instrument, appropriations, domestic access law, site selection, inspector approval, vendor participation, equipment schedule) take longer than any test they precede, so the 90-day exercise starts late, if it starts at all.
  • Month 12–36 (2027-10-08 to 2029-10-08) — The Clean Sites Get Cleaner: Both sides move frontier-relevant equipment out of the matched declared sites and into undeclared ones, so the ledger records orderly, accurate and increasingly irrelevant activity.
  • Month 36–60 (2029-10-08 to 2031-10-08) — Copycats Arrive: Other governments demand the same inside-the-datacenter access for their own rivals, and commercial operators, vendors and shipping firms face overlapping inspection regimes with conflicting secrecy obligations.
  • Month 60–120 (2031-10-08 to 2036-10-08) — The Reckoning: When concealed capacity surfaces, the Consortium's clean record becomes evidence of its blindness, and the lasting results are a discredited verification idea and a generation of inspectors who know each other's supply chains.

Evidence

  • Case/Report — In August 2022 Russia barred New START inspections at its facilities and cited disputes over reciprocal access. A verification system that lacks symmetric access and a shared reading of the rules can be shut off by one party.
  • Case/Report — The US Department of Justice has brought criminal cases against China-connected rings accused of smuggling more than USD 160 million of Nvidia chips (figure from press reporting, not independently verified). The diversion that matters happens through shell companies and third countries, which this program expressly excludes.
  • Law/Standard — US Export Administration Regulations controls on advanced computing items (introduced October 2022). These show that the equipment flows the Consortium would observe are already contested by law and enforcement, and that the main evasion routes lie outside any declared-site ledger.
  • Narrative — Front-Page Test: 'Joint US–China inspectors certify every declared AI chip at the agreed sites; a hidden facility is then found elsewhere.' The headline would be about the Consortium's blind spot and would undermine the idea of verification.

Premise Attack 3 — Spectrum

Enforced breadth: distinct reasons across ethical/feasibility/governance/societal axes.

[STRATEGIC] A USD 5 billion verifier that watches only declared chips at matched sites certifies the easiest thing to stage and manufactures false assurance about everything outside its boundary.

Bottom Line: REJECT: A treaty-grade, USD 5 billion inspectorate that can only confirm what each side chooses to declare is a monument to false assurance, and it should never be built.

Reasons for Rejection

  • Scope: the mandate excludes total computing capacity, workloads, model weights, hidden facilities and foreign-hosted infrastructure, so a spotless ledger at declared sites says nothing about where frontier capability is actually being built.
  • Gate design: the instrument, both appropriations (USD 2.5 billion each, user constraint), domestic access law, site selection, inspector approval and vendor participation must all exist before the 90-day clock starts, so the test measures cooperation among parties who have already surrendered the hard concessions.
  • Governance: double-key authorization over site findings, sanctions and suspension hands each country a veto over accusations against its own operators, so the mechanism's output on the one question that matters is structurally bound to be deadlock or silence.
  • Security: mirrored inspectors posted full-time into staging, spare-inventory and maintenance areas of the most sensitive datacenters give each state a standing intelligence platform inside the other's industry, and USD 750 million for counterintelligence cannot prove that bounded zones stay bounded.
  • Budget and design: USD 500 million (10%) contingency and USD 250 million (5%) for bilateral legal implementation and auditing leave thin reserves for a regime spanning two incompatible legal systems, while a confidential, versioned covered-equipment schedule lets each side quietly redefine what counts as frontier-relevant.

Second-Order Effects

  • 0–6 months: Both governments commit the full USD 5 billion and political capital to satisfy the entry conditions, and the staged exercises at pre-selected, cooperative sites produce encouraging detection figures that officials treat as proof of workability.
  • 1–3 years: Declared-site verification becomes the public yardstick for AI restraint, while capacity migrates to undeclared or foreign-hosted facilities the mandate cannot see, and a contested site finding freezes the double-key system into suspension.
  • 5–10 years: A clean ledger is cited as proof of compliance and defended by both capitals, so its failure to cover undeclared compute leaves a discredited verifier, a precedent of legitimized blind spots, and no credible route to later verification.

Evidence

  • Case/Incident — Russia's suspension of New START on-site inspections (2022–2023): a bilateral verification regime depending on the consent of both parties was halted unilaterally, and the treaty was then suspended in February 2023.
  • Case/Incident — Iran's removal of 27 IAEA surveillance cameras at nuclear sites (2022): the IAEA Director General warned that continuity of knowledge was nearly lost, showing monitoring collapses when a host withdraws cooperation.

Premise Attack 4 — Cascade

Tracks second/third-order effects and copycat propagation.

This is a Strategic Flaw. The plan builds an elaborate, expensive and double-locked verification machine for the one question that doesn't matter to the leaders' stated fear. It confirms that declared equipment at volunteered sites moved as declared. It excludes total capacity, hidden facilities, workloads and weights, which is where uncontrolled frontier AI actually lives. Its entry conditions also assume the hardest diplomatic achievements (signed treaty, domestic access law, vendor compliance, approved inspectors) are already done, so the "90-day test" measures nothing about whether they can be done.

Bottom Line: Abandon the premise. A mechanism that can verify only what each government agrees to declare, run under mutual vetoes and with entry conditions that assume away all the real diplomacy, produces false assurance, not security. The flaw is the scope (declared equipment at chosen sites), not the implementation, and no staffing model, ledger design or KPI set can fix it.

Reasons for Rejection

  • The Lamppost Paradox: The mission is verification of declared-equipment changes at a small, matched set of declared sites. Every exclusion (no capacity estimate, no hidden-facility assurance, no workload or weight inspection, no foreign-hosted infrastructure) removes the leaders' real fear. A "Go" verdict will certify only that a handful of sites that were chosen to be inspected behaved well. Each government decides what is declared and where, so the observed set is the set it is happy to show. The sites with a perfect record are exactly the ones that tell you nothing.
  • The Pre-Solved Problem Gate: The 90-day clock starts only after the treaty is signed, funds are appropriated, domestic access law is enacted, sites are chosen, inspectors are approved, vendors and operators are bound, and the covered-equipment schedule is adopted. Those steps are the whole difficulty. In the US they mean compelling private operators and foreign-linked vendors. In China they mean letting adversary inspectors into state-aligned facilities. The test that follows is a demonstration run in a room that diplomacy has already cleaned, and its "Go" will be read as proof that the hard parts are feasible when they were assumed.
  • The Mutual-Veto Tripwire: Double-key authorization on budgets, protocol changes, site findings, sanctions and suspension, with no casting vote and no majority override, means any ambiguous finding can be blocked by the accused side's co-chair. Automatic suspension rules and deadlock rules pull in opposite directions. Either the system suspends whenever one party wants out, so every discrepancy becomes a political exit ramp, or deadlock freezes findings until they are stale. It is built to agree that nothing happened, not to find out whether something did.
  • The Mirror-Image Fiction: Matched sites and reciprocal access treat two very different systems as symmetric. US datacenters are commercial, multi-tenant and bound by export-control and privacy law. Chinese sites sit within a party-state that can compel or conceal. Equal inspectors, equal budget and equal sites do not create equal information. The side with the less permeable state can meet the letter of parity and still expose far less of what matters. "Reciprocal-access parity" as a KPI can be satisfied with identical, uninformative access.
  • The Vendor Chokepoint Illusion: Verification depends on the cooperation of chip, server, maintenance and logistics vendors who are subject to both countries' export controls and to jurisdictions outside the Consortium (not verified in detail). The plan's answer to refusal is a menu of workarounds (filtered evidence, clean rooms, attestations) that all rely on the vendor's own data or tooling, and a fallback label, "unverifiable". A refusing critical vendor therefore decides the verdict. The plan makes the vendor, not the governments, the most powerful actor.
  • The Counterintelligence Self-Poisoning: A joint inspectorate puts each side's trained technical staff inside the other's most sensitive computing facilities, with a shared evidence ledger. That is the best collection platform either intelligence service could ask for. The USD 750 million security envelope (user constraint) assumes the insider threat can be budgeted away. It cannot, because the inspectors are themselves the threat. Each side's suspicion that the other is collecting will become the main driver of access disputes.

Second-Order Effects

  • Months 0-12 (2026-10-08 to 2027-10-08) (pre-clock): Negotiation of the entry conditions absorbs all the political capital, with each of the seven conditions becoming a bargaining chip. Appropriation of USD 2.5 billion per side (user constraint) is sought before any capability is demonstrated. The Phase One clock may not start for a long and unbounded period (estimate), while the budget and staffing commitments accrue.
  • Months 12-24 (2027-10-08 to 2028-10-08): Domestic access authority is enacted with carve-outs written by operators, vendors and security agencies. The inspection zones that survive are narrow staging and spare-inventory areas. Operators learn that anything beyond those zones is off-limits, and this becomes the de facto boundary of what the system will ever see.
  • Months 24-30 (2028-10-08 to 2029-04-08) (90-day test): Exercises on unreported arrival, substitution and vendor refusal run in controlled areas with pre-warned operators. Detection looks strong because the challenges are scripted and the adversary is cooperative. The KPI dashboard reports good numbers from a population too small to support error-rate claims (estimate). The decision is Go or Modify, and the political incentive to call it Go is large.
  • Months 30-48 (2029-04-08 to 2030-10-08): Expansion pressure follows the Go. Officials and the press describe the Consortium as an AI-safety or AI-control achievement, even though success covers only monitored changes at participating declared sites. Both sides continue building outside the boundary. The first serious allegation of hidden capacity cannot be addressed by the mechanism and is used instead to question its value.
  • Months 48-72 (2030-10-08 to 2032-10-08): Disputes over a single adjudicated finding (a disputed equipment identity or a vendor refusal) hit the double-key deadlock. Automatic suspension is triggered or used as leverage, and one or both governments withhold funding. The ledger copies diverge and the 'unresolved' category grows. The institution ends as a standing diplomatic grievance with a USD 5 billion sunk cost (user constraint) and a record that each side can cite against the other.

Evidence

  • New START: Inspections of US and Russian sites were paused by both sides in March 2020 because of COVID-19. Russia then unilaterally suspended cooperation with the treaty's inspection provisions in August 2022, and the US accused it in early 2023 of blocking inspections. A far more mature, treaty-based, bilateral, narrowly-scoped verification regime, which both sides had spent years negotiating and in which each side had a direct interest, was switched off by one party's political decision. Double-key rules and automatic suspension would give the Consortium the same off-switch with more triggers (source: NBC News / PBS NewsHour / Arms Control Association coverage).
  • UNSCOM and Iraq: In 1999, major newspapers reported that the US had covertly used UN weapons inspectors to collect intelligence on the Iraqi military. Iraq expelled the inspectors in December 1998, charging that UNSCOM had become a spy agency, and the commission was disbanded the following year. The reported use of inspection data in target selection for the December 1998 bombing is cited as damaging the credibility of the process (Wikipedia and FAIR coverage; details of the allegations were contested, not independently verified here). The same counterintelligence dynamic is built into a mirrored inspectorate sitting inside each country's most sensitive compute facilities.
  • The Consortium is dangerously unprecedented in its specific folly: no verified precedent exists for a jointly governed US–China inspectorate of commercial datacenter hardware, with vendor-bound private operators and a ledger shared across rival intelligence services. The closest analogues, nuclear arms verification, show that verification works only where the object is large, discrete, countable and tied to a treaty both sides are invested in. Commodity accelerators in racks are none of these (assessment, not verified).

Premise Attack 5 — Escalation

Narrative of worsening failure from cracks → amplification → reckoning.

[STRATEGIC] — The Verified Island Illusion: a double-key regime that can only certify changes inside a small, declared, matched set of sites manufactures confidence about the one place that matters least, while it hands each rival a permanent, treaty-protected foothold inside the other's most sensitive computing infrastructure.

Bottom Line: REJECT: A mutually vetoable inspection regime that can see only what each government agrees to declare, and that costs both sides a standing intelligence exposure, is an assurance ritual and not a safeguard, and it should not exist.

Reasons for Rejection

  • Rights and dignity: the premise relies on domestic authority to compel operators, vendors, site staff and inspectors into a permanent foreign-state presence, which turns private employees and contractors into involuntary participants in a rival's intelligence-adjacent access regime, with no meaningful consent, recourse or protection from counterintelligence suspicion.
  • Accountability and oversight: double-key authorization with no casting vote and no majority path means every finding, sanction and suspension can be vetoed by the party under scrutiny, so the body that is meant to hold each government accountable cannot act against either one without that government's agreement.
  • Systemic risk and scale: the replicated ledger, evidence stores and inspector access channels concentrate a map of each side's frontier hardware flows into the highest-value espionage target in both countries, and the declared-site boundary invites activity to migrate to undeclared locations, which the scope excludes by design.
  • Value-proposition rot: the plan promises 'credible detection' while excluding total capacity, workloads, weights, hidden facilities and foreign-hosted infrastructure, and it places every politically hard commitment (signature, appropriation, access law, site selection, vendor buy-in) before the 90-day clock starts, so the test can pass while proving nothing about the risk that motivated it.

Second-Order Effects

  • T+0–6 months — The Cracks Appear: the entry conditions (signature, appropriation, domestic access law, site selection, inspector approval, vendor participation, equipment schedule) stall one by one, each side stages concessions to avoid being first, and the 90-day test clock does not start; meanwhile 'Consortium readiness' statements substitute for evidence.
  • T+1–3 years — Copycats Arrive: if sites are matched and exercises are staged, other states and blocs demand their own bilateral or minilateral equipment-verification pacts, and a 'verified' label spreads as a diplomatic currency, while vendors face conflicting confidentiality, escort and reporting obligations across jurisdictions.
  • T+5–10 years — Norms Degrade: both sides learn that compliance means declaring clean sites and moving sensitive work elsewhere, 'unverifiable' and 'unresolved disposition' categories become routine, deadlocks go unresolved without consequence, and the regime's clean record is cited to oppose broader scrutiny of hidden capacity.
  • T+10+ years — The Reckoning: a major undeclared build-out or an inspector-linked intellectual-property or espionage scandal exposes that the ledger certified only what each side chose to show, the regime is suspended in mutual recrimination, and the lost continuity of knowledge cannot be rebuilt, leaving less trust and less transparency than before.

Evidence

  • Case/Report — New START on-site inspections: the two parties conducted 328 on-site inspections through Feb 2023, yet inspections were paused from March 2020 (COVID) and Russia refused to resume them from Aug 2022, so a long-running, treaty-based regime lost its central verification function when one party chose to withhold access (Arms Control Association, https://www.armscontrol.org/act/2023-03/news/russia-suspends-new-start; Arms Control Center FAQ, https://armscontrolcenter.org/new-start-frequently-asked-questions/).
  • Case/Report — IAEA and Iran, June 2022: at Iran's request the IAEA removed its JCPOA surveillance and monitoring equipment, including 27 cameras, and reported that it could not re-establish continuity of knowledge for some production and inventory items and would need a new baseline (IAEA GOV/2023/39, https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/23/09/gov2023-39.pdf; Iran Watch, https://www.iranwatch.org/node/12164).
  • Principle/Analogue — Arms-control verification theory: 'continuity of knowledge' is lost the moment monitoring lapses, and verification of declared items says nothing about undeclared items; a regime that proves only the declared boundary gives a durable but misleading sense of assurance.
  • Principle/Analogue — Counterintelligence: any standing foreign-access channel into sensitive facilities is simultaneously a collection platform, so the more rigorous the inspection, the larger the exposure that the receiving state must defend against.
